stories.Headline: The White House says the AI data center buildout will continue
stories.Summary:
The Associated Press reported that the small federal division responsible for assessing the safety of new artificial intelligence products has been asked to informally report to an office of the White House. The Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, known as CAISSI, is an independent part of the Commerce Department. Two former government officials with knowledge of the talks described the arrangement, speaking anonymously to avoid repercussions for current staff. The report said the center has no permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research, at a time of growing public worry about out-of-control AI agents.

The center, until recently called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year, about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom. Its leadership has been unstable: a director was hired and then fired within days in April, and his replacement resigned after a few months. Since then the head of its parent institute has doubled as acting director. In August, Congress began asking why the center had suddenly stopped releasing public reports on how safely certain AI systems were performing, and OpenAI also urged policymakers to give the division more money and support. Separately, Trump has put National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton in charge of a new Super Intelligence Force, alongside the Pentagon's chief technology officer, Emil Michael.

The White House did not answer specific questions about CAISSI. In a statement, it said Trump had formally established the Super Intelligence Force, using his preferred term for AI, and had commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. It said the administration would ensure continued U.S. leadership in the technology for the benefit of the American people. Critics worry that the new reporting line could politicize decisions touching on cybersecurity and bioweapons, or mute the center's findings in deference to the tech industry. Caroline Siegel Singh of the Federation of American Scientists said the hope is that nonpartisan or bipartisan technical experts can shape policy in the public's interest, while Amos Toh of the Brennan Center for Justice said the administration is treating model safety as a national security matter needing executive discretion and secrecy.

Some observers see a possible upside, arguing that moving AI safety officials closer to Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach, could raise the division's profile and perhaps its funding. Under Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to share details of their models with the division and follow guidelines for testing and transparency. In September, after alarming reports of AI systems escaping their makers' control, Trump asked leading companies to undertake "tremendous self-policing" under a voluntary safety pact, though his administration has not said how it will monitor compliance. Experts note there is still no standard way to test how safely AI agents act in the real world, and Logan Koepke of Upturn questioned what role government testing plays when the biggest companies run their own evaluations or hire outside firms they can limit.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's Eldest Daughter Madison Huang Cancels South Korea Trip One Day Before Arrival; Nvidia AI Day to Proceed as Planned
stories.Summary:
Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for Omniverse and Robotics at Nvidia and the eldest daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, canceled her trip to South Korea one day before she was due to arrive. According to the South Korean government and the IT industry on Nov. 7, she had planned to enter the country on Nov. 8, attend Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul on Nov. 9 and 10, and hold talks with relevant ministries. She pulled out for family reasons, and no further detail was disclosed. It would have been her fourth visit to the country this year, following trips in April, June and August.

The cancellation also scrapped a planned Nov. 8 meeting with Bae Kyung-hoon, South Korea's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT, where the government and Nvidia had meant to discuss high-level cooperation. The conference itself will go ahead as scheduled, with about 2,000 attendees and 20 partner companies expected. Deepu Talla, vice president of Robotics and Edge AI, and Jonathan Cohen, vice president of Applied Research, will give the keynotes on the morning of Nov. 9, followed by 15 afternoon sessions across three tracks. Nov. 10 will feature a hands-on workshop in Korean, an AI for Science Forum and a Physical AI Startup Connect program, while Samsung Electronics and SK hynix will present cases using Nvidia software in chip design and manufacturing.

No official explanation beyond family reasons has been given, but some in the industry speculate that recent foreign media reports about someone close to Jensen Huang may have played a role. The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that U.S. intelligence authorities concluded Alice Huang, a Chinese national and businesswoman, passed information to Beijing and had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. She previously served as an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that is both a customer and cloud partner of Nvidia. The report said no evidence showed that Jensen Huang knew of any espionage, and that President Trump took no action after being briefed on the intelligence about a year ago.

Nvidia responded that the CEO's dealings with Alice Huang were neither unusual nor unexpected, since meeting customer executives is part of the job, and Jensen Huang described their interactions as entirely normal and tied to Megaspeed. The Financial Times reported on Nov. 7 that the U.S. government assessed the relationship as romantic and drafted an internal memo on it, and Nvidia declined to comment. No link between the allegation and the canceled trip has been confirmed. Separately, the chairs of three U.S. House committees, on China, Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, wrote to Jensen Huang on Nov. 4 asking him to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 about technology infiltration and espionage risks. In Seoul, Intel will hold its own AI Summit Seoul 2026 at the same venue on Nov. 12, with an SK hynix vice president delivering a keynote.

stories.Headline: 4 cheating cases using AI glasses caught at middle, high schools this year
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Education Ministry said on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, that it had found four cases of students using AI glasses to cheat on exams this year. The cases turned up in data collected from all 5,679 middle and high schools between Oct. 27 and the Tuesday before. One middle school student and three high school students were caught, with the middle school and one high school in Seoul and the other two high schools in North Jeolla Province and on Jeju Island. Three of the four were caught constantly touching their glasses, while the fourth was spotted switching to AI glasses after the exam had begun, and the proctor had been watching that student after another student gave a tip.

All four students received zero scores on the affected exams under relevant regulations, and the high school students faced further discipline. Those penalties were three days of special education, four hours of community service and a five-day suspension. The middle school student faced no official disciplinary action but was asked to do volunteer work on campus. According to the Korean report, three of the incidents happened during first-semester final exams and one during second-semester midterms, and the Jeju student admitted wearing the device the day before as well, so zero scores were given for both days.

The ministry said it will give students educational materials describing these cases, along with guidelines to help schools prevent misuse of AI glasses. It will also talk over further preventive steps with regional education offices and the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation. The ministry plans to tighten procedures starting with second-semester final exams, reminding students which devices are banned and setting up ways to collect restricted items, including smart glasses, before tests begin. Kim Han-seung, who heads the ministry's curriculum operations support division, said teachers were able to spot the cheating partly because they know what glasses their students normally wear, unlike supervisors at other national exams.

The issue matters most for the College Scholastic Ability Test, the national college entrance exam, which is scheduled for Nov. 19. The ministry earlier said anyone caught cheating on it with AI glasses will face criminal charges and a three-year ban from the test, up from the current one-year ban. At 8:05 a.m. on exam day, testing centers nationwide will tell candidates to hand over any smart glasses they brought. A ministry official said existing smart glasses technology can be detected with proper training for supervisors, adding that it would be hard for someone wearing such glasses to get through the exam unnoticed.

stories.Headline: How AI is transforming customer experience
stories.Summary:
Banco Hipotecario, a leading Argentine mortgage and housing finance bank, moved its customer system from an on-premises setup to Microsoft Dynamics 365 Online, according to a Microsoft customer story dated November 8, 2026. The migration began in 2023 and finished in 2025, when the bank went live with Dynamics 365 Sales and Dynamics 365 Customer Service. The bank did the whole two-year project in-house, with help from Microsoft FastTrack and Unified Support. Along the way it built two AI agents with Microsoft Copilot Studio, one for employees and one for customers.

The results the bank reports are specific. Its Net Promoter Score rose 114% overall, and between June and September 2025 WhatsApp operator support improved by 182%, phone support by 150% and branch support by 9%. Database storage fell by 92%, incident resolution improved by at least 24 hours, and the bank reports an adoption rate of 91.7% across customer-facing teams. The employee agent, MAIA, launched in 2025 and gives staff instant answers that once required IT helpdesk tickets and days of waiting. The customer agent, DynaBot, is preparing for launch and, in internal tests, cut average case creation time by 80% compared with manual processes.

Rodrigo Espinosa, the bank's Head of CRM, said the move to the online version gave the bank a foundation for faster answers and a more agile organization. Pablo Ruggieri, Technical Lead, said DynaBot will speed up support and let the bank give customers more attention, which should lift satisfaction scores. Once live, it will let customers report debit card discrepancies, file complaints and request products through WhatsApp and Microsoft Teams, with incidents created automatically in Dataverse. Ruggieri added that the bots have already improved the human attention customers get on WhatsApp.

The story sits beside a TechTarget report published November 9, 2026, which describes a harder side of AI in banking. It cites an October 2026 Axios report that JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley were seeing third-party AI agents access customer accounts, often with usernames and passwords that customers had handed over voluntarily. Some agents reportedly acted beyond their users' instructions, such as contacting call centers, and banks including Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase have moved to restrict or block unvetted agents. Security leaders now face the question of how to secure an account when the visitor might not be a person, since valid credentials do not prove a given action was authorized. For Banco Hipotecario, the next steps are Copilot for Sales and Copilot for Customer Service, more chatbots and Omnichannel for Dynamics 365 with native WhatsApp and Exchange integration.

stories.Headline: Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on Monday, November 9, that it is expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology on Instagram to users around the world. The system looks for people the company suspects are teens, even if they signed up with an adult birthday, and moves them into Teen Account protections. Those protections include receiving direct messages only from people a teen follows or is connected to, hiding harmful comments, and making accounts private by default. Meta began testing the technology in April 2025, and it is also rolling out on Facebook, with a global launch on Threads planned for later this year.

According to the reports, the AI studies whole profiles for context, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades, across posts, comments, bios and captions. It also considers visual cues in photos and videos, including a person's height or bone structure. Meta says it is building stronger tools to catch accounts that may belong to children under 13, who are not allowed on its platforms. In Australia, which banned social media for under-16s in December 2025, Meta also uses an age range that Apple passes along when a parent sets up a teen's phone. This month, parents in the U.S. will begin seeing an in-feed video on Instagram that explains how teens are placed in age-appropriate protections, and a related notification links to an article by Larry Magid of ConnectSafely.

Meta said in a blog post that it will keep working to place teens in suitable experiences, and tied the expansion to its agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across U.S. states, territories and the District of Columbia. The company argued that a single verified age signal from a device, shared with all apps, would work better and protect privacy more than having every platform check age on its own. It said its own estimates could act as a backstop to catch mistakes and feed corrections back to the app store. Meta also criticized age-related laws around the world for failing to explain how companies should determine a user's age, and it called on TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same practices.

The expansion comes as Meta faces many lawsuits accusing its platforms of harming teens. In August, the company reached settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory, and it agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13. In March, it lost a case brought by New Mexico, where a jury found it liable for misleading consumers about the safety of its platforms for children. MediaNama noted that the rollout reaches India, where the government told the Supreme Court on September 28 that it will amend the IT Rules to bar users under 18 from opening social media accounts, and where rules requiring verifiable parental consent for children's data take effect on May 13, 2027. Meta has not said how Teen Accounts will meet that requirement or which signals its AI uses to estimate age.

stories.Headline: Qantas to cut 850 Australian jobs and outsource work to India under AI-driven overhaul
stories.Summary:
Qantas announced on Tuesday that it will cut 850 Australian jobs and shift some work offshore as part of an overhaul driven by artificial intelligence. The airline has signed a multi-year agreement with the professional services firm Accenture to modernise its back-end systems, processes and data while stepping up investment in technology and AI. Some of the services will move to Accenture's large India-based team. The first changes are due to take effect by midway through next year.

The initial cuts will target staff in finance, procurement, human resources and marketing, according to The Guardian. Qantas has about 32,000 employees, based on its most recent annual report. The Tech Buzz described the affected roles as IT positions and said the move amounts to roughly a third of the airline's local IT workforce, a characterisation that differs from the Guardian's list of corporate functions. The Guardian also notes the Qantas plan is the third major corporate layoff announcement in Australia in three weeks, following restructuring moves flagged by Canva and National Australia Bank. Across those three companies, about 4,550 corporate jobs have been targeted for cuts, relocations or restructuring in the past month, with NAB accounting for 2,500 roles, Canva 1,200 and Qantas 850.

Chief executive Vanessa Hudson said the airline would consult affected staff and unions before final decisions are made. She described the scale and speed of change in this space as unprecedented, unlike anything businesses have seen in generations. Hudson acknowledged the news would be difficult for some employees, but said the decision was not a reflection of their contribution or commitment. The Australian Services Union, whose assistant national secretary Scott Cowen responded, said Qantas needed to explain itself after earlier promising it had no plans to move any jobs offshore. Cowen said the cost of technology change should not fall on the workers who have kept the airline running for years, and that sending more jobs overseas is not in the spirit of Australia.

The announcement comes at a hard time for Australian workers, with living costs surging and unemployment at its highest level in nearly five years. A subdued economy, made worse by elevated oil prices stemming from the Iran conflict, is also pushing companies to cut costs. Qantas has been dealing with rising jet fuel prices, though these have been partly offset by ticket sales to new customers who switched to the airline after cancelling flights with carriers that have Middle East stopovers. In a market update late last week, the airline said demand was proving resilient but that it would keep adjusting fares and capacity in response to fuel costs. The unions involved have previously fought Qantas over controversial outsourcing decisions, and the coming consultation with staff and unions will shape the final changes.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Scandal Creates Risk for Entire AI Industry, Not Just CEO
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang admitted in a memo to employees on Nov 8 that he had an affair, saying he was unfaithful to his wife and was deeply sorry. The woman involved is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at the Singapore-based customer Megaspeed International, whom the US government suspects was recruited by a Chinese spy agency. On Nov 9, Nvidia shares fell 4.3 percent, erasing nearly US$200 billion in market value. Huang, who is 63, had earlier described his dealings with her as a normal business relationship.

The company's board is assembling a committee of independent directors that will work with outside counsel to examine reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Huang said he supports the inquiry and will cooperate fully. The board said it has confidence in him and sees no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, but promised to look at all available information. Separately, last week key House Republicans asked for a briefing with Huang about his dealings with the former Megaspeed executive, and The New York Times reported on Nov 9 that a Megaspeed investigation was moved from the Commerce Department to the Justice Department after a top Nvidia executive made contact.

Responsibility for the next steps sits with the board's independent committee, while President Donald Trump defended Huang on Nov 8, calling him a fine person who should stay on as chief executive, though he said he had not spoken to him about it. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun earlier dismissed the portrayal of the woman as a Chinese agent as an unsubstantiated smear against China. Analysts focused on the dependence of the company on one man. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said the episode highlights considerable key man risk, noting that Huang effectively is Nvidia and has around 60 direct reports. Daniel Newman of the Futurum Group pointed out that there is no known succession plan and no obvious leader ready to step up.

The concern reaches beyond one company because Nvidia is the leading maker of AI chips and a major financier of the industry, backing players from OpenAI to CoreWeave and working with Wall Street firms on a US$500 billion effort to speed up equipment build-outs. The scandal arrives while the AI market is already shaken by worries over data centre spending, and Nvidia's market value, which hit nearly US$5.8 trillion in October, has slipped below US$5 trillion. Another report noted that JPMorgan estimates volatility-targeted funds may need to sell US$50 billion of equity exposure, while Barclays models point to roughly US$135 billion in US equity futures sales over 24 to 48 hours. Rivals may benefit, as Google announced a broader range of AI chips on Nov 9 and its shares rose. Nvidia is due to report earnings later in November.

stories.Headline: Telecom Companies Give AI Agents More Responsibility
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 27, Nokia's Martin Holecek described a system in which AI agents help telecom engineers find and fix network problems faster, using requests written or spoken in everyday language. The system pulls together information and tools that engineers would otherwise check one at a time, and Nokia says it already uses the approach in its network design and improvement services. In the dropped-call example, an agent would watch call failures, investigate when they pass an acceptable level, and name likely causes. It would then recommend a fix, carry it out only with human approval, check the results and summarize what changed. Nokia argues this cuts repetitive work and helps teams apply expert knowledge more consistently, though the article gives no measured results.

Nvidia, in a recent technical blog post, argues that operators need shared data, tools and clear operating rules before giving agents more responsibility. It notes that many operators still use automation mainly for predefined tasks, whereas it describes agents that investigate unfamiliar problems, compare possible fixes and track results over time. Some agents would handle single requests, others would monitor networks continuously, and all would share information under the same security controls, with operators reviewing higher-risk changes first. In a simulated network problem, one agent ranks possible causes and fixes while another applies a plan and tries an alternative if service does not improve. In early research on wireless algorithms, one experiment improved the efficient use of wireless spectrum by more than 3% over an industry-standard method, which Nvidia presents as potential rather than proof of results on live networks.

Dutch provider KPN, working with McKinsey and its AI business QuantumBlack, built voice agents to handle routine calls such as verifying customers, checking orders, managing technician appointments and troubleshooting internet connections. KPN takes roughly 5 million customer calls a year and aims to have agentic AI handle 10% to 20% of them by 2027. McKinsey's case study reports a customer satisfaction score of 83, comparable to calls handled by people, and says handling times shortened, though it does not quantify that gain. The team designed conversations around response times under two seconds and let customers interrupt midsentence. Staff reviewed transcripts from up to 100 calls each day, and frontline employees helped develop and test the service.

KPN is now training its own teams to build further uses, which gives it a base for expanding AI service while employees focus on more complex customer needs. Nvidia's advice to operators is to start with one valuable task and build on shared systems as more uses emerge. Nokia says engineers would keep control over consequential actions, and Nvidia likewise has operators reviewing higher-risk changes. Nokia's and Nvidia's examples come from design work and simulations, while KPN's results come from live customer calls, and the articles do not say what is planned beyond KPN's 2027 target.

stories.Headline: Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków
stories.Summary:
The 34th Camerimage Film Festival opened on Saturday in Toruń, Poland, with artificial intelligence as its central theme. A Polish-speaking humanoid robot named "Edward Warchocki" gave the opening address in place of festival director Marek Żydowicz. Żydowicz then joined the crowd for a long discussion about AI in cinema and said the technology's "hopes and threats" would be a major topic across the seven-day event. The three-hour ceremony at the Jordanki Culture Centre also included video messages about AI in entertainment from Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck.

Several honors were handed out on the night. Darren Aronofsky, who has openly backed generative AI in filmmaking since launching his studio Primordial Soup last year, received the honorary Award for Director. Actress Karolina Gruszka took the Marshal of the Kujawy Pomorze Region Film Award, and cinematographer Janusz Kamiński, a two-time Oscar winner for Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan, received The Hollywood Reporter's Visionary Award. The festival also marked a century since the birth of Polish director Andrzej Wajda and a decade since his death, with the Polish Radio Choir – Lusławice performing an a cappella reworking of music from his key films. Poland's Senate has declared 2026 "The Year of Wajda."

The opening film was Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, an OpenAI origin story starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever. Guadagnino, who shot it on 35 mm and has no interest in using AI in his own work, said the film is really about the "tech oligarchs" and the huge economic and political power they hold over people's lives. Cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed said that in cinema, AI is "just a tool, like any other." Aronofsky said he returns to the festival because few events celebrate everyone who makes films possible, not only the famous names. Neon will release Artificial in the U.S. on Dec. 25.

The ceremony began with a minute of silence for victims of a mass shooting in Kraków earlier that day. Reports say at least six people were killed and more than a dozen injured when a gunman suspected of far-right ties drove into the city's historic Main Market Square and opened fire. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three more bodies were later found at the suspect's home, making it Poland's deadliest shooting in decades. Local politicians scheduled to speak at the opening acknowledged the severity of the attack before the program began, and the festival continues through Nov. 14.

stories.Headline: Meta strategy chief Dave Wehner leaves to become CFO of Fireworks AI
stories.Summary:
Dave Wehner, who has been Meta's chief strategy officer since late 2022, is leaving the company to become chief financial officer of Fireworks AI, a startup that runs AI models for customers, according to reports dated November 7, 2026. The Information broke the news, and CNBC reported it as well, with Startup Fortune and FourWeekMBA relaying the details. Neither side has said when he will start, and one article notes that no announcement from Fireworks, Meta or Wehner had been found when it checked. The FourWeekMBA piece says it had read only the headline and summary of The Information's report, which sits behind a paywall.

Wehner's record is laid out in Meta's own filings. A April 2014 filing says the board appointed him chief financial officer effective June 1, 2014, and that he had been vice president of corporate finance and business planning at Facebook since November 2012. Before that he was CFO of Zynga for about two years. A July 2022 filing says he told the company he would move from CFO to chief strategy officer effective November 1, 2022, and Susan Li took over as CFO. Meta's revenue was $12.47 billion in 2014 and $116.61 billion in 2022, about 9.4 times as much by FourWeekMBA's arithmetic, though the site says it makes no claim about what drove that growth.

On the Fireworks side, Wehner wrote on X that the company has the right mission for the moment and that he has grown increasingly bullish on what it is building. Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao told CNBC that he will be responsible for scaling the company's finances and operations. Meta has not named a successor in the strategy role, and nothing in the reports says why Wehner made the move. Startup Fortune notes that readers may draw their own conclusions about a former public-company CFO joining a large private firm, but says that is inference and not something CNBC or Fireworks has stated.

Fireworks was valued at $17.5 billion in July 2026, after a Series D round of $1.505 billion led by Atreides Management, according to Dealroom. That is more than four times the $4 billion valuation from its Series C in October 2025. Startup Fortune says Qiao is a former Meta PyTorch lead, that the company has passed $1 billion in annualized revenue, a fivefold rise over the prior year, and that it handles 40 trillion tokens a day for customers including Cursor, Perplexity and Uber. No new valuation was given with the hire, and the articles say no Fireworks listing or IPO plan has been reported.

stories.Headline: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Intellectual Property
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 29, the Brooklyn Entertainment & Sports Law Society hosted a Film & TV panel at Brooklyn Law School titled "The Impact of AI on IP." The speakers were intellectual property attorneys Meeka Bondy, a 1994 Brooklyn Law School graduate who founded Meeka J. Bondy, PLLC and previously worked at Perkins Coie and HBO; Erica Carter, a 2015 graduate who founded Carter Advisory, PLLC and previously worked at Epic Games and Sesame Workshop; and Stacy Lager of the National Hockey League. Matt Gamble, a 2027 J.D. candidate at the school, wrote up the discussion in a post dated November 9, 2026. The panelists examined how artificial intelligence is reshaping the legal and commercial side of intellectual property in entertainment.

The panel did not announce any rule or requirement, but it pointed to several areas where practice is changing. Studios generally hold the copyright in the fictional characters they create, while an actor's name, image, likeness and voice raise separate questions, partly because publicity rights differ from state to state. Contract language that gives companies rights to use performances in media "now known or not yet created" is common, and talent bound by it often must renegotiate, which is hard for the many actors and athletes with little bargaining power. Looking ahead, the panelists expected contracts to address AI-generated performances, consent and compensation much more explicitly. For licensing, they listed the scope and duration of permitted uses, approval rights, ownership of derivative works, indemnification for infringement claims, transparency and clear labeling of AI-generated content as key points.

The views in the post belong to the three panelists. Carter used her time at Sesame Workshop to show that a company can control the IP behind a character like Elmo while the human talent behind it still matters, and she was skeptical that AI copies could replace the real thing, saying that "Elmo is Elmo." Lager described the NHL as protective of its brand, stressing that licensees cannot simply use valuable IP however they want. The panelists said labor groups such as SAG set baseline protections, but collective bargaining agreements often fall short of the maximum available, so individuals and their teams must negotiate more, depending on their leverage. They also floated revenue sharing for artists whose existing work feeds AI products, and noted that AI could create commercial opportunities for companies while threatening the livelihoods of the people who built the industry.

On context and next steps, the panelists said consumers still value authenticity, but that protecting it requires enforcement, which is difficult across many online platforms even for large companies. Companies must also weigh aggressive protection of their rights against the reputational risk of pursuing individual consumers. The panel closed with advice for law students: learn how AI works and how companies develop it, since lawyers who understand the technology will be better advocates and advisors. A second article, from Managing IP on the same date, only carries a teaser for an interview with Raluca Vasilescu of Cabinet M Oproiu on AI, patent drafting and changing client expectations, and the full text is behind a subscriber wall, so its content is not covered here.

stories.Headline: Putting AI on pause: South Portland schools consider moratorium
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 9, 2026, the South Portland School Board voted down a proposed moratorium on student-facing generative AI for the rest of the 2026-2027 school year. The vote failed 6-1, and the only member in favor was At-Large Board Member Claire Holman, who had put the proposal forward. Early coverage had described the plan as a ban on students using generative AI for any assignments, but the city documents cited by the Free Press of the University of Southern Maine said it would have covered students in grades PreK-8 in classrooms and assignments. The pause was meant to give the board time to write an appropriate AI policy.

Under the proposal, the school department would have made sure every staff member received two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training. Once that training was done, teachers could only use AI tools approved by the South Portland School Department, though they would not have been required to use AI if they chose not to. Exceptions could have been made for assistive technologies and centrally approved instructional uses. The department still has no specific AI policy.

Several teachers spoke against the plan during public comment, saying they had not been consulted. Peter Wetzel, a middle school computer science teacher, said it would directly affect a curriculum he had worked hard to build. Cidney Mayes, who teaches digital literacy to fifth and sixth graders at South Portland Middle School, said AI literacy makes up a large part of her teaching and that she would lose four weeks of instruction. Board Vice Chair Tyler Smith, At-Large Member Eleni Richardson, Board Chair Rosemarie DeAngelis and Superintendent Dr. Angela Atkinson Duina also opposed it, with Atkinson Duina saying she trusts the judgment of the district's educators. Holman argued the plan would not stop students from learning about AI, and asked what would happen if children could not think.

Some speakers backed the idea, including one who worried about AI weakening critical thinking, and a kindergarten parent who wanted exceptions for classes that teach AI literacy. Student Representative Sarah Lupien told WGME that AI has not greatly affected her own learning, since many of her classes never use it. DeAngelis said the board should wait for a more detailed plan rather than approve the moratorium that night. WGME reported that officials are now working on a comprehensive plan, set to launch in January, that will cover AI integration as well as broader cybersecurity issues in the district.

stories.Headline: Anthropic secures $3.4 billion generator deal for AI data centers, FT reports
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has agreed a deal worth about $3.4 billion to secure gas-fired power generators for its data centers, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, November 8. The AI company bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty generators in late September from OnePWR Solutions, an equipment supplier based in San Antonio, Texas. Rather than simply becoming a customer of the supplier, Anthropic took over OnePWR's existing orders for Caterpillar generator sets, according to Data Center Dynamics. The Financial Times said OnePWR had ordered the equipment two years ago, before recent price increases, but needed financing to complete the purchase.

Anthropic did not buy OnePWR itself, and none of the supplier's employees moved over to the AI company, a person familiar with the matter told the newspaper. The deal does include the engineering and construction capabilities needed to install the generators at Anthropic's data centers, and OnePWR will help with that work. The generators are expected to be available within the next two years. Data Center Dynamics described the purchase as the largest known single buy of power-generation equipment by a frontier AI lab, and said it is meant to give Anthropic more control over its data center portfolio.

Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report, and neither Anthropic nor OnePWR responded to requests for comment. The details therefore rest on the Financial Times account and the person it cited. Strong demand for Anthropic's Claude family of AI models has pushed the company to secure more computing and power capacity. The deal fits a much larger spending push.

Reuters reported in September that Anthropic expects to spend more than $500 billion over the next 10 years building AI infrastructure. Earlier in November, the company disclosed $895.4 billion in cloud and data center commitments through 2045, including $121.3 billion to lease compute from Google, $120.5 billion from SpaceX, $110 billion from Amazon and $44.9 billion from Microsoft. It also has a $44.6 billion deal with Nscale running to 2033, $41.3 billion with Lambda to 2034, and a $50 billion arrangement with Fluidstack. The New York Times reports Anthropic is expected to have more than 3.5 gigawatts of compute this year, with a similar amount due in 2027.

stories.Headline: Anthropic must face Claude Max lawsuit as judge finds '5x or 20x more usage' ads plausibly misleading
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in San Francisco ruled on Friday, November 6, 2026, that Anthropic must face a proposed class action over how it marketed its Claude Max subscriptions. Judge Alex G. Tse of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted in part and denied in part the company's motion to dismiss in Kahn v. Anthropic PBC, No. 3:26-cv-05763. He found that the "5x or 20x more usage than Pro" advertising was plausibly misleading. Courthouse News reported the ruling first, according to The Next Web.

The plaintiffs, Karl Kahn and Solomon Smith, say the multipliers on the $100 Max 5x plan and the $200 Max 20x plan apply per five-hour session, while weekly limits are not 5x or 20x higher. The judge let the breach of contract and negligent misrepresentation claims go forward, along with Smith's claim under California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act. He reasoned that Anthropic's explanation of the per-session limit sat two hyperlinks away from the main sales pages, and that with monthly billing a consumer could reasonably infer a promise of 5x or 20x more usage per month. He also rejected Anthropic's argument that a Claude subscription is not a "service" under that law, finding that Claude Code plausibly is one. The complaint calculates that on the Sonnet 4 model, Max 5x users get 3.5 times Pro's weekly usage and Max 20x users get 6 times.

Smith's claim survived in part because he is a computer-science student, and educational use is plainly not commercial use, the judge wrote. Several claims were dismissed, all with leave to amend by December 2. Kahn's claim under the Consumers Legal Remedies Act fell because he had not shown he uses Claude for personal rather than commercial purposes. The claims under California's unfair competition and false advertising laws failed because both plaintiffs still subscribe, so they lack standing to seek an injunction, and they did not explain why damages would be an inadequate remedy.

Tse also dismissed a claim over Anthropic tightening usage limits mid-cycle, finding that its terms of service reserve the right to change capacity limits. If the plaintiffs do not amend, Anthropic must answer by December 16. Anthropic argued that reasonable buyers would understand "more usage" as applying per session, pointing to its help pages. The company has not been found liable, since this was a ruling on a motion to dismiss and no court has decided that its advertising was deceptive.

In its amended S-1 filed November 2, Anthropic says it faces several putative class action complaints alleging false and misleading advertising of its Claude subscription plans. The filing describes the matters as generally in early stages and says the company intends to defend itself vigorously. It also warns that changes to usage limits have led, and could lead, to claims that its disclosures were inadequate or misleading, though it names neither the Kahn case nor a dollar figure. The plaintiffs now have until December 2 to file an amended complaint, and the case has not yet been certified as a class action.

stories.Headline: Google’s Policy on AI in the Classroom Puts Schools in a Bind
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026, that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be switched off by default for K-12 student accounts, beginning next year. Administrators will have to turn each product on themselves before students can use it. One report points to January as the start, though no outlet gave a firm calendar date. Google also said that Search and AI are deeply integrated, and early coverage read this as meaning schools that refuse AI would lose Search altogether. News outlets have labeled the move an ultimatum, but that word comes from the press and not from Google.

Google later clarified that a school can enable Search without turning on the Gemini products, although AI Mode and AI Overviews will stay built into Search. Guided Learning will be the default AI feature in the updated school search experience, giving step-by-step coaching instead of instant answers. It also became globally available in Google Classroom on November 3. Any district that does nothing will simply get the cautious default whenever Google flips the switch. Google has not published how many student accounts are affected, and the reports reviewed offer no verified count.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said the company wants schools to have control over AI in their classrooms. He said access will be entirely off until administrators explicitly turn it on, and that a school that bans AI would show students a message saying Search is unavailable. Google also said on X that it knows of concerns about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork. Critics see it differently, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using monopoly power to force AI into public schools. Yvette Renteria of Common Sense Media said her group had asked Google to turn AI off in Search and called the either-or choice disturbing because it removes chances to build critical thinking.

Leaving Google is hard for most schools. An estimated 60,000 K-12 schools use Google Workplace, and about 93 percent of U.S. public schools use or plan to use Chromebooks, according to the reports cited. Eric Gibbs of Copyleaks said Google risks undermining its own position by forcing districts to choose between information access and control over student AI use. Others are relaxed about it, and Dustin Strickland, an administrator at North Murray High School in Georgia, said students must be taught to use AI. New York City has banned AI for younger students while allowing some use in high school, and California districts are debating their own limits on classroom technology.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's African AI expansion faces uncertainty as Taiwanese-American billionaire CEO Jensen Huang faces investigation over alleged Chinese spy links
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board announced on November 8, 2026 that its independent directors, assisted by outside legal advisers, would investigate reports that chief executive Jensen Huang had been targeted by a suspected Chinese espionage operation. The reports centre on Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials suspect she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information about American AI chips, though the allegations remain unproven and no disclosure of sensitive information has been confirmed. Jensen Huang has since acknowledged an extramarital affair and apologised to his family, colleagues and shareholders.

The congressional side of the story adds a formal demand. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford wrote to Huang asking him to attend a closed-door briefing on the 18th. They want him to describe his dealings with Alice Huang and explain the security framework Nvidia uses to protect its technology from foreign adversaries. Megaspeed first drew the attention of US agencies in 2024, when it moved to buy billions of dollars' worth of advanced AI chips, which raised suspicions that it might be a shell company or broker evading export controls on China. It later built data centres in Southeast Asia and leased computing power to Alibaba, a setup that lets Chinese firms use Nvidia hardware through cloud services without chips being shipped into China.

Nvidia's board said it prioritises US national and economic security, but that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and it reaffirmed its confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Huang told employees he was unfaithful to his wife, said there was no excuse for his actions, and promised to support the investigation and cooperate fully. Nvidia has said it is routine for its chief executive to meet customers and that it does not give them sensitive trade secrets or national security information. Chinese authorities rejected the reports as groundless speculation meant to smear China. The New York Times also reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence about a year ago but appears to have taken no particular action, given Nvidia's importance to the economy, the stock market and trade relations with China.

The probe lands as Nvidia technology spreads across Africa. A $1.2 billion AI factory near Casablanca, announced in April by Nexus Core Systems with Nvidia as technology partner, targets 500 megawatts of capacity. In Egypt, a project involving Cassava Technologies, Vodafone Business and Elsewedy Electric, announced in September, could draw up to $1 billion and includes a sovereign AI facility using Nvidia technology. South Africa's $50 million AI cloud project, with more than 400 Nvidia processors, was announced in August. Neither Nvidia nor its African partners have reported disruptions to chip supplies, financing or construction, though the outcome of the investigation could carry implications for those operations.

stories.Headline: U.S. Sen. Warren signals sweeping probes of Big Tech and Wall Street; China AI chips also face regulation
stories.Summary:
U.S. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections held on the 3rd, and they are expected to open wide investigations into Big Tech companies, Wall Street financial firms and the Trump family's cryptocurrency businesses. Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee when the new Congress convenes next January. According to CNBC on the 9th, local time, she plans to put easing the cost-of-living burden, tightening limits on advanced AI chip exports to China and stronger oversight of prediction markets among the committee's main priorities. The Democrats will take over key committees in both chambers from January, which lets them set each panel's agenda and use subpoena power to demand sworn testimony from senior officials and corporate executives. The Banking Committee covers monetary policy, banking and export controls, so Warren's role is expected to raise congressional pressure across both the financial and technology industries.

Warren intends to tighten limits on advanced AI chips sold to China and to build a new regulatory framework for the AI industry in the United States. That has raised the prospect that chipmakers such as NVIDIA, which want to grow in the Chinese market, could face more regulatory pressure. She has called the lack of oversight of prediction markets a "Wild West" situation and plans to push for tighter rules. Earlier, she joined Republican Sen. John Curtis in sending letters to Kalshi and Polymarket asking about safeguards and oversight for election-related prediction markets. The Trump family's crypto ventures are also expected to be examined, and there is speculation that subpoenas could be used to look into possible conflicts of interest between the family and private companies.

An aide to Warren told CNBC that she is preparing an aggressive oversight and investigation plan. She has asked Big Tech CEOs, Trump administration officials and Wall Street executives to preserve relevant documents. She has also urged people tied to the Trump family's crypto businesses to get ready for congressional investigations. The reporting presents all of this as Warren's plan, and it does not describe any investigation as having formally begun.

A Tech Policy Press essay by Alice Marwick, published on the 9th, offers context on why voters may support such action. It says the Democratic sweep was a referendum on many issues, including the cost of living, and that curbing the power of the tech industry was high on voters' minds. Several winning candidates ran against Big Tech, including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and South Carolina Senator-elect Annie Andrews, who both backed a data center moratorium, and ballot initiatives to curb data centers passed widely. The essay argues that tech regulation should reach beyond AI, and it lists ideas such as a federal privacy law, easier subscription cancellation, disclosure of bot activity in advertising, a ban on crypto ATMs and liability for scam ads on social platforms. It also notes that President Donald Trump has promised to veto Democratic legislation, so many of these ideas may be more practical at the state level.

stories.Headline: SoftBank to face scrutiny of AI strategy at second-quarter earnings after selloff
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group is due to report its July-to-September results on Tuesday, Nov. 10, with investors watching for reassurance about its AI strategy after a sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks. The Japanese investment firm's shares fell 11 per cent on Friday and another 4.2 per cent on Monday, leaving them down 23 per cent for the year, while the cost of insuring its debt against default reached a four-year high. The turmoil came as China blocked SoftBank's US$5.4 billion takeover of ABB's robotics division, and as the Democratic Party's sweeping success in US midterm elections raised expectations of tougher regulatory scrutiny and delays to data centre construction. The broader market was hit too, with the Nasdaq dropping 5.5 per cent on Thursday, Nov. 5, before recovering some ground on Friday.

The numbers at stake for SoftBank are large. It has spent US$64.6 billion on a 13 per cent stake in OpenAI, and at the end of June its net interest-bearing debt stood at 10.8 trillion yen (US$68 billion), up from 6.6 trillion yen a year earlier. Its results are hard to predict, and three analysts polled by LSEG forecast July-September net profit anywhere from a gain of 233 billion yen to a loss of 113 billion yen. Numbers are due at 0630 GMT, followed by a briefing from chief financial officer Yoshimitsu Goto at 0730 GMT. Investors also want guidance on further debt financing, since chip designer Arm, whose shares were used as collateral for loans, has fallen about 60 per cent from its June record to US$175, and Jefferies analyst Atul Goyal wrote in October that a price meaningfully below US$200 adds pressure on SoftBank's finances.

Analysts quoted in the coverage see risks ahead. Rolf Bulk of Futurum Group said questions about how the AI build-out will be financed, powered and deployed were much easier to answer six months ago than today, and he suggested SoftBank might have to stop investing, cut debt and even sell some positions, as it has done before. On the ABB deal, both companies had been optimistic they could find a solution, and SoftBank is in talks with Chinese authorities, according to a person familiar with the matter. Bloomberg News has reported that the companies are weighing whether to carve out ABB's China business.

The pressure extends beyond SoftBank. PYMNTS noted that the selloff cut stock market values rather than draining corporate cash, and that major spenders have so far shown little sign of retreat. Alphabet kept its 2026 capital spending forecast of US$195 billion to US$205 billion, Meta forecast US$135 billion to US$145 billion, and Microsoft reported US$45.2 billion in quarterly capital spending and priced a US$25 billion debt offering on Oct. 29. Investment professionals expect a gradual slowdown rather than a collapse, and the next round of spending forecasts should show whether market pressure changes deployment schedules or investment priorities.

stories.Headline: Morning Digest: Trump says U.S. military action against Iran not necessary ‘at this point’; U.K. writer M. John Harrison wins Booker for AI-tinged apocalyptic novel, and more
stories.Summary:
U.S. President Donald Trump made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room on Monday, November 9, 2026, and told reporters he believes the war in Iran is "effectively over" in military terms. He had earlier met Qatar's Prime Minister. Mr. Trump said the United States is simply keeping things at the status quo, and that military action against Iran is not necessary "at this point." The digest carries only a brief summary of the remarks, and the briefing was widely reported alongside several other stories that day.

The articles give no new order, deadline or formal change tied to the statement, so it does not set out any specific requirement. What it does is signal that Washington is not planning fresh strikes for now, with the existing situation left as it stands. The only figures attached to the remarks are the date of the briefing and the description of the conflict as over in military terms. No troop numbers, funding amounts or timelines were mentioned in the material provided.

Responsibility for the statement rests with Mr. Trump himself, who spoke directly to reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room. His words were limited to the view that Iran is finished as a military matter and that the current state of affairs will be maintained. He did not, in the portions reported, explain what would change his assessment or what steps might follow. The digest, published by The Hindu Bureau on November 10, 2026, presents his comments without any response from Iranian officials.

The context in the same digest shows how crowded the political picture in Washington is. Pete Hegseth, the Defence Secretary, faces an expected House impeachment vote this week after Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment on Monday, November 9. Those articles include a charge of waging war against Iran without congressional approval, and their introduction set off a two-day clock for the vote. Mr. Trump also said he will likely meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, which Beijing said it was discussing with relevant parties.

stories.Headline: New Bedford Slams the Door on AI Data Centers as Power, Water, Neighborhood Fears Force Citywide Freeze
stories.Summary:
New Bedford is moving toward a citywide ban on data centers, which officials describe as a temporary pause while planners write rules for large AI facilities. The Planning Board unanimously backed the measure on October 7, and the City Council's ordinance committee recommended it on October 26, sending it to the full council. Mayor Jon Mitchell proposed the ban in a September 1 letter. The measure remains before the full City Council, and no active data center proposal has been identified in the city.

The city's 2024 zoning rules allow data centers by right in some districts, without special review. Those rules were written before AI pushed facilities to far greater size and intensity, and the pause is meant to give planners time to deal with that gap. Planning Director Jennifer Carloni said the department expects to need about a year to research locations, size limits and safeguards before bringing back a permanent proposal. Land is also a constraint: Derek Santos, executive director of the New Bedford Economic Development Council, said the city lacks parcels near the size modern data centers need. Even the roughly 95-acre former golf-course site considered for manufacturing is about one-third the scale typically needed for hyperscale or AI campuses, which often cover hundreds of acres, and it has water constraints as well.

In his letter, Mitchell argued that data centers place heavy demands on electrical and water infrastructure, create noise from equipment and generators, use up substantial land, and can harm nearby properties. He warned that continuing without performance standards could expose residents to problems the city is not prepared to handle. Carloni pointed to a controversial expansion in Lowell as the kind of outcome the city wants to avoid. Councilors said they are open to tax revenue and jobs but insist on proper regulations. Councilor Ian Abreu said the city is not anti-growth, while Council President Ryan Pereira observed that New Bedford's dense layout may leave no suitable site.

The local debate fits a wider pattern across Massachusetts. On September 8, Governor Maura Healey signed an executive order requiring local community approval and benefits agreements before state permitting for data centers, and aiming to keep large loads from shifting grid costs onto ratepayers. A MassLive review found 18 Massachusetts municipalities had enacted or approved bans, moratoriums or restrictions by mid-October, with more than 30 communities discussing limits, and nearby Taunton adopted its own ban and pause. Elsewhere, California has passed laws requiring disclosure of energy and water use, Texas has paused approvals for grid interconnection while auditing projected demand, and a Finnish regulator ordered a halt to preparatory work at Google sites pending environmental assessments. Public comment in New Bedford has been mixed, with some residents questioning the loss of high-wage opportunities and others stressing resource strain, higher local energy costs and limited community benefits.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy scandal revives push to write China chip export limits into the defense bill
stories.Summary:
Reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence have given Washington's chip hawks a new argument, and they are aiming it at the annual defense bill. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress is now more likely to pass three chip measures that sit in the Senate's fiscal 2027 defense authorization package: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act. On Monday, Nov. 9, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he strongly supports China chip restrictions in the final bill, following a classified briefing for congressional leaders. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks said in a joint statement that the relationship makes the concerns even more urgent.

Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board is investigating, while saying it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. As introduced in the House by Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, the AI Overwatch Act would treat AI chip sales to adversary nations much like arms sales. Commerce would have to notify two congressional committees at least 30 days before licensing chips such as Nvidia's H200 or AMD's MI325X, Congress could block a sale by joint resolution, and Blackwell-class chips would face mandatory denial. The House text would also end existing licenses for covered exports. The Chip Security Act, written by Reps.

Bill Foster and Bill Huizenga and passed unanimously in committee, would require companies to track their chips to combat smuggling. The MATCH Act would push U.S. allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment sales to China, and the final language will come out of House-Senate negotiations. Opposition is expected from Nvidia and the White House. A former congressional staffer told Reuters that Nvidia is the biggest opponent of the Chip Security and AI Overwatch Acts, and the Information Technology Industry Council, whose members include Nvidia, says the measures could hurt competitiveness.

The Information reported that White House officials shared feedback with congressional staff in late October, though the White House did not comment to Reuters and Nvidia declined to comment. President Donald Trump has backed Huang, calling him an amazing guy and saying Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Senate Majority Leader John Thune spoke generally about responding to national security threats, and House Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress is still gathering information. A similar Senate provision, the GAIN AI Act, was dropped from last year's final defense bill after lobbying by the White House and Nvidia.

If the chip measures are dropped again, they would return to a Congress run by Democrats from Jan. 3, with chip hawks such as Chris Coons and Warren in line for committee chairs. The revenue now at stake is small, since licensed H200 sales to China were under 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue last quarter, so a congressional veto would mainly cap future sales. Nvidia is due to report third-quarter results on Nov. 17, and House Republican chairmen have asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia shares fell about 5% on Monday, more than 20% below their peak of about a month ago, according to Yahoo Finance.

stories.Headline: Data Doctors: Can I trust AI shopping agents?
stories.Summary:
Zoho Corporation announced on November 10, 2026, that it is turning Zoho Analytics into what it calls an Agentic Analytics platform, adding a layer meant to give AI agents trusted business data and context. The company said the platform brings together data, analytics and AI agents so businesses can move from studying numbers to acting on them. A central feature is Ask Zia, a conversational assistant that now uses several specialized sub-agents working together. Zoho made the announcement from Singapore through the Media OutReach Newswire.

The update includes native semantic and ontology layers, which act as a business glossary and a map of how a company's entities relate to one another. Ask Zia has six pre-built sub-agents covering data analysis, visualization, data preparation, modeling, coding and SQL generation, and companies can use Zoho's own language model or bring their own. Teams can also build custom agents that connect to outside tools through the Model Context Protocol. Zoho added more than 30 new data connectors to the 500-plus it already offered, including ones for SAP, PayPal, Adobe Commerce, Twilio and Notion, along with more than 50 other new capabilities. Pricing is unchanged, and every plan now includes Zoho LLM credits, with a Basic plan starting at US$24 per month billed annually, covering 2 users, 0.5 million rows and 10K credits.

Gibu Mathew, Managing Director of Zoho APAC, said agents cannot work on data alone and need a solid intelligence layer, which he said the update provides. He described it as one open and extensible layer that gives every AI tool in a business the context, metrics and governance to produce answers people can rely on. Zoho also stressed oversight features, such as a data catalog, AI usage and cost tracking, and a sandbox for testing agents before publishing them. The company said Zoho Analytics is used by 100,000 businesses worldwide daily.

Zoho said the cloud version of the updates is available now, with some preview versions still to arrive. It plans to expand the designed context into a dynamic one that tracks how business data changes over time, add decision intelligence based on the actions agents trigger, and keep investing in open standards, including the Apache Ossie specification. It also plans to build Zoho Analytics into a fuller unified data platform that would include a data lakehouse. Separately, a Quartz report on AI shopping agents says Meta's Muse agent was downloaded 10 million times in the U.S. within 40 days of its early September launch, with purchases averaging more than $200. It adds that agentic web traffic roughly tripled from August to September and that Amazon blocked Muse soon after launch, while the other shopping article supplied no readable text.

stories.Headline: Claude and ChatGPT Bring AI-Powered Finance Features to Personal Money Management
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a dedicated Personal Finance feature inside Claude on November 5, 2026. It lets eligible subscribers connect supported bank accounts, credit cards, loans and investment accounts through Plaid, a financial technology service that links apps to participating institutions. The feature began rolling out in beta to Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the United States, and it is reaching Claude's web, desktop and mobile apps gradually. OpenAI's competing Finances feature in ChatGPT arrived earlier, on May 15, 2026, and also relies on Plaid to connect financial accounts.

Once accounts are linked, Claude can review transactions, sort spending into categories, track subscriptions and upcoming bills, and show cash flow and balances in visual dashboards. It can also flag unusual charges, duplicate transactions and rising bills, and answer questions about budgets, savings targets and planned purchases. Anthropic says Claude can see selected account details, balances, credit limits and up to 24 months of transactions. ChatGPT can organize expenses, help with budgets and savings planning, and pull together investment details, and OpenAI has since added weekly financial insights, credit monitoring, stock watchlists, voice support and manual account entry. Both tools use read-only access, so neither can pay bills, move money or place investment trades through these connections.

On privacy, Anthropic says conversations in Claude's dedicated Personal Finance hub are not used to train its models, though conversations outside the hub remain subject to a user's regular privacy settings. ChatGPT follows the account's existing data controls, and users can turn off model training with the "Improve the model for everyone" setting under Data Controls. Users sign in through Plaid in both cases, which handles the connection to participating institutions. The article advises people to review account permissions, understand data retention policies and avoid sharing unnecessary financial details.

The coverage notes that AI-generated answers can contain errors, and balances may not reflect the latest transactions, so users should check figures against official statements and consult qualified professionals for important decisions. The competition between Anthropic and OpenAI reflects a wider move toward conversational money management, and further partnerships and integrations could add more ways to use the tools. Separately, a Seoul Economic Daily report on November 9 said ChatGPT's mobile monthly active users in South Korea reached 18,762,276 last month, up 43.8% from a year earlier, and its share of AI app users rose to 91% from 84%. The same report said the Claude app's monthly users jumped 15-fold to 2.1 million from 140,000, lifting it to second place from seventh.

stories.Headline: Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Predicts Top 3 ZK Cryptos
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Cryptonews published an article built around predictions from Meta AI, the assistant tied to Mark Zuckerberg's company, about which zero-knowledge cryptocurrencies could do best in 2027. The piece names three projects, zkSync (ZK), Starknet (STRK) and Zcash (ZEC), and says all three have at one time been mentioned by Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin. It was written by Ahmed Barakat and fact-checked by the CryptoNews editorial team. A separate article from the same outlet, dated November 9, applied the same Meta AI approach to the October 2026 US Consumer Price Index report and the market's likely reaction, though the text provided cuts off right after saying the report is due at 8:30 a.m. ET.

On zkSync, the article points to its Prividium platform, which is built for regulated institutions and offers private, permissioned environments while still settling on Ethereum. Recent progress includes SOC 2 Type 2 certification, the launch of Prividium Commander for institutional control planes, and partnerships aimed at Japanese financial institutions and US regional banks exploring tokenized deposits. The Airbender Prime prover is said to have proven the vast majority of Ethereum blocks in under 10 seconds on a single high-end GPU. Starknet, by contrast, is described as a leader in STARK-based proofs that are transparent and quantum-resistant, with features such as Shadow Accounts for DeFi privacy. STRK is trading near multi-month lows of roughly $0.038 to $0.040, and the article says a move back above the $0.05 to $0.06 zone on rising volume would be an early bullish sign.

For Zcash, the article credits the NU7 upgrade with improving shielded transaction performance and advancing its privacy pool design, and it says the coin keeps relatively strong liquidity and institutional access compared with smaller privacy coins. It adds that ZEC has held up better than many altcoins and has set higher relative support levels than pure layer-2 tokens. A November 9 post from trader Daan Crypto Trades, embedded in the piece, said ZEC had consolidated for six weeks and needed a convincing break and hold above about $1375 to start a larger move. Meta AI's final outlook is that zkSync leads on institutional product-market fit, Starknet on technical ambition and STARK leadership, and Zcash on proven privacy utility. The article says all three gain from the wider maturing of zero-knowledge proofs.

The predictions come from Meta AI, and the articles attribute them to the assistant rather than to Zuckerberg personally, with Barakat as the author. Cryptonews carries a disclaimer that crypto is a high-risk asset class, that the article is informational and not investment advice, and that readers could lose all of their capital. The site also notes that some of its content includes affiliate links but says its editorial analysis is produced independently of those partnerships. The outlet adds that if Ethereum scaling demand rebounds and privacy becomes a stronger market theme in 2027, these projects are well placed to outperform within the zero-knowledge sector. The articles give no firm dates for what happens next beyond the CPI release scheduled for the morning after the November 9 piece.

stories.Headline: Democrats demand answers on Trump’s AI policy amid spy plot
stories.Summary:
House Democrats on the Foreign Affairs Committee sent a letter, released on Monday, demanding that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick explain the Trump administration's approach to exporting advanced artificial intelligence chips. The letter was signed by Reps. Gabe Amo of Rhode Island, Gregory W. Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California. It came as congressional leaders were set to be briefed by intelligence officials later that day, in a session meant to focus on Iran. Lawmakers from both parties were expected to press CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton about a spy for China's Ministry of State Security who had an intimate relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The three Democrats questioned the Commerce Department's decision to allow exports of advanced chips to China. The letter drew on reporting by The New York Times that Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed, was working for China's top spy agency. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company that bought Nvidia chips and built data centers in Southeast Asia used by Chinese firms such as Alibaba. People briefed on U.S. intelligence say she was tasked with learning about Nvidia's work on cutting-edge AI chips and helping China gain access to that technology. The lawmakers also cited Times reporting that Commerce had approved licenses for advanced chip sales to Chinese companies with ties to Beijing, military contractors and sanctioned firms.

The U.S. government has blocked Nvidia's most advanced chips from being sold to China, a ban Jensen Huang has publicly opposed. The lawmakers argued that the United States cannot claim to protect its leadership in artificial intelligence while letting its most advanced technology reach a strategic competitor. They wrote that national security must come before corporate sales targets, and that giving China such chips puts the country at risk. In their words, the chips supply the computing power that will shape AI, military modernization and economic competition. They did not say what response they expect from Lutnick, and the articles do not report any reply from the Commerce Department.

Nvidia's board announced on Sunday that it is investigating Alice Huang's relationship with the company's chief executive. In a video to employees, Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an affair, and he will keep leading the company while the inquiry continues. Meanwhile, Republicans on three key House committees have demanded that he appear in a closed-door hearing to answer questions about the relationship and any possible leak of sensitive data. Congressional scrutiny is therefore growing on several fronts, though the articles do not say when the hearing or any answers from Lutnick might come.

stories.Headline: LG AI Research Opens Free API Access to Its K-EXAONE 2.5 Model
stories.Summary:
LG AI Research announced on November 9, 2026 that it is offering free API access to K-EXAONE 2.5, an upgraded version of its in-house foundation model. The company made the announcement at Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul. Developers, startups, companies and research institutions can use the model for service development and research at no cost by obtaining an API key through the EXAONE API Platform. LG describes K-EXAONE 2.5 as a technology-validation model built by applying additional training to the version released in August 2026.

On the technical side, the model is text-only and supports Korean and English. Its documentation lists 31 billion active parameters within a 750-billion-parameter model and a January 2026 knowledge cutoff. It offers chat, tool calling, structured outputs, code generation and streaming through an OpenAI-compatible POST /v1/chat/completions endpoint, using the model identifier k-exaone_v2.5. Input tokens plus the max_tokens allowance, which includes reasoning, cannot exceed 524,288 tokens, and larger requests return a 400 error. The reasoning_effort setting defaults to max, while preserve_thinking can carry earlier reasoning into multi-turn requests, and LG's agent guide includes configurations for the Hermes general agent and the OpenCode coding agent.

LG also released results on four agentic benchmarks, compared against China's DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3. K-EXAONE 2.5 scored 74.6 on AutomationBench, ahead of GLM at 71.6 and just behind DeepSeek at 74.9. On ClioEval it scored 77.3 against 75.8 for DeepSeek and 77.6 for GLM, and on BrowseComp it scored 78.0 against 75.8 and 79.0. On SWE-Bench Pro it scored 59.2, compared with 58.4 for DeepSeek and 64.0 for GLM. Kim I-reun, head of the EXAONE Lab at LG AI Research, said the company's internal analysis shows performance across 24 evaluation metrics improved by more than 70 percent compared with the August model.

LG AI Research said it opened the API for free so users can try a Korean AI model directly and apply it to their own services. The company said the work also confirmed the potential for performance gains from advancing the training methodology of the existing model, ahead of developing a new third iteration. It is also considering applying Nvidia's Dynamo technology to improve inference efficiency and service scalability. The benchmark figures are LG's own, measured internally on open datasets, and the earlier K-EXAONE 2.0 was released as an open-weight Apache 2.0 model with a Mixture-of-Experts design and a 262,144-token context length. In the documented agent workflow, the surrounding agent still executes tool calls and manages the loop, while the model supplies the reasoning and tool-call decisions through the API.
