stories.Headline: How sustainable is the AI investment boom after Thursday’s selloff? By Investing.com
stories.Summary:
Capital Economics, a research firm, warned in a report that the AI investment boom is getting harder to sustain at its current pace, because technology companies are spending billions on infrastructure without a matching acceleration in revenue. The article, published by Investing.com on November 8, 2026, came in the wake of a Thursday selloff in AI-linked stocks. The firm said it remains positive about AI's long-term potential to lift productivity, but questions whether revenues will grow fast enough to justify the spending. It expects growth in AI investment to slow in 2027, followed by a fall of around 10% in total investment in 2028.

The numbers behind the warning are large. The five biggest US hyperscalers, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle, are set to spend a combined $800 billion on capital expenditure this year, with $1 trillion or more expected in 2027. Capital Economics estimates that annual AI revenues from external customers would need to reach between $1.7 trillion and $1.9 trillion by 2030, against roughly $150 billion to $200 billion now, a rise of about nine to 12 times in four years. AI investment has recently added around 0.3 percentage points to annual US GDP growth, a boost that could largely vanish next year, and a 10% drop in 2028 could take off another 0.1 point. Taiwan and South Korea are more exposed, with annual real GDP growth possibly cut by about three points and one point respectively next year, deepening to 5.5 and 1.5 points in 2028.

The firm laid out three possible sources of extra revenue: productivity gains that let AI providers capture part of the added output, the displacement of existing software and business-services providers, and savings from lower labour costs. It said reaching the required returns would take much bigger productivity gains, and a larger shift of income from workers to capital, than it currently expects. It also pointed to physical limits, including shortages of advanced chips and electricity and growing opposition to data centres over their use of land, power and water. Capital Economics added that political pressure after Democratic gains in the US midterm elections could bring tighter planning rules, especially at state level.

On the financial side, the report noted that AI spending, once funded mostly from companies' own cash flow, now leans more on debt, equity, leases and private credit. Outstanding hyperscaler bonds come to about $500 billion, or roughly 6% of the $8.3 trillion US non-financial corporate bond market, so the risks would stay fairly contained if the boom turned soon. A longer debt-financed boom could create much larger vulnerabilities. Even so, the firm does not expect an abrupt collapse in AI investment or a severe downturn, saying existing infrastructure, replacement spending and continued investment should support further adoption. Its central view is that the boom will settle at a more sustainable pace, with software and applications likely to prove more resilient than spending on GPUs, servers and networking equipment.

stories.Headline: Robots Head Into Older Chip Fabs as Samsung, SK hynix Push Charging Standard
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron, the three largest memory chipmakers, have begun working on a charging standard for the mobile robots they plan to use in semiconductor plants. Seoul Economic Daily reported on November 8 that working-level staff from the three companies have formed an early-stage consultative body, and that major industry associations including SEMI, the global association for semiconductor equipment and materials, are taking part. A report the following day said talks with SEMI had begun and that discussions shelved for a decade were gaining momentum as the rush to adopt robots coincides with a chip boom. The effort is aimed at older fabs, which have little automated equipment such as overhead hoist transport systems or stockers, so workers often move wafer carriers on manual carts.

The project would unify battery specifications and charging station operating methods that currently differ from one robot vendor to another. Items under consideration include battery specifications for various mobile robots, communications and equipment for charging stations, charger connection parts and battery management systems. The standard is limited to mobile robots to be deployed in chip plants, including humanoids, autonomous mobile robots and mobile manipulators. Unifying station specifications would also let fewer units serve robots of different types. As a later step, charging data could be linked to manufacturing execution systems so that robots' working and charging time is allocated according to production schedules.

The reports name no single owner of the effort beyond the three chipmakers and the industry associations involved. Jang Young-jae, head of the Manufacturing Physical AI Research Center at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, said a standard prepares the way for using a wide range of robots as production equipment in chip plants. He added that common charging systems across manufacturers can reduce the burden of adopting, validating and maintaining robots while lowering dependence on any single vendor. Park Soo-han, a professor in the School of Robotics at Kwangwoon University, said an industry standard would shorten safety certification and accelerate actual robot adoption.

The articles describe the work as a milestone in the drive toward unmanned factories, as chipmakers seek to automate aging facilities. The robots meant to replace manual carts have different specifications depending on the developer, which is the gap the standard is meant to close. The reports give no timetable for completing the standard, and the consultative body is described as being at an early stage. For now, the three companies and the associations are still working out the guidelines on charging components, equipment, communications and system interfaces.

stories.Headline: [Law Firms Now] Bae, Kim & Lee to Hold Seminar on 'Current Issues and Challenges in AI Regulation' on Nov. 16
stories.Summary:
Bae, Kim & Lee, a Korean law firm, announced on November 9, 2026 that it will hold a seminar titled "Current Issues and Challenges in AI Regulation" at GLAD Yeouido in Seoul at 2 p.m. on November 16. The forum is the firm's second-half AI Law and Policy Forum for this year. It is held in response to the spread of agentic AI and physical AI, which follow generative AI as new areas needing regulation, at a time when the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act takes effect this year. The event is aimed at examining regulatory trends and legal issues and finding reasonable ways to improve the system.

The seminar is co-hosted by Bae, Kim & Lee, the offices of Assemblymen Lee Juhee and Choi Hyungdoo of the National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee, the Korea Association for ICT Law, the Korea Association for Data and AI Law and Policy, and the Korea Information Society Development Institute (KISDI). Opening remarks will come from Ryu Jemyung, Second Vice Minister of Science and ICT, both assemblymen, Jo Kyungsik, an advisor at the firm and a former vice minister, and Lee Sangkyu, KISDI's president. Kang Jiwon, an attorney at the firm, will analyze regulatory issues from the Basic Act's implementation and how it affects business. Jung Junhwa, a legislative researcher at the National Assembly Research Service, will discuss legal questions raised by agentic and physical AI and the legislative work ahead.

Lee Seongyeop, a Korea University professor and president of the Korea Association for ICT Law, will moderate a panel. Panelists include Sun Jiwon of Hanyang University School of Law, Seo Younghoon of Kakao, Park Jiyeon, head of the firm's TMT Group, Moon Jeongwook of KISDI, Jang Doowon of the Ministry of Science and ICT, and Kim Hyesook of the Broadcasting, Media and Communications Commission. The organizers say the panelists will offer a range of views on regulatory approaches that can support AI innovation while keeping it safe. The announcement does not say how many attendees are expected or whether the forum will produce any formal recommendations.

stories.Headline: Nigeria: Manufacturers Charged to Deploy Ai, Energy-Efficient Technologies to Cut Costs
stories.Summary:
The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has urged manufacturers to adopt artificial intelligence, advanced technologies and energy-efficient solutions to counter rising production costs and weak energy supply. The call was made on November 9, 2026, at the 2026 Manufacturers Energy Security and Energy Efficiency Summit in Lagos, which was jointly organised by Manufacturers Power Development Company Ltd. (MPDCL), GIZ and the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP). Industry leaders and government representatives discussed how technology, reliable energy supply and structured financing could help manufacturers meet their energy challenges. The summit drew attention to the difficulties that continue to hurt Nigerian industry. Reporting for Vanguard, Yinka Kolawole described the event as a platform for practical solutions.

MAN's President, Ifeanyi Okoye, said an industrial energy cost reduction and adoption programme would promote factory rooftop solar installations, battery energy storage systems, captive natural gas solutions and smart energy management networks. He said the programme targets the rising cost of energy, which has significantly weakened manufacturing operations and competitiveness. According to him, manufacturers spend about 40 per cent of their profits dealing with energy problems, while high electricity tariffs, unreliable grid supply and dependence on fossil fuels continue to undermine production. He added that the summit aims to help manufacturers gain access to long-term financing, climate funds, green investments and asset-financing mechanisms for moving to more efficient energy systems. Okoye framed these measures as a route to a steadier industrial base.

MAN's Director-General, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, said emerging technologies have become essential for raising production efficiency, cutting energy use and making manufacturing operations more resilient. He noted that AI and smart manufacturing systems could help factories optimise energy use, reduce production losses, lower operating costs and improve product quality, especially given persistent electricity shortages. John Aluya, Chairman of the Board of Directors of MPDCL, said the high cost of self-generation has reduced manufacturers' profit margins and weakened their competitiveness. He stressed that reliable and affordable power is critical to the survival of Nigerian industries, and that the summit was meant to explore solar photovoltaic systems, battery storage, captive gas power, energy efficiency and carbon credit monetisation.

Ulf Brackmann, Chief Executive Officer of IKAPITAL Family Office & Friends, delivered the keynote and argued that AI could significantly raise industrial productivity and create new jobs rather than displace workers. He cautioned, however, that AI can cut costs and improve efficiency only where factories have dependable electricity and sound digital foundations. Brackmann also warned manufacturers against treating AI as a quick fix for their production problems, rejecting the idea that it will solve every difficulty. The article presents his remarks as a note of realism in an otherwise optimistic discussion. The summit therefore left manufacturers with a mix of encouragement to invest in technology and a reminder that reliable power must come first.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
stories.Summary:
MIT and New York University researchers have introduced FLEX, a flexible feature-editing pipeline that lets robots read more into natural language commands. The study, led by Andreea Bobu of MIT with co-authors Audrey Lee and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University, is set to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month. FLEX allows a person to instruct a robot conversationally, and the robot can follow those instructions literally while also drawing broader generalizations that improve its motion planning. The team tested the system in simulated scenarios, including one where a robotic arm carries a cup of coffee over a cluttered table. In that simulation, a person typed a command such as "Don't spill on the laptop!"

and the robot reasoned about why it should avoid the laptop. FLEX uses a large language model, an AI system trained on large volumes of text from the internet, to identify patterns and generalizations. Dennler noted that such models have absorbed common associations, such as liquids plus devices leading to things not working. As a result, the robot adjusted its path to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone without the person spelling that out. The approach means users do not need to specify every object or rule, which the researchers say is a change from earlier methods that added one feature per correction.

The researchers describe the platform as a three-step process that takes about five seconds. In the "Add" step, the robot adds an object mentioned in a command to its list of features to avoid. In the "Generalize" step, a large language model, identified in the article as GPT-4o, looks for patterns among the listed features and infers broader categories, such as fragile objects. In the "Mask" step, the robot's computer vision system checks its surroundings and removes features for objects no longer present. In simulations of three tasks, serving coffee, moving a candle, and carrying a bowling ball, volunteers typed commands and the robot followed them while also avoiding electronics, flammable objects, and fragile items.

The work comes from Bobu's Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research Lab at MIT, where her group builds autonomous agents that learn to work with and around people, with a focus on assistive and household robots. Bobu said that because every home differs and every person cares about different things, no robot arrives knowing what matters to a given owner. She argued that FLEX can learn those preferences from a sentence or two rather than requiring a long list of rules. The article notes that the wider robotics community is also exploring language-based methods for clarifying goals and redirecting trajectories, but the article does not describe any deployment in real homes or any next steps beyond the presentation of the study.

stories.Headline: Congress’s Permitting Bill Is a ‘Massive Giveaway’ to the AI Data Center Industry, Critics Warn
stories.Summary:
The Senate voted on Monday to advance a bipartisan bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which is meant to ease the construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill has support from labor leaders, who say it will produce thousands of jobs, and from clean energy advocates, who think it could unlock wind and solar projects. Its sponsors want it passed before the current Congress ends in January. Critics, however, say it would speed up an AI data center buildout that voters rejected in the midterm elections.

BAAJA would force data centers to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they trigger and includes transmission reforms meant to modernize the grid. It would also weaken some environmental protections and could lead to more gas-powered data centers and more construction on public lands. Its permitting provisions could fast-track projects that are now waiting for approval and limit judges' ability to halt construction over environmental review. One study estimates data centers would pay about $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years, roughly $35 billion more than under current policy. Hundreds of local and national groups, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, have urged Congress not to pass the bill as written.

Supporters, including Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic sponsor, argue the bill ends data center cost-shifting onto households and businesses. Sierra Club's Holly Bender and Earthjustice's Meg Slattery have warned that gas and fossil fuel investment could rise instead. Oil Change International's Allie Rosenbluth called the bill a massive giveaway to the data center industry. President Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass it, saying China would take any data center the United States does not want. Tribal leaders have written that the bill would weaken their ability to protect historic and cultural sites threatened by federally connected projects.

The vote is a test for Democrats after the midterms, since the bill must still pass a Senate vote to take it up, face amendments, and then pass the House in identical form before reaching Trump. Gas-powered data center projects have grown sharply, from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026, according to Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired. Critics on the left, including Michele Jawando of Omidyar Network, want Democrats to wait for the next Congress, which will include many new House members. Supporters hope to pass it this year as a rare bipartisan win on affordability.

stories.Headline: Macron wants AI banned wherever it threatens children
stories.Summary:
On Monday, November 9, 2026, French President Emmanuel Macron said that artificial intelligence should be banned wherever it poses a risk to the mental health of children. He made the remarks in an interview with the French daily Les Echos, on the eve of the adoption of a charter on the subject at the Paris Peace Forum. Macron, who is also pushing for a ban on certain social networks for under-15s in France, said that if certain uses of AI put children at risk, those uses must be prohibited. He argued that AI should not be an unregulated space and said it should be barred when it threatens children's mental health or their brain.

The charter is meant to protect citizens from the threats posed by AI and to inform national and European legislative debates. Under it, research labs would commit to measures including independent evaluations of generative AI systems placed on the market and access to their models' data. Macron said companies would accept a pre-audit and pre-certification, with models reviewed before they are placed in children's hands. A committee of experts was due to give him recommendations on protection against AI on November 10, an area the articles describe as less explored than the impact of social networks. The charter is expected to bring together US firms OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Macron's office.

Macron framed the initiative as a call on Europe to lead, saying the EU would advance its own regulation and push Americans, Canadians and others to follow. He said the aim was a framework covering three categories of danger: children, democratic security, and major national security issues. On the same occasion, he held a videoconference with around 50 heads of state and government, international organisations, companies, researchers and laboratories to discuss AI risks to collective security. The British, Canadian, Norwegian, Dutch and Japanese prime ministers took part, as did the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral and Microsoft. Macron wrote on X that the diagnosis was shared and that action must be taken together.

The announcement comes as regional approaches to AI regulation diverge sharply among the United States, the European Union and China. The EU was due to hold its first summit of national AI ministers in Dublin on the Friday after, under the Irish rotating presidency, to help governments agree a new path for regulating AI and revive the bloc's sluggish economic growth. Leaders were also to review safeguards such as the AI Act. The articles do not say what outcome the Dublin meeting produced.

stories.Headline: The finance professionals scared of AI might just be using the wrong tools
stories.Summary:
Cornell University has launched an online certificate called AI in Finance, aimed at financial professionals who want to understand how artificial intelligence can be used in their work. The program, offered through eCornell, is a collaboration between the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering and the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business. It debuted in spring 2026 with 37 participants and is taught live online so students can interact directly with faculty and industry practitioners. The idea grew out of Victoria Averbukh's work directing the Cornell Financial Engineering Manhattan program, where practitioners kept raising AI questions. Averbukh said many experienced professionals feel overwhelmed by new terms and models and do not know where to start.

The certificate is intended less as training in a specific software tool than as a way to build enough understanding to make informed choices about AI. Participants do not need deep technical backgrounds, Averbukh said, since the focus is on understanding what AI models do, where they fall short, and why they were not built specifically for finance. The curriculum moves from AI foundations to financial use cases such as investment research, credit risk, fraud detection, compliance, client engagement and operational efficiency. It also covers hallucinations, data security, regulation and governance. The program ends with participants identifying AI opportunities in their organizations and developing strategies to pursue them.

The instructors include Cornell faculty such as Averbukh, Jamol Pender, David Goldberg and Jeffrey Varner, along with faculty from the SC Johnson College of Business. Industry contributors include Andrew Chin of AllianceBernstein, Dhagash Mehta of BlackRock, Kathryn Zhao of OKX, Mohamed Khalifa of J.P. Morgan Global Private Bank and Joseph Sommer of EY. Averbukh said Cornell faculty set the conceptual foundations, and practitioners then show how those ideas play out in financial institutions. Pender, who taught the data and AI portions, said accurate data can still lead to poor decisions if it is outdated or unavailable when needed.

Registration for the spring 2027 offering is now open. Classes will meet live online on Tuesday and Thursday evenings from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. beginning May 18, 2027, with the final class on Thursday, June 24. Details and enrollment are available on the eCornell website.

stories.Headline: Deepfake CEO Impersonation Scam Steals $129M From Companies
stories.Summary:
Three men arrested in Europe now face extradition to the United States, accused of using AI-generated deepfakes to defraud thousands of companies of more than $100 million. Jacob Soall, 41, of Spain and the United Kingdom, and Sharon Hazan, 54, of Israel, were arrested in Spain on June 17 and Aug. 5, respectively. Guy Sheetrit, 42, of Israel and the United Arab Emirates, was arrested in the U.K. on Sept. 7. Prosecutors say the suspects posed as CEOs using AI-generated voices and images and also posed as attorneys from major international law firms to make their requests seem credible. Reporting on the case dates to November 9, 2026.

The men face seven charges: conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy, and two counts of money laundering. A recently unsealed indictment alleges the scheme drew about $129 million from corporate executives between 2024 and 2026. Among the targets were a New York investment bank, a Rhode Island bank, hospital systems in California and Missouri, a U.K. financial technology company, a Massachusetts mutual fund company, and a Florida pet food company. The money went into attacker-controlled bank accounts in several countries, was converted into cryptocurrency to hide its trail, and was then divided among the conspirators. The maximum potential sentence is 20 years for most of the charges.

According to the indictment, the suspects sent phishing emails through electronic signature services such as DocuSign to accounting employees who could authorize large wire transfers. Those employees were asked to sign a nondisclosure agreement for a confidential deal, often a corporate acquisition, and to join a "compliance call" with a law firm the scammers had impersonated. On those calls, AI mimicked the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO to persuade the employee the deal was real, and an impersonated attorney then requested the wire. The indictment says Soall mainly impersonated real attorneys in the European offices of the target firms, using a written script to sound authentic. It describes Hazan and Sheetrit as responsible for laundering the funds, and says Hazan boasted of laundering more than $400 million in the past three years.

Hazan had previously been convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in a New York district court in 2008. Federal Bureau of Investigation Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. said in a press release that the alleged scheme shows how advanced technology can be misused for large-scale fraud. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald urged individuals and businesses to consider how to protect themselves from the growing threat of AI-enabled crime. The case highlights how deepfake impersonation is being used against corporate finance staff, not only against the executives being copied. The articles do not state whether extradition has been granted or when any trial might take place.

stories.Headline: Sh13bn initiative targets global healthcare gaps through AI
stories.Summary:
The AWS Health Impact Initiative, launched by Amazon Web Services, will provide $100 million (Sh13 billion) in AI and cloud computing resources over five years to healthcare nonprofits, government agencies, research institutions and technology companies. The programme aims to close gaps in healthcare access and medical research, and it reaches projects ranging from early prototypes to systems ready for large-scale use. It arrives as health systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, struggle with staff shortages, rising demand and unequal access to treatment. The World Health Organisation estimates a global health worker shortage that could reach 11 million by 2030, and Africa alone faces a projected gap of about 5.85 million.

The initiative focuses on three areas: expanding access to healthcare services, advancing research in women's and children's health, and improving access to nutritious food. Under healthcare access, support will go to community healthcare, outpatient services, hospitals, diagnostic testing and medical research, with particular attention to rural communities. The women's and children's health category targets research gaps, with AWS citing estimates that only five per cent of healthcare research funding goes to women's health. The food category will back technology for food distribution, forecasting food insecurity and expanding access to nutritious food. Eligible organisations can apply through their AWS account teams or a public portal, and awards of up to $10,000 (Sh1.3 million) are available for initial support.

AWS said Dr Rowland Illing, its chief medical officer and director of healthcare and life sciences, argued that AI tools often fail to reach the communities that need them most unless organisations know how to deploy them. The company says the initiative builds on support for more than 600 healthcare organisations in over 80 countries since 2021. Credits generally remain valid for 12 months, extendable to 24, and applications are reviewed weekly. Critics and observers note that AI cannot on its own solve shortages of staff, medicines or public funding, and that concerns persist over patient data privacy, clinical reliability, regulation and the cost of maintaining systems after initial funding ends.

Kenyan organisations are already using digital and cloud-based tools for healthcare, including AAR Healthcare's management system for rural hospitals and Cogni-X Kenya's MOYO wellbeing platform. Jacaranda Health uses two-way text messaging to help mothers get care across sub-Saharan Africa, while Savannah Informatics runs an electronic medical records platform. TibERbu Healthnet says its systems, built on Amazon Bedrock, reach more than 200 facilities that serve 30.4 million Kenyans. The WHO reports that 2 billion people face financial hardship from out-of-pocket health spending and 4.5 billion lack full coverage of essential services.

stories.Headline: NAVER's $9 Billion AI Factory Is Built on a Fee Contract Banks Can Lend Against
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA paid $1 billion for a 4.13% stake in NAVER on November 6, completing the final step of a deal that began with a condition. The chipmaker would invest only after NAVER secured at least $9 billion in separate committed financing for computing infrastructure. Brookfield signed that infrastructure agreement with NAVER on October 27. The headline frames this as an equity story, but the articles describe a credit structure underneath it.

Under that structure, a Brookfield-funded company will buy the GPUs and data center assets and lease computing to NAVER Cloud. NAVER Cloud will run the facilities and pay usage fees, which NAVER says are tied to its business revenue. Korean banks plan to lend against those fees, with KB Kookmin Bank announcing on November 1 a mandate to arrange about KRW 10.7 trillion of loans for a KRW 12.6 trillion project. Hana Bank, Shinhan Bank, Woori Bank and NH Investment & Securities are reported as participants, though final commitments have not been disclosed. NAVER also guarantees NAVER Cloud's fee obligations for up to eight years, with a nominal amount of KRW 18.74 trillion, but the guarantee does not cover the syndicated loan itself.

The articles also set out the capacity plan and what remains unsettled. At the GAK Sejong data center, capacity is staged at 55 MW in the first half of 2027, 100 MW by the end of 2027 and 200 MW in 2028, within a wider project NAVER describes as a 1-gigawatt-scale global AI factory. NAVER issued a little over 6.5 million new shares on November 6, raising about KRW 1.3 trillion. The articles say the fee formula, including any minimum payment and how fees move when sales are slow, is not disclosed. NAVER is expected to consolidate the Brookfield-owned company as a subsidiary under K-IFRS, so its borrowings and assets would appear in NAVER's own accounts.

NAVER has not named customers for the capacity, though it targets enterprise and government clients in Asia, Europe and the Middle East. In October, NAVER Cloud and Vietnam's FPT announced cooperation on AI factories and GPU-as-a-service across Asia-Pacific. The articles say no purchase commitment for this capacity has been disclosed. Separately, NVIDIA and NAVER are expanding their AI model work, with NAVER Cloud taking part in NVIDIA's Nemotron Alliance and using related technology for its HyperCLOVA X model, according to a November 9 report.

stories.Headline: Judge urges expert witnesses to declare AI use right away
stories.Summary:
Joanna Smith, interim deputy president of the UK High Court's business and property division, has told expert witnesses to disclose their use of artificial intelligence now rather than wait for a formal rule. She made the point at the Bond Solon Expert Witness Conference at Church House in Westminster, as reported by the Law Society Gazette on 7 November 2026. Her warning was that experts whose evidence is shaped by AI they have not declared could face searching questions under cross-examination. She told the audience that there is currently no rule requiring such disclosure, but that experts who stay silent may find themselves open to criticism.

The instruction follows a report from the Civil Justice Council published in late October 2026, on AI and the preparation of court documents. Smith co-chaired the working group behind it. The council recommended that experts make a declaration where AI tools have generated or influenced the substantive content of a report, and that this requirement be added to the 2014 guidance on instructing experts in civil claims. Smith said the declaration should give enough information to allow effective scrutiny, which could include the method used, confirmation that AI was appropriate for that purpose, and, in exceptional cases, the tool itself. She also advised experts to check at the point of instruction whether AI use is permitted, citing intellectual property, data protection and regulatory compliance.

Smith placed the responsibility on experts themselves, reminding them that their credibility depends on their fundamental duties to the court. She said AI has not changed those duties, and that the obligations of independence, objectivity, transparency and professional competence remain exactly as they were. In her keynote she identified the main danger as the erosion of independent judgment, where experts hand their opinions over to an AI agent and lose their integrity. She listed practical risks including inadequate oversight, poor training, and a weak understanding of what AI can do. She also advised experts to disclose intended AI use to their instructing solicitors even when the instructions say nothing about it.

The context includes a recent case, Cornwall Council v M & Ors [2026] EWFC 306, in which an independent social worker used Microsoft Copilot to prepare a parenting assessment, assessments of potential kinship carers and an addendum report. The judge found that AI use had influenced a significant part of the report and therefore gave the evidence limited weight. The articles do not say whether a formal rule will follow or when. Smith concluded that experts who understand both the capabilities and limits of AI, and use it transparently where necessary, will be best placed to meet their overriding duty to the court.

stories.Headline: Missoula AI company files lawsuit challenging city's data center restrictions
stories.Summary:
A Missoula artificial intelligence company, CubCloud AI, has sued the City of Missoula over zoning rules that restrict data centers. The lawsuit was filed in Missoula County District Court, according to the reporting, and the company's complaint says the city's ordinance is unconstitutionally vague. The Missoulian and Montana Free Press both reported the filing on November 9, 2026. The articles describe the lawsuit as the company's challenge to the city's new local zoning rules. The company says it has 16 employees and has put money into research and development that it says would be wasted under the restrictions.

Its leaders told reporters they want the city to allow the project to proceed while the case is decided. The company is also seeking to build a new 4,200-square-foot research facility in the area, a plan the Missoulian says is tied to the changes the city has proposed. The city has said it intends to tweak its data center regulations, but the articles say the city will not comment on pending litigation. The city's rules were adopted after a city council discussion, and the company argues that the restrictions amount to a de facto ban on data centers in parts of town. Its representatives say the city was working toward a new proposal that would give them a path to build.

Officials with the city defended the ordinance as a legitimate exercise of local land-use authority. The Goldwater Institute, a Phoenix-based free-market think tank, is representing the company, the articles report, and says the restrictions go beyond what the law allows. The case comes as Missoula weighs how to handle data centers and other high-energy uses, a question many Montana communities are also debating. The articles do not say when a hearing is scheduled or when the court might rule. The city has indicated it will revise its regulations, and the outcome of the lawsuit could determine whether CubCloud AI can move ahead with its planned facility.

The Global Medical AI Summit 2026 (GMAI 2026) was held on October 30 at the Grand Hall of True Digital Park in Bangkok, drawing more than 400 senior executives from 263 organisations. Attendees included medical professionals, investors, technology entrepreneurs and experts from countries such as the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines. The event also featured 25 exhibition booths showing innovations from startups and technology companies. The Artificial Intelligence Entrepreneur Association of Thailand organised the summit with the Technology and Innovation in Life Sciences National Agency (Public Organization). Its theme centred on making Thailand a gateway for medical AI innovation.

Prof Dr Yodchanan Wongsawat, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, gave the opening keynote. He described a plan for Thailand to move beyond its role as a healthcare service hub and become a regional centre for medical AI research and innovation. He pointed to the country's strengths in tropical medicine, cancer, stroke and health data as a base for AI-enabled healthcare. He also called for technology transfer, shared research infrastructure, and incubation and accelerator programmes to strengthen the ecosystem. The summit also formally announced the Medical AI Network (MAIN), which is intended to link government agencies, universities, hospitals and private companies.

Organisations named in connection with the network included the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, TILSNA, AIEAT, the Artificial Intelligence Association of Thailand, Thammasat University, Khon Kaen University and the Digital Council of Thailand. The network aims to support collaboration from research and technology development through clinical testing to commercial use in Thailand and overseas. International speakers included Dr Supachai Parchariyanon of SeaX Ventures and RISE, who discussed Thailand as a base for testing medical AI for global markets. Dr Ashraf Zarkan of BioTryp Therapeutics, based in the United Kingdom, spoke about AI in drug discovery. Five panel discussions and a Medical AI Showcase of seven companies, along with a pitching competition, rounded out the programme.

stories.Headline: Samsung, Hyundai Motor Deepen Physical AI Alliance
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and Hyundai Motor Group, two long-standing rivals that have cooperated across three generations of their founding families, have announced a deeper strategic alliance aimed at future industries. The partnership, which began in semiconductors, batteries and automotive electronics, now extends to robots and artificial intelligence. On November 9, Samsung hosted an event called "HMG Appreciation Day" at its Seocheon Training Institute, inviting key Hyundai executives in what was the first large-scale invitation of its kind from Samsung to a major domestic conglomerate. The gathering was held under the theme "One Harmony Toward the Future" and drew 177 people, including Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun and Hyundai Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon.

The cooperation is already producing business results. Samsung Electronics agreed to supply its Exynos Auto V920 in-vehicle infotainment chip to Hyundai Motor Company, and Samsung SDI signed its first long-term electric vehicle battery supply contract with Hyundai in 2023. Its high-nickel prismatic batteries are slated for Kia's compact electric SUV, Hyundai's Ioniq 3, and the Genesis GV90 flagship. The two sides have also begun jointly developing batteries for robots, widening their work into the robotics sector. Analysts quoted in the report suggest that combining Samsung's semiconductor, sensor and battery technology with Hyundai's robotics and autonomous driving know-how could strengthen their future mobility competitiveness.

Jun Young-hyun said in his welcoming speech that the two groups are reliable partners that have written Korean industrial history together, and he hoped their combined strengths would open up new possibilities. Chang Jae-hoon said that cooperation now reaches beyond vehicle components into robots and energy, and that the strengths built over three generations would create greater synergy. The article also recounts the history between the groups, including a 1985 birthday visit by Samsung founder Lee Byung-chull to Hyundai founder Chung Ju-yung, and a 2020 meeting between Lee Jae-yong and Euisun Chung to discuss next-generation electric vehicle batteries. Observers quoted in the report describe the groups as moving from eternal rivals to pragmatic strategic partners.

A separate report from the same period describes Nvidia's AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX, where the company outlined its physical AI cooperation with South Korean firms, including Hyundai Motor Group, Doosan, SK Hynix and LG Electronics. Nvidia is working with Hyundai on robot simulation for automotive production lines using its Omniverse and Isaac platforms, and with Doosan on robotic precision polishing of car body surfaces. Dipu Talla, Nvidia's vice president of robotics and edge AI, said South Korea would play a very important role in physical AI over the next decade. Nvidia positions itself as a platform company supplying core technology rather than building robots itself, with South Korea serving as a proving ground.

stories.Summary:
GeniosAI, a financial intelligence startup that builds AI software for financial analysis and modeling, has raised $19.1 million across seed and Series A funding, according to CEO PD Singh, who spoke to Axios Pro exclusively. The announcement came on November 9, 2026, and it positions the company as a provider of AI that shows the reasoning behind its outputs. The funding comes from FactSet, Zoom and General Catalyst, with FactSet leading the Series A and acting as a strategic partner. The company says finance teams need to check the numbers and assumptions behind AI analysis before acting on it.

The company is building products for corporate finance teams, investment professionals and the office of the CFO. Its core pitch is that financial institutions need to keep the assumptions, calculations and review decisions behind each analysis, so staff can verify results, challenge conclusions and build on earlier work. Under its partnership with FactSet, geniosAI will bring FactSet's financial data into its platform. Zoom will support the settings where financial decisions get made, such as internal finance reviews and earnings calls.

The company said finance and investment teams at Fortune 500 banks and technology companies already use the technology to prepare for earnings and compare results with analyst expectations. FactSet's chief executive, Sanoke Viswanathan, said that the value of data depends on how well it can be acted upon, and that pairing FactSet's data with geniosAI's traceable analysis could help financial teams decide with more confidence and speed. The timing reflects a wider shift in enterprise finance, where companies are adding technology and must work out how to connect systems, keep controls in place and decide which capabilities to own. For CFOs, the expense of a modern finance stack often lies less in software licenses than in the effort needed to keep applications, data and processes linked.

AI adoption is also rising in financial services back offices, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence study. That study found that at least half of surveyed financial services firms used AI in 27 of 75 business tasks examined, with revenue recognition leading at 65 percent and credit risk assessment and sales forecasting at 60 percent each. Fragmented or poor-quality data, however, remained the largest obstacle to wider deployment for 30 percent of financial services leaders. Taken together, the reporting suggests that geniosAI is betting banks and investment firms will pay for AI that can explain its results, not just produce them.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, long one of the most influential figures in the artificial intelligence boom, now faces a serious threat to his position. Reports published on November 9, 2026, say Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board said it would investigate the matter, and Huang said he fully supports the review and will cooperate with it. The incident has also drawn the attention of a US congressional investigation, according to Asian business reporting on the matter.

The stakes for the industry are large. Nvidia controls about 90 percent of the market for chips used to train frontier AI models, and it has invested billions in companies that buy those chips, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Corporate filings show Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of the company as of March, and he is an at-will employee who can be dismissed at any time without severance. Analysts note that Nvidia has no other executive of comparable prominence and no apparent successor. Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday while broader market indices rose.

Experts say the board's inquiry will likely focus on whether Huang broke company policy, though the FBI could examine whether any laws were broken. Congress may also look into whether the affair influenced US policy on chip sales to China, and some analysts say it raises questions about whether sensitive information about AI companies or US strategy reached China. Huang has been outspoken against tougher export controls on China, which could leave his credibility on that issue in doubt. The Trump administration loosened some restrictions in its second term, giving China access to older Nvidia chips.

Researchers at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology expect the scandal to speed efforts to tighten chip exports, with more scrutiny from the Commerce Department over shipments routed through third countries such as Singapore and the Middle East. In South Korea, semiconductor and manufacturing firms that have built plans around Nvidia's AI technology are watching closely, and analysts say the impact on memory chipmakers may be limited given ongoing shortages. Some observers also warn that possible changes in Congress after the US midterm elections could bring stricter rules on AI data centers, which could affect investment across the supply chain. Nvidia's board has not yet said how long its investigation will take.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Still Plans to Go Public as Soon as Next Week: Report
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, still plans to go public later this month, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Gizmodo, even as investor anxiety about AI valuations has grown. Shares could begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT as soon as October 19 or 20, the Journal reported. The expected valuation has fallen sharply, from speculation of about $2 trillion earlier in the year to a range of $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion, according to CNBC. The drop followed a rough October for AI-adjacent stocks, when the Nasdaq had one of its worst months in a while.

The company's regulatory filings show it brought in $33 billion in revenue from January through September 2026. Those filings also warn that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Separately, Anthropic has announced plans to commit 5 per cent of its shares to an Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, with additional contributions tied to the company's growth in value. The company says the fund would support people affected by AI rather than go toward executive pay. Gizmodo noted that the company's own data shows hiring of junior technical workers fell sharply last year as it expanded its use of Claude AI agents.

Economists and policy experts quoted by The Globe and Mail are skeptical that the fund would do much for affected workers. Rafael Gomez, director of the Centre for Industrial Relations and Human Resources at the University of Toronto, called the proposal very conceptual and said it could pre-empt government regulation by defining rules on the company's own terms. Barry Eidlin, a McGill University sociologist, described such funds as a public-relations effort to keep control over how regulation is shaped. Rosalie Wyonch of the C.D. Howe Institute argued the funds could instead signal commitment to investors and reduce the chance of forceful political action. Anthropic did not respond to the Globe's questions about these criticisms.

The debate sits against a backdrop of limited regulation, since neither Canada nor the United States has a comprehensive AI law like the European Union's AI Act. Canada's federal AI minister, Evan Solomon, has warned against governments ceding control of AI regulation to frontier platforms. OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, filed confidentially to go public in June but will not list before the end of the year, Gizmodo reported. In May, OpenAI's foundation announced a $250 million commitment to help workers, of which $50 million has been distributed so far. Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed a one-time 50 per cent tax on the equity of large AI companies, and Gomez pointed to past labour and industry coalitions as a model for consultation.

stories.Headline: Health researchers warn proposed federal privacy law could expose sensitive medical data
stories.Summary:
Health researchers have warned that Canada's proposed federal privacy legislation contains gaps that could leave sensitive medical information open to commercial exploitation as artificial intelligence spreads through the health-care system. Their concerns centre on Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, which the Carney government introduced in June as part of an effort to modernize private-sector privacy rules. The critics published their commentary in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, arguing that some provisions would let companies collect, use or disclose personal information without direct consent in certain circumstances. One provision in particular allows organizations to rely on a legitimate business interest when they judge that the expected benefits outweigh reasonably foreseeable harm to individuals.

Dr. Sheryl Spithoff, a clinician scientist at Women's College Hospital in Toronto and a co-author of the commentary, says this gives companies too much discretion over how personal data is used. She argues that firms should have to inform regulators from the start and that the clause should apply only in rare cases, with higher standards for sensitive information such as health records. The researchers also point to the European Union's data protection regulation, which sets a higher bar of proof and says legitimate interest does not override the fundamental rights of data owners. Teresa Scassa, a research chair in information law at the University of Ottawa and another co-author, warns that advances in AI may make it impossible to fully anonymize data, since records can be linked with other information and used to profile people as high-risk for costly conditions. Under the bill, deliberately re-identifying personal information would be an offence, though Scassa noted that this could be hard to prove.

The bill requires that personal information be de-identified by modifying details such as names and health card numbers, but it does not protect anonymized data, which is stripped of personal information so that no reasonably foreseeable risk of identification remains. The researchers say anonymized data often carries societal biases that can be built into AI systems and lead to discrimination, and they cite a widely used American hospital algorithm that allocated fewer resources to Black patients. Ottawa's position is that the legislation would strengthen privacy protection, improve corporate accountability and introduce safeguards on automated decision-making. AI Minister Evan Solomon's office repeated the bill's definition of legitimate interest and said organizations relying on it would have to assess and mitigate privacy risks, without detailing those safeguards. Some physicians, including Dr. Amol Verma of St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto, argue that de-identified health data is valuable for research and hospital efficiency when handled safely, and that privacy protection and innovation can go hand in hand.

Bill C-36 remains before Parliament, and the debate reflects a broader tension between technological innovation, commercial use of data and Canadians' privacy rights. Other jurisdictions are facing similar problems, including a class-action lawsuit filed earlier this year against Chicago-based Tempus AI, which the plaintiffs allege obtained patients' genetic and clinical data and sold it without consent. Last year, a study that Spithoff worked on found that millions of Canadians' de-identified health records, including medical histories and prescriptions, were being sold to pharmaceutical companies. The study's authors warned that such sharing could improve care but could also let drug companies put their economic interests ahead of patients' and push up prices. Critics say stronger restrictions and independent oversight are needed to prevent commercial misuse of sensitive information, and the bill's path through Parliament will determine whether those changes are made.

stories.Headline: Lawyers need AI education, not AI legislation
stories.Summary:
Nicole Black, a Rochester, New York attorney and legal technology writer, has argued in a column that lawyers need more AI education rather than new AI legislation. Her piece responds to California's SB 574, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed on September 30 and which is likely to take effect January 1, 2027. She points out that bar associations have issued at least twenty ethics opinions and guides on AI since ChatGPT's public release in November 2022. Her view is that these existing guidelines already cover the field. She writes that AI is simply a new technology, no different for practice purposes than the tools that came before it.

According to Black, the California law does little more than restate duties lawyers already owe. It bars lawyers from delegating the practice of law to AI, and it prohibits entering confidential or nonpublic information into systems not restricted to authorized persons. It also requires lawyers to verify the accuracy of AI outputs, correct hallucinated material, and personally verify every citation in court filings. Another provision requires disclosure of AI use to the court for submitted documents and consideration of disclosure for public-facing content. Black argues that this disclosure rule is both unnecessary and duplicative, since many recent ethics opinions already address it.

Black says the law will complicate and discourage technology adoption rather than improve compliance. She draws on past experience with email, the internet, social media, and cloud computing, noting that early requirements such as client consent often faded once those tools became routine. She expects AI to follow the same path, only faster, because it is already built into the workflows of nearly every legal and general-purpose technology in use at law firms. In her telling, lawyers are already using AI, sometimes without realizing it, so new rules that duplicate existing duties hurt their ability to compete. She concludes that the better response is more education that helps lawyers use the technology to serve clients, and she says she hopes other states will not follow California's example.

stories.Headline: UC Law SF scholars drive solutions to AI legal challenges - UC Law San Francisco | (Formerly UC Hastings)
stories.Summary:
UC Law San Francisco scholars are developing legal and policy proposals for artificial intelligence, and some of their ideas have already drawn interest from lawmakers. Professors Prithika Balakrishnan, Dave Owen, Seema N. Patel and Robin Feldman are at the center of this work, which examines how AI affects workers, artists, consumers, political debate and criminal evidence. Their recommendations include new laws to encourage AI innovation, stronger consumer rights, clear liability standards and a greater role for employees in workplace technology decisions. Chancellor and Dean David Faigman said the school's scholars are proposing concrete measures to protect people's rights and promote accountability while still encouraging innovation. The articles describe the research as an effort to give policymakers a workable path forward.

Professor Robin Feldman, who directs the AI Law & Innovation Institute at the Center for Innovation, has focused on who should answer for harm caused by AI agents. She asks whether the developer, the deployer or another party is responsible when such a system causes damage. Feldman suggests Congress could create clearer rules and "safe harbors" that shield companies from liability when they follow them, which she says would promote accountability while reducing litigation risk. The Institute receives more than 50 requests a year from government officials, she said, increasingly about AI regulation. Her broader work includes a 2025 book, "AI Versus IP: Rewriting Creativity," and a forthcoming book, "The Human Zone," which proposes a New Deal-style patronage and licensing system to support new human-generated creative work.

Professor Ben Depoorter, who has studied copyright for more than 15 years, argues in a forthcoming paper that it is too early to decide whether training AI models on copyrighted works counts as fair use. He says more evidence is needed on whether AI can produce innovative work or only lower-quality imitations, and on its effect on the creative economy. He recommends that judges and lawmakers keep copyright rules flexible as that evidence develops. Professor Dave Owen, working with Alexandra Klass of the University of Michigan, proposes requiring data centers to accept power interruptions during peak demand, which could help keep household and business electricity costs from rising. Owen said the study has drawn inquiries from state lawmakers and attorneys general's offices.

Professor Prithika Balakrishnan, a former public defender, questions how AI-enabled license plate and analytical tools decide that a pattern of travel is suspicious. She cites a 2022 case in which New York police stopped David Zayas after software flagged his vehicle for possible drug trafficking based on nine trips between Massachusetts and New York over about two years. To guard against errors, she proposes requiring a warrant to search a vehicle's license plate location history and expert testimony to help judges assess algorithm-driven conclusions. Professor Seema N. Patel, meanwhile, examines how low-wage workers' personal data is collected, sold and used to train AI without their consent or compensation. She notes that 94% of low-wage workers lack union representation and recommends stronger data rights and new laws and enforcement strategies at the federal, state and local levels.

stories.Headline: The impact of AI on youth unemployment
stories.Summary:
The London Assembly's Economy, Culture and Skills Committee is holding a public meeting on the effect of artificial intelligence on youth unemployment in the capital. The session, chaired by Bassam Mahfouz AM, is set for Tuesday 10 November at 10am in the Chamber at City Hall. The background is a Greater London Authority report from April 2026, which estimates that around 46 per cent of London's workforce is in roles that could be at risk of automation, compared with 38 per cent across the wider UK. Media and members of the public are invited to attend, and the meeting can be watched live or later by webcast or on YouTube.

The Milburn Review's interim report found that AI and automation are likely to add further pressure to the entry-level labour market. A key concern is that the vacancies traditionally filled by young first-time job seekers are often the same roles most exposed to automation. The Committee will continue its investigation into youth unemployment in London with a focus on how AI is affecting job availability. It will also hear from employers about the barriers and opportunities facing young people looking for work in the capital. Panel speakers include representatives from the West London Alliance, NHS North East London, UKHospitality, the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, and the Institute for the Future of Work, along with GLA officials.

The material supplied does not set out any policy change, legal requirement or formal finding from the Committee, so it is not clear what the session will produce beyond the hearing itself. The Assembly describes its role as investigating issues that matter to Londoners and acting as a check and balance on the Mayor. The page is an announcement from the London Assembly and the GLA, and it attributes the workforce estimate to a GLA Economics report and the entry-level concern to the Milburn Review's interim report. stories.Headline: AI freezer cyberattacks: Hackers are using cheap technology to melt supermarket stock in Europe
stories.Summary:
Freezers in dozens of supermarket stores across at least 11 European countries were remotely switched to very high temperatures on November 2, with some reaching 50 degrees. Chains including Carrefour and Ikea in Belgium, ICA and Coop in Sweden, Kesko in Finland and SuperValu in Ireland were among the victims. It was the second such wave in a matter of weeks, following an earlier attack on hundreds of French supermarkets around October 12. The attacks targeted the small controllers that set refrigeration temperatures, which can be reached over the internet.

The articles do not say that any formal rules were changed, but they point to what the attacks expose. The same controllers also run cold storage in hospitals, medicine warehouses and data centres, and in France hackers reached the cold storage of at least three blood banks, though the blood was moved and no patients were harmed. Security agencies have warned since 2014 that these controllers should never be placed directly online. Australia's critical infrastructure laws cover the supply networks of major grocers such as Woolworths, Coles and Aldi, but do not explicitly cover the freezer aisle, and it is unclear whether a single store's freezers would count. The Australian Signals Directorate issued an alert to businesses running refrigeration and cooling systems two days after the French attack.

Security researchers and officials placed much of the blame on weak basic protections. France's cyber agency chief told the French Senate the controllers sat on the open internet with no firewall and weak admin passwords, while Danfoss said the Dutch systems hit had no secure network and still used factory passwords. Danfoss also said most affected equipment was old and no longer received security updates. Belgium's refrigeration industry group Sabcobel said the damage would have been worse had its members not begun patching vulnerabilities after October 12. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot named Iran as the country behind the hacks and called for European sanctions, while a SentinelOne researcher said Russian-aligned groups were also credible suspects, and no group has claimed the attacks or demanded money.

The articles note that breaking in has become cheaper, partly because of AI. In August, Claroty described security holes in controllers from Danfoss and Copeland, and a day after the French attack its researchers showed an AI tool could build a working attack on a test device in about 28 minutes at a cost of US$6. Belgian butcher Luc De Laet told Reuters he lost about €15,000 of meat in one night. No attacks have been reported in Australia, and Woolworths and Aldi are understood to have no refrigeration controllers connected to outside networks, while Coles did not respond. CyberCX's Leah Pinto said attackers are increasingly targeting internet-connected building equipment, and researcher Samuli Bergström argued that any device not needing internet access should not be online at all.

stories.Headline: From Fake CEO Calls To Garland Police Briefings: Texas And Federal Moves Against AI Impersonation
stories.Summary:
Federal prosecutors in New York unsealed charges on November 5 against three people, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, accusing them of running an international impersonation fraud. According to the Justice Department, the conspirators targeted companies around the world between 2024 and 2026, using artificial intelligence to imitate corporate executives and lawyers. The indictment describes purportedly confidential business deals in which the conspirators allegedly posed as chief executives, used synthetic voices or images during calls, and sent employees to supposed attorneys who directed large wire transfers into accounts they controlled. Prosecutors allege the scheme stole more than $129 million from businesses, including hospital systems and financial firms.

Authorities arrested the defendants in Spain and the United Kingdom between June and September, and extradition requests were still pending when the charges were announced. The defendants face allegations rather than convictions and are presumed innocent. On the federal side, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14390 on March 6, directing agencies to develop measures against international scam centers and cyber-enabled financial fraud, including ways to return money to victims from recovered criminal proceeds. The Justice Department also announced on November 5 a Super Intelligence Task Force to address malicious uses of emerging technology by foreign actors and criminal groups. The article notes that the task force's mandate extends beyond impersonation scams and that the announcement does not show it has already stopped any fraud.

Texas has taken its own steps. Senate Bill 2373 took effect September 1, 2025, and makes certain financial abuse using artificially generated media or phishing a crime, while also giving some victims a civil route to damages. House Bill 149, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, took effect January 1, 2026, setting rules for specified AI uses, including some government and health care disclosures, and giving the attorney general enforcement power. The article stresses that this law does not ban every synthetic voice or image. Locally, Garland police scheduled a November 5 presentation at the West Garland Library on deceptive calls, messages, and AI voice cloning.

The FBI, which warned in July that criminals had used AI-generated videos resembling its personnel to lure earlier fraud victims toward fake complaint websites, advises people to verify unexpected requests through a previously trusted phone number or channel. It also recommends multi-factor authentication and caution with unsolicited links. For employers, a separate confirmation before releasing funds can stop a scam even when the caller sounds convincing. The article presents these measures as a patchwork of prosecutions, new laws, and public education still responding to a threat that is growing.

stories.Headline: Has Wales already lost the AI revolution?
stories.Summary:
Wales has fallen behind in the artificial intelligence sector, according to research published by the UK Government last week and discussed by business commentator Dylan Jones-Evans. The Artificial Intelligence Sector Study 2025 counts 10,488 AI businesses across the UK, generating £33.6 billion in revenues and employing more than 130,000 people. Wales hosts just 1.6% of those businesses, well below Scotland at 3.7%, the North West of England at 5.9% and the West Midlands at 4%. Only Northern Ireland and the North East of England have smaller shares. The gap is striking because generative AI, which took off after ChatGPT launched in November 2022, gave regions a chance to build new economic strengths quickly.

The author argues that Wales had real assets to draw on, including talented researchers, established universities and specialist expertise in semiconductors, cybersecurity and financial technology. He notes that AI firms do not need expensive factories and that small teams can build competitive products with modest funding. He suggests that Wales could have launched a national programme in early 2023 to find, develop and invest in hundreds of new AI businesses. Such a programme could have focused on healthcare, manufacturing, education and financial services. Instead, the Welsh Government published its AI Plan in November 2025, nearly three years after ChatGPT appeared.

The Welsh Government has since announced £2.1 million to support AI adoption, including £600,000 for Business Wales, £1 million for skills and £500,000 for tourism and events. The author welcomes these measures but says they mainly help existing companies use AI rather than create firms that develop and sell the technology. He argues that creating Welsh AI businesses with products for international markets could generate jobs, intellectual property, exports and wealth on a much larger scale. He says the article's conclusion is that there is still an opportunity to change course, but that this requires the Welsh Government, Business Wales and the Development Bank to act.

The Motley Fool analysis published November 9, 2026 argues that Broadcom, rather than AMD or Intel, is the AI chip company that Nvidia should fear most. The piece describes Nvidia as the dominant supplier of graphics processing units used in generative AI, while noting that Broadcom designs application-specific integrated circuits, or custom chips, for large AI customers including Alphabet, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. The article says Broadcom's stock had fallen about 39% from its all-time high by early November.

Broadcom's fiscal third quarter, which ended August 2, showed AI semiconductor revenue of $16.7 billion, more than triple the prior year, with custom chips making up roughly 73% of that total. Management guided for $21.7 billion in AI semiconductor revenue in the fourth quarter. Looking further out, Broadcom expects AI semiconductor revenue of roughly $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and potentially $230 billion in fiscal 2028. The article links these figures to a shift toward inference, the stage where trained models generate responses, which it says favors specialized processors over general-purpose GPUs. It also notes Broadcom's forward price-to-earnings multiple of about 15 as of November 6, the lowest of the AI era.

The author, Adam Spatacco, presents these developments as a challenge for Nvidia and a reason for long-term investors to consider Broadcom. He argues that Broadcom can benefit from AI infrastructure growth even if customers keep buying Nvidia GPUs, since it also supplies networking and connectivity technology. A separate Motley Fool piece in the Globe and Mail, published November 8, 2026, takes a contrasting view, saying Nvidia is the better buy over AMD because its shares trade near 13 times next year's expected earnings compared with about 30 times for AMD. That article notes Nvidia reports its fiscal third-quarter results on November 17, and that its data center revenue rose 117% to $89 billion in its prior quarter.

stories.Headline: A.I.Matics' AIM-T1 Named CES Innovation Awards® 2027 Honoree in Two Categories
stories.Summary:
A.I.Matics, a South Korean vision AI company, announced that its AIM-T1 AI vision inspection platform has been named a CES Innovation Awards 2027 Honoree in two categories, Artificial Intelligence and Construction & Industrial Tech. The award was announced on November 9 and 10, 2026, and the platform is aimed at electronics manufacturers that need to identify defects and adapt inspections to new products. The company says the system is built for quality, process and manufacturing engineers who work with camera modules, semiconductor packages and printed circuit board assemblies. Its recognition comes from the Consumer Technology Association, which organizes the program.

The announcement presents AIM-T1 as a response to a recurring problem in electronics production, where inspection has to stay consistent even as product designs and manufacturing requirements change. Introducing a new product can require manufacturers to gather defect images, revise inspection criteria and adjust imaging equipment, tasks that place extra demands on experienced inspectors and AI engineers. According to the company, AIM-T1 pairs modular imaging hardware with software-defined inspection so teams can adapt workflows on a common platform. The system uses reference samples of acceptable products to set inspection criteria and flag deviations that may signal defects. Its optical system uses liquid lens technology and electronic focus stacking to capture images at several focal planes without mechanical Z-axis movement, and camera resolution, lens magnification, lighting and inspection settings can be adjusted for different applications.

A.I.Matics is the party responsible for these claims, and the company describes the platform's aim as making inspection knowledge easier to reuse so that each product changeover depends less on specialized expertise. It says this matters for manufacturers reshoring production or adding regional capacity, since transferring inspection know-how helps new facilities come online. The company also plans to showcase AIM-T1 at CES 2027, taking place January 6 to 9 in Las Vegas, and to meet with manufacturers, automation equipment integrators and potential distribution partners. The CES notice adds that its awards are based on materials submitted to judges, that CTA did not verify the accuracy of submissions or claims, and that CTA did not test the product. Booth and meeting details are to be announced once confirmed.

A.I.Matics is a subsidiary of Dreamtech and began as an in-house venture at Hyundai Motor Company in 2000, before being incorporated in 2003. The company built its expertise by supplying lane departure warning systems to automakers and now develops AI solutions for transportation, logistics and manufacturing. Its portfolio also includes AI-powered driver safety cameras, the aid fleet management platform, intelligent process and operations management tools, and AI chatbots for logistics call centers. The company says it will continue pursuing industry partnerships at the show, and further product information is available on its vision website.

stories.Summary:
Kyndryl and ServiceNow announced on November 9, 2026, that Kyndryl Autonomous Operations for ServiceNow is now available on the ServiceNow Store. The offering was co-developed by the two companies and runs on Kyndryl Bridge, the operational data platform. It combines the ServiceNow AI Platform with Bridge's data, AI agents and operational intelligence. The aim is to detect incidents automatically, analyze their causes, assess risk and guide remediation.

The product feeds operational context from assets, configurations, dependencies, events, changes and past incidents into Bridge, and specialized agents use that context to find issues from failure patterns. Each resolved incident sends its insights back into the platform, which is meant to improve later automation and recommendations. The Store listing names dashboards, root-cause analysis, playbook generation and change-risk scoring among its features. It is a paid, certified generative-AI application that requires several ServiceNow components and may consume Assists from the customer's account.

Giovanni Carraro, Kyndryl's global strategic alliances leader, said customers want practical ways to improve operations and get more value from AI, and that the collaboration aims to produce meaningful business outcomes. Michael Park, ServiceNow's senior vice president of global partnerships and channels, said the combination gives customers proven patterns for their own environments, which he said means less time on incidents and more time on innovation. Kyndryl says Bridge, which launched in 2022, is used by more than 1,400 enterprises and generates over 16 million AI insights monthly. Its runbooks and remediation practices number more than 10,000.

Bridge is also described as an agentic control plane that applies policy at the point of action, keeps an auditable record of agent activity and requires human approval when risk warrants it. Its services catalog holds more than 190 services. The companies recently extended their work on employee experience through Kyndryl AI Front Door, which is powered by ServiceNow EmployeeWorks. The articles present the offering's value as depending on whether the incident feedback loop consistently improves remediation over time.
