stories.Headline: Meta Forms Sales Group to Sell AI to Small Businesses
stories.Summary:
Meta has reportedly formed a sales organization to sell its artificial intelligence products to businesses, according to a report from The Information published Monday, November 9, 2026. The report cited a source familiar with the matter and job postings the outlet viewed. The new group will target both small and mid-sized businesses and corporate clients. The move is part of a plan to recoup Meta's large investments in AI.

The push follows Meta's September introduction of the Meta Enterprise Platform, a business unit focused on selling software products to corporate customers and developers. Those products include the Muse Code coding tool, business agent software and Muse Spark models. Former MongoDB CEO Chirantan "CJ" Desai has been appointed to head that unit, which Mark Zuckerberg called the company's "next major pillar." Meta is also forming partnerships with consulting firms and systems integrators, including Accenture, Deloitte and IBM, to speed corporate deployment and reduce its reliance on internal engineers. The report compares this approach to enterprise sales strategies used by OpenAI and Anthropic.

The commercial effort reflects more than a year of market testing. In 2024, Meta saw strong demand from small and mid-sized businesses using its automated customer agents to handle inquiries around the clock. Winning large enterprise deals, however, remains difficult. Meta's earlier Workplace communication software reached 7 million paid subscribers at its peak in 2021 but was discontinued in 2024 after struggling against Microsoft and Slack. An October pitch urging retailers such as Amazon and Booking.com to place Meta's business agent on their websites also met resistance, sources said.

Context from PYMNTS Intelligence research suggests strong interest among smaller firms in AI. The company reported that 60% of small and mid-sized businesses using AI said it lets them produce more without hiring more employees. In an October report, 16% of growing businesses said they skipped a full-time hire because of AI, compared with 10% of businesses with flat revenue. Meta is planning to spend up to $145 billion in capital expenditures this year alone to support its AI infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Meta Forms Sales Group to Sell AI to Small Businesses

stories.Headline: Sierra Leone : President Bio Joins Macron in Global Push for Stronger Artificial Intelligence Safety and Accountability
stories.Summary:
On 9 November 2026, Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio joined French President Emmanuel Macron and other world leaders in calling for stronger international safeguards on artificial intelligence. Speaking at a high-level virtual meeting convened by Macron that day, Bio laid out three priorities for cooperation on frontier AI security. The meeting drew representatives of several countries, international institutions and technology companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Mistral AI and Hugging Face. Bio's intervention reflects growing international concern about how quickly advanced AI systems are being developed and deployed.

Bio's first priority was credible and common safety evaluation standards, which would help governments, researchers and independent experts identify risks in powerful models. His second was clear accountability for the developers and operators of advanced systems, so that responsibility is defined when systems fail or cause harm. His third was an effective way to report serious incidents and share information about emerging threats across borders. Bio said Sierra Leone welcomes the proposed Paris Declaration and supports its focus on shared evaluation standards, accountability and incident reporting. The proposed Paris framework seeks to advance these goals through greater transparency and better coordination among governments, companies and independent experts.

The articles place Sierra Leone's position within a wider African effort to take part in shaping global technology rules. The country had already joined an earlier initiative in September 2026, advanced by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, calling for stronger safety protocols and independent testing. Kenyan President William Ruto and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa have also backed international efforts to strengthen safeguards. The articles argue that Africa has a stake in these rules because AI affects economic opportunity, digital sovereignty and public security, and many African countries lack the technical capacity to assess advanced systems on their own.

The articles also note that turning these commitments into action remains difficult, since governments must still decide how standards will be implemented, how evaluations will be conducted and how developers will be held to account. Differences in national regulation, competing commercial interests and the fast pace of AI development could complicate a coordinated framework. For African countries, the articles say meaningful progress will depend on access to expertise, stronger domestic institutions and sustained participation in international talks. Bio's remarks, as the articles present them, signal that Sierra Leone wants to move from being a consumer of AI technology to a participant in its governance.

Articles.Title: Sierra Leone : President Bio Joins Macron in Global Push for Stronger Artificial Intelligence Safety and Accountability

stories.Headline: Computational Framework Maps Regional Skin Aging Through Spatial Omics and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Diala Haykal, Jovian Wan, Kyu-Ho Yi, TingSong Lim, and Soo Ick Cho introduced a computational framework called the predictive dermatome in a theoretical paper published in Frontiers in Digital Health. The framework is designed to map skin aging in localized regions rather than treating the skin as one uniform organ. The authors argue that conventional aging clocks and chronological measures miss the fact that nearby facial areas can age at different rates. The paper was reported on November 9, 2026, by bioengineer.org. The predictive dermatome is explicitly non-neurological, unlike classical dermatomes that follow spinal nerve territories.

Instead, it defines microregions linked by shared or probabilistically connected molecular trajectories. The proposed architecture combines spatial transcriptomics, spatial or targeted proteomics, histology, and extracellular matrix measurements in a discovery phase, with these invasive assays serving as reference maps rather than routine diagnostic tools. Non-invasive imaging, including optical coherence tomography, reflectance confocal microscopy, high-frequency ultrasound, and digital photographs, would then feed surrogate models calibrated against those reference maps. The authors also call for exposomic data, such as ultraviolet dosimetry, air pollution, and lifestyle questionnaires, to be harmonized to specific body sites and time windows. The article says the framework relies on graph attention networks and transformer-based fusion, and it stresses quality control and dimensionality reduction to prevent overfitting.

The authors frame the work as a step toward precision dermatology, which they say requires looking beneath visible surface features to the molecular and structural mosaic of tissue decline. They note that cutaneous senescence involves mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, telomere attrition, and low-grade inflammation, while external stressors such as ultraviolet radiation and pollution act in anatomically variable patterns. The article describes the work as theoretical, so the framework has not been validated in clinical cohorts. The source text was cut off before its discussion of validation and next steps, so I cannot report what the authors plan to do next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Computational Framework Maps Regional Skin Aging Through Spatial Omics and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Show HN: STE80 Humanizer – de-AI text by writing 80% of the way to ASD-STE100
stories.Summary:
The article describes a GitHub project called STE80 Humanizer, posted to Hacker News as a "Show HN" under a headline that uses the phrase "de-AI text." The repository, published on 9 November 2026 at 06:00 UTC by the account Dodaios, is an agent skill that removes common signs of AI-written prose and rewrites text to be closer to ASD-STE100, the controlled English used in aircraft maintenance manuals. The project combines two methods: a list of 26 AI writing tells taken from Wikipedia's guide to signs of AI writing, and a set of 15 structure rules that the author calls STE80, meaning writing about 80 percent of the way to the full specification. The skill can be installed for Claude Code, Claude.ai, and agents supported by the skills.sh tool, and it can run in three modes. The skill works in two passes, and the author argues that the passes cover different problems.

The first pass removes phrases such as "Great question!" and empty claims of significance, while the second pass rebuilds sentences into short, active, one-idea statements. The repository gives a Kubernetes example in which the rewritten version uses short sentences and keeps the facts, and it says the goal is text that people can read easily rather than text that evades AI detectors. Users can ask for light edits, full strict STE, or a version that matches a sample of their own writing. The skill is designed to keep every fact, to keep hedges such as "may" where the source uses them, and to flag contradictions in the original text.

The method draws on a post by Andrej Karpathy dated 2 October 2026, in which he suggested asking an LLM to explain things in ASD-STE100, or in a softened form at 80 percent of the way, because he found the output more readable. He described this as part of a shift in which work moves toward oversight and understanding of model output, with clear writing as the first step. The ASD-STE100 specification dates from the 1980s aerospace industry and limits instructions to 20 words and descriptions to 25, with one instruction per sentence and a small approved vocabulary. The repository notes that a later fact check found errors in one of the dictionary details in Karpathy's graphic, and says the skill follows Issue 9 of the specification. The article does not say how many people have adopted the tool or what the author plans next, and it contains no independent evaluation beyond the author's own tests.

Articles.Title: Show HN: STE80 Humanizer – de-AI text by writing 80% of the way to ASD-STE100

stories.Headline: Y/N (YC S23) is hiring a growth lead to distribute superhuman A.I. storytelling
stories.Summary:
Y Combinator has posted a job listing for a Founding Growth Marketer at Y/n, a San Francisco startup from its S23 batch, with the listing appearing on November 9, 2026. The company describes itself as building interactive stories, where people play a character in a book and their texts shape the plot. Its stated mission is to build a superhuman A.I. storyteller and distribute it to billions of people. The posting says the company has already seen more than one billion messages sent on its platform.

The hire would be the company's first growth employee, and the listing calls for someone who can find marketing channels that work and then own them from start to finish. Responsibilities could include running ads and the creative pipeline across Meta, TikTok, or Google, or building creator partnerships with BookTokers, YouTubers, and a user-generated content program. The listing pays between $130,000 and $300,000 a year, offers equity of 0.30% to 2.00%, and says the company will sponsor visas. Candidates would take two team interviews and a paid day-long work trial, and the role is full-time and on-site in San Francisco.

The company is led by founders Gabriel Birnbaum and Eric Meier, and the listing says Y/n has raised $14 million from top investors and has a team of four. The founders say story quality determines the company's success, and they describe the culture as commercially minded, with a focus on measuring results and cutting what does not work. The posting also predicts that by 2030 playing stories will become the dominant form of entertainment. The articles do not describe any further hiring plans beyond this role or any timeline for the company's growth.

Articles.Title: Y/N (YC S23) is hiring a growth lead to distribute superhuman A.I. storytelling

stories.Headline: KAIST vs. MIT: Which University Is Harder to Get Into, More Prestigious, and Better for Artificial Intelligence?
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, so I cannot end it with "More to follow." The article is an opinion-style comparison piece, not a report of a recent event, so the required structure of what happened, what it changes, who is responsible, and what comes next does not map onto it cleanly. Below is a faithful account of what the article says, in three paragraphs of five sentences each. The article, published by Rebellion Research on November 9, 2026, compares the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology on admissions difficulty, prestige, and strength in artificial intelligence. It describes MIT as a long-established engineering and computer science powerhouse and KAIST as South Korea's leading science and technology institution.

The piece argues that both schools attract highly talented students but differ in admissions standards, reputation, resources, and career opportunities. It frames the central question as which university offers the better education for students interested in AI or advanced engineering. On admissions, the article says MIT admits roughly 4% to 5% of undergraduate applicants in recent cycles and concludes it is generally the harder school to enter. It cites a KAIST domestic early-admissions competition ratio of about 8.47 applicants per place for the 2026 academic year, while cautioning that this does not translate directly into a comparable acceptance rate. On prestige, the article holds that MIT has far greater recognition among American employers, investors, and the general public, while KAIST is well respected in specialized scientific circles.

For AI, it describes MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and KAIST's Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI, established in 2019, and says MIT offers the stronger startup and American industry ecosystem while KAIST suits those interested in robotics, semiconductors, and South Korea's technology sector. The article's final verdict is that MIT is the stronger overall choice for global prestige and opportunity, but that KAIST is a formidable technical university deserving more recognition in the United States. It notes that both schools offer financial aid and scholarships, so students should compare net costs rather than published tuition. The piece makes no predictions about future rankings or policy changes, and it does not name a specific author or cite outside sources for its claims.

Articles.Title: KAIST vs. MIT: Which University Is Harder to Get Into, More Prestigious, and Better for Artificial Intelligence?

stories.Headline: Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems
stories.Summary:
Doximity said on Thursday, November 5, 2026 in its fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings call that more than 190 health systems have now bought its AI suite, up from 165 last quarter. The customers include 10 of the nation's top 20 hospitals. NewYork-Presbyterian has built Doximity's AI tools into its electronic health record workflow for clinicians across NewYork-Presbyterian, Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Weill Cornell Medicine. UCSD Health is among the first hospitals to adopt the company's new patient context feature, which lets the AI read charts, labs and patient history. The company is also opening API access to its clinical intelligence layer.

The company's CEO, Jeff Tangney, said the patient context feature is now available to thousands of doctors and cuts the length of their prompts from an average of 24 words to 12. Tangney described Doximity's offering as a full suite covering telehealth, AI documentation, scheduling, clinical questions, patient context and clinical evidence. He argued that larger health systems are tightening AI governance over concerns about patient data, liability and security, which he believes favors approved platforms with enterprise privacy and security controls. He said the company has more than 300 enterprise clients, which together reach nearly half of all U.S. physicians.

Tangney also said accuracy is the top concern doctors have about AI, and he pointed to Doximity's recently launched DoseCheck medication safety verifier. Through a partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health, UpToDate's evidence-based content is now embedded in Doximity Ask, and Tangney said he expects the partnership to grow over time. Physician engagement is rising as well, with quarterly active workflow prescribers up 34% year over year and about 900,000 of the 1.8 million U.S. prescribers using its workflow products during the quarter. Chief financial officer Matt Sonefeldt said that engagement lays the groundwork for future monetization.

Doximity reported $174.5 million in revenue for the quarter ending September 30, up 4% year over year and above guidance, with adjusted EBITDA of $89 million. It raised its full-year revenue outlook to $678 million to $683 million. Its AI Search product for pharmaceutical companies, launched in late April, has been bought by 16 of the top 20 drugmakers, with three more in contracting. Shares fell after the report over margin compression, and the stock is down nearly 25% this year. The company plans to pursue pharma paid search spending, which Tangney estimated at $14 billion a year in the U.S.

Articles.Title: Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems

stories.Headline: Is AI A Financial Bubble? – OpEd
stories.Summary:
An opinion piece published on Eurasia Review on November 9, 2026, and republished from the Mises Institute, asks whether the artificial intelligence boom is a financial bubble. Its author, Frank Shostak, an Associated Scholar of the Mises Institute, argues from Austrian-school economics that it is. He contends that AI's apparent strength is not the whole story, and that the boom may reflect resources being shifted by loose monetary policy rather than genuine growth. He says the piece is an analysis rather than reporting, so its claims are his own reasoning and not established facts.

Shostak's central argument is that expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates through artificial increases in the money supply, which makes projects look profitable that would otherwise have a negative net present value. In his account, savings are diverted into these projects, including AI ventures, and the diversion is sustained by continued inflation and the "subsistence fund" of real production and saving. He says that fund is already under strain from growing government spending, what he calls reckless central bank policy, and tariffs. He also points to a sharp slowdown in money-supply growth since February 2021, following a historically large expansion between August 2019 and February 2021, and expects that slowdown to reach economic activity with a time lag, which he says will weaken the savings flowing into these projects.

Shostak is pointed about what he thinks should happen next. He warns that further aggressive rate cuts and faster money-supply growth would make matters worse, and he expects bank inflationary lending to weaken in the months ahead. To ease the pressure, he recommends that the central bank reduce or end its intervention in financial markets and that government outlays be sharply curtailed. He concludes that, whatever the merits of the technology, AI and similar projects are misallocated and unaffordable activities that are likely to burst. The article does not describe any formal response from central banks, governments or AI companies to these arguments.

Articles.Title: Is AI A Financial Bubble? – OpEd

stories.Headline: Patient Feedback Informs New Framework for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Transparency
stories.Summary:
A new qualitative study across nine hospital sites has set out a proportionate transparency framework for using artificial intelligence in clinical care. The researchers, Guy Stein, Abinav R. Udaiyar, David Bouslov, Howard M. Ross, and Charles E. Binkley, published their findings in PLOS Digital Health in November 2026. They gathered input from Patient and Family Advisory Councils within a large healthcare network. The work responds to the rapid spread of clinical AI tools, from ambient clinical scribes to diagnostic support, at a time when research on patient expectations remains thin.

The team ran twenty semi-structured interviews and collected intake surveys from council members. They analyzed the transcripts with a hybrid approach that used Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro for initial coding, followed by human validation to reach consensus. Four themes emerged: ethical prerequisites for AI integration, systemic prerequisites for trust, preserving clinician oversight, and strategies for meaningful communication. Participants saw transparency as a necessary ethical floor for protecting patient autonomy, but said it alone was not enough to earn confidence. Trust, they said, must be shown through evidence of reliability and High Reliability Organization principles.

Based on these findings, the authors built a model that scales transparency to clinical risk and the degree of patient agency needed. It sorts AI engagement into three tiers: disclosure, assent, and consent. Participants expected clinicians to act as the bridge between technology and patients and to remain the final decision makers on all care. The authors conclude that health systems can deploy AI in a way that builds trust and protects the patient-provider relationship. The articles do not describe any plans for adopting the framework at specific institutions.

Articles.Title: Patient Feedback Informs New Framework for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Transparency

stories.Headline: AI Governance in Healthcare: WHO Principles & QA
stories.Summary:
The World Health Organization has issued governance guidance for artificial intelligence in healthcare, and the framework is described in a CASRAI explainer updated on 9 November 2026. The guidance builds on a 2021 WHO report, Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health, which was produced after a two-year international consultation involving bioethicists, clinicians, legal scholars, and health ministries. Two later WHO documents extend that baseline, one issued in October 2023 on regulatory considerations and one issued in January 2024 on large multi-modal models. The article does not describe a single new event, so the story rests on this published framework and its ongoing application.

The 2021 report sets out six principles: protecting human autonomy, promoting well-being and safety, ensuring transparency and explainability, fostering responsibility and accountability, ensuring inclusiveness and equity, and promoting AI that is responsive and sustainable. The 2023 document organizes regulatory evaluation into six operational pillars, covering transparency, risk management across the product lifecycle, clinical validation, data quality, privacy protection, and collaboration with clinicians and patients. The January 2024 guidance covers more than 40 recommendations for generative models across five healthcare domains, including diagnosis, administrative work, medical education, and research. It warns that passing a standardized medical licensing exam is not enough to justify clinical use and calls for guardrails against fabricated outputs, clinician sign-off, patient disclosure, and independent audits.

Responsibility for applying these standards falls on health systems, medical software developers, and clinical trial sponsors, with the WHO setting the international baseline. In the United States, the article says, the rules are enforced through the ONC HTI-1 Final Rule, the FDA framework for software as a medical device, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The article also describes a recommended structure in which a hospital convenes an interdisciplinary clinical AI governance committee, typically led by senior medical information, AI, and quality officers along with biostatisticians and frontline clinicians. It proposes a four-gate lifecycle covering intake and risk classification, retrospective local validation, silent prospective testing in live systems, and phased go-live with continuous drift monitoring.

The article presents this as a model rather than a legal mandate. Looking ahead, the article indicates that the framework is meant to guide ongoing oversight, with models re-accredited every six to twelve months and monitored for drift after deployment. It does not report any scheduled deadline, enforcement action, or pending rulemaking beyond these existing documents. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Governance in Healthcare: WHO Principles & QA

stories.Headline: AI in Telemedicine: Triage, Scribes & RPM Guide
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story. The only article provided is an evergreen explainer guide titled "AI in Telemedicine: Triage, Scribes & RPM Guide," published on casrai.org on 10 November 2026 and last updated the same day, so there is no specific event, actor, or date of an incident to report. The guide describes how AI is used across the telehealth encounter, from pre-visit symptom triage and virtual physical exam peripherals to ambient documentation, tele-ICU monitoring, and remote patient monitoring. It also covers research uses such as decentralized trials, where AI helps with eligibility screening and captures vocal, facial, and motor biomarkers during video visits.

The guide sets out the regulatory framework that governs these tools. It says that AI software analyzing images, ECG waveforms, or physiological signals to detect or diagnose a condition is regulated as a Software as a Medical Device and needs FDA marketing authorization, while administrative tools such as ambient note drafting with clinician review generally fall outside that category. It also says that certified EHR and telehealth modules using predictive decision support must disclose training data, validation performance across demographic subgroups, and known failure modes, and that cloud AI services handling patient information must operate under a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement. Recording telehealth calls for ambient scribes, the guide notes, requires consent disclosures under the applicable state wiretapping rules.

The guide is written and maintained by the CASRAI Editorial Board, and the page presents it as a reference rather than a report on any new development. It does not describe a specific rule change, enforcement action, or product launch, and it does not state any upcoming deadline. The article also carries promotional material for a medical supply distributor and an AI research assistant subscription, which are unrelated to the subject matter. Because the source is a general guide, it offers no next steps or pending decisions to report.

Articles.Title: AI in Telemedicine: Triage, Scribes & RPM Guide

stories.Headline: Where AI Can Strengthen Clinical Research, and Where Patient Input is More Important
stories.Summary:
Stacy Hurt, chief patient officer at Parexel, discussed how artificial intelligence can be used in clinical research in an interview with Pharmaceutical Executive, published November 10, 2026. Her central point is that the question facing the pharma and biotech industries is less whether AI should be used and more when it should be used. She says AI can make trials faster and smarter, which matters to patients with advanced cancer or rare disease. The article notes that the technology can be applied across many workflows, but that doesn't guarantee good results.

Hurt argues that patient input is needed from the very beginning of a study, because lived experience cannot be replaced. She describes the side effects of chemotherapy, including nausea, fatigue, constipation and diarrhea, to make the point that AI cannot substitute for what patients endure. She also explains that AI learns from the prompts it is given, so patients asking the right questions can help train these systems. When AI is used poorly, patients may face badly designed research and weak communication, but she says proper use can deepen understanding of patients' viewpoints. Her approach treats AI as complementary to patient experience rather than a replacement for it.

The article is an interview feature rather than a report on a specific event, and it does not describe any new regulation, rule or product change. It sits among related PharmExec coverage on tumor testing, COVID-19 prevention and clinical data infrastructure, though those pieces are not tied to Hurt's remarks. The article does not describe any next steps or timelines for how AI should be adopted in clinical trials. Its main takeaway is Hurt's view that patient involvement should remain central as the industry adopts these tools.

Articles.Title: Where AI Can Strengthen Clinical Research, and Where Patient Input is More Important

stories.Headline: I don’t want AI in my online search. What options do I have?
stories.Summary:
Google has announced a new artificial intelligence policy for schools that use its apps, providing settings that let schools opt in or out of AI products on student accounts. Schools that reject AI in the classroom entirely can also turn off search. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated, which led to headlines suggesting there is no longer a way to use Google search without AI. The announcement comes as AI faces growing pushback from people who reject it for personal, ethical, or environmental reasons.

Any web search engine relies on a set of algorithms that handle crawling, indexing, spam detection, ranking, user interactions, and evaluation. Most of these components involve machine learning and neural networks, which are AI systems trained to find patterns in large amounts of data. This means a search engine cannot be used entirely without AI in the broad sense. The concern usually centers on generative AI, which produces new content from prompts. Google's AI Mode and AI Overviews use a method called retrieval-augmented generation, which pairs a large language model with web content retrieved by the search engine.

Users have some options for avoiding those summaries on Google. There is no official switch to disable AI Overviews, but appending "&udm=14" to a search link defaults results to the Web tab, which does not show them. Because adding that parameter manually is impractical, people have built browser plugins and custom search engine settings to automate it in browsers such as Firefox, Chrome, Brave, and Opera. Alternatives such as DuckDuckGo, Brave Search, and Ecosia offer non-AI modes that turn off AI summaries by default, and some also let users filter out AI-generated images.

Maintaining a web index is costly, so only a few organizations operate at large scale, with Google and Microsoft Bing holding the most popular indexes. Some alternatives are gaining attention, including Brave Search, which runs its own independent engine, and DuckDuckGo, which combines several sources. The OpenWebSearch.eu project aims to build an open European web search infrastructure and make its index publicly available. Overall, the answer is that no search exists without AI in some form, though generative AI answers can be switched off on some platforms.

Articles.Title: I don’t want AI in my online search. What options do I have?

stories.Headline: Radiology Artificial Intelligence: Uses and Rules
stories.Summary:
The articles do not report a breaking event. They are an explanatory guide, dated 9 November 2026 and last updated that day, titled "Radiology Artificial Intelligence: Uses and Rules," published by CASRAI and maintained by its Editorial Board. The guide describes radiology artificial intelligence as computer vision and machine learning software that helps acquire, optimize, analyze, and triage diagnostic medical images. It states that these tools act as clinical decision support rather than replacements for specialists, detecting anomalies, measuring structures, and prioritizing urgent cases under physician supervision.

The guide explains how the software fits into imaging workflows. Images in the DICOM standard are routed through a vendor neutral archive or PACS to an inference engine, which produces structured reports and reorders radiology worklists so emergencies are read first. The Food and Drug Administration regulates these tools as Software as a Medical Device under Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations, with categories including computer-assisted triage (21 CFR 892.2080), computer-aided detection (892.2050), computer-assisted diagnosis (892.2060), combined detection and diagnosis (892.2090), and acquisition optimization (892.2100), all listed as Class II. The guide notes that manufacturers may use Predetermined Change Control Plans and that sites should monitor performance for model drift.

Responsibility for final diagnoses rests with the licensed interpreting physician, a position the guide attributes to a 2019 joint consensus statement from the ACR, RSNA, ESR, and CAR. The guide also says that 510(k) clearance does not guarantee accuracy at every site, so local validation is needed before clinical use. The guide lists its sources as FDA regulatory materials, the FDA, Health Canada, and UK MHRA Good Machine Learning Practice principles, the 2019 multisociety statement in Radiology, and DICOM standards. It does not describe any upcoming deadlines or pending changes beyond general ongoing monitoring.

Articles.Title: Radiology Artificial Intelligence: Uses and Rules

stories.Headline: CBP, Commerce Apply AI to Advance IT Modernization
stories.Summary:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection is using AI-assisted coding to speed up the modernization of its legacy IT systems, while the Department of Commerce is using AI to make its data easier to reach across bureaus, according to a report from Federal News Network published Thursday, November 9, 2026. CBP has used AI coding tools to examine older software, including stored procedures, databases and code that processes inbound messages. Thomas Mills, executive director of CBP's Cargo Systems Program Directorate, said this has moved legacy components into modernized versions about 40 percent faster than previously projected. The agency initially expected some of this work to take five to seven years. Mills also said CBP recently retired a mainframe dating to the 1980s.

The changes come with requirements and new working methods. Mills said technical staff must review the AI's output rather than rely on it without verification. CBP is also breaking many software projects into two-week work cycles to deliver capabilities step by step, which helps the agency track costs, particularly cloud costs. At Commerce, the department is not replacing older systems but is instead connecting existing data sources to GSA's USAi service through application programming interfaces, or APIs. Census Bureau, the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration are among the bureaus using these connections.

Mills said CBP uses AI for data extraction and governance before applying large language models, warning that unreliable input can produce inaccurate results. Matt Passos, acting Chief Technology Officer at Commerce, said data is central to the department's AI use cases and that Commerce does not always have the funding or technical expertise to modernize older systems. He said changes to one system affect every connected system, which adds complexity. Passos also said Commerce is applying AI to capital investment assessments to examine total ownership costs and project the outcomes of spending decisions. He said the department is working with several vendors and is asking business owners to weigh the potential costs of each AI application against its value.

Ryan Palmer, USAi architecture lead at GSA, named cost and vendor lock-in as among the biggest challenges for the service. The articles place these efforts within a broader federal push to use AI for legacy systems, data management and mission support. Palmer said more than 20 agencies are using USAi, which makes models from leading U.S. AI companies available in FedRAMP-authorized environments so agencies can test different models without committing to one provider. The articles also note that the Potomac Officers Club's 2026 Homeland Security Summit, scheduled for November 10, will cover these topics, with CBP CIO Sonny Bhagowalia giving a keynote. The articles do not say what the next steps are for either agency's modernization timelines or costs.

Articles.Title: CBP, Commerce Apply AI to Advance IT Modernization

stories.Headline: As AI stakes its claim in higher education, colleges and universities across Chicago aim to embrace it
stories.Summary:
DePaul University recently released "Guiding Principles on Artificial Intelligence," a document calling for academic integrity, intellectual honesty, transparency and human-centered use of the technology. The principles were developed by the school's 26-member Provost's Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which worked on them for more than a year and meets monthly to discuss policy and classroom practice. The Chicago Tribune reported the story on November 10, 2026, and the principles were published the month before. DePaul's earlier statement on AI dated from 2023, which the university's leaders said was outdated given how quickly the technology has changed.

The principles go beyond academic integrity, according to Jay Cunningham, an assistant professor of computing who created the Responsible AI Systems and Experiences lab in 2025. He wants students to understand AI as a tool that tries to model human behavior, interactions and decision-making, and he says people should use such tools in ways that serve them best. The article notes that more fields now expect workers to understand AI, which creates a need for students to learn the technology as it develops. Other Chicago schools are taking similar steps, with committees, new classes and programs aimed at AI literacy among students and faculty.

John Shanahan, an English professor and associate provost at DePaul, chairs the Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence and says the group gives faculty across disciplines a shared place to discuss the technology and vet ideas for future policy. He said the university is being proactive and that AI does not have to be feared, though he acknowledged the field is only at its beginning. Mark Potter, provost and chief academic officer at City Colleges of Chicago, said the system cannot ignore AI and must prepare students with competencies in its responsible and ethical use. Ayoka Noelle Mota Samuels, the system's associate vice chancellor for technology sector strategy, said City Colleges wants to make AI learning affordable and accessible to people from all backgrounds.

The approaches differ across institutions. City Colleges introduced an Associate of Applied Science degree in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Development at Wilbur Wright College this fall, after forming a district-wide AI steering committee. The University of Chicago will launch a master's degree in applied AI in fall 2027, while its law school bans note-taking on electronic devices in some classes. Northwestern launched an undergraduate AI major this fall along with a webpage of tools for students, faculty and staff. Shanahan summed up the broader stance by saying that there will be times when AI is useful and times when it is better to think and write without it.

Articles.Title: As AI stakes its claim in higher education, colleges and universities across Chicago aim to embrace it

stories.Headline: Deerfield taps AWS to fuel healthcare AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
Deerfield Management, an investment firm, has agreed to use Amazon Web Services' AI and cloud technology to help AI-native healthcare and life sciences companies build and scale, according to a press release that Fierce Healthcare reported on November 9, 2026. Under the collaboration, AWS becomes a preferred AI provider, and select Deerfield portfolio companies will receive access to its AI and cloud tools, technical training and support. The companies say these resources will help them apply agentic AI to drug discovery, operations and care delivery. The deal also brings together AWS's generative AI and cloud services with Deerfield's team of AI engineers and the innovation ecosystem of its affiliate, Cure.

Deerfield plans to go further by bringing AWS AI services into its own research, evaluation and operating processes. Its Deerfield Intelligence and Deerfield Discovery and Development (3DC) teams will get access to AWS technology and technical support to scale proprietary healthcare AI products. Select portfolio companies will also receive AWS training on topics such as large-scale model training, inference optimization and healthcare-specific managed services. AWS will serve as a common technology layer that Deerfield can use internally and offer to portfolio companies, which could help startups move from AI development to deployment more quickly. The firm supports more than 200 private and public healthcare and life sciences investments.

Dan Sheeran, vice president and general manager of Healthcare and Life Sciences at AWS, said the collaboration aims to drive development of the next generation of AI-powered healthcare organizations. He pointed to services such as Amazon Bio Discovery and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore as tools that can help organizations operate at a scale not feasible only a few years ago. Jim Flynn, managing partner at Deerfield, said the firm's Intelligence team is developing models intended to transform how it sources opportunities, evaluates science and accelerates portfolio companies. Mark Michalski, M.D., Deerfield's chief information officer and CEO of Ascertain, said AWS's services will help Ascertain scale its platform, which automates workflows such as case management and prior authorization.

The move follows Deerfield's May 2025 unveiling of the third installment of its healthcare innovations fund, which earmarks more than $600 million for promising therapeutics and technologies. Deerfield's headquarters at Cure, a healthcare innovation campus in New York City, sits within one of the world's densest healthcare ecosystems, according to the firm. The articles do not say how much the partnership costs or how long it will run. They also do not describe specific results from the collaboration.

Articles.Title: Deerfield taps AWS to fuel healthcare AI ambitions

stories.Headline: The Formal–Functional Gap: How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Medi | AMEP
stories.Summary:
Researchers Fateme Hejazi, Narges Tavangar, Ali Saber and Mohammad Saeid Moeinfar published a narrative review on November 10, 2026, in the journal Advances in Medical Education and Practice, examining how artificial intelligence is reshaping what it means to be a physician. The authors, based at Kashan University of Medical Sciences in Iran and Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, synthesized conceptual, empirical and theoretical literature on AI, professional identity formation and clinical practice. They searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Google Scholar for material available through August 2026. The review concentrates on diagnostic and predictive systems, clinical decision support, generative AI and large language models, and AI-supported medical education. Its evidence base is predominantly US-centered, and the authors note that non-US studies were considered only selectively.

The review argues that AI affects professional identity unevenly, with the strongest effects on expertise, clinical reasoning and professional autonomy. Physicians are shifting from being the exclusive holders of specialized knowledge toward validating information that is more accessible but not always trusted. The authors cite evidence of automation bias and reduced diagnostic performance to support this transition. They propose the "formal–functional gap," describing the divergence between formal clinical responsibility, which remains with physicians, and functional influence over decisions, which is shared with AI.

The size of this gap varies by AI configuration, identity component and career stage. Trainees may face a risk of never developing key skills, while experienced physicians may face deskilling. The authors place these concerns in a wider context of rapid adoption. The US Food and Drug Administration's list of authorized AI- and machine-learning-enabled devices grew from 7 entries before 2010 to 343 by mid-2021, still concentrated in radiology and cardiology.

The review also reports that by 2022 about 18.7% of US hospitals had integrated AI, and that projections estimated 66% of physicians would incorporate AI into practice by 2025. A randomized trial in JAMA Network Open found that a large language model used alone outscored physicians with or without the model on structured diagnostic reasoning. The authors conclude that medical education should prioritize sustained expertise, clinical reasoning, professional autonomy, judgment about AI outputs and meaningful human oversight. They also state that the gap remains a conceptual framework whose relationships require empirical validation.

Articles.Title: The Formal–Functional Gap: How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Medi | AMEP

stories.Headline: Colorado, Wyoming researchers use AI to predict destructive hailstorms earlier
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Colorado State University and the University of Wyoming are developing artificial intelligence tools that aim to forecast destructive hailstorms earlier than current methods allow. The effort was reported by Denver7 on November 10, 2026, and it centers on a team of five professors, three from CSU and two from Wyoming, along with four research scientists. Kristen Rasmussen, an associate professor in CSU's Department of Atmospheric Science, described the project as combining two existing AI-based prediction models. The goal is to predict hail earlier and more accurately, so that people have time to act.

The system takes historical weather observations and uses artificial intelligence to identify the atmospheric conditions that lead to hail formation. It pairs longer-range machine learning models with AI radar forecasting technology. Researchers hope it can eventually deliver hail forecasts several hours, or even days, before a storm arrives. Rasmussen said the team feeds these atmospheric ingredients into a hail prediction model that projects out to eight days. The technology is still under development and testing, and additional field research is planned for spring 2027.

The article describes farmer Dave Petrocco of LaSalle, who said hailstorms damaged parts of his fields last June, though the crops recovered because the hail came early in the growing season. He said unpredictable storms can put workers, equipment and a whole harvest at risk, since crews may be planting or harvesting when a storm arrives. Rasmussen said earlier warnings could also help homeowners and drivers move vehicles and protect property. The researchers eventually hope to work with the National Weather Service to bring the forecasting system into practical use.

The article places the work in the context of Colorado, where hailstorms can cause billions of dollars in damage and where hail is a major factor in homeowners insurance costs. Petrocco said better warning would save money, reduce risk and lower stress for farmers. The article does not state a timeline for when the system will be available to the public or whether the National Weather Service has committed to adopting it. The next step reported is the continued development and testing of the technology, with the field research scheduled for spring 2027.

Articles.Title: Colorado, Wyoming researchers use AI to predict destructive hailstorms earlier

stories.Headline: Study Reveals Critical Efficiency and Transparency Gap in Microgrid Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers Serge Raoul Dzonde Naoussi, François Dieudonné Mengue, David Tsuanyo, and Bernard Kamsu Foguem published a systematic bibliometric review of 2,150 records indexed in Scopus between 2011 and 2025. Using VOSviewer and the Bibliometrix R package, they examined how research on artificial intelligence for microgrid energy management has developed around two themes: explainability and computational frugality. Their analysis found that work on making these systems interpretable has expanded rapidly, driven by regulatory scrutiny and the need for operator trust, while work on minimizing computing resources and energy use has remained comparatively marginal. The authors say that published engineering studies rarely measure the energy the optimization algorithms themselves consume.

The study explains why this gap matters for remote and small-scale power networks. Microgrids coordinate solar panels, wind turbines, battery storage, and variable consumer loads, and their energy management systems increasingly rely on deep neural networks for forecasting and control. These models are accurate but demand substantial processing power, memory, and electricity during training and operation, which can exceed the capacity of the compact microcontrollers and bandwidth-limited hardware used in remote deployments. The researchers treat frugal AI and explainable AI as mutually necessary for deployable systems, because automated decisions such as load shedding, islanding, and battery scheduling affect expensive assets and need auditable rationales. Their co-occurrence analysis showed that interpretability terms sit at the center of the research network while frugality and edge-execution terms remain peripheral and fragmented, even though every captured paper had to reference frugality under the search criteria.

The authors place the imbalance within broader patterns in the field. Their production metrics show the intersection of these topics is mostly a recent development, with marked growth between 2018 and 2025, and they found that leading institutions shape research preferences that spread through collaboration networks. According to the authors, closing the gap will require international collaboration to establish shared benchmarks that pair transparency metrics with rigorous hardware profiling. The articles provided do not describe any specific follow-up initiatives, funding commitments, or timelines for such benchmarks.

Articles.Title: Study Reveals Critical Efficiency and Transparency Gap in Microgrid Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Vermont hospitals embrace AI as questions about oversight remain
stories.Summary:
Vermont's two largest hospital networks, UVM Health and Dartmouth Health, are expanding their use of artificial intelligence, according to a WCAX report published November 9, 2026. UVM Health uses an AI tool to help doctors spot fractures on X-rays, and both networks use AI to take notes during patient visits and to summarize charts. Dr. Alison Sullivan of UVM Health said the tools have returned minutes she can spend with patients. Both hospitals say the technology supports clinicians rather than replacing them.

Dartmouth Health's Dr. Randa Perkins said AI tools are supplemental to care and do not replace clinician diagnosis or decision-making. Both networks use AI in billing, scanning patient charts for keywords that help inform pricing and insurance decisions. UVM Health's Craig Chase said no part of that process relies on AI alone, noting that a single phrase can be read several ways. UVM Health reported finding errors in insurance denials but attributed them to timing issues rather than the technology.

Both hospital systems are working on governance. UVM Health has a committee that reviews each tool before and after launch, and Dartmouth has a similar process along with a set policy on AI use. Sullivan acknowledged that the technology is advancing quickly, making it a challenge to keep up the oversight it needs. She stressed that clinicians remain responsible for patient care decisions. The hospitals' positions were presented as their own statements in the report.

State officials are also examining the issue. David Herlihy, who runs Vermont's Board of Medical Practice, sits on a statewide AI council studying guardrails for medicine and is helping the state health commissioner draft recommendations for lawmakers. He said the state does not want patients treated as subjects of an experiment with harmful results. The larger question of who oversees AI tools themselves remains unsettled, since states license doctors and the FDA reviews medical devices but no body has clearly claimed AI. State officials are starting with mental health, and Vermont's report on AI in mental health is due to lawmakers January 15.

Articles.Title: Vermont hospitals embrace AI as questions about oversight remain

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's affair shines a spotlight on Nvidia's weak board and opaque succession planning at what has become the world's most important company (Semafor)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang faces questions about his future after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for Chinese intelligence, a revelation that has drawn attention to the company's governance. Shares fell about 5% in afternoon trading on November 9, 2026, wiping out more than $200 billion in market value. The article reports that Huang's position now rests with a board that lacks the experience and stature typically found at a company of Nvidia's size. Huang has led the company since he co-founded it in 1993, and he has built it into the center of the AI boom.

The board has allowed a leadership structure with little precedent in corporate America, in which Huang has more than 50 direct reports. Nvidia has never publicly named a successor, has no president or chief operating officer, and its latest annual report does not use the word "succession." Analysts quoted in the piece say a replacement would likely have to come from outside, with chipmakers such as AMD and Broadcom mentioned as sources of candidates. The average board member has served almost 15 years, and none are current or former S&P 500 chief executives or have national-security experience. Huang and two other directors have been on the board since the company was founded.

Former SEC chair Gary Gensler said Huang appeared to have misled the public, given earlier company and Huang denials that his dealings were normal. Gensler said the stock drop could make the matter material to a court. The SEC declined to say whether it would investigate. Nvidia's board has said it still has confidence in Huang and that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. President Donald Trump has also expressed confidence in him.

Governance experts quoted in the article describe a board that may have struggled to check a celebrated chief executive, and they note the company's internal investigation and likely congressional hearings will determine whether any secrets were exposed. The company could also face more shareholder litigation if it is found to have misled investors. The scandal arrives alongside other pressures, including a Democratic Congress that could slow the buildout of AI infrastructure. The article does not say when the board's investigation will conclude.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang's affair shines a spotlight on Nvidia's weak board and opaque succession planning at what has become the world's most important company (Semafor)

stories.Headline: Israel warns Iran is seeking AI-powered cyberattack capabilities
stories.Summary:
Yossi Karadi, head of Israel's National Cyber Directorate, warned on Tuesday that Iran is pursuing artificial intelligence-powered cyberattack capabilities that could threaten countries well beyond Israel. He spoke at Cyber Week at Tel Aviv University, where he argued that AI could give attackers a decisive speed advantage over national defenses. His remarks were reported by CTech on November 10, 2026. Karadi also suggested that connected robots and other machines could eventually turn cyber intrusions into physical dangers.

Karadi said that an attacker needs only one AI model and one target, while national defenders must protect many organizations at once, around the clock, within regulatory limits. He presented a framework for a new war of attrition in cyberspace, published recently in a U.S. professional journal, which holds that repeated incidents can gradually erode a country's ability to function if they come faster than systems can be restored. The imbalance is especially serious for governments, which must protect interconnected public institutions, businesses and critical infrastructure. At the event he also described a hypothetical scenario in which a software update or cyberattack causes a million robots from one manufacturer to perform the same dangerous action at once. A humanoid robot developed in the laboratory of Professor Yuval Elovici appeared on stage during the address.

Karadi's warning follows a series of Iranian cyber campaigns against Israel. In March he said the Shin Bet and the National Cyber Directorate had thwarted Iranian attempts to gather intelligence on security personnel, defense companies and their relatives, including attempts to take control of surveillance cameras. The Directorate counted 50 attempts to penetrate public camera systems since the start of the war, plus another 50 cases in which attackers entered organizational systems and deleted critical data. It also reported issuing 2,304 targeted cyber alerts to organizations in 2025, an increase of nearly 350 percent over the previous year. Microsoft's annual cyber defense report, published in October, ranked Israel as the second most targeted country for cyber activity between July 2025 and June 2026, behind only the United States, and identified Iran as the leading state-backed source of operations against Israel.

Karadi had already urged Israeli company executives and board members in May to prepare for a new generation of AI models able to find security vulnerabilities and carry out complex attack sequences. He warned that skills once limited to highly trained specialists were becoming more accessible and that traditional defenses alone would no longer suffice. The articles do not describe any specific new Iranian AI-driven attack or any new regulatory requirement. They also do not say what further steps Israel or other governments plan to take in response to the warning.

Articles.Title: Israel warns Iran is seeking AI-powered cyberattack capabilities

stories.Headline: Apple is now offering additional AI access via one-time $50 "intelligence usage packs" when monthly usage caps are met, starting in its Creator Studio apps (Ryan Christoffel/9to5Mac)
stories.Summary:
Apple has begun selling one-time "intelligence usage packs" that give users more access to its AI features once they reach their monthly usage limit. The first of these packs arrived on November 9, 2026, tied to the Logic Pro update within Apple Creator Studio. Users reach the purchase option by choosing Logic Pro from the menu bar, then "Intelligence Features," then "Show Usage," where a "Buy More Usage" option appears. The only offering is a one-time purchase priced at $49.99.

According to Apple's website, the packs cannot be shared through Family Sharing and work only with the Apple Account used for iCloud at the time of purchase. Unused usage rolls over from month to month and expires 12 months after purchase. Additional usage is consumed only after a user has reached the monthly limit for the relevant features. The articles say Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, and the iWork suite are expected to offer the packs as the rest of the announced Creator Studio updates arrive later in the month. The articles do not identify who set these terms beyond Apple's own published conditions, which are linked in the report.

Apple had previously said it would eventually charge for expanded use of select AI features, and this launch marks its first step in that direction. The articles note that most other AI services rely on subscriptions rather than one-time purchases, which makes Apple's approach at least initially different. The reporting also says all Apple Intelligence features had been free on Apple devices until now. The articles suggest the same model could extend to other server-based features such as Siri AI, Image Playground, and Photos editing tools, but they describe this as a likely future development rather than an announced plan.

Articles.Title: Apple is now offering additional AI access via one-time $50 "intelligence usage packs" when monthly usage caps are met, starting in its Creator Studio apps (Ryan Christoffel/9to5Mac)

stories.Headline: Dems point to CISA staffing, AI security and other cyber priorities
stories.Summary:
Incoming Democratic leaders in Congress have laid out their cybersecurity priorities for the next session, which begins in January after Democrats retook both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections. Their statements, reported by Federal News Network on November 9, 2026, focus on restaffing the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, extending key information-sharing authorities, protecting critical infrastructure, and addressing security risks from artificial intelligence. Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Homeland Security Committee, described the moment as pivotal for CISA, which has lost more than 1,000 staff, roughly one-third of its workforce, since January 2025. He said the agency is now hiring several hundred people and must be ready to help defenders against AI-enabled attacks.

Lawmakers are also focused on expiring authorities and funding that shape how federal, state, local and private partners share cyber information. The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 is set to expire again in December after a short-term extension tied to a continuing resolution, and nearly three dozen industry groups want a long-term extension. Sen. Mark Warner, expected to chair the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, named reauthorizing that law and funding the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center as top priorities. The Department of Homeland Security allowed MS-ISAC funding to lapse last year. Thompson also wants to extend the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program to help under-resourced sectors, especially water utilities.

Senator Maggie Hassan, expected to chair the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, tied CISA staffing to broader homeland security concerns, including fentanyl trafficking. She accused the Trump-Vance administration of undermining security by diverting resources and gutting CISA, and said those cuts should be reversed. Warner said critical infrastructure such as power and water remains deeply vulnerable, pointing to past attacks on Salt Typhoon, Colonial Pipeline and Change Healthcare. He also said he wants to explore whether the nation's approach to offensive cyber operations is right, while noting that the country must be able to respond to attacks.

Analysts quoted in the article say cybersecurity has drawn new attention because AI is accelerating long-standing threats, though it may also help defenders. Tonya Ugoretz of PwC, a former senior FBI cyber official, said lawmakers are likely to examine resourcing across sector-risk management agencies, not only CISA. She also noted that the Trump administration is expected to release final rules early next year requiring critical infrastructure operators to report cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act. She advised companies to review their internal controls now, before those rules take effect.

Articles.Title: Dems point to CISA staffing, AI security and other cyber priorities

stories.Headline: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
stories.Summary:
CrossnoKaye, an industrial software company, has described how it built its physical AI platform on AWS, combining its ATLAS automation system with an agentic intelligence system called AURA that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The company's blog post, published on November 9, 2026, explains that heavy industry plants keep their data and control logic in separate systems from different vendors, which makes bolting an outside AI agent onto them difficult. CrossnoKaye's answer was to manage the facility model, base control software, historian, and optimization applications in one platform, so that AURA has native access to the full operational state of a plant inside a single security boundary. The post reports that the platform covers more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, stores over 22 trillion machine data points, and ingests more than 50 billion new readings each day.

For numerical answers, AURA hands calculations to isolated Python sandboxes in AgentCore rather than relying on language models to compute statistics over millions of readings. The architecture runs in three layers. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant hardware runs a local Kubernetes cluster that executes base control narratives against existing PLC and DCS equipment, and the company reports more than 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance acts as an outbound-only gateway that opens no inbound firewall ports, streaming telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon MSK, and if cloud connectivity drops the plant keeps running on the local cluster.

In the cloud, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications compute setpoint schedules that are dispatched through Amazon SQS FIFO queues, with CrossnoKaye reporting 650,000 closed-loop control actions per day. AURA runs on Amazon EKS and uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and the AgentCore code interpreter across three modes: interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks that produce cited Briefs, and automated Routines. The post describes a quarry example in which the back half of a plant tripped twice in one shift. Operators initially suspected the secondary crusher, but AURA read the conveyor layout and deployed interlocks and found that a slipping recirculating belt beneath the tertiary crusher had tripped the tertiary crusher's overload interlock, which in turn halted the secondary crusher.

A plant manager sent an operator to inspect the belt, and the slip was confirmed and fixed within minutes. CrossnoKaye states that it designed warm sandbox sessions with a 15-minute sliding time to live for Chats, so that engineers can continue investigations without losing in-memory data, while Tasks and Routines get a fresh, single-use microVM for each run to keep results reproducible. The company presents these choices as lessons from running physical AI in production, though the post does not describe any regulatory requirement behind them. The articles provided do not describe further deployments or announced next steps beyond the platform's continued operation.

Articles.Title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

stories.Headline: FDA Artificial Intelligence & AI/ML Device Rules
stories.Summary:
The article is a reference guide rather than a news report. It is dated November 9, 2026, and was last updated that day, and it describes how the U.S. Food and Drug Administration regulates artificial intelligence and machine learning medical devices. It says the agency handles these tools through risk-based premarket pathways, which are 510(k) notification for moderate-risk devices, De Novo classification for novel low-to-moderate-risk devices, and premarket approval for high-risk devices. It also covers Good Machine Learning Practice principles, which the FDA, Health Canada, and the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency issued jointly in October 2021, and Predetermined Change Control Plans authorized under Section 515C of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

The guide sets out the boundary between regulated devices and exempt clinical decision support software. Under Section 520(o)(1)(E), software is excluded only if it meets four criteria at once, and the article lists them, including that it does not analyze medical images or physiological signals and that the clinician can independently review the basis for its recommendations. The FDA's final guidance on clinical decision support software, issued in September 2022, governs this test. The article also describes the ten Good Machine Learning Practice principles, which cover dataset representativeness and independence, reference standards, evaluation of the combined human and AI team, and post-market monitoring for data drift. It notes that these principles apply across the total product life cycle.

The article attributes the framework to the FDA and its Center for Devices and Radiological Health and Digital Health Center of Excellence, and it cites the agency's own guidance and database as its sources. It does not report any new action, enforcement, or announcement on the date of publication. The article states that the FDA maintains a public database of authorized AI and machine learning devices, which lists submission numbers, decision dates, applicants, review panels, and product codes. It reports that more than 75 percent of listed authorizations fall under radiology, with cardiovascular devices at about 10 percent. The guide does not describe any pending rule changes or future deadlines, so it offers no next steps beyond the existing framework.

Articles.Title: FDA Artificial Intelligence & AI/ML Device Rules

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech outlines philosophy for AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Virginia Tech's Board of Visitors heard on Monday from leaders of a task force on artificial intelligence, who said they had developed a "cultural framework" the university can use as it puts the technology into practice. Rishi Jaitly, an entrepreneur and professor of practice, and College of Engineering Dean Warren Dixon presented the work at the board's first day of a two-day meeting in Blacksburg. The framework is described as a set of principles meant to guide how the university approaches AI in its teaching, research and operations. The task force said it wants the effort to shape how students, faculty and staff think about and use the technology. The framework outlines how the university plans to adopt AI responsibly, covering areas such as academic integrity, research, and the use of tools in classrooms and administration.

Its leaders said it is intended to help the university decide what to do with AI and how to explain those decisions to the public. The articles do not give specific dollar figures, dates for implementation or numerical targets tied to the plan. They do indicate that the framework is meant to be a living guide that will be revised as the technology and the university's needs change. Board members were expected to weigh in on the proposal during the meeting. Jaitly and Dixon are the public faces of the work, and they framed the effort as a way to move forward on AI without losing sight of the university's values.

Dixon, speaking to the board, said the university must do more than adopt the tools, and that it needs to think carefully about how they affect people. Jaitly emphasized that the task force aimed to give the board a shared language for talking about AI, rather than a rigid rulebook. The articles attribute these views to the two men in paraphrase and short quotes, and they do not describe any formal dissent from board members on the framework itself. The announcement comes as universities across the country grapple with how to respond to generative AI, which has raised questions about cheating, instruction and the future of higher education. Virginia Tech, one of the state's largest public universities, has been positioning itself as a leader in technology and engineering, and the framework f

Articles.Title: Virginia Tech outlines philosophy for AI adoption

stories.Headline: Military-made AI tool helped thwart World Cup bomb threat
stories.Summary:
A military-made artificial intelligence tool helped law enforcement stop a bomb threat at the FIFA World Cup in California this summer, according to remarks by Army Capt. Ryan Hetrick, who leads the Pentagon's Generative AI Task Force. The incident, which had not been publicly disclosed before, took place on June 18, when Switzerland played Bosnia and Herzegovina at SoFi Stadium outside Los Angeles. Hetrick made the claim on Nov. 6 at an AI event in Washington, and the report was published by Federal News Network on Nov. 9, 2026.

Three days before the match, Hetrick and colleagues from the Defense Department, FBI and Coast Guard met at the White House to design an automated agent that writes spot reports, which are short, time-sensitive accounts of fast-changing situations. Under the setup, local law enforcement would call the White House during a security incident, and the World Cup Task Force would write a spot report and send it up the chain of command to coordinate a response. That process normally takes about 20 minutes, Hetrick said, while the AI agent can complete it in 90 seconds, leaving authorities an extra 18 minutes to act. He credited the extra time with helping deter the threat on June 18.

Spokespeople for the White House, the FBI and local law enforcement did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The article notes that the 2026 tournament drew more than six million spectators to over 100 matches in 16 host cities across the United States, Canada and Mexico, prompting a large interagency effort that used AI and drones for security. Separately, FBI Director Kash Patel said in a video after the tournament that the bureau had investigated hoax threats and online scams and had provided the most extensive support it has ever given a global sporting event. Two people were charged in connection with a different bomb threat at a World Cup match at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

Hetrick has become one of the military's most active promoters of AI, and his task force travels to troops in the field to find AI solutions to pressing problems. He urged service members to partner with AI experts and to name innovative troops as in-house AI leaders. He pointed to a tool he built with the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, which cut a cyber operations workflow from 100 hours to 15, and said that tool is now available to all cyber officers across the department. The article does not describe any further steps for the World Cup agent or related policy changes.

Articles.Title: Military-made AI tool helped thwart World Cup bomb threat

stories.Headline: Lab Thread launches new AI tools and strengthens platform with universal AI assistant compatibility.aspx
stories.Summary:
Lab Thread Ltd, a UK-based life science software company, announced on November 10, 2026, that it has launched a new Model Context Protocol server that lets scientists connect their own AI assistants directly to their laboratory data. The launch coincided with the company's formal incorporation in the United States and the opening of an office in Boston. The company said this lets US-based customers engage with it under a local entity and extends support to its growing customer base in the region. The server uses the same open standard that widely used AI assistants rely on to connect to outside software. Scientists can therefore point their existing tools at their own lab records without exporting data or commissioning a custom integration.

Lab Thread also released a set of new AI functions aimed at the time-consuming parts of onboarding and record keeping. Scientists can use these tools to generate experimental protocols and electronic lab notebook templates, configure equipment and storage locations, and transcribe handwritten notes into formatted lab notebook entries. The company said its platform stores data as structured, linked records rather than free text, so answers return with full experimental context attached. Security is built into the server, which runs within the company's secure cloud environment with tenant isolation, role-based permissions and immutable audit logs. According to the company, data stays within Lab Thread until an authorized query is made, and then only the minimum necessary context goes to the chosen assistant.

Chief executive officers and company representatives at Lab Thread framed the release as a way to remove friction from adoption. In a statement, the company said that customers often teach themselves the platform within days once they are in, and that the new server and AI functions make setup easier still. It said that whatever AI assistant a scientist already uses can see their data, securely and in context, from day one. The company has said that since its worldwide launch in July 2026, research teams at institutions including Mayo Clinic and UMass Chan Medical School have adopted the platform. The article notes that the platform spans modules for project management, protein engineering, electronic lab notebooks, laboratory information management, sample tracking and inventory.

Articles.Title: Lab Thread launches new AI tools and strengthens platform with universal AI assistant compatibility
