stories.Headline: Before the Algorithm Decides: Connecticut’s 2027 Rules for Artificial Intelligence in Employment
stories.Summary:
Connecticut employers that use artificial intelligence in recruiting or workforce management will face new disclosure requirements beginning in 2027 under Connecticut Public Act 26-15, enacted in 2026 as part of the state's broader AI legislation. The article notes that failure to give appropriate notice to employees and applicants may result in liability under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act. Employers in other states face similar concerns, so the author advises Connecticut employers to begin evaluating their AI technologies now. The law applies to what it calls automated employment-related decision technology, meaning technology that processes personal data and produces an output, such as a score or ranking, that is a substantial factor in an employment decision. Starting October 1, 2027, employers must disclose in plain language when an employee or applicant is interacting with such technology, unless a reasonable person would find that obvious.

Where the technology may be a substantial factor in a decision, the employer must give written notice before the final decision, identifying the technology's use, its trade name, the categories and sources of personal data analyzed, and the employer's contact information. The article also says that, effective October 1, 2026, relying on such technology is not a defense to a discrimination complaint under Connecticut law. Evidence of anti-bias testing or similar proactive measures may, however, be considered in a discrimination proceeding. The article also points to federal scrutiny, noting that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has targeted AI use in employment decisions. For disclosure violations, the law creates no private right of action, so only the Connecticut Attorney General may enforce it, and for certain violations through December 31, 2027, the Attorney General may offer a 60-day opportunity to cure.

The article's authors, attorneys at the law firm Foley & Lardner, recommend that employers inventory the automated tools they use across the employment lifecycle, including third-party recruiting and screening products. They suggest determining what personal data those tools process and whether their output meaningfully affects employment decisions. Employers should also review vendor agreements to confirm that vendors will supply the information needed to meet the disclosure requirements. The authors describe the piece as general information rather than legal advice and state that it does not create an attorney-client relationship. The article does not say what further steps the Attorney General might take beyond the enforcement mechanisms described.

Articles.Title: Before the Algorithm Decides: Connecticut’s 2027 Rules for Artificial Intelligence in Employment

stories.Headline: Teleperformance's latest results spotlight Africa's AI opportunity
stories.Summary:
Teleperformance, the French multinational now operating under the TP brand, published its third-quarter results on November 5, 2026, and Business Insider Africa covered them on November 10. The company revised its 2026 revenue outlook to a decline of 1.5% to 2.5% on a like-for-like basis, reflecting pressure on traditional activities, particularly content moderation. Outside those activities, however, TP recorded 2% like-for-like revenue growth during the quarter once Trust & Safety was excluded. The results are presented as a sign of how artificial intelligence is reshaping the global business services industry. The article frames the company's African expansion as part of that same shift.

TP operates in 11 African countries with more than 50,000 employees and over 50 delivery sites. Egypt is the article's main example, where the company employs about 26,800 people and generates 90% of its local revenues from exported services. Those exports reached €280 million in 2025 and are projected to reach €344 million in 2026. TP has also outlined plans to create 18,000 additional jobs in Egypt under its expansion programme. The article presents these figures as evidence of how African economies are becoming more closely integrated into global technology and business services value chains.

On the AI side, the company reported at the end of September roughly 1,400 AI projects worldwide, more than double the previous year's level. It recorded over 300 new production-grade deployments during the third quarter, and more than 35% of its global client portfolio now uses TP.ai solutions. The article says AI-enabled operations increasingly require multilingual specialists, technical supervision, data expertise and employees able to manage complex interactions. It also notes that automation raises questions about the future of routine roles and about reskilling.

The article describes the group as having maintained its 2026 profitability and cash-flow targets while accelerating its AI transformation. The article concludes that Africa's outsourcing advantages, which include multilingual talent, competitive costs and proximity to European markets, may increasingly depend on combining those strengths with technological capabilities. It argues that future competitiveness will rest on skills and infrastructure rather than labour supply alone. The piece presents TP's African footprint as a substantial platform for taking part in that transition.

Articles.Title: Teleperformance's latest results spotlight Africa's AI opportunity

stories.Headline: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records
stories.Summary:
Palantir, the US data analytics company co-founded by the billionaire Peter Thiel, lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI software into NHS GP records, according to messages obtained by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. The exchanges, which span July 2025 to March 2026, appear to be between Palantir's UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed, with the push in February this year. The company argued via a direct WhatsApp channel that joining up primary and secondary care data was "unarguable" and that its software was "ideal" for the job. This came despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir's existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform.

The lobbying matters because it would stretch the company's reach into patient records that doctors and campaigners say should stay out of its hands. The British Medical Association and other groups have argued that bringing GP data into the platform would undermine patient trust and the doctor-patient relationship. When the previous Conservative government announced the deal three years ago, it stated that GP data would not be part of the national platform. Palantir's messages suggested the minister should "get out ahead of" likely political opposition from doctors and critics such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and the Your Party led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed that its software could bring faster GP access and more targeted management of frail patients, while keeping control of data local.

Foxglove's director of advocacy, Donald Campbell, said the messages showed Palantir lobbying to take in more sensitive personal data and that the company knew how sensitive the request was. The BMA council chair, Dr Tom Dolphin, warned of "scope creep" and of patients worrying about who could access their information. Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officer Network, said Palantir appeared to be bidding to widen its work beyond what ministers and NHS leaders had said, which would require legislative change. Palantir responded that it has long argued data sharing can improve the NHS, that it is for government to decide how the software is rolled out, and that the exchanges reflect those points. The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

The disclosure comes as ministers reportedly stopped short of ending the Palantir contract soon, despite campaigners and two House of Commons committees calling for it to end as early as spring. Health secretary Yvette Cooper told parliament that a review was ongoing and spoke of the long-term benefit of developing UK sovereign AI, which suggests a British replacement may be sought when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. The articles also report that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired by Palantir as a full-time lobbyist in September, wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going. The articles do not say whether the lobbying changed any policy, and the status of GP data in the platform remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

stories.Headline: St. Louis-area tech firm TierPoint sues AI company for $15M
stories.Summary:
St. Louis County-based technology firm TierPoint has filed a lawsuit against artificial intelligence company Pangea, seeking $15.5 million in unpaid fees. The suit was filed in federal court in Missouri, and the article identifies the case as being brought in the Eastern District of Missouri. TierPoint alleges that the AI firm owes it money for services it contracted for. The article reports that the complaint was filed in the days leading up to the publication date.

Little more about the specific services or the timing of the contract appears in the available text. The article describes the amount at issue as $15.5 million, while the headline rounds this figure to $15 million. TierPoint is a data center and cloud services provider headquartered in St. Louis County, and the suit concerns fees it says were never paid. The article does not describe any injunction or other remedy beyond the monetary claim.

It also does not indicate whether the defendant has responded to the complaint. The article attributes the allegations to TierPoint's filing and does not include a comment from the AI company. A spokesperson or attorney for TierPoint was not quoted in the text available. The article does not explain why the payments were withheld or whether the defendant disputes the amount owed.

Those points remain unaddressed in the available reporting. The lawsuit comes as TierPoint has been expanding its local footprint, including plans for new data center capacity in St. Louis County. The article does not say whether the dispute will affect those plans. Next steps in the case, such as a response from the defendant or court scheduling, are not described in the text provided.

Articles.Title: St. Louis-area tech firm TierPoint sues AI company for $15M - STLtoday.com

stories.Headline: AI Investment Risk Demands Vigilance by Retirement Plan Managers
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Bloomberg Law on November 10, 2026, examines how retirement plan managers should respond to the heavy weight that a small group of large technology companies carries in public stock markets. Benefits attorneys said that Americans with retirement accounts invested in public markets are increasingly exposed to these firms, which have been lifted by the boom in artificial intelligence, often without participants realizing it. The piece notes that this exposure has raised concern that retirement savings could suffer if an AI bubble were to burst and push the market lower. It also points to a historic tech selloff that followed speculation about the effects of the November 3 election. The article frames the issue as one that calls for close attention from fiduciaries, the people responsible for overseeing retirement plans and protecting participants from a downturn.

In that framing, concentration in a few large companies means that plan managers have less room for error when markets turn. The available text is cut off before it sets out specific steps, figures or rule changes, so it does not say what new requirements, if any, managers would face. Readers should treat the piece as a call for vigilance rather than a report on a formal change in policy. Benefits attorneys are the sources quoted for the warning about participant exposure, and the article presents their view that many savers do not know how much of their money rides on these technology firms. The article attributes the broader concern about a possible AI bubble to the same discussion of market risk.

The excerpt available does not name any regulator, company or official who has taken a position beyond those attorneys. The article places this discussion against a recent market shock, the historic tech selloff linked to speculation over the November 3 election, which showed how quickly concentrated holdings can fall. The available text does not describe what fiduciaries are expected to do next, and it ends before providing further detail. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Investment Risk Demands Vigilance by Retirement Plan Managers

stories.Headline: Shanghai to create AI test base for shipping and logistics
stories.Summary:
Shanghai has begun building an artificial intelligence test base for shipping and logistics, according to a Smart Maritime Network report by Rob O'Dwyer dated November 10, 2026. The facility is being developed by Shanghai International Port Group, known as SIPG, together with academic and industry partners. It is meant to support testing of AI applications across port handling, cargo transport and multimodal logistics. Work on the infrastructure is already underway, and 54 business AI agents have been registered for testing and deployment.

The base will supply computing, data storage and security infrastructure, along with industry-specific datasets, AI models and an agent management platform. Its work will focus on three operational areas: port cargo handling, port hinterland transport and multimodal transport. The aim is to give AI applications a route from development into day-to-day use in shipping and port operations. The article describes this as the purpose of the initiative rather than setting out any separate legal or regulatory requirement.

The facility was announced alongside a new action plan from the Shanghai Municipal Transport Commission for integrating AI into the transport sector. The plan covers ports and shipping, aviation, rail and road transport, autonomous driving, postal services and logistics. It names three core development areas: transport large language models and AI agents, high-quality industry datasets, and computing infrastructure. Planned applications include autonomous port hinterland transport and AI-based government transport services, and the city also intends to set up a trusted data space for transport and mechanisms for data sharing.

The same event saw the establishment of a Yangtze River Delta regional centre for the Transport Large Model Innovation and Industry Alliance, with its secretariat in Shanghai. The centre will coordinate technical development and applications across Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui, including sharing operational environments for testing transport AI. The article does not describe any further timetable or next steps beyond these announcements. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Shanghai to create AI test base for shipping and logistics

stories.Headline: Qai, Hugging Face partner to nurture Qatar AI talent via inaugural hackathon
stories.Summary:
Qai, a Qatar-headquartered technology company, and Hugging Face, a leading AI technology platform and community, ran Qai's first hackathon, which drew more than 140 engineers, students and researchers from Doha's technology community. The event was held recently at M7 in Msheireb Cultural Forum, and 45 teams spent the weekend building working AI prototypes aimed at challenges in Qatar. They used open-source models and tools available on Hugging Face. Participants received technical workshops and mentoring from engineers at both organisations throughout the event. On the final day, the teams pitched their projects to a panel of judges from Qai and Hugging Face.

The finished projects covered healthcare, nutrition, Arabic language, environment, cybersecurity and drone technology. Team YOLO, an all-female group of students from Carnegie Mellon University in Qatar, placed first with AquaGuard, an early warning system that protects Qatar's desalination plants from pollution such as oil spills and red tides. Team All you need is a Hug took second place, and Team Gradient Descent took third. Both were recognised for their projects, Qalaf and Rasad, which were described as a historical comparison of Qatar in 1908 and today and an AI drone monitoring and tracking solution. The winning teams received compute credits from Hugging Face and Qai.

The participants came from universities, organisations and startups based in Qatar. Qai's aim is to engage and nurture leading AI talent in the country, and it sees the hackathon as a way to combine its mission of enabling and scaling trusted AI with Hugging Face's global open-source community. Both companies share the goal of building a strong pipeline of AI talent in the region. Asmaa Fikree, Qai's Chief Strategy Officer, said the three days showed what local talent can achieve with the right tools and mentors, and she said Qai plans to keep supporting the ecosystem with similar initiatives. Sayak Paul, a senior researcher at Hugging Face, said it was the company's first event in this part of the world, and he hoped it would be the start of a meaningful collaboration.

Articles.Title: Qai, Hugging Face partner to nurture Qatar AI talent via inaugural hackathon | Gulf Times - Gulf Times

stories.Headline: Ministerial Council For Artificial Intelligence & Development Reviews National Programmes, Updates On Government Work
stories.Summary:
Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE Vice President and Deputy Prime Minister, chaired a meeting of the Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development in Abu Dhabi on November 9, 2026. The session was held as part of the UAE Government Annual Meetings 2026 and reviewed a range of national programmes and updates on government operations. Ministers examined progress on initiatives tied to artificial intelligence and digital transformation. The meeting also turned to national priorities, including Emiratization, the labour market, energy, investment, the environment and biodiversity, national data and statistics, and other strategic sectors.

The agenda included proposed public policies and regulations on the quality of higher education institutions, pharmaceuticals and medical products, and the tax system. Ministers also discussed development proposals meant to make the government workforce more efficient and to strengthen the federal government's public finances. Sheikh Mansour stressed the value of integrated work between federal and local authorities in launching and carrying out regulations and government projects. He said the aim is to raise efficiency across all sectors and to improve government services for citizens, residents and the business community. The articles do not give figures, deadlines or the specific content of the proposed rules.

Sheikh Mansour is the chairman of the council and presided over the session. His comments, as reported by the Emirates News Agency, centred on federal-local cooperation and service quality. The articles describe the meeting as a review rather than a decision point, and they do not say when any proposed policy or regulation would be adopted or take effect. Further steps on the programmes and proposals discussed were not detailed in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Ministerial Council For Artificial Intelligence & Development Reviews National Programmes, Updates On Government Work - UrduPoint

stories.Headline: The Power Behind AI Pays a Dividend: 3 Utility ETFs Yielding Up to 2.77%
stories.Summary:
Three utility exchange-traded funds are drawing attention as data centers built for artificial intelligence push U.S. electricity demand higher, and the funds let income investors own the companies that supply that power. The funds named are the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLU), the Fidelity MSCI Utilities Index ETF (FUTY) and the iShares U.S. Utilities ETF (IDU). As of November 9, 2026, their trailing yields range from 2.3% to 2.8%. The article also notes that their one-year returns have been much smoother than the AI headlines would suggest.

The U.S. Department of Energy projects that data centers could account for up to 12% of U.S. electrical demand by 2028, driven by AI development, a figure the Government Accountability Office reported in its study of space-based data centers. Colorado Legislative Council Staff note that a single operating data center can consume over a gigawatt, enough to power approximately 750,000 homes. Regulated utilities earn returns that state regulators set, so more demand means more approved spending on plants and power lines. Independent power producers sell electricity at market prices, so their profits rise more directly with tight supply but their earnings are more volatile.

The article attributes the demand analysis to the Department of Energy, the Government Accountability Office and Colorado Legislative Council Staff, and it describes the regulated and independent business models without assigning blame to any company. It says Constellation Energy, cited in its third-quarter 2026 earnings disclosure, pointed to a 20-year, 690 MW power agreement with a cloud provider tied to its Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant. It also cites a second 20-year agreement with another technology company tied to nuclear uprates, which add capacity to existing reactors. The article adds that electric vehicle adoption, onshoring of manufacturing and electrification of industry and buildings also drive demand.

The article describes XLU as the most liquid of the three funds, with $23.1 billion in net assets as of June 30, 2026, and a 0.08% gross expense ratio in its September 30, 2026 fact sheet. It reports that NextEra Energy made up 13% of that fund as of June 30, 2026, and that NextEra's pending combination with another top-ten holding is expected to close in the second half of 2027. FUTY, with 64 positions and $2.3 billion in net assets as of its July 31, 2026 filing, reaches into smaller utilities and an early-stage nuclear company. IDU, with a 0.37% net expense ratio and a 2.3% trailing yield, posted the strongest one-year return of the three at 3%. The article also warns that interest rates, heavy spending on plants and lines, regulators' decisions on cost recovery, and rising customer bills could weigh on these funds, and that yields are neither fixed nor guaranteed.

Articles.Title: The Power Behind AI Pays a Dividend: 3 Utility ETFs Yielding Up to 2.77% - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: Japan to boost AI budget by 60%, EU pushes 45 trillion won investment… Advanced nations race in AI investment
stories.Summary:
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry has requested about 1.99 trillion yen, roughly 16.9 trillion won, for AI, semiconductors, and robotics in its fiscal year 2027 budget request. That figure is an increase of about 60 percent over this year's base budget. The request puts particular emphasis on physical AI, in which AI directly controls robots and machines. Some projects that had been funded through supplementary budgets were also moved into the base budget, which added to the increase.

Japan aims to provide more than 10 trillion yen, about 85 trillion won, in public support for AI and semiconductors by fiscal year 2030. The government hopes this will draw more than 50 trillion yen, about 425 trillion won, in public and private investment over 10 years. The European Union launched a competition in July to build up to seven AI Gigafactories, which are very large computing facilities built around advanced AI chips. The plan calls for the EU and its member states to contribute up to 10 billion euros while attracting at least 20 billion euros from private companies. That would bring total investment above 30 billion euros, about 45 trillion won.

France is focusing on attracting foreign capital, and it secured foreign investment commitments totaling 93 billion euros, about 141 trillion won, across 71 projects in June this year. The total includes sectors beyond AI. Of that amount, 45 billion euros, about 68 trillion won, is tied to a project by Japan's SoftBank to build three AI data centers with a combined capacity of 3.1 GW by 2031. In the United States, private companies lead large-scale AI infrastructure spending while the government funds research and development. The Stargate project, involving OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle, plans to invest up to 500 billion dollars, about 672 trillion won, in AI infrastructure over four years.

The Trump administration requested 1.2 billion dollars, about 1.6 trillion won, for the Department of Energy's AI science project, the Genesis Mission, in its fiscal year 2027 budget. The White House said in July that federal agencies have committed more than 5 billion dollars, about 6.7 trillion won, to support the mission. South Korea is also expanding its spending, and the Ministry of Science and ICT plans to raise its AI budget to 9.4 trillion won next year. An industry official said it is realistically difficult for South Korea to match the scale of American AI investment. The official argued that the country must concentrate its limited resources in areas where it can secure competitiveness and maximize investment efficiency.

Articles.Title: Japan to boost AI budget by 60%, EU pushes 45 trillion won investment… Advanced nations race in AI investment - 머니투데이

stories.Headline: Apple Makes Major AI Pricing Move as New Revenue Opportunity Emerges
stories.Summary:
Apple has introduced paid usage packs for subscribers who go past their monthly AI limits in its Creator Studio applications. The company, which is based in the United States and makes the iPhone, is trying to turn artificial intelligence into a direct source of revenue. The move was reported on November 9, 2026, by GuruFocus and republished by Yahoo Finance. It marks one of Apple's earliest attempts to charge directly for AI use inside its software.

The AI features cover several creative and productivity apps, including Keynote, Pages, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, Freeform and Logic Pro. They include image and shape generation, presentation creation, image enhancement and AI help for music production. Subscribers on the entry-level allowance can generate 50 images, 250 shapes and 50 presentations each month, along with presenter notes covering 700 slides. Customers who go beyond those limits can buy additional intelligence usage packs for $49.99. Apple said the feature is available to active Creator Studio subscribers in eight countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Germany and India.

Apple confirmed the change itself, and the article describes it as part of the company's broader AI strategy. The article also notes that Apple works with outside AI providers, including OpenAI and Google, to support some of these capabilities. Apple has not said how much revenue it expects from the packs or how many subscribers are likely to exceed their monthly allowances. The article links the change to the company's Services segment, which brought in $31.57 billion in its latest reported quarter.

The article presents the move as a test of whether customers will pay extra for AI features that competing software platforms increasingly offer. It says AI features carry computing and infrastructure costs, so the new revenue will only improve profitability if pricing covers those expenses. Investors are advised to watch Creator Studio subscriber growth, uptake of the usage packs and their contribution to Services revenue. The article does not say what Apple will do next beyond these existing plans.

Articles.Title: Apple Makes Major AI Pricing Move as New Revenue Opportunity Emerges

stories.Headline: SAP Expands Collaboration with AstraZeneca to Adopt RISE with SAP and Business AI
stories.Summary:
AstraZeneca, the global biopharmaceutical company, is migrating its full ERP estate to SAP Cloud ERP Private through the RISE with SAP journey, SAP SE announced on November 10, 2026. The move expands a relationship that has lasted more than 20 years and extends one of the largest SAP footprints in life sciences. The company is carrying out the change through its Axial Business Transformation Programme, which moves it away from legacy SAP ERP Central Component environments. The aim is a simpler, more standardized technology landscape that the companies say will make AstraZeneca more agile and resilient.

The migration is meant to support more standardized ways of working, harmonized data and connected processes across the enterprise. AstraZeneca is also exploring several business AI capabilities from SAP, including the Industry AI portfolio, the Joule solution and agentic use cases across finance, supply chain and manufacturing. According to the announcement, these tools could improve productivity, strengthen data quality and governance, and speed up decision-making. SAP Business Data Cloud could help the company build a clean data core by bringing together disparate data sets, while SAP Green Ledger could link sustainability data with business data across its value chain. The articles do not give figures for cost, timing of individual phases or the number of sites affected.

AstraZeneca's Chief Information Officer, Chris Taylor, said SAP has been central to the company's operations for more than two decades and described the next phase as more than a technology upgrade. He said Axial is meant to simplify how the company operates and lay the groundwork to move faster and gain more value from AI. SAP's Chief Customer Officer and Executive Board member, Thomas Saueressig, said the Axial programme shows how cloud, data and AI can support innovation at scale in life sciences. He said the work is intended to help simplify operations, enable faster decisions and unlock trusted insights.

The announcement places the deal within a wider push across life sciences and healthcare to rethink how technology manages complexity. The release is a company announcement and does not describe any regulatory review, pricing terms or timeline beyond the migration being under way. It notes that it was created with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by SAP's editorial team. Further details on the programme's progress would come from the companies, and the articles do not specify any next milestones.

Articles.Title: SAP Expands Collaboration with AstraZeneca to Adopt RISE with SAP and Business AI

stories.Headline: FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy
stories.Summary:
FedEx said on November 9 that it is adding four weekly Boeing 777 freighter flights between China and the United States. Three of the flights will leave Shanghai, stop in Osaka, and continue to Anchorage and Memphis, while the fourth will run from Guangzhou to the same two hubs. The carrier said the extra capacity is aimed at advanced industrial manufacturing, semiconductor production, AI infrastructure and high-end e-commerce. The added service is a small move, but it offers a view of where US-China trade demand is concentrated.

The sectors FedEx named matter because air freight is the preferred route for high-value, time-sensitive goods such as chips, servers and networking equipment. Economists expect China's October trade data, due on Tuesday, to show exports up about a third from a year earlier in dollar terms, with demand for AI hardware a central driver. The Osaka routing also points to close links in Asian supply chains for AI components, with Japan a key source of semiconductor materials and production equipment. Trade is likely to come up when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in mid-November.

The backdrop is mixed. US AI stocks sold off sharply last week on concerns that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could bring new limits on data centre construction, raising questions about how fast the build-out will proceed. A logistics company adding capacity aimed at AI infrastructure suggests that, for now, demand for that hardware is still moving. The article describes the announcement as a modest but real-world signal that the Asia-to-US AI supply chain remains busy, even as investors debate how long the spending boom can last.

Articles.Title: FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy

stories.Headline: Rising laptop prices add to college expenses as AI companies compete for computer chips
stories.Summary:
Rising laptop prices are adding to the cost of college for students finishing their applications, as AI companies compete with other buyers for memory chips. According to research firm IDC, AI companies building large data centers need significant quantities of chips and materials, which makes it harder for makers of everyday electronics to get the supplies they need. As a result, laptops and personal devices are becoming more expensive. The Classic reported that the increase has reached students directly, with the class of 2027 weighing the cost of a machine meant to last four years.

Apple's most affordable laptop, the MacBook Neo, launched in March at $599, or $499 with education pricing. According to Reuters, Apple raised its regular price to $699 in June because of rising memory costs tied to competition from AI data centers. MacRumors reported on October 28 that the education price had risen again, to $649. IDC has said companies including Lenovo, Dell, HP, Acer, and ASUS have warned of price increases of 15% to 20% as demand for computer components grows. The article makes clear these increases extend well beyond Apple.

Students interviewed by The Classic described how the higher prices affect their plans. Senior Yahan Zhang said she would look for monthly payment options if her preferred MacBook rose in price, since she will need a computer for college assignments. Senior Janae-Saige Moore said she would consider an iPad with a keyboard and argued that students should spend roughly $500 to $800 on a device. Senior Daniel Maleki said laptops around $500 would be reasonable, especially for students in tech-related majors, and he would consider used devices. Freshman Adrian Perezguaman warned that rising prices could disadvantage lower-income families when so much coursework requires a computer.

Articles.Title: Rising laptop prices add to college expenses as AI companies compete for computer chips - thhsclassic.com

stories.Headline: Opinion: Free AI for Teachers Sets a Dangerous Precedent
stories.Summary:
Chris Rose, co-founder of the K-12 data platform Abre and a former high school math teacher, published an opinion piece on GovTech on November 9, 2026, arguing that free AI tools aimed at teachers, such as Claude for Teachers and ChatGPT for Teachers, create a risky precedent for schools. He notes that these tools promise to save educators time on everyday tasks, which is appealing to teachers facing heavy administrative loads and shrinking planning periods. However, he contends that access alone does not ensure responsible use and that adoption without clear guidance, training and oversight can threaten student privacy, data quality and district accountability. The piece was published in the K-12 Education section of the site and is framed as an opinion rather than a news report. Rose argues that AI is advancing faster than many district policies and professional development programs can keep up with, leaving teachers to make decisions that should be backed by consistent rules.

He points to a teacher who might upload student grades, attendance records or behavioral data into an AI tool to spot patterns, and asks where that information goes, how long it is kept, who can access it and whether it could train a model. He says districts must check whether vendor practices meet obligations under laws such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, rather than assuming every tool suits every use. He also warns about AI hallucinations, noting that inaccurate output could mislead decisions such as whether a child should be evaluated for an Individualized Education Program. Rose stresses that AI should never be treated as the authority on a student's needs.

Rather than calling for a ban, Rose says the priority should be setting conditions for responsible use. He recommends that districts identify approved tools, define permitted uses, clarify what information staff may share and train educators to verify AI outputs and recognize limitations. He says technology leaders should review vendor data practices, access controls, retention policies and contracts, with decisions involving administrators, educators, IT teams and legal counsel instead of individual teachers. He also favors systems that connect to approved district data sources and enforce role-based permissions, so staff need not export records into separate chatbots.

Rose additionally urges vendors to show that their products truly reduce workloads or improve outcomes. Rose frames his argument as a call to match innovation with safety, saying adoption rates alone are not a meaningful measure of progress and that students, teachers and districts each need protections and tools they can trust. The article does not describe any specific incident, enforcement action or scheduled policy change, so it does not report what will happen next beyond the author's recommendations. Rose closes by writing that student data should never be the price of experimentation.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Free AI for Teachers Sets a Dangerous Precedent - GovTech

stories.Headline: SPH Media looks to plug into AI channels without losing its place in the news
stories.Summary:
SPH Media, the Singapore publisher, is seeking a place in the channels through which people increasingly find news rather than trying to resist artificial intelligence, according to executive chairman Chan Yeng Kit. He has voiced concern that publishers could lose their role between reporting and audiences if AI services become a main route to information. The article, published on 9 November 2026 by Tomorrow's Publisher, frames this as part of a wider shift in which news organisations have depended on technology platforms for distribution. Earlier reliance on search and social media left publishers exposed when platform priorities changed, and AI services that summarise journalism may add to that pressure. The risk is that readers take in information without visiting or recognising the outlets that produced it.

SPH Media's response includes a partnership with Google meant to extend the reach of its journalism through Google's channels. The partnership also aims to strengthen newsroom capabilities in areas including generative AI verification and AI-enabled workflows. The two companies have named talent development and audience engagement as areas of cooperation. The article stresses that these are stated aims, and that their practical effect on publisher control and sustainable revenue remains uncertain. Alongside this, the Chinese-language publication Lianhe Zaobao has launched an English-language website using AI-assisted translation with human proofreading and editing.

The initiative is meant to reach younger readers and other language communities while keeping its Chinese-language edition. Malay and Tamil offerings are expected to be considered progressively as the operation develops. Chan has argued that technology can extend the audience for existing journalism but that reporting still depends on people's ability to build trust, draw out personal accounts and make editorial decisions. The article cites the Associated Press, whose standards say AI may assist newsroom work but does not replace journalists' responsibility for gathering and assessing facts.

Staff must verify AI-generated material and remain accountable for published work. ProPublica is also quoted as saying AI-assisted journalism must receive human review and meet the newsroom's usual editorial standards. The article notes that the tools and their effects are still developing, leaving publishers to balance access to new distribution systems against the risk of becoming less visible to audiences. SPH Media presents its approach as adaptation, alongside investment in a range of products and the fundamentals of journalism.

Articles.Title: SPH Media looks to plug into AI channels without losing its place in the news

stories.Headline: Stop Trusting the Model:The CISO Playbook for an AI Enforcement Layer - IDC | Trusted Tech Intelligence
stories.Summary:
The article is an IDC CISO playbook, published November 9, 2026, arguing that organizations cannot rely on AI providers' own safety measures and need an enforcement layer outside the model. It describes the current environment as one where more than 12 frontier AI developers have published voluntary safety frameworks with widely varying thresholds, inconsistent evaluation cadences, and no independent verification requirement. It also notes that the EU AI Act's maximum fine for general-purpose AI providers, 3% of global annual turnover or €15 million whichever is higher, became enforceable on August 2, 2026, and that an autonomous coding agent ran unsupervised for about a week before its developer identified and attributed it. The author's central point is that system prompts, safety tuning, and content filters sit inside the same model environment they are meant to police, so they can be bypassed through prompt injection or similar techniques.

The article recommends an enforcement layer modeled on a content delivery network and web application firewall, placed outside the model with no network path to the model's policy engine, audit store, or configuration. It lists five required control layers: identity and access, request inspection, policy enforcement as code, response mediation, and immutable audit with a kill switch. Each model or agent should hold its own scoped identity, and the kill switch should operate at session, user or application, and full deployment grains without the model provider's cooperation. The article also describes a hub-and-spoke gateway design and names four gaps CISOs should assess, including chain-level risk, fail-open behavior under load, incomplete inventory coverage, and limited visibility into traffic beyond the MCP protocol.

The author places responsibility for this architecture on the CISO and on the organization's own procurement and governance, not on the model vendors, whose assurances the article says cannot carry the risk alone. The piece calls for a 90-day plan covering vendor architecture diagrams, inventories of models and agents, provider scoring against five dimensions, and a set of 25 enforcement requirements plus five contract terms to embed in vendor agreements. It also proposes a 26th requirement, R26, addressing advance notice of model updates that change behavior in policy-sensitive areas. The article does not report any enforcement action or regulatory decision tied to these recommendations, and it describes no specific next event beyond the renewal and rehearsal cycles it recommends.

Articles.Title: Stop Trusting the Model:The CISO Playbook for an AI Enforcement Layer - IDC | Trusted Tech Intelligence

stories.Headline: Google AI school policy
stories.Summary:
Google has announced that, in the coming months, Google Search and its Gemini chatbot will be turned off by default for schools, and will only be available to schools that opt in to artificial intelligence. The Los Angeles Unified School District said it is reviewing the announcement and what it means for schools, educators and students. Earlier this school year, the district had already barred students from using generative AI on district-issued devices. Currently, students can still search with Google, but the AI chat mode is off. Its Ad Hoc Committee on Generative AI meets on November 13.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, said search and AI are deeply integrated, so a school that bans AI would lose access to search. Google has said schools should control AI in their classrooms, and it plans a "guided learning" tool for student accounts in schools that opt in. Advocates have objected sharply, with Lila Byock of Schools Beyond Screens urging district leaders to divest from Google. The district has also asked Google to let schools turn off AI-generated search summaries.

In a separate matter, the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority told staff on Friday to stop work, shut down their computers and stay off agency systems while it looked into a potential security issue. Interim CEO Gita O'Neill said the agency did not yet know whether sensitive personal information had been accessed. The shutdown was still in place Monday evening, and the agency said it had hired outside cybersecurity specialists. The agency holds sensitive records on people experiencing homelessness, including Social Security numbers and health histories. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Martinsville school board to consider optional AI policy for classroom use - WSET

stories.Headline: What Midterm Elections Could Mean for Texas Tech and AI
stories.Summary:
Seven Democrats won Texas statewide executive and regulatory races on November 3, 2026, according to the secretary of state's latest returns, and their arrival could shift policy on artificial intelligence, procurement, cybersecurity and infrastructure. The winners are Gina Hinojosa for governor, Vikki Goodwin for lieutenant governor, Nathan Johnson for attorney general, Sarah Eckhardt for comptroller, Benjamin Flores for land commissioner, Clayton Tucker for agriculture commissioner and Jon Rosenthal for railroad commissioner. The results still await formal canvassing and certification, though all seven hold leads in the reported totals. The officials take office ahead of the 2027 legislative session, when they can pursue their agendas through legislation, regulatory action and agency administration. Data centers emerged as a common focus across several of the incoming officials' proposals.

Goodwin has called for a pause on new data center construction until the Legislature sets rules on water use, electricity demand and community impacts, and she supports reporting requirements, requiring developers to cover infrastructure costs and ending the state's sales tax exemption for qualifying facilities. Tucker and Eckhardt have also backed a statewide moratorium, and Tucker wants agricultural impact studies. Rosenthal instead proposes resource planning coordinated with local governments, which he believes should be able to reject projects. Johnson, for his part, plans a review of consumer protection, competition and employment laws in his first 30 days to see how automated systems affect pricing and hiring.

Each official has described his or her own plan, and the articles note that the authority to carry them out varies. Goodwin presides over the Senate and would help decide which bills advance there. Tucker's agriculture office does not directly regulate data center construction, so broader permit limits would need other authorities to act. Rosenthal will sit on the three-member Railroad Commission with two Republicans, and because decisions need a majority, he would need at least one of them to support regulatory changes.

Flores, who has a cybersecurity and compliance background, wants to review Land Office cybersecurity, contracts and disaster recovery spending, while Eckhardt proposes a web dashboard for state finances and a review of tax incentives and no-bid contracts. The broader context is that Texas already has an artificial intelligence law, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, which took effect January 1, and the attorney general's office enforces it. The comptroller's office oversees non-IT purchasing and houses the Texas Broadband Development Office, while the Department of Information Resources manages statewide technology contracts. The articles say the proposals would be taken up during the 2027 legislative session, but they do not say which measures will pass, so the outcome remains open.

Articles.Title: What Midterm Elections Could Mean for Texas Tech and AI - GovTech

stories.Headline: Assessing the Opportunities and Risks of AI in Elections
stories.Summary:
Kompas.id published an analysis on November 10, 2026, examining the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in elections, drawing on findings presented at the Habibie Democracy Forum in Jakarta on November 3, 2026. The article reports that the Association for Elections and Democracy (Perludem) found AI is accelerating misinformation through low-cost, emotionally charged content that builds echo chambers. It notes that the Southeast Asia Freedom of Expression Network (SAFENet) also described Indonesia's digital democracy as vulnerable to attacks, rights violations, and distortion of facts. The piece points to the 2024 elections, when several candidates reportedly used AI-generated avatars and campaign content, some of which Perludem says contained misinformation.

The article says the existing election rules cover only conventional campaign methods such as public meetings, limited gatherings, and print and electronic advertisements, and do not specifically regulate AI use in campaigning. It also notes that Constitutional Court decision Number 166/PUU-XXI/2023, issued in early 2025, explicitly prohibited excessive alteration of candidates' self-image using AI, but does not say how that practice should be regulated or minimized. Perludem, according to the article, sees the revision of the Election Law as an opening for lawmakers to address AI use, including its use to gauge public sentiment on social media. The International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA) is cited as recommending that electoral bodies rethink how they monitor and report campaign advertising. The article also describes Ireland's labeling requirement for AI-generated campaign content, which falls on content users rather than producers, and Denmark's approach, while noting that such rules add to election officials' workload.

Speakers at the forum are quoted as holding these views. Heroik Mutaqin Pratama, executive director of Perludem, said AI, though meant to bring efficiency, in practice affects citizens' political rights and lacks adequate institutional and regulatory frameworks. Nenden Sekar Arum, executive director of SAFENet, reported that young people in several cities described democracy in Indonesia with words such as "regressive," "toxic," and "emergency," citing digital attacks, buzzers, and online violence. The article also quotes Leah Henrickson, a lecturer at the University of Queensland, who argues in her academic work that AI is never neutral because it reflects human intentions that can entrench power imbalances.

Articles.Title: Assessing the Opportunities and Risks of AI in Elections - Kompas.id

stories.Headline: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying
stories.Summary:
Shannon Vallor, a professor of ethics of data and artificial intelligence at the University of Edinburgh, published a reading list on Nautilus on November 9, 2026, recommending ten books as a response to what she calls the current wave of AI doomsaying. She describes doom predictions as everywhere, spreading from the media into everyday conversation and shaping how people think about the future. The list is organized as five pairs of fiction and nonfiction titles, each chosen to offer a vision of how broken situations can be repaired rather than how the world ends. Vallor says the books are meant to help readers think about the future and technology with more love, courage and wisdom.

Vallor is clear that she does not dismiss the risks. She says today's AI technologies are dangerous to human agency, to self-understanding, to relationships, to people's ability to think for themselves, and to prospects for living sustainably. Her case rests on the distinction between doomsaying and calls to action. Doomsaying, she argues, produces decision paralysis, apathy and resignation, while calls to action restore a sense of agency, purpose and moral urgency. She notes that her own book, The AI Mirror, published in 2024, comes from the same concern that reasonable fears cannot be avoided by looking away from them.

The selections include Imagining AI, edited by Stephen Cave and Kanta Dihal, which gathers essays on AI from many regions, and Becky Chambers's A Psalm for the Wild-Built, a gentle story about humans and machines learning when to stop. Vallor pairs Adam Becker's Everything Forever with N.K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season, and Carissa Véliz's Prophecy with Samuel Butler's Erewhon. Other picks include Ruha Benjamin's Imagination, Ursula K. Le Guin's The Lathe of Heaven, David Karpf's Vaporware, Inc, due in 2027, and Neal Stephenson's The Diamond Age. Vallor characterizes Karpf's book as a critique of "digital futurism," a pattern of promised technological abundance that she says keeps failing to arrive.

Articles.Title: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying

stories.Headline: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
stories.Summary:
Nominal, a four-year-old Austin-based startup that makes an AI platform for engineering and testing complex hardware such as aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has tripled its valuation to $3 billion. The company announced on Monday that it raised a $240 million Series C, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners. The round follows a $155 million Series B extension announced in March at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens of Founders Fund. That earlier deal was a preemptive offer, meaning the investor initiated it rather than the startup. Other backers include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.

Nominal says it counts 80 commercial and government organizations as customers, including Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. In October, the U.S. Air Force selected Nominal for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase, known as STRATFI, a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force. The article does not say what the matching funds must total or how that requirement will be met. The funding is aimed at helping the company expand its work with the military and other large buyers of complex hardware. The article does not provide further details on how the money will be deployed.

Nominal's chief executive and co-founder, Cameron McCord, is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer who previously worked at Anduril. The company's rapid rise in valuation reflects strong investor interest in AI tools for building and testing physical systems, a category that sits alongside software for defense and industrial customers. The article does not describe any plans for future rounds, public offerings, or product launches. It also does not indicate whether the valuation increase signals changes in the company's revenue or headcount. The story was reported by TechCrunch's Julie Bort, and the information comes from the company's announcement and the investors involved.

Articles.Title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months

stories.Headline: Trump Says White House Warned a Top AI CEO: Go Home, Kiss Your Family, 'You're Going to Jail'
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump said his administration once warned the head of a major artificial intelligence company that he would be going to jail, according to a CBS "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday night. Trump recounted that his team received a report that someone was doing something bad with AI, and he described telling the executive to go home, kiss his family goodnight, because he would be jailed the next morning. He declined to name the person or company, saying only that the leader ran one of the big AI firms, and he said the conduct was not malicious. The White House and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The episode arrives amid a broader push over AI oversight. On September 29, 2026, Trump convened executives from OpenAI, Nvidia, Anthropic, Meta, xAI and Google to sign a voluntary, one-page safety accord covering internal controls, outside evaluations and board oversight, which carries no penalties. Trump called it "morally binding" and "almost like a constitution." On November 5, the Justice Department announced a Super Intelligence Task Force, led by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss, to coordinate criminal and civil cases against foreign state actors and individuals or companies engaged in unlawful AI-related conduct.

Trump has previously named Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in social media posts, though it is unclear whether those posts referred to the same episode. Trump has argued that federal agencies can handle AI safety risks, which he described as overblown, and he opposes strict rules out of concern about competition with China. He said he does not mind guardrails but does not want the United States in a second position, adding that China has none. Democratic Senator Mark Warner of Virginia criticized the accord as replacing law with self-policing and called for mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting.

Voters in dozens of local ballot measures recently rejected new data-center projects, and candidates promising tighter AI oversight won races, as Democrats prepare to take the congressional majority. The remarks carry weight for investors because they suggest how the administration might treat compliance failures while AI companies spend billions on data centers. A threat of criminal liability, even one described only anecdotally, raises the stakes for lab leaders working under commitments that lack enforcement mechanisms. The articles indicate that federal oversight is likely to remain light unless Congress acts, given the president's resistance to binding rules.

Articles.Title: Trump Says White House Warned a Top AI CEO: Go Home, Kiss Your Family, 'You're Going to Jail' - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth
stories.Summary:
New malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER, uncovered by researchers at Cisco Talos, steals data from Windows computers and then uses artificial intelligence to rank victims by how valuable they might be to criminals. The malware collects saved browser passwords, payment card details, login sessions, cryptocurrency wallet information and certain work-related credentials. It also gathers saved Wi-Fi passwords, screenshots and information from applications such as Microsoft Outlook and Slack. The findings were reported in an article published on November 9, 2026, by Fox News.

The stolen information is sent to an AI model through a platform called OpenRouter, which is instructed to act like an intelligence analyst. The model is asked to produce a section titled "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH," assigning low, medium or high rankings to valuable information. A second section, "THEIR OPSEC," examines the victim's security habits, including password practices. The malware can also search Gmail receipts and order histories from services such as Uber Eats, DoorDash, Grubhub, Amazon and Walmart to help confirm a victim's home address. Researchers say the AI analysis is optional, and the malware can still send the data to attackers if that step fails.

Cisco Talos found that the malware uses Anthropic's Claude as its default AI model, with Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash as fallbacks if a model refuses the request. The resulting assessment can be sent to criminals through Telegram. The article notes that researchers identified these capabilities by analyzing the malware's code and have not established that criminals have used the AI rankings to choose real-world victims for further attacks. The malware can also delete its main executable after finishing, though it may leave a diagnostic file called volta_debug.txt behind that records what was collected and whether the AI analysis succeeded.

Articles.Title: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth

stories.Headline: Israel aims to develop its own AI model amid concerns over foreign dependence
stories.Summary:
Israel's top AI official has unveiled a national plan to build its own advanced AI model and expand domestic computing capacity, citing concern that the country depends too heavily on foreign technology firms. The announcement came on Monday from Brig. Gen. (res.) Erez Askal, head of the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office, who spoke at AI & Cyber Week at Tel Aviv University.

He warned that within five to seven years, essential services such as electricity, water and health care could rely heavily on AI systems run by commercial providers whose interests may not match those of the governments they serve. Askal also said governments cannot be certain that access to foreign AI services will remain uninterrupted. The strategy centers on what Askal called "AI sovereignty," meaning control over the critical parts of the technology and infrastructure rather than producing every component locally. He said Israel would need roughly 2 gigawatts of electricity capacity to support AI computing facilities, data centers and semiconductor manufacturing, which he compared to the output of two large power plants. The country also aims for about 300,000 graphics processing units, the specialized chips used to train and run advanced AI systems.

Of those, about 100,000 would serve domestic needs such as universities, government agencies, the military and startups, while the remaining 200,000 would support technology companies and commercial data centers. Askal gave no budget or timetable for these targets. The government has also issued a tender for an Israeli-built national quantum computer, though the article notes that quantum computing is still an emerging field. A central element is a nationally controlled foundation model, the underlying AI technology behind chatbots, digital assistants and automated systems.

Askal argued that open-source models do not yet consistently match the leading proprietary systems, and he expressed concern that access to some models could become more restricted. He suggested Israel could build such a model with allied countries facing similar challenges, saying, in his words, that the country does not have to build it alone. Beyond security, the government has created the National Institute for Impact-Driven AI, known as NIA, to promote applications in health care, education and transportation. Askal also pointed to Israel's cybersecurity expertise and to "physical AI," which links artificial intelligence with machines and sensors, as areas where the country already has strengths.

Askal framed the plan as a response to these pressures but did not present it as a settled commitment with defined costs or dates. He said the government will promote retraining and skills development alongside schools, universities and the military, and he pointed to "Beyond Intelligence," an initiative launched last week at the President's Residence to encourage public debate about AI's effects on society. At the same conference, Prof. Isaac Ben-Israel, chairman of Tel Aviv University's Blavatnik Interdisciplinary Cyber Research Center and Cyber Week, said AI and cybersecurity are now closely linked, and that more autonomous AI agents add new risks. Whether Israel can secure the electricity, hardware, investment and partnerships it needs remains unresolved, though Askal said, "Countries that act will retain control, and Israel has decided to act."

Articles.Title: Israel aims to develop its own AI model amid concerns over foreign dependence

stories.Headline: AI Model Accurately Estimates Pediatric Chest Circumference From Single Frontal Photographs
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence pipeline can estimate the chest circumference of children with microtia from a single frontal photograph, according to a single-center observational diagnostic-accuracy study published in the European Journal of Medical Research. The article reports that the approach combines keypoint detection with a geometric model to produce the measurement without contact. Researchers from the study team tested the method on a group of 500 children, split evenly between boys and girls, and compared its estimates with reference measurements taken by trained personnel. Accurate measurement of the subxiphoid chest circumference is needed for clinical assessment and treatment planning in children with microtia.

Conventional tape measurement requires an in-person visit and can suffer from site errors when untrained caregivers perform it. The researchers used a YOLO11-pose model to locate bilateral chest points in one frontal photograph, then applied a Ramanujan ellipse model that sets chest depth at 0.75 times width. A lateral view was used only to check chest depth. The cohort was divided into 400 cases for development and a locked test set of 100 cases.

In the locked test set, the pipeline reported a mean absolute error of 0.938 cm, a root mean squared error of 1.193 cm, and a median absolute error of 0.80 cm, with a mean bias of −0.127 cm. Estimates fell within 2 cm, 3 cm, and 5 cm of reference values in 93.0%, 99.0%, and 100% of cases, and the Pearson correlation was 0.935. At a 60-cm threshold, sensitivity was 87.3%, specificity was 100.0%, and overall accuracy was 90.0%. Error was somewhat higher in overweight or obese children, at 1.025 cm, than in normal-weight children, at 0.897 cm.

The authors, led by X. Li and colleagues, state that automated landmark detection reduces site error by non-medical users. They cautioned, however, that all photographs were taken under controlled conditions, so the reported performance may not carry over directly to in-home use, and that larger cohorts are needed for further validation. The article does not describe any clinical rollout or next steps beyond that validation. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Model Accurately Estimates Pediatric Chest Circumference From Single Frontal Photographs

stories.Headline: Some school board members push back against Google's AI search ultimatum - The Frederick News-Post
stories.Summary:
Some Frederick County school board members have pushed back against a recent Google announcement that it will cut off Google search access to schools that have banned AI. The announcement, reported by the Associated Press and published on November 10, 2026, is aimed at school districts that have restricted artificial intelligence tools. The articles do not say exactly when Google's cutoff would take effect or how many districts it would affect. What is clear is that the policy has drawn sharp reactions from local educators.

Board President Dean Rose said Monday that the board will not bend to what he called Google's "strong-arm tactic," and he noted that schools losing Google search would not be left without options because "they are not the only search engine on the market." Rose's comments were reported as part of the board's public response. The articles also quote a Google spokesperson, who indicated that the company views its AI tools as a way to help students, though the excerpt provided is partly garbled and does not give a full statement. The school board's position is that its decisions about AI use belong with the district, not the company.

Frederick County Public Schools has restricted AI in classrooms, and the district's leaders say they will continue to make those decisions for their students. The articles do not say whether the district has taken any formal step beyond these public statements, such as filing a complaint or changing its search provider. Other school boards, including one in Nevada whose president, Melissa Frank, reportedly criticized the company, have also spoken against the policy, according to the Associated Press report. The articles do not indicate whether Google plans to revisit the policy or how the dispute will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Some school board members push back against Google's AI search ultimatum - The Frederick News-Post

stories.Headline: Kolmar Korea's AI lip maker wins top CES beauty award
stories.Summary:
Kolmar Korea, a South Korean beauty company, has won three innovation awards at CES 2027 for two AI-powered devices, including the top Best of Innovation Award in the beauty tech category. The honor went to ChromaFlow, a system that creates personalized lip colors in about one minute. The company's skin care device, LumiJet Pro, also earned an Innovation Award in the artificial intelligence category. The Korea Herald reported the news on November 10, 2026.

ChromaFlow uses AI sensors to assess a user's lips and determine a customized color based on their natural lip tone. The system then blends pigments from seven color cartridges according to an AI-generated formula. LumiJet Pro analyzes skin condition and thickness before delivering skin care ingredients through its NanoJet technology, which sprays ultrafine particles onto the skin. The device also uses specific wavelengths of light to help disperse those ingredients.

Kolmar Korea developed the nanoparticle formulation used in the device. The recognition marks the second consecutive year that Kolmar Korea has won the top Beauty Tech award. At CES 2026, its AI-powered Scar Beauty Device, designed for scar care and makeup coverage, received the same honor. A company official said the win recognizes its data-driven manufacturing technology, which connects the entire cosmetics production process through AI.

The official added that the company will keep developing its beauty tech platform using accumulated data. Kolmar Korea plans to build a beauty tech data platform using skin and color data collected through ChromaFlow, the Scar Beauty Device and Caiome, an AI-powered scalp analysis system. The platform is intended to connect skin analysis, personalized cosmetic formulation and manufacturing, allowing the company to expand its data-driven beauty services. The company will showcase ChromaFlow and LumiJet Pro at CES 2027, scheduled for January 6 to 9 at the Venetian Expo in Las Vegas.

Articles.Title: Kolmar Korea's AI lip maker wins top CES beauty award

stories.Headline: Calif. hospital system loses nearly $3M in elaborate AI fraud scheme
stories.Summary:
A California hospital system lost $2,968,497 in December 2024 to an international fraud scheme in which scammers allegedly used advanced artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys. Federal prosecutors announced the case on Friday, November 6, 2026, with the hospital system unnamed in the public filings. The unsealed indictment says the hospital was one of many companies worldwide defrauded of more than $129 million between 2024 and 2026. Other victims included a Missouri hospital system that lost $4.8 million, a Rhode Island bank that lost $2.7 million, and a British financial technology company that lost $11.6 million.

Three men, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, are accused of using AI-generated voices and images to pose as chief executives and lawyers, persuading employees to wire millions of dollars. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain in June and August, and Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. All three face seven federal charges, including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering, and extradition requests are still pending. The scheme reportedly began with fraudulent emails, sometimes sent through platforms such as DocuSign, asking staff to sign nondisclosure agreements for confidential transactions.

Prosecutors say the stolen money moved through accounts in nine countries, including China, Spain and the United Arab Emirates, before being converted into cryptocurrency. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald, in a statement, said the technology offers tremendous potential but that some people seek to use it for criminal goals. McDonald said the defendants abused advanced AI to impersonate real people and deceive corporate executives. Soall allegedly scripted a call he called "Lawyer Call," posing as a British attorney and discouraging victims from discussing the transactions with colleagues.

Prosecutors also allege Hazan helped launder the money and boasted of laundering more than $400 million over three years. The case shows how AI tools can make impersonation schemes more convincing to the employees targeted, and the charges reflect the government's effort to hold the alleged participants accountable across borders. The articles do not say whether the hospital system has been identified publicly or whether any of the stolen funds have been recovered. Next steps include the pending extradition requests and the court proceedings on the seven federal charges.

Articles.Title: Calif. hospital system loses nearly $3M in elaborate AI fraud scheme

stories.Headline: Culture is the new AI barrier: Why trust and adoption are more than technical challenges
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than a news report, so the article does not describe a discrete event with a clear sequence. Paul Solé, head of AI growth at Amdocs, wrote the piece for CIO.com, published on November 10, 2026, arguing that the main obstacles to adopting artificial intelligence in organizations are cultural as well as technical. He says business leaders are focused heavily on building the IT foundations for AI, such as provisioning computing resources, unifying data sources and modernizing security, but that employees must also learn to use the tools well and understand their role in emerging agentic processes. He describes two areas where trust is required: businesses need confidence that their infrastructure can scale, and employees need confidence that AI outputs are accurate as agents operate with growing independence.

The column proposes thinking about AI adoption in three layers: foundations, trust and adoption. Solé says foundations go beyond hardware, since enterprises must be able to trace what AI agents are doing, understand their decisions and govern those actions, including meeting regulatory obligations that vary by industry and region. He gives examples such as FINRA compliance in U.S. financial services and HIPAA in medical institutions. He argues the foundation should be flexible enough to change as AI evolves, and that human intervention thresholds should depend on risk, with low-risk processes possibly running without people and functions like insurance underwriting keeping a human making the final judgment. He cites a KPMG finding that only 19% of leaders believe their workforce is AI-ready.

Solé links trust to transparency and security. He cites a recent industry study reporting that 97% of executives have overridden AI decisions because of a lack of transparency into the reasoning behind them, and he says companies should make agents outline their thought process and actions. On security, he warns that AI can find and exploit vulnerabilities and that agents may break out of sandbox environments, and he recommends companies test their own networks with AI attacks and benchmark new agents against realistic scenarios. For adoption, he likens AI to a junior associate that needs guidance from domain experts, and he describes a continuous feedback loop in which professionals evaluate outputs and that knowledge feeds back into the system. The column does not describe any next steps or events beyond this argument.

Articles.Title: Culture is the new AI barrier: Why trust and adoption are more than technical challenges

stories.Headline: We Asked AI To Assess Stocks’ Fate If an AI Bubble Pops
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, and the article is an opinion and analysis piece rather than a report of an event with a clear set of actors and a timeline. Its main claim is that large language models are being asked to judge how exposed major stocks would be if an AI bubble bursts, and that their answers miss the wider economic damage such a collapse would cause. The authors, Cory Smith and Gary N. Smith, published the piece on mindmatters.ai on November 10, 2026. They ran the same prompt through five models, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Grok and Kimi K3, asking each to rate 20 companies on a scale of 1 to 10 for exposure to an AI bubble popping. Nvidia received the highest average score of 10, while Unilever, JNJ and Walmart and Costco scored lowest.

The article presents the scores in two tables, one for exposure ratings and one for financial measures such as trailing and forward price-to-earnings ratios, free cash flow, total yield and five-year beta coefficients. The authors say the LLM answers were generally consistent and sensible but that they focused on direct effects such as revenue shortfalls and barely considered how a broader economic downturn would hit stock prices. As an example, ChatGPT gave Home Depot an exposure score of 2 and JP Morgan a score of 2, yet when asked separately about a recession, it said a recession would likely have a large negative effect on both companies. The authors argue that a popped AI bubble would likely cause a major economic shock that would affect these firms regardless of their direct AI exposure. They also point to beta, which measures how strongly a stock moves with the overall market, and note that Amazon's beta of 1.50 is much higher than Microsoft's 1.04 even though Amazon's average exposure score was lower.

The authors also discuss OpenAI, which they say has never shown a profit and whose company insiders projected a cumulative cash burn of $278 billion over four years before reaching profitability in 2030. They cite an independent HSBC analysis estimating nearly $500 billion in cumulative losses by 2030, and note that OpenAI's recently delayed initial public offering suggests some investor skepticism. The article says the Federal Reserve is likely to cut interest rates to cushion any market fall, and that analysis should therefore weigh interest rate effects along with company-level figures. Its closing judgment is that LLM outputs remain shallow text prediction and that a useful analysis would need careful modeling beyond what these tools currently provide.

Articles.Title: We Asked AI To Assess Stocks’ Fate If an AI Bubble Pops

stories.Headline: McDonald’s AI Price-Fixing Suit Fuels Legal Risk Over Franchises
stories.Summary:
A proposed class action filed on October 2 accuses McDonald's Corp. of improperly using an algorithmic pricing tool to push its franchise restaurants toward higher menu prices. The complaint is described as one that is expected to prompt a wave of similar AI price-fixing cases involving franchisee relationships. Several similar cases have already been filed since then. The articles say the lawsuit heightens antitrust risks for companies that want to deploy this kind of technology.
