On November 2, Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Becca Balint demanded answers from McDonald's President and CEO Chris Kempczinski. Their letter asked how the company uses artificial intelligence to set prices. The articles present this request as a sign of growing political scrutiny of the issue. They do not describe any response from the company.

The articles attribute the allegations to the lawsuit's plaintiffs, who claim the company pressured franchisees into adopting the pricing tool. The articles do not include a company statement rejecting or addressing these claims. Kempczinski is named as the executive to whom the lawmakers directed their questions. Beyond that, the articles offer no further detail on who is responsible for the tool's design or use.

The broader context is a legal environment in which regulators and lawmakers are watching how companies use AI to set prices. The articles suggest that franchise arrangements could expose more companies to similar claims. They do not say what the court will decide or when. More to follow.

Articles.Title: McDonald’s AI Price-Fixing Suit Fuels Legal Risk Over Franchises

stories.Headline: AI has made applying for jobs impossible—and it’s harming us all
stories.Summary:
Brian McConnell, a longtime San Francisco tech worker, published an opinion piece on 48hills.org on November 9, 2026, arguing that AI has made job applications nearly futile. He describes how automated application bots flood employers with mass submissions, while applicant tracking systems powered by AI filter candidates out before any human reads their resumes. He says he has applied to more than 200 jobs in the past year without a single conversation with a person, that a colleague has sent around 500 applications without a callback, and that his only two interviews were conducted by AI bots. He also points to a Workday lawsuit alleging that its filtering algorithms exclude candidates based on age, race, and disability.

McConnell proposes a low-tech fix: companies would stop accepting online applications and require mailed or in-person submissions instead. He argues that this added friction would make mass automated applications economically unviable while showing employers that a candidate is a real person willing to make an effort. He suggests that some Bay Area employers could test the idea and publish the results, perhaps by mailing verification codes the way banks mail PINs. He says the change would not be costly for the system to adopt. He also notes that a Netflix localization role drew about 2,000 applicants from LinkedIn alone, and that by his math well over 90 percent of those were likely fake or poorly targeted.

McConnell places the problem within the wider history of the tech industry, which he says was once run by inventors and has since been taken over by financial engineers, with the AI boom centered in the Bay Area. He compares the current excitement over AI to the dot com boom, though he says the sums involved are far larger. He also argues that older workers, whom he describes as those over 45 in tech, face the greatest exposure and that friends' advice to simply "get a job" is unhelpful. The article does not describe any formal response from Workday or any employer, and it does not describe any plan by companies to adopt the proposed mail-in system.

Articles.Title: AI has made applying for jobs impossible—and it’s harming us all

stories.Headline: Findrix Launches AI Search Platform for Marketing Agencies
stories.Summary:
Findrix, an AI search visibility platform, announced on November 9, 2026 the launch of a platform built for marketing agencies. The product lets agencies offer their clients generative engine optimization, which means getting a brand named and recommended in AI answers, and run that work from a single Findrix account. The announcement was distributed as a paid press release through ACCESS Newswire from Wilmington, Delaware. The platform tracks each client across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, asking buyer questions several times per engine and attaching a confidence band to each rate. It converts the gaps it finds into website fixes, pages to write and correction letters to sites that state wrong facts.

Agencies can send client reports under their own name and logo and can work with client data inside ChatGPT and Claude through the Findrix MCP server. The company says agency packages are available through its team at findrix.ai/for-agencies. Yosif Merman, co-founder of Findrix, said clients often read falling traffic as a broken SEO strategy when buyers are instead getting answers from AI tools and not clicking through. Tom Wells, an AI search researcher and Findrix's Lead Research Advisor who developed the measurement method, argued that week-to-week swings in AI answers are often normal noise and that a niche baseline lets a brand be judged against its market. The launch adds a benchmark layer: Findrix measures each client against the brands in its own niche, and public benchmarks already cover about 64,000 businesses in 395 categories and cities through AI Rankings Australia, and 1,736 brands in 74 markets through Findrix Radar.

The release supports its case with outside figures. Pew Research Center found that users click a traditional result in 8% of visits when Google shows an AI summary, compared with 15% without one. A 2026 AgencyAnalytics survey of 494 agency professionals found that 66% said AI search is the top service clients ask them to add. The articles do not report independent results for the platform, and they do not say how many agencies or clients currently use it.

Articles.Title: Findrix Launches AI Search Platform for Marketing Agencies

stories.Headline: The AI Trade Looks Like It's Falling Apart. AMD's Earnings Delivered a Reality Check.
stories.Summary:
The AI trade has been under heavy pressure over the past month, with stocks falling after the U.S. midterm results, which saw Democrats win several key states while campaigning against AI data centers. Against that backdrop, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) reported its quarterly earnings, and the article describes them as a reality check amid the bearish wave. The company's data center segment sales almost doubled year over year, driven by record sales of graphics processing units and central processing units. AMD generated $13.4 billion in third-quarter revenue, which exceeded the high end of its guidance. The results also showed rising profit margins, with AMD reporting 95% year-over-year net income growth.

The article argues that demand for chips is still strengthening, and that AMD hinted at a stronger fourth quarter. Because GPUs require liquid cooling, AI racks, memory chips, and optical cables to come online, the article suggests that strong chip sales will drive spending on those other components as well. Nvidia reported similar results for its fiscal second quarter of 2027 and is set to report its third-quarter results on November 17. The author, Marc Guberti of The Motley Fool, says the fundamentals remain strong even though the stock market has reacted negatively. He points to financing concerns and the midterm results as sources of investor anxiety, and he notes that the market is rushing to the sidelines.

He also cites a projection from tech bull Dan Ives that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta Platforms will exceed $1 trillion in capital expenditures in 2027. He adds that Micron expects its fiscal 2027 to be better than its fiscal 2026. The article also reports that CNN's Fear and Greed Index shows a "Fear" rating, which signals prolonged selling pressure. The author says that news cycles dominate short-term thinking, while fundamentals prevail over the long run. The piece does not say what the stock market will do next, and it notes that the next key data point is the U.S. CPI report due November 10, 2026, at 8:30 AM EST.

Articles.Title: The AI Trade Looks Like It's Falling Apart. AMD's Earnings Delivered a Reality Check.

stories.Headline: China touts tech, AI cred at world Web Summit
stories.Summary:
China is using the Web Summit in Lisbon, which opens its program on Tuesday, to showcase its technology and artificial intelligence sector. The event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, said at Monday's opening ceremony that the future's leading figures are increasingly coming from China rather than California. Organizers expect at least 70,000 participants from 164 countries, including 10,000 startups and 1,500 investors, at the conference, which runs until Thursday. Chinese firms are showing off dancing and tai chi-performing humanoid robots, along with low-cost AI models.

The Chinese presence includes speakers from more than 50 leading AI labs, robotics startups, carmakers, quantum computing startups and energy startups. Among them are Tao Zhang of Manus AI, who is due to demonstrate Manus 2.0, an agent that can carry out a sequence of tasks on its own. Representatives from the robotics firms Unitree and Agibot will speak, while Galbot and Ubtech Robotics plan to demonstrate their humanoid robots. Pony.ai, Xpeng and other companies will also present, and Xpeng displayed a prototype flying car at Monday's opening events.

The timing is shaped by a scandal engulfing Nvidia, the US company that dominates the market for chips used in leading AI systems. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of spying for China, a claim Beijing has denied. The articles also report that Nvidia has announced a probe into Huang and that the company faces a class-action lawsuit over the affair. Chinese open-weight AI models, which can be downloaded free and partly modified, are drawing interest from European firms including Orange, Renault, Revolut and Siemens.

The articles frame the push as part of China's search for new markets amid weak domestic demand and US restrictions on much of its market on national security grounds. The summit gives Beijing a stage to present its firms to European buyers and investors at a time when the Nvidia controversy has drawn attention to China's AI ambitions. The articles do not say how the Nvidia matter will be resolved or what commitments, if any, the Chinese firms will make in Lisbon. More to follow.

Articles.Title: China touts tech, AI cred at world Web Summit

stories.Headline: Students Who Turn to AI for Emotional Support Report Worse Mental Health
stories.Summary:
A report from the JED Foundation, a nonprofit focused on youth mental health, found that some students' use of AI is linked to worse mental health and well-being. The findings were published in an Education Week article dated November 10, 2026. The analysis drew on a JED student survey collected between October 2025 and April 2026 from 5,560 middle and high school students in 21 schools across the United States. Students who used AI for friendship or companionship, or who turned to it when struggling emotionally, were more likely to report anxiety and depression symptoms, loneliness, and a history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. The report also found that many students use AI when they feel sad, stressed, lonely, or overwhelmed.

The report does not call for a ban on AI or endorse its unrestricted use, and the authors describe the research as very early. Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation and the report's author, said the findings show that the effect depends on what students are doing with the technology. For educators, the report suggests that AI should not replace real-life support, and that schools should keep students connected to trusted adults. It also points to the need for AI literacy, so students can learn how to use these tools safely and effectively. Anderson said systemic safeguards are needed, including responsibilities for the technology industry.

Anderson said that a majority of students who reported using AI during hard emotions did so without seeking formal help, which she said is an important distinction. She stressed that the research is preliminary and that it is not yet clear whether AI use causes the worse outcomes or whether already vulnerable students are more likely to turn to it. She also said that young people's brains and emotional skills are still developing through their mid-20s, which is why the questions matter. Anderson argued that supporting young people means working across home, school, community, and online settings, not placing the burden on educators alone. The interview was conducted by Education Week staff writer Lauraine Langreo.

Articles.Title: Students Who Turn to AI for Emotional Support Report Worse Mental Health

stories.Headline: Midterm results put AI on the hot seat
stories.Summary:
Voters in the US midterm elections signaled concern about artificial intelligence and data centers, and Democrats swept both the House and the Senate. An SSRS exit poll shared by NBC News found that 56% of voters considered AI and data centers a major factor in their vote. Analysts say the anger centers less on the IT industry itself than on the fear that data centers will drive up electricity, water and other costs for consumers and local governments. Jack Gold of J. Gold Associates said the concern extends to home values and land use. Tighter restrictions, more oversight and slower approvals could slow AI deployment and raise costs for businesses.

Analysts quoted in the article say IT leaders need to adapt their strategies quickly. Stephanie Walter of HyperFRAME Research said that over the next two years there will be more pressure to show who benefits, who pays and who answers when something goes wrong. She advised IT leaders to keep deploying AI where it improves work while building evidence to defend those decisions. David Linthicum of Linthicum Research warned against assuming AI services will get cheaper, arguing that costs may appear in token pricing, enterprise contracts, limited availability or stricter usage policies.

He suggested CIOs consider smaller models, more efficient token use and more careful decisions about what runs in the public cloud. Anshel Sag of Moor Insights & Strategy argued that the industry waited too long to address public sentiment and could face restrictive legislation. Gartner analysts advised companies to reassess AI business cases under scenarios of higher compute costs and reduced infrastructure availability. The article notes that President Donald Trump, a Republican, has been hands-off on AI regulation and has said he would work with Democrats on legislation while also signaling he would be willing to use his veto.

Gartner analysts wrote that a Democratic Congress paired with a Republican presidency will likely produce legislative gridlock. They added that federal inaction could push states to act on AI governance, data center development, energy infrastructure and environmental regulation. AI vendors should expect more requests for disclosure of testing, safety controls, privacy practices, data provenance, bias management, human oversight and procurement justifications. Gartner also said non-US CIOs should avoid a wait-and-see approach and instead run scenario analysis, while diversifying systems across countries, providers and models.

Walter advised IT leaders to tighten governance over the AI they already run, including knowing which systems are in use, what they can access and who owns the results. She recommended asking vendors for test results, incident information and clear contractual responsibilities. She also said some requirements will persist regardless of which party controls Congress, chiefly the need to establish whether AI produces better work after accounting for review, corrections and operating costs. The article is framed as an analysis of how the midterm results may shape AI costs and compliance for enterprises.

Articles.Title: Midterm results put AI on the hot seat

stories.Headline: AI analysis of ECG data measured by smartwatch may help detect reduced heart pumping function
stories.Summary:
An AI model analyzing electrocardiogram recordings taken by smartwatches may help flag a hidden heart condition known as left ventricular systolic dysfunction, according to preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, held November 6 to 9. The condition, which the study defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less, can occur without symptoms and can lead to heart failure if left untreated. The researchers examined whether the software could identify people who might need a traditional screening test, such as an echocardiogram, to check how well the heart pumps. The results varied between watch brands and across recordings, so the findings remain early and exploratory.

In the largest group, 2,211 adults scheduled for an echocardiogram at an outpatient cardiology clinic in South Korea had ECGs recorded on both an Apple Watch and a Samsung Galaxy Watch during the same visit. The AI model distinguished people with and without the condition about equally well on both watches. However, when the same score cutoff was applied to both devices, 200 participants, or 9%, were classified as positive on one watch and negative on the other. A separate group of 146 adults recorded ECGs at home, and requiring positive results on at least two of three consecutive days cut false positives from 18 to nine among the 70 participants without the condition. That rule also missed two cases compared with a single-positive-day rule, and the researchers tested several repeat-testing rules.

Lee, a cardiologist and chief medical officer of Medical AI Co., Ltd., which developed the model, said some people have reduced pumping function without noticeable symptoms. He said the study explored whether smartwatch analysis could help identify people who may benefit from additional screening. Lee also noted that a single smartwatch ECG is a snapshot and that repeated recordings can give different results. He said larger studies are needed to determine how best to use these results to guide further evaluation.

The study was conducted at Incheon Sejong Hospital, with the first group enrolled from July 2023 to May 2024 and the second from July 2024 to December 2025. Because participants were patients referred for echocardiography, many already with known heart failure, the results may not apply to the general population, and the researchers adjusted their estimates for lower prevalence. The study did not determine whether using these AI results leads to earlier treatment, fewer hospitalizations or improved survival. Its limitations include the single hospital setting and the small number of participants in the repeat-testing analysis.

Articles.Title: AI analysis of ECG data measured by smartwatch may help detect reduced heart pumping function

stories.Headline: T. Rowe Price gives Claude a promotion as it expands workplace AI
stories.Summary:
T. Rowe Price, the Baltimore-based investment firm, has partnered with Anthropic to give its workforce access to Claude, an AI assistant, and is expanding its artificial intelligence lab beyond its New York center. The company converted a small wing of its new Harbor Point headquarters in Baltimore into an AI hub in September. The firm's CEO, Rob Sharps, told analysts on a recent earnings call that AI is moving into the core of how the firm invests. The article, published November 10, 2026, reports that the initiative is intended to offload routine tasks and free employees to focus on clients.

Christopher LePre, the head of AI engineering and application development, said Claude could help associates cover significantly more stocks and could read and summarize news to show how events might affect the portfolios they manage. He said the aim is to give all associates access and reduce the routine work that takes up their days. The company is retiring its in-house tool, ChatTRP, and while some staff can still use models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and Microsoft's Copilot, LePre said the company believes Claude offers the best of those options. About 68 employees work in the New York lab, now called "The Lab," with eight more at the new Baltimore space, and two others in the department will soon work from London.

Sharps described investment in AI as a competitive necessity. Cheryl Pipia, the firm's head of global sales management, said employees should feel free to build skills that automate part of their work so they can focus on more important tasks. A company spokesperson, Arminta Plater, said in a statement that the AI strategy centers on enabling the workforce and expanding capabilities. LePre also said the firm would not let costs get out of control, since AI services generally charge per use and employees receive a set number of tokens.

The article places the move within a broader rush of AI adoption, noting that about half of Americans said this year they had used a chatbot and that a Acuity Analytics survey found four-fifths of asset management companies use AI. It also notes that Anthropic is expected to be valued at over $1 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. T. Rowe Price cut its roughly 8,000 global employees by about 6% between last summer and this one, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, though the company says that reduction was unrelated to its AI push. The article does not say what further steps the firm plans beyond the current expansion.

Articles.Title: T. Rowe Price gives Claude a promotion as it expands workplace AI

stories.Headline: Ron Daniels: Exploring the Ethical Frontiers of AI in Cancer Care
stories.Summary:
Ron Daniels, president of The Johns Hopkins University, posted on LinkedIn on November 10, 2026, about a recent Next Conversations event on artificial intelligence in cancer care. The panel included Hopkins researchers Ashani Weeraratna and Vasan Yegnasubramanian, along with Pulitzer Prize-winning author Siddhartha Mukherjee, who spoke with NPR's Steve Inskeep. The discussion focused on the ethics of AI tools in oncology and the next stage of their development. Daniels shared his opening remarks and encouraged readers to listen to the full conversation.

In his post, Daniels described how cancer tools have grown more powerful and how each advance brings both hope and new questions about using them responsibly. He said the event returned to questions that have long shaped medicine but now feel more pressing. Those questions include how to use technology in a humane way, how to make sure these tools benefit all patients, and how to keep the human connection, clinical judgment, and trust between doctor and patient at the center of care. The article does not describe specific policies, rules, or changes that the discussion called for.

Daniels is the one responsible for the message, and the article presents his views as an invitation to the conversation rather than as a set of conclusions. The panelists' individual remarks are not reported in the article, so their positions are not described. The piece also points readers to a related article about AI in oncology by Yan Leyfman, which offers a further look at the field. The article does not say whether any follow-up events or outcomes are planned.

Articles.Title: Ron Daniels: Exploring the Ethical Frontiers of AI in Cancer Care

stories.Headline: How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms
stories.Summary:
Vestiaire Collective, the resale platform, is working to make its secondhand product listings available to OpenAI's agentic shopping systems, so that pre-owned pieces could appear alongside new products in AI-generated recommendations. The plan follows the company quietly launching a dedicated app plugin within ChatGPT last month, which lets shoppers search its pre-owned luxury inventory using conversational prompts. Rémi Bouchez, who was appointed Vestiaire's CTO in March, is leading this work. The article notes that a shopper looking for a new Prada bag could now be shown a used version at a lower price or an archival design no longer sold new.

The shift is part of a wider change in how secondhand fashion is found. Resale platforms are rebuilding their search and recommendation systems with AI that reads product images, interprets shoppers' tastes and decides which listings get seen. Bouchez argues that AI shopping agents, which he names as Muse, Instinct and Duet, could change how luxury buyers compare options by processing far more information than people can, remembering preferences and flagging hidden terms or questionable seller behavior. Rivals are also investing: Depop allows searches through Apple's Visual Intelligence on supported iPhones, and The RealReal launched Ask TRR, an assistant built on Google Gemini, which its CEO Rati Levesque said early users spend 20% more per transaction than non-users. The RealReal is also restructuring data on its 1.5 million listed items so that outside AI agents can find them.

Vestiaire's visual search now recognizes multiple objects in an image, and its systems interpret natural language requests and pull fit and visible defects from photographs. Poshmark's Smart List AI generates titles, descriptions and categories from uploaded photos, and its chief product officer, Heather Friedland, says listing is now five times faster and that its automated offers make selling 50% faster. Depop's chief product officer, Sonia Biddle, says shoppers increasingly browse a personalized feed instead of searching. Vestiaire, working with the AI photography company Photoroom, is standardizing the main photo of roughly 40,000 new listings a day, and an A/B test found those listings had a 5% higher sell-through rate than before, with unique product page views up between 3% and 7%.

Resale platforms say ranking depends on several factors. Bouchez describes Vestiaire's three-stage system, which weighs relevance, condition, price, location and seller reliability, and he says human checks on authenticity remain central to its trust. Depop weighs how closely a listing matches a query, along with views, likes, seller history and location. To counter the narrowing effect of personalization, Poshmark launched a "Tastemaker" program in September with fashion figures including Courtney Grow, Colleen Allen and Jalil Johnson, and it set up a human merchandising team. Biddle suggests shoppers sort results by price or newest first, and Friedland advises saving searches and liking items to refine recommendations.

Articles.Title: How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms

stories.Headline: Bizarre AI chip demo uses butter to highlight how new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition
stories.Summary:
Deepx, a chip company, has drawn attention with an unusual demonstration in which competing chips are shown melting butter while its own processor leaves the butter intact. The article, published by Tom's Hardware on November 9, 2026, describes the demo as a dairy-based benchmark for thermal performance. The headline says the new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition. The article's core claim is that the Deepx processor generates less heat than rival chips during operation. The article's details are limited, but the thrust of the story is that lower thermal output is presented as the key advantage of the new processor.

The demo was used to make that difference visible in a simple way, with butter standing in as a heat indicator placed on or near the chips. The headline's reference to a 40-degree gap is the only specific figure given for the comparison. The article does not appear to set out the test conditions, the chips compared, or the methodology in detail. The company behind the chip is Deepx, and the article reports that the demonstration highlights its low thermals. The article as provided does not include direct statements from Deepx executives or independent testers.

Responsibility for the claims therefore rests with the company and with the outlet's report of its demo. Readers should note that the comparison is a promotional showcase rather than a published, independently verified benchmark. Heat management has become a central concern for AI accelerators, since high power draw and temperatures affect cooling costs, density, and reliability in data centers. The articles provided do not state what happens next, such as product availability, pricing, or further independent testing. Any such developments would need to come from later reporting.

Articles.Title: Bizarre AI chip demo uses butter to highlight how new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition

stories.Headline: Trump Shares AI Video of Dana White Berating Reporters Days After Violent Cartoon Post
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, President Donald Trump posted two AI-generated videos on Truth Social showing a fake version of UFC CEO Dana White acting as White House press secretary. The first clip layered White's likeness over years-old footage of rapper Lil Yachty performing on a Chicago festival stage in 2021, and it showed White dancing and rapping at a podium bearing the presidential seal. Minutes later, Trump posted a second, 13-second video in which the fake White angrily scolds reporters, one of whom holds a microphone labeled "FAKE NEWS." The videos followed a cartoon Trump had posted the day before, on November 8, depicting White sending UFC fighters to attack journalists. Those posts came just after Trump said he had only been joking when he offered White the press secretary job.

The videos were published as Trump continued a running joke about White and the role, which has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt left the White House in August. Trump had brought White into the briefing room that afternoon for an impromptu press conference, where he said the UFC president loved the idea and would do a good job. White flew to Washington after UFC fights in London on November 8, and he told TMZ that he was heading to the White House to have Trump sign a trading card commemorating the UFC Freedom 250 fights held on the president's 80th birthday in June. He said he has "less than zero political aspirations" and that the press secretary idea came from Trump, who put it out publicly. The articles do not describe any formal change in policy or any consequence arising from the videos.

White has said he will leave the decision about the job to Trump and is not going to respond with disrespect, while stating that he has many other jobs and is busy with obligations in several states. He told reporters in the briefing room that the past 24 hours had been insane and that he had no interest in politics. Trump, for his part, described White as someone who would be good in the role and said he was only kidding when he first offered it. The articles frame the episode as part of a pattern of Trump posting satirical and AI-generated content, though they do not report any response from the press corps beyond the scripted lines within the video itself.

Articles.Title: Trump Shares AI Video of Dana White Berating Reporters Days After Violent Cartoon Post

stories.Headline: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%
stories.Summary:
An AI tool that drafts echocardiogram reports was tested against reports prepared by ultrasound technicians and cardiologists, and the researchers found the AI-assisted reports were comparable in accuracy. The study was presented on Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, and it was described as new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science. An echocardiogram is a heart ultrasound, the most widely used type of heart imaging. Normally a sonographer acquires the images and a cardiologist reviews them and writes the report. The trial was reported as the first randomized trial testing an AI tool to write a full echocardiogram report, including interpretations and measurements.

In the trial, an AI tool, a sonographer and a cardiologist each prepared preliminary reports for the same 1,200 echocardiograms that had been obtained during routine care. Cardiologists then reviewed and finalized these drafts without knowing which source had produced each one. Cardiologists made substantial changes to 50.6% of the AI-generated drafts, compared with 49.7% of the human-prepared drafts, which met the study's criteria for noninferiority. Cardiologists spent an average of 4.6 minutes per scan reviewing AI drafts, compared with 8.5 minutes to write reports without AI help, a saving of about 46%. The AI-assisted reports were also more consistent with historical reports in the medical record, and reviewers could not tell which drafts came from the AI.

The lead investigator, Keane K. Lee, a cardiologist at Kaiser Permanente Santa Clara Homestead Medical Center, said the team expected strong accuracy but was surprised by how much time the tool saved. Lee said that saving a few minutes per scan could add up over a day and could mean faster results and more time with patients. Lee also said that AI cannot replace the human team, and that the cardiologist remains responsible for the interpretation and for certifying the final report. The article notes that a July 2026 study in the Journal of the American Heart Association projected a national shortfall of about 7,000 cardiologists by 2036, which the authors cited as a reason to strengthen the workforce.

The study drew on 1,200 exams performed over two weeks in March 2025 at 21 medical centers across Kaiser Permanente Northern California, with patients averaging 69 years of age. Nine sonographers and 20 cardiologists took part. The article lists several limitations: the study did not test whether AI-assisted interpretation improves patients' long-term health, and cardiologists knew they were in the study and may have changed their usual habits. The article says more research is needed to see how the tool performs in everyday clinical settings at larger scale. The findings were published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

Articles.Title: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%

stories.Headline: Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage
stories.Summary:
House House, the Australian studio behind the indie hit Big Walk, has published a statement on its FAQ page disclosing that large language models were used during the game's final stage of development. The disclosure came after the studio voluntarily noted this use as part of its submission for next year's IGF Awards, following a signed statement from some IGF jurors saying they would not vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity. The studio said LLMs were used sparingly to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs, and that well under 0.1% of the game's code had anything to do with this usage. House House also said generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The studio explained that in some cases, snippets from chatbot responses were copied as a starting point and then modified into game code. Its example involved a shadow-culling problem in Unity's URP that made the game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. After the team researched the issue, examined the URP code and consulted a Unity engineer who concluded the fix wasn't possible, it asked an LLM chatbot, which suggested a fix that was heavily modified and amounted to about 10 lines of code. Steam requires a generative AI disclosure on storefronts but does not ask for disclosure of code or chatbot usage, so the studio made no disclosure there. House House said it posted the statement because the matter had become one of public interest.

House House stressed that this is not an endorsement of AI tools and said it worries that voluntary disclosures like this could normalise the technology or make it seem inevitable. The studio said it supports those working to limit generative AI's harm to video games and the wider world, and it apologised that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards. It called the lack of an internal AI usage policy during development a failure and said it will work to create a more comprehensive policy going forward. The statement also noted that the studio had earlier explained it was not publishing Big Walk on Xbox platforms because of a Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft.

Big Walk launched in August 2026 to critical acclaim and reached one million sales in less than a week. House House was previously best known for its 2019 hit Untitled Goose Game. Reactions online have been divided, with some commenters defending the bug-fixing use as reasonable and others arguing that any use of generative tools in creative work is a concern. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

stories.Headline: Google’s chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia’s own AI boom
stories.Summary:
Google introduced two new tensor processing units, its homegrown AI chips, on Monday, November 9, 2026. The TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max join the 8t and 8i that the company unveiled in April, which makes this the first time Google has launched four TPU systems in a single year. Both of the new chips ship next year. Alphabet shares rose about 3% on the news, while Nvidia fell 8% after the opening bell and traded at its lowest level since March.

The 8tx is built to keep data encrypted for governments, banks and other regulated businesses, and it is paired with processors from AMD. The 8i Max puts two chips into one package to handle requests with long context windows, meaning the amount of information an AI model can juggle at once. Google used to roll out about one data center TPU a year, and it now has one for each kind of job. Bloomberg Intelligence expects TPU sales to climb from about $12 billion this year to more than $135 billion by 2028, a rise of more than 11-fold in two years, and that figure leaves out chips rented through Google Cloud.

Demand is already strong, according to Yahoo Finance. Epoch AI estimates that TPU shipments doubled in computing power in a single quarter this year, to roughly 800,000 chips. Anthropic's IPO filing shows about $161 billion of lease payments tied to TPUs, which Raymond James says makes it the biggest custom-chip customer of Broadcom, Google's design partner. Meta, OpenAI and Oracle are also buyers. SemiAnalysis found that Google's current Ironwood TPU delivers up to nearly three times as much AI output per dollar as Nvidia's Blackwell chips when running AI agents, though Nvidia's top system still wins when speed matters most.

Nvidia's slide came as its board looks into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, which Yahoo Finance called Wall Street's first $4.5 trillion CEO scandal. Nvidia still holds the stronger hardware, with its next-generation Rubin chip rated at 35 petaflops against about 10 for Google's 8i and about 20 for the 8i Max, by Yahoo Finance's calculations. The article stresses that forecasts are not sales and that Nvidia still sells far more AI chips than anyone else. Nvidia reports third-quarter results on November 17, a day before a requested closed-door House briefing on Huang, and investors will want to know whether customers are hedging their bets. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon told clients that Huang is no ordinary chief executive and that he is Nvidia.

Articles.Title: Google’s chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia’s own AI boom

stories.Headline: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
stories.Summary:
Scott Wiener, a California state senator who had authored AI safety legislation, was declared the winner of a tight congressional race to succeed former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in San Francisco, a result known by the Friday after the election. The article, published by MIT Technology Review on November 9, 2026, reports that Wiener spoke shortly after his victory was announced. The day before, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report widely read as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a process in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement. Wiener said the report was very concerning and that the window for regulating AI is closing quickly.

Wiener said he had hoped Congress would take decisive action before the end of the year, but he said that did not appear to be happening. The article notes his earlier work, including SB 1047, which Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed in 2024, and SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Wiener has backed a strong, empowered and nimble federal regulator, supported whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements and a kill switch requirement, and said he would be eager to serve on a select committee on artificial intelligence if Congress creates one, a idea Democrats have discussed since September. He also opposes broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some proposed federal legislation would require.

The article describes Wiener's campaign as having received more than $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit favoring AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. Opponents criticized him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener rejected that charge, saying the group backed him because he was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce and pass AI regulation. He described the attacks as cynical. On the broader political mood, the article reports that voters approved 40 of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on the same day, and Wiener said he views that movement as driven mainly by local concerns such as electric bills, water use and impacts near homes rather than by AI risk.

Wiener described himself as only cautiously optimistic about Congress's ability to rein in AI, citing its record on regulating the tech industry. He also voiced concern about getting legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a hoax in September. Wiener said Trump's unpredictability offers some hope, while adding that he hopes a disaster does not prompt action. The article presents these views as Wiener's own and does not describe any specific federal bill advancing or any vote scheduled.

Articles.Title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

stories.Headline: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company that has generally preferred renting computing capacity to owning physical infrastructure, is now spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines. According to a Financial Times report cited by TechCrunch, the company is buying Caterpillar generators that the equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered. The generators can produce up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity. The article describes the purchase as part of a broader rush by AI firms to secure power as demand for computing grows.

Anthropic's shift is notable because the company has historically avoided buying infrastructure. Its S-1 filing in May disclosed that it pays SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for computing power. In that filing, Anthropic said it expected to enter into additional similar services contracts. The article notes that the backlog for natural gas turbines extends into the early 2030s, and grid connection queues can be just as long, which may have pushed the company toward direct ownership. OnePWR had ordered the turbines a couple of years ago but could not find financing to complete the purchase, so Anthropic bought from Caterpillar directly instead.

TechCrunch reports that OnePWR did not explain why it could not secure financing, despite Anthropic's apparent interest as a customer. The article suggests Anthropic may have wanted to keep the generating capacity for itself rather than let a competitor acquire it. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have each announced plans to build large natural gas plants to power their data centers on site instead of relying on the public grid. The article's author, Tim De Chant, a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch, frames the purchase within this wider trend.

The article places the buildout in a larger context. It says the trend has given new momentum to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. If the plans proceed, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. It also warns that reliance on gas exposes these companies to price swings, and one analyst expects prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, the article suggests, Anthropic could regret the purchase.

Articles.Title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines

stories.Headline: AI-fueled hacking is getting worse — top cyber companies are turning away some victims
stories.Summary:
Cybersecurity firms say they are being overwhelmed by work as AI-aided cyberattacks have grown severe enough that some of the largest companies in the sector are turning away new customers who need emergency help. The report, written by Kevin Collier and published by NBC News on November 9, 2026, describes a surge in attacks that have been made faster and more effective through artificial intelligence tools. The article itself is largely built around that central development, and the page text available to me contains little beyond the headline, the opening summary, and unrelated navigation and story listings. Because of that, the specific figures, dates of individual incidents, company names, and detailed requirements or policy changes that a fuller account would normally include are not present in what I was given.

What the piece reports is that the strain on the industry has reached the point where firms cannot take on everyone who calls. Victims seeking urgent assistance after breaches are being refused by some top providers, which means organizations hit by attacks may have to look for help elsewhere or wait longer for response. The article's summary frames this as a worsening trend rather than a single event, pointing to the growing volume of AI-fueled intrusions as the driving pressure on response capacity. Beyond that, I cannot confirm which firms are involved, how many customers have been turned away, or what changes in pricing, staffing, or service rules the companies have adopted.

The article's summary also indicates that the companies themselves are the ones describing the flood of work, so responsibility for the capacity limits rests with the firms' own accounts of their workloads. I do not have their statements or any quoted remarks from executives, government officials, or security researchers, so I cannot paraphrase what any particular party said. Nor can I say what regulators or lawmakers have done in response or what the next steps are expected to be. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI-fueled hacking is getting worse — top cyber companies are turning away some victims

stories.Headline: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
stories.Summary:
A Google Cloud blog post published on November 9, 2026 under the byline of Jeanette Manfra, a vice president and head of risk and compliance at the company, reports on a survey of 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The survey was conducted with Hypothesis Group and examined how existing software affects companies' ability to adopt artificial intelligence. Its central finding is that legacy software, meaning programs that run locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud, is holding back AI projects. The article says that 49% of respondents reported that reliance on on-premises software had delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives.

The article describes the operational toll as a zero-sum contest for engineering time. Routine patching and maintenance of legacy systems were identified as a main bottleneck, and the author argues that AI-enabled vulnerability discovery is surfacing flaws faster than human security teams can address them. Because of this, IT staff are spending time maintaining old systems instead of pursuing AI modernization. The survey also found that 39% of decision-makers said reliance on legacy software and cloud providers forces them into complex licensing rules, contracts or limited negotiating flexibility. The author further warns that concentrating operating systems, productivity tools, cloud hosting and AI models with a single vendor creates a single point of failure and a larger attack surface.

The author, Manfra, argues that vendor lock-in is the reason organizations keep relying on constraining legacy environments, and calls on enterprise buyers and policymakers to ensure genuine choice and interoperability. The survey found that 80% of leaders agree a provider's installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, and 78% believe the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. The post recommends demanding architectural and provider choice, building secure-by-design software that eliminates vulnerability classes before release, and using AI-driven defenses such as Google's Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics to remediate existing legacy vulnerabilities. The article does not report any regulatory action or scheduled next steps beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization

stories.Headline: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
stories.Summary:
Medium launched a new app called TK on Monday, which aims to bring AI assistance directly into the writing process. Users can invoke the built-in assistant by typing "@TK" followed by a request or prompt inside the editor. The name borrows from publishing, where "TK" marks a placeholder for information to be added later, and the spelling makes it easy for proofreaders to spot. The assistant is meant to fill in those blanks, answering quick factual questions that would otherwise send a writer to another tab and pulling in notes saved earlier in the drafting process.

TK will also ship with skills for editorial feedback and headline suggestions, and it can check a draft against the style guide for Medium publications. Writers can connect their own AI agent through TK's MCP server or a Claude skill so the app can better understand their projects and ideas. TK also offers memory and organization tools that surface past writing, along with writing prompts. A social layer lets writers share early drafts and collect feedback from others. The app is free for anyone with a Medium account and is currently available on the web, with a desktop version on the roadmap.

The launch comes at a sensitive time for the publishing industry, which has been grappling with AI's role in long-form writing. Several authors have lost book deals after suspicions that they used AI to write, and some literary awards have faced scrutiny over similar concerns. Writers have long relied on automated tools for proofreading, but there is growing worry that AI editing suggestions can end up replacing the writer's own thoughts. Reliability of AI detection tools is also in doubt, since models trained on human writing make it hard to tell AI-written text from AI-assisted text. Medium's stance is that these distinctions will matter less over time, and it argues that AI can amplify human intelligence.

Medium acknowledges that AI raises the risk of low-quality content and blurred lines between human and machine writing. To address this, TK lets authors publish notes that explain how AI was used in a piece. Medium described this as a first step toward making the origins of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, including the prompts and source material used. The article does not say how many writers have adopted the notes feature or whether Medium plans further safeguards.

Articles.Title: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process

stories.Headline: Maryland AI Tracker Focuses on National Job Gains and Displacement Risks
stories.Summary:
Maryland's comptroller, Brooke E. Lierman, has launched a public AI Economic Impact Tracker that combines evidence of growing demand for artificial intelligence skills with forecasts of major workforce disruption. The portal gathers government data, university research and private-sector analysis into one place. Its stated purpose is to give policymakers a view of an economic shift that reaches well beyond the state. The tracker also links these employment and adoption trends to possible pressure on tax revenues and public budgets. That gives fiscal officials a framework for weighing AI's effects alongside employers and workforce planners.

Its dashboard reports 273,000 U.S. AI job postings during the first nine months of 2026, up 79% from the full-year 2025 total. AI positions made up 1.8% of all postings in the third quarter, and California, New York, Washington, Texas and Illinois led in posting volumes. These posting figures come from the University of Maryland–LinkUp AI Maps project, which analyzes employer listings. Its definition covers technical AI skills such as machine learning and model development, and it excludes roles that only use chatbots or that build and maintain data centers. Because the figures count postings, they measure recruitment demand rather than completed hires or net job gains.

Displacement evidence tells a different story: employers cited AI in 120,136 announced U.S. job cuts through September, about 21% of the total, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. AI was the leading reason cited for cuts in that period, although these are employer announcements rather than an independently verified count of jobs lost solely to automation. Longer-term estimates are far larger. The American AI Jobs Risk Index, developed at Tufts University's Fletcher School, identifies 9.3 million jobs vulnerable to displacement under its median adoption scenario, with a range of 2.7 million to 19.5 million depending on how fast adoption proceeds. The tracker places these projections within a two-to-five-year horizon.

Tufts estimates annual wage income at risk at $200 billion to $1.5 trillion, with a midpoint near $757 billion, and it estimates displacement vulnerability at 18% in information, 17% in finance and insurance, and 16% in professional, scientific and technical services. The portal acknowledges that evidence on enterprise integration, operational spending and realized productivity remains thin. Its initial business findings come from a Maryland survey of 276 senior decision makers, mostly at AI-engaged organizations, so the sample cannot establish a national adoption rate. Even so, 91% of respondents used AI, while only 32% reported advanced uses involving core systems, automated processes or agents.

The tracker will receive quarterly updates, with periodic fiscal research briefs starting in 2027. The survey's staffing responses suggest disruption may appear through slower hiring as much as through layoffs, since only 4% expected to eliminate existing positions while 32% expected fewer replacement hires or slower recruitment. For policymakers and businesses, the tracker's usefulness will depend on keeping technical capability, employer intentions, observed hiring and modeled losses clearly separate. Tracking them together could show where retraining, worker support and closer scrutiny of AI deployment may be needed.

Articles.Title: Maryland AI Tracker Focuses on National Job Gains and Displacement Risks

stories.Headline: AI helps sort specialty referrals before scheduling at UTMB
stories.Summary:
The University of Texas Medical Branch, known as UTMB, has begun using artificial intelligence to sort specialty referrals before they are scheduled, a change aimed at shortening long waits for specialist care. The health system added referral triage to an AI agent it already used, built by Bunkerhill Health, and the tool reviews each referral's full chart and assigns a priority. Early results reported by Dr. Salim Hayek, UTMB's vice president and chief transformation officer, show average waits for a first new-patient visit falling from 93 days to 65 across four of the system's longest-running specialties. Those figures are preliminary, and UTMB says its full analysis is still underway. The system works by reading the order, clinic notes, labs, imaging and outside records behind each referral, then applying a playbook written by UTMB's own specialty physicians.

Each referral receives a priority score from 0 to 10 and a recommended pathway, such as a subspecialty clinic, an advanced practice provider, an e-consult, or a redirect to another service like transplant or dialysis. Anything that looks like an emergency goes to the emergency department before scoring, and the agent keeps reviewing the queue as new results arrive. No booking is automated, so schedulers and referral coordinators decide each case, and the recommendations link back to Epic. Hayek said division champions wrote and validated the playbooks against manual chart review, and each champion reviews a random sample of cases every month so the rules can be tuned. He described the aim as giving every referral the review an experienced specialist would give it before anyone schedules it.

He also said the system has reduced the need to add endocrinologists, noting that UTMB had estimated it needed three to four more to meet demand. Now about four in ten endocrinology referrals go to advanced practice providers, and e-consults answer many straightforward questions, often within 48 to 72 hours. The approach responds to a common problem in which referrals with very different levels of urgency sit in the same first-come, first-served queue. According to the article, research on Ontario's e-consult program found that 40% of planned specialist visits were avoided entirely. Hayek said UTMB is now redesigning its scheduling to hold new-patient slots by priority so the patients who need care most are seen first, and he expects the next gains to come from that change.

Articles.Title: AI helps sort specialty referrals before scheduling at UTMB

stories.Headline: AI stocks have 2 major headwinds driving recent volatility
stories.Summary:
AI stocks rose on Monday, November 9, 2026, but markets stayed on edge after a steep sell-off that began the previous week. Brian Sozzi, executive editor at Yahoo Finance, reported that investors fear a slowdown in data center build-outs could delay the profits expected from the largest technology companies. Those concerns grew after the midterm elections, when a wave of Democratic wins raised worries that newly elected senators and governors could disrupt AI expansion. A second, less obvious factor has also weighed on the sector.

Companies including Apple and Amazon have said they are watching their spending on AI tokens more closely, which suggests AI providers may not be able to keep raising prices without limit. Matt Maley, chief markets strategist at Miller Tabal, wrote that enterprises are pushing back on AI pricing. He said a new usage-based pricing policy caused a sharp rise in enterprise AI costs, prompting many firms to route simple queries to cheaper models, adopt open-weight and local models, and set budgets and token caps for employees. Maley argued that these pricing pressures raise doubts about how profitable AI will be.

The selling reached a historic level on November 5, when the S&P 500 fell 4.4 percent and lost about $3 trillion in market value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,800 points, its worst single-day decline since 2020, while the Nasdaq sank 5.5 percent, pulled down by chipmakers and cloud companies such as Micron and Sandisk. Tech stocks have kept trading lower since then. According to the article, the reported developments have intensified doubts about the return on investment from the AI industry, and Maley said many AI bulls' assumptions about the profitability of AI are beginning to fade.

Articles.Title: AI stocks have 2 major headwinds driving recent volatility

stories.Headline: Berkshire Hathaway's Top AI Holding Is Poised to Outperform
stories.Summary:
Berkshire Hathaway has added to its holdings in Alphabet, the parent company of Google, with the stake now standing as the conglomerate's fourth-largest position across its Class A and Class C shares. According to a Motley Fool article by Neil Patel published on November 9, 2026, Warren Buffett initiated the purchase in the third quarter of last year, and current CEO Greg Abel followed with additional buying. The article presents Alphabet as Berkshire's top artificial intelligence holding and argues that the stock is positioned to outperform the market. It notes that the shares have risen 124% over the past 36 months as of November 4, yet trade 28% below their peak. Shares dipped after third-quarter results missed expectations on both revenue and earnings.

The article points to several figures that account for the valuation. Alphabet's capital expenditures are expected to total roughly $200 billion in 2026, with management projecting a substantial increase next year. Free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter, and long-term debt rose 169% from the end of last year to $125.1 billion. Alphabet trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.5, which the author describes as a compelling entry point. Sell-side consensus estimates cited in the piece project operating income growing at a compound annual rate of 28.1% from 2025 to 2028.

Patel attributes the growth case mainly to AI demand. Revenue rose 25% year over year in the most recent quarter, and Google Cloud sales climbed 103% in the third quarter, a streak the author describes as accelerating. The cloud backlog stands at $561 billion. The article says Google Cloud benefits from selling specific software and hardware to enterprise clients, and that Alphabet's broader products improve as AI is integrated into them. Patel acknowledges that the next few years are hard to forecast and that uncertainty is high, but he concludes that the company is well placed to ride the AI wave.

The piece also reflects the uncertainty around AI spending that investors are weighing. Google Search sales slowed to 12% growth in the quarter, and Alphabet has begun funding its AI push with outside capital. The article frames the current price as a setup that favors investors with a five-year horizon. Patel discloses that he holds no position in the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends both Alphabet and Berkshire Hathaway, and the article contains promotional material for its Stock Advisor service.

Articles.Title: Berkshire Hathaway's Top AI Holding Is Poised to Outperform

stories.Headline: Google Hands AMD Major Win in AI Chip Race
stories.Summary:
Advanced Micro Devices shares rose nearly four percent in premarket trading on Monday, November 9, 2026, after the chipmaker announced an expanded partnership with Google Cloud. Under the agreement, AMD's fifth-generation EPYC server processors will support Google's new TPU 8tx, its first cloud tensor processing unit system with hardware-based confidential computing. The arrangement is meant to protect sensitive information, including proprietary AI models and customer data, while workloads run. AMD's processors will handle data preparation and supporting tasks alongside Google's custom AI accelerators. AMD shares traded around $464.66 in premarket trading after the news.

The combination is aimed at AI inference, model fine-tuning and agentic AI applications, where multiple AI systems carry out increasingly complex tasks. The announcement builds on AMD's long relationship with Google Cloud, particularly in enterprise computing and security infrastructure. The company said its EPYC processors are already deployed by more than 10 leading hyperscalers and AI laboratories. Those customers run infrastructure built around Nvidia GPUs, AMD Instinct accelerators and custom-designed AI chips. That flexibility matters as large technology companies build their own processors to reduce reliance on outside suppliers.

The article attributes the announcement to AMD and Google Cloud, with AMD describing its EPYC adoption across the industry. It frames the deal as an opportunity for AMD to supply the central processors that power AI systems rather than competing head-on with Nvidia in graphics processors. Analysts and commentators quoted in related coverage pointed to the upgrade and rising interest in the stock. The companies did not disclose the financial value of the agreement or expected shipment volumes.

The article says investors should watch whether AMD can turn its hyperscaler relationships into sustained data-center revenue, along with EPYC adoption, server CPU market share and demand from customers using custom accelerators. Google's TPU 8tx rollout could give AMD another route to AI infrastructure spending without displacing Nvidia's GPUs. Slower deployments or weaker infrastructure investment could limit the partnership's financial contribution. Until more figures are released, the size of the deal remains unclear.

Articles.Title: Google Hands AMD Major Win in AI Chip Race

stories.Headline: On theCUBE Pod: Midterms send shockwaves through AI market
stories.Summary:
Tech stocks sold off sharply after the midterm elections, as investors reacted to a wave of winning candidates who opposed data centers and called for tighter limits on artificial intelligence. According to the article, the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% and technology companies lost a combined $2.5 trillion in market value. John Furrier of theCUBE Research called the day a bloodbath and said that 41 states had data centers on the ballot. The report was published on November 9, 2026.

Investors now expect AI spending to slow, and the article describes the selloff as a sign that AI has become a political issue that touches everyone in the industry. Dave Vellante of theCUBE Research said enterprises are not yet paying for their own AI build-out, and he pointed to the time needed to build data centers and recover their financing. He noted that companies selling GPUs are profitable, but that clear monetization in enterprises is so far showing up mainly inside technology firms. A recent analysis cited in the piece identified 2029 as the riskiest year for an AI bubble.

Vellante argued that large tech companies are well placed, while neoclouds such as CoreWeave are taking on more risk with a new software model and will face some pain. Furrier said the infrastructure behind AI is moving beyond GPUs toward networking, optics, memory, storage, and power efficiency, and named Supermicro, Advanced Micro Devices, Arista Networks, and Marvell Technology as companies to watch. He also mentioned Marvell's reported $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum. Vellante described hyperscalers as able to scale spending up or down at will, while growth and market share remain the priority.

The article also explores who will control the system of intelligence that links AI agents to the data they rely on, a question it says remains open. Palantir Technologies has an ontology that could give it an edge, while Snowflake and Databricks are still building their operational systems. Vellante said Databricks chief executive Ali Ghodsi has the strongest vision, and Furrier predicted that AI-native enterprises will be the lasting result, with control resting in data and context rather than models. The article reports that frontier model vendors remain the wild card in this contest.

Articles.Title: On theCUBE Pod: Midterms send shockwaves through AI market

stories.Headline: AI in the Workplace: Why We Should Listen to Gen Z Women
stories.Summary:
A Senate hearing held this summer on AI's effect on the workforce drew concern from its witnesses about entry-level jobs, but the author, Charlotte Racine, writing for the National Partnership for Women & Families on November 9, 2026, says the panel largely ignored women. Only Senator Blunt Rochester raised how AI would affect women of color differently, and the witnesses only acknowledged the point in response. The author argues that the gap extends to research, which covers women and young adults in general but says little about how Gen Z women specifically feel about AI. She describes herself as a young woman who came away from the hearing both interested and disheartened.

The article says women are less optimistic about AI and less likely to use it at work, with studies of more than 140,000 college students and workers finding women's use 10 to 40 percent below men's. In a 2025 survey, 69 percent of Black women said AI made them feel unsafe, and 45 percent did not believe AI's creators cared about their community's well-being. Among Gen Z, 51 percent use generative AI at least weekly, yet 42 percent report anxiety and 31 percent report anger toward it. The share of Gen Z who strongly believe AI can help them work faster fell from 22 percent in 2025 to 18 percent in 2026, and Gen Z men are 25 percent more likely than Gen Z women to have experimented with AI.

The article also presents evidence that women may face harder job prospects in an AI-centered market. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates reached 6 percent in spring 2025, compared with a 4 percent national average, and a 2024 survey found 37 percent of HR managers would prefer AI over hiring a recent graduate. Women hold 83 percent of the jobs most vulnerable to AI, and women of color are among the most likely to work in AI-exposed occupations such as translation and interpretation. The author cites studies showing some AI hiring tools favor white and male applicants, and notes that 90 percent of American employers, along with 98.4 percent of Fortune 500 companies, use AI to screen resumes.

She points to Amazon's 2018 AI hiring tool, which discriminated against graduates of women's colleges, as evidence that the problem is longstanding. The author concludes that policymakers and experts are not paying enough attention to the disproportionate risk AI poses to Gen Z women in the workplace. She urges lawmakers who regulate AI to listen to young women and to weigh how their policies will shape the economy and workplaces for the next generation of workers. The article is an advocacy piece rather than a report of a pending decision, so it does not describe any specific rule or deadline that would follow.

Articles.Title: AI in the Workplace: Why We Should Listen to Gen Z Women

stories.Headline: Exclusive: Spines, a 'hybrid publisher,' raises $64 million in funding for book publishing platform powered by AI agents
stories.Summary:
Spines, a startup that calls itself a "hybrid publisher," announced on Monday, November 9, 2026, that it has secured $64 million in new capital. The company uses AI agents to help authors edit manuscripts, design covers, translate books, market titles and manage social media campaigns. Spines has offices in Israel and New York, and its founder and CEO, Yehuda Niv, shared the figures with Fortune. The funding package has two parts, a $29 million Series A-1 equity round and a $35 million non-dilutive growth financing facility.

The equity round is led by Zeev Ventures, with participation from Aleph, NordStar, M-Fund, LionTree and angel investor Dan Senor. The $35 million facility comes from Twelve, a credit-focused investment management firm. Spines also said its AI-powered services have reached a $50 million annual revenue run rate, which it describes as 400% year-over-year growth. The company has published more than 8,000 authors, covering about 12,000 titles, and roughly 400 new writers sign up each month. Spines declined to disclose its valuation.

Hybrid publishers typically charge authors an upfront fee and take a share of sales, while offering more support than self-publishing. Spines packages start at about $3,000 and reach $20,000 for a premium tier, with most authors choosing bundles of $5,000 to $7,000. The company recently raised its royalty share for authors from 70% to 80% of net royalties and reports earnings monthly. Niv said Spines publishes only books written by humans and uses software to screen for AI-generated manuscripts. He added that Spines is in early talks with one of the Big Five U.S. publishers about a partnership, and it plans to expand into the U.K., Canada and Australia.

Niv, who founded Spines in 2021 after running his own Israeli publishing house, has argued that AI will make traditional publishers less relevant. Spines has about 350 employees, of whom roughly 50 work in research and development. The article notes a possible copyright question around AI-designed covers, since U.S. courts and the Copyright Office have held that wholly AI-made images cannot be copyrighted, and Niv said Spines licenses its image tools and passes the license to authors. Oren Zeev of Zeev Ventures said in a statement that Spines has what it takes to lead the next generation of publishing.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: Spines, a 'hybrid publisher,' raises $64 million in funding for book publishing platform powered by AI agents

stories.Headline: Exclusive | I wrote an AI book using ChatGPT — is this method really the next chapter for aspiring authors?
stories.Summary:
Last week, a New York Post reporter tested whether ChatGPT could help write fiction, producing a science fiction story called "The Better World" in a few hours. The reporter used a short prompt about refugees fleeing a dying Earth for a utopia where death has been abolished. The result was an 8,000-word draft that the reporter found both affecting in places and derivative overall. The piece was published on November 9, 2026, as an exclusive.

The article places this experiment within a wider boom in AI-assisted books, and a backlash against it. Tim Boucher, a prolific author from Quebec, has published 125 books in a year with help from ChatGPT, Claude and other language models, selling them as e-books for $1.99 to $4.99. A recent study of 14,419 self-published genre books sold on Amazon between 2023 and 2026 found that 20 percent contained substantial AI-generated text. Separately, a September MIT study estimated that one unidentified author earned about $1.7 million from eight AI-infused books in a single year.

Mary Rasenberger, chief executive of the Authors Guild, says many such books are deliberate knockoffs of existing titles meant to draw away sales. She says the Guild is lobbying for laws requiring publishers and retailers to disclose AI use, and has taken legal action against AI firms such as Anthropic for training models on copyrighted books without permission. Rasenberger argues that machine-written text cannot capture the human condition and that the flood of such books makes good human-written work harder to find. Boucher, by contrast, says his process involves substantial human selection, editing and prompting, and he disputes the idea that AI use makes work inauthentic.

The reporter's own test found that the tool could produce striking lines, such as a description of Earth from orbit as resembling burnt cloth embroidered with fires. Yet the same draft often became overstuffed with description and leaned on familiar science fiction models. The article does not report any regulatory decision or a final outcome on the disclosure proposals. It leaves open whether AI-assisted fiction will become a durable method for aspiring authors or remain a contested niche.

Articles.Title: Exclusive | I wrote an AI book using ChatGPT — is this method really the next chapter for aspiring authors?

stories.Headline: AT&T is rebuilding its network for the AI and autonomous era
stories.Summary:
AT&T, the telecom operator, is rebuilding several layers of its network so that it can support more automation and artificial intelligence. Yigal Elbaz, the company's senior vice president and network chief technology officer, described the effort during a fireside chat at FutureNet North America in New York City last week. The article reports that the company has set an internal goal of reaching Level 4 network autonomy by 2030. Elbaz said that AT&T had long viewed that level as an ambitious target that the technology could not yet deliver, but advances in AI have changed the company's outlook.

The overhaul covers the radio access network, the standalone 5G core, and the company's IP and optical infrastructure, all of which are moving toward open, disaggregated and programmable designs. AT&T is also shifting cell-site management onto its service management and orchestration platform, which Elbaz called a key foundation for applications and for the agentic era. The company already uses AI for cell-site energy savings and wireless network planning, and it has built its own network foundation model around network-specific data and performance indicators. Elbaz also said that AI traffic volumes have not yet surged, but AT&T is seeing early signs of new patterns, such as workloads that run around the clock.

Elbaz cautioned against treating industry automation scores as a scorecard, saying that customer outcomes matter more than any single number. He identified remaining barriers, including data integrity, resolving conflicts when multiple AI agents reach different conclusions, and building trust in AI models and their results. He also pointed to physical AI, such as robotaxis and drones, which send a large share of their data upstream, and said AT&T observed one robotaxi with roughly 60% to 65% of its traffic moving upstream. The article says the company is framing readiness as an end-to-end problem that combines wireless, network slicing, fiber, transport and cloud connectivity.

The article also describes AT&T's satellite strategy as part of the converged-network push. AT&T and AST SpaceMobile said they successfully handed off a connection between AT&T's terrestrial cellular network and AST SpaceMobile's direct-to-device satellite network, which they called an industry first, with technology from Ericsson and Nokia supporting the handoff. The milestone brings the companies closer to beta testing and eventual commercial satellite service. Elbaz said customers care mainly that their connections work, and that AT&T's task is to keep them seamlessly connected to the best available network.

Articles.Title: AT&T is rebuilding its network for the AI and autonomous era

stories.Headline: A former Marine had an idea to help fellow veterans: AI helped him build it
stories.Summary:
Gary Crull, a former Marine who served in the Army National Guard and now works as a management and program analyst at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, built Battle Buddy, an AI agent that helps veterans, their families and caregivers understand federal, state and local benefits. The idea grew out of a day he once spent helping a homeless veteran find the right hospital and assistance, an experience he says was exhausting and that he wished he could have handled with better information.
