stories.Headline: EXL Acquires Aimpoint Digital, Adds 250 AI and Data Experts
stories.Summary:
EXL, the data analytics and AI services company, has acquired Aimpoint Digital, a data and AI consulting firm, to expand its forward-deployed AI engineering capabilities. The deal, reported on November 9, 2026, adds about 250 AI engineers, platform architects, analytics consultants, decision scientists and AI strategists to EXL's workforce. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction. The purpose is to help enterprises move AI projects out of pilot stages and into production.

The acquisition is meant to strengthen EXL's capabilities across the full enterprise AI lifecycle, including strategy, architecture, engineering, deployment, evaluation and managed operations. It also broadens the company's expertise across AI and data platforms such as Anthropic, Databricks and Snowflake. The combined offering is designed to give clients a single partner from initial strategy discussions through architecture, production deployment and ongoing operations. EXL said this should reduce handoffs between teams and create clearer accountability for business outcomes. Aimpoint Digital brings experience building enterprise data and AI platforms, along with engineers who work closely with client teams.

EXL's chairman and chief executive, Rohit Kapoor, said clients need a partner who can take them from AI ambition to impact at enterprise scale. He said Aimpoint Digital's strategists and engineers bring hands-on expertise to turn AI strategy into production on the platforms clients trust most. Ben Yopp, chief executive and co-founder of Aimpoint Digital, said the firm's AI strategy and engineering talent, combined with EXL's industry expertise, global reach and ability to run AI in operations, lets them take clients' most important AI initiatives into production. The acquisition comes as enterprises increase AI spending but still struggle to move projects beyond pilots.

The deal follows EXL's earlier purchase of AI model training and evaluation company iMerit, which expanded EXL's work in model training, evaluation and reinforcement learning. With Aimpoint Digital, EXL is focusing on the engineering and deployment side of its AI business, complementing the model development capabilities gained from iMerit. Together, the two acquisitions are intended to cover the AI lifecycle from model development and evaluation to enterprise deployment and managed operations. The articles do not say what further steps EXL plans beyond this integration.

Articles.Title: EXL Acquires Aimpoint Digital, Adds 250 AI and Data Experts - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Denmark wants its AI supercomputer to power new businesses and jobs
stories.Summary:
Denmark has announced an additional 500 million DKK (about €67 million) for its AI supercomputer Gefion, according to an announcement on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. The funding was disclosed by the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark and is aimed at the machine's infrastructure and operations at the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which runs it. The new money comes on top of an initial 700 million DKK (about €93.8 million) from Denmark's state investment fund and the Novo Nordisk Foundation, which backs the supercomputer. Gefion was launched in 2024 with 1,528 Nvidia chips, and the centre says it is now nearing full capacity. Details on how the funds will be spent and when the extra capacity will become available have not been revealed.

The government's stated goal is to turn wider access to computing power into economic growth. Martin Lidegaard, Denmark's minister for business and competitiveness, said the funding would give Danish companies and researchers more computing power to turn ideas into new solutions, companies and jobs. He also argued that it strengthens national competitiveness and keeps ownership of future technology from passing to others. A second aim is to help public institutions and businesses adopt AI while keeping sensitive data under their own control. Netcompany, a Danish technology firm that builds and runs public-sector IT systems, is joining the centre's investors and will supply software for access management, monitoring and security.

The announcement sits within a broader European effort to gain more control over the infrastructure used to develop AI. The United Kingdom invested £225 million (about €269 million) in an AI-focused supercomputer in 2023, and Finland hosts LUMI, a supercomputer jointly funded by the European Union and participating countries at a lifetime cost of more than €200 million. In July, the European Commission opened a call for up to seven AI gigafactories, large data centres for training and running advanced AI models, backed by up to €10 billion in EU and national funding. Christina Egelund, Denmark's minister for research, education and digitalisation, said Europe must do much more for itself and that Denmark should contribute to technological independence so that technology can be regulated and developed in line with democratic values. The article does not say what further steps are planned beyond the funding itself.

Articles.Title: Denmark wants its AI supercomputer to power new businesses and jobs

stories.Headline: Cephalopod-inspired embodied camouflage system for simultaneous evasion of artificial and human visual perception
stories.Summary:
Researchers have described CephCam, an embodied camouflage system that aims to hide a vehicle from both human observers and modern object detectors at the same time. The work, published in Nature Communications with a date stamp of November 9, 2026, is built on the camouflage of cephalopods such as cuttlefish and octopus. Prior approaches tended to fool either people or artificial intelligence, not both, and their patterns were often static. The system follows an eye-brain-skin design. Specialized cameras act as eyes to capture the surroundings and extract dominant colors, while processors and cloud servers serve as the brain to generate camouflage textures.

OLED screens on a model vehicle act as the skin, and a color mapping network corrects for how colors shift at different viewing angles. The brain uses two modes, a template matching mode and a real-time learning mode, along with an ensemble of detectors to improve how well the camouflage transfers to unseen models. The authors report that CephCam was tested across six environmental scenes: beach, city, desert, forest, night, and snow. In digital tests, the evasion rate was computed as the proportion of undetected vehicles among 1,000 rendered images per scenario, and 107 volunteers rated how natural the vehicles looked. The article also states that CephCam achieved higher evasion rates than prior methods against both white-box and unseen black-box detectors.

The authors say these results suggest that camouflage which looks plausible to humans can also suppress modern detectors, pointing to failure modes shared by human and artificial vision. The article does not indicate who funded the work or whether the system has been deployed beyond the research setting. Further physical testing and independent evaluation would be needed before any real-world use. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cephalopod-inspired embodied camouflage system for simultaneous evasion of artificial and human visual perception

stories.Headline: State space model for new generation network alternative to transformers: a survey
stories.Summary:
The article is an academic survey published on 9 November 2026 by Springer Nature in the journal Visual Intelligence, with authors including a first author listed under ORCID and co-authors Chenglong Li, Yaowei Wang, Yonghong Tian, and Jin Tang. It reviews the state space model (SSM), a framework originally used for modeling dynamic systems in control theory and computational neuroscience, as a possible alternative to the Transformer architecture. The authors say the Transformer has performed strongly in large pre-trained models but its heavy computational demands have discouraged many researchers. The survey presents what it describes as the first comprehensive review of SSM works, along with experimental comparisons. Because the source material is an academic abstract and introduction rather than news coverage, it does not report a single event with a date and actor beyond the publication itself.

The paper says it will walk readers through the principles of SSMs, review existing SSM models across natural language processing, computer vision, graphs, multimodal and multimedia data, point clouds, event streams, and other domains. It also offers statistical comparisons meant to show how different structures affect performance on various tasks. The experiments cover single- and multi-label classification, visual object tracking, pixel-level segmentation, image-to-text generation, and person or vehicle re-identification. The authors state that they will propose possible research directions for both the theory and applications of SSMs. The article explains that SSMs can be discretized so that they can be computed either recurrently or as convolutions, which is part of what makes them attractive for long sequences.

The authors are listed as responsible for the survey, and the abstract describes their goal in their own words as helping readers understand SSM features and advantages. They present their work as a review and comparison rather than as a claim that SSMs have replaced Transformers. The introduction places the work in the context of deep learning's development since AlexNet in 2012, the rise of convolutional and recurrent networks, and efforts to reduce the cost of attention through sparse methods and new paradigms. The paper includes a timeline of representative SSM algorithms from 2020 to July 2026. The article does not describe any outcome beyond the survey itself, so what happens next for the field is not stated in the material provided.

Articles.Title: State space model for new generation network alternative to transformers: a survey

stories.Headline: Red Hat OpenShift 5 adds AI capabilities, agent for workflow automation
stories.Summary:
Red Hat has extended its OpenShift platform with new artificial intelligence capabilities and an AI agent, aiming to simplify Kubernetes cluster management and automate workflows for IT teams. The company revealed these extensions at the KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America 2026 conference, and the report was published on November 10, 2026. The update is part of OpenShift version 5. Red Hat says the platform now includes a built-in Model Context Protocol server that makes OpenShift available to any AI agent through a simple update. The company has also expanded its Lightspeed AI tools with an agent that lets IT teams invoke multiple AI models for workflow automation.

OpenShift 5 also adds hardened multi-tenant isolation, automated certificate lifecycle management, and a control plane for managing post-quantum cryptography. The platform can analyze application programming interfaces to produce risk assessments, which allows updates without manual cluster reboots. Amazon Web Services is using this feature to extend support for OpenShift updates from 18 to 24 months, and it will also provide up to three years of extended lifecycle support. The embedded AI capabilities can identify root causes of issues, isolate anomalies, analyze log streams, and carry out supervised remediation across clusters from a single console. Version 2.1 of Red Hat Developer Hub, currently in preview, gives AI agents direct command-line access to an organization's software catalog.

Mike Barrett, vice president of Hybrid Cloud Platforms at Red Hat, said the Model Context Protocol server makes OpenShift available to any AI agent through a simple update. The AI agent has been trained to automate tasks across cloud-native platforms, including the Argo continuous delivery platform. Red Hat is also positioning OpenShift to run diverse workloads, including monolithic legacy applications deployed on virtual machines encapsulated in containers. Several organizations, including NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Brigham Young University, Allianz Turkey, Alior Bank, Hospital Diagnóstico, and Bharti Airtel, have adopted OpenShift Virtualization.

The article notes that many organizations struggle to manage fleets of Kubernetes clusters because they lack the software engineering expertise needed to operate at scale. The report suggests AI agents could make cluster management simpler for the average IT administrator. This matters more as AI coding agents make it faster to build cloud-native and AI applications. The article does not describe specific next steps beyond the preview availability of Developer Hub version 2.1.

Articles.Title: Red Hat OpenShift 5 adds AI capabilities, agent for workflow automation

stories.Headline: The Judgement and the Machine. School Assessment and Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Perspective
stories.Summary:
I can't write this one as a news story, because the article doesn't report an event. It is a Zenodo record for an Italian book, "Il giudizio e la macchina" (The Judgement and the Machine), about artificial intelligence in school assessment. The record is dated 9 November 2026 and gives the book's DOI, a CC0 licence, and a note saying the text was written by Claude Opus 5.5, an Anthropic model, at the request of Antonio Vigilante, who defined the topic and prepared the book for publication. The source gives no breaking news, no new incident, and no decision or announcement with a date, so there is nothing to build a timeline around.

What the source does provide is the book's scope. It reviews the Italian debate on docimology and school assessment, from Visalberghi and Gattullo to Corsini. It traces changes in the rules on school assessment, from Law 517/1977 to the return of summary judgements under Law 150/2024. It covers the current framework for AI in schools, including the EU AI Act, Ministerial Decree 166/2025, Law 132/2025, and a ministerial pilot.

It also looks at the history of assessment machines, from Pressey and Skinner's teaching machines to automated essay scoring and the Ofqual algorithm case. The book argues that automated assessment should be placed within datafication and education governance, and it discusses effects on social and linguistic inequality and on the teacher-student relationship. It closes with principles for a democratic use of AI in assessment, or a reasoned refusal of it. If you would like, I can write a short descriptive piece on the book's contents using only the information above, or a news story if you can point me to a separate article reporting an event, such as a ministerial decision or a court ruling.

stories.Headline: TraSPIN: inferring transporter specificity through language model-guided graph learning
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Tong Pan and Jiangning Song, with co-authors at several Australian, Chinese and university institutions, has published TraSPIN, a computational framework for predicting which chemical substances membrane transporters bind. The paper appeared in Genome Biology as an early-access article, with a publication date of November 9, 2026, and carries a permanent DOI while the authors' final version is still pending. The authors explain that membrane transporters move chemicals across cell boundaries, but their substrate preferences are poorly mapped because the proteins are hard to keep stable in laboratory experiments. Existing prediction tools, they note, tend to cover only narrow groups of substrates or fail when applied to transporters that are distantly related to those in their training data.

TraSPIN uses a geometric deep learning approach that models transporter proteins and small-molecule substrates together, and the article says it outperforms existing methods. The authors report that it generalizes to substrates it has not seen before and to transporters whose sequences differ substantially from the training set. The study also describes the framework identifying structural features and sequence motifs that appear to govern whether a transporter recognizes a given substrate. The authors further tested it on cross-species inference and on de-orphanization of uncharacterized solute carrier proteins, which are transporters whose functions are not yet known, presenting these results as evidence of its usefulness for functional annotation. The article gives no specific accuracy figures in the abstract.

Responsibility for the work rests with the listed authors, and the article credits the publisher's editorial team, including editors Qin Ma and Tim Sands, with managing peer review. The funding statement attributes support to the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia, the Australian Research Council, Monash University and the South Australian immunoGENomics Cancer Institute, and it notes that Jiangning Song served as a guest editor for the collection but was not involved in this manuscript's editorial process. The article is released under a Creative Commons licence that permits non-commercial reuse with attribution. It is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record once the publisher completes its production process.

Articles.Title: TraSPIN: inferring transporter specificity through language model-guided graph learning

stories.Headline: Scaling AI agents: AWS Lambda to EKS Auto Mode decision framework
stories.Summary:
An autonomous AI agent, first built to run on AWS Lambda, was designed to automate bug ticket filing for Quality Assurance teams, according to a TechGig report published on November 9, 2026. The agent watches test results, makes judgment calls, and files structured bugs, which its developer says saves 8 to 10 hours per week for each team. For a single team, the Lambda-based setup costs under $5 per month. Lambda was picked for its low operational overhead, costs that track usage, and fast iteration.

The article says that growing the agent to 10, 50, or 100 teams changes the workload itself. Work moves from stateless events to long-running context needed for cross-project correlation, and from isolated invocations to shared resources that need centralized rate limiting. Although newer Lambda features such as Managed Instances and Durable Functions address some of these needs one at a time, the proposed framework points to container-native execution for the full set of needs, including persistent connections, cross-tenant analysis, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode is presented as that environment, provisioning nodes only when pods require them and supporting immutable Bottlerocket AMIs, automatic node rotation, and reactive scaling for GPU workloads.

The multi-tenant design described includes shared platform services for rate limiting and connection pooling, isolated agent namespaces for each tenant, and a shared machine learning inference namespace with GPU-enabled pods that scale to zero when idle. The agent's decision logic stays in Python, but it would run as a long-lived asynchronous loop, which the article says allows cross-team intelligence such as correlating failures across teams and ML-based bug classification. The framework recommends starting with Lambda for single-team automation and moving to EKS Auto Mode as the platform layer for persistent multi-tenant services. The article quotes the developer as saying that Lambda validates the pattern while EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale, describing the two as stages in a journey rather than competitors. The article does not say when or whether any team will make this transition.

Articles.Title: Scaling AI agents: AWS Lambda to EKS Auto Mode decision framework

stories.Headline: Atlassian Connect end-of-life poses migration challenges for Jira apps
stories.Summary:
Atlassian has announced that its Connect platform will reach end of support on January 31, 2027, which means developers of existing Jira applications will need to migrate them to Forge. A developer tested this transition by porting the open-source app atlassian-labs/figma-for-jira to Forge on a live Jira Cloud site. The Figma for Jira Marketplace listing had 48,052 installs as of November 7, 2026, and lacked a Forge manifest, according to Marketplace and forge-apps.com data. The case study was published on November 9, 2026, by TechGig.

The migration required substantial code changes because many Connect features disappear once Forge takes over hosting, installation identity, and request authentication. Connect's JWT middleware and installations table were removed, and Forge renders admin pages through UI Kit instead of iframe-served pages. The Jira Designs panel, which Connect provides through the jiraDesignInfoProvider module, has no direct Forge equivalent, and the Forge scope list has no design scope. Background API calls also required a custom OAuth flow, since Forge's withProvider only supports user-invoked actions. The developer built this flow with a signed state, a one-time PKCE verifier, and secret storage for tokens.

Atlassian has said Connect apps will keep running after the deadline, but only critical security patches will be issued, and some changes could break apps without advance notice. The article notes that an app remains a Connect app until all Connect modules are removed, so keeping the Designs panel does not avoid the January 2027 deadline. Atlassian staff confirmed the limits of the provider behavior that forced the custom OAuth work. The developer's findings are presented as a practical account rather than as an official Atlassian statement.

For Marketplace apps, the article identifies a notable architectural difference: Forge assigns a different callback URL for each customer site, whereas Connect used a single base URL. Developers may need a fixed relay to forward callbacks or one OAuth application per customer, so the article advises planning for this early. The ported app demonstrated sign-in, a connected Figma account email, and background jobs reading a Figma file with a stored token, and the project reported zero vulnerabilities from an npm audit. The article also warns that adding an egress host forces a major version upgrade and removes "Runs on Atlassian" eligibility, and it recommends storing client secrets with encrypted forge variables.

Articles.Title: Atlassian Connect end-of-life poses migration challenges for Jira apps

stories.Headline: IIT Delhi launches 6-month cybersecurity and AI security course
stories.Summary:
IIT Delhi has launched a six-month Certificate Programme in Cybersecurity and AI Security aimed at working professionals. The course is offered through the institute's Continuing Education Programme and was reported on November 9, 2026. It responds to the security risks that come with artificial intelligence built into enterprise systems. The curriculum covers adversarial machine learning, prompt injection in large language models, exploitation of agentic AI, and attacks on model supply chains.

The programme includes 78 hours of live instruction across five modules, followed by a capstone project. Its five agentic AI attack areas are multimodal jailbreaks, Model Context Protocol prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool-calling exploitation, and model hub supply chain attacks. Participants will use tools such as PyRIT, Garak, Sigstore, OPA and Falco. Classes are held live online on Saturdays, and for the capstone, participants build and deploy a production-grade AI security solution that IIT Delhi faculty will evaluate.

The course is intended for cybersecurity professionals, AI and machine learning engineers, data scientists, DevOps and platform engineers, and governance, risk and compliance professionals. Applicants need a Bachelor's or Master's degree in a related discipline, at least 50 per cent marks, and familiarity with one programming language. Reports put the total fee at about ₹1,40,000 plus 18 per cent GST, or ₹1,65,200. Prof Subodh Vishnu Sharma, an associate professor in IIT Delhi's Department of Computer Science and Engineering, said security can no longer be separated from AI engineering. He said the programme takes a threat-first approach, teaching how AI systems are attacked before defences are built, in line with India's evolving regulatory requirements.

Articles.Title: IIT Delhi launches 6-month cybersecurity and AI security course
