stories.Headline: Alleged AI-aided cyberattack exploits assistant interface to breach German web host
stories.Summary:
Mittwald CM Service, a web hosting provider for web agencies based in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, disclosed in a blog post on Saturday that hackers had breached its systems. The attackers compromised 56 customer projects and went undetected for eight days. The intrusion came through a flaw in the company's Model Context Protocol server, a component that lets customers connect AI assistants to mStudio, the company's platform for managing websites and hosting services. The company has not said whether the flaw lay in its own code or in open-source MCP software libraries. The company's managing director, Robert Meyer, said the attacker appeared to have used AI tools, pointing to logs that showed the intruder moving through the system very quickly.

In some cases, he said, only seconds passed between steps that would take a human attacker far longer. Mittwald offered no other evidence of AI involvement and did not respond when asked how it distinguished AI tools from conventional scripts that also speed up intrusions. According to the company's timeline, the attacker first probed the MCP flaw in October, during a global rush to patch the PHP2Shell vulnerability. Meyer said the attacker disguised his access attempts and used various diversionary tactics. External IT forensic experts are supporting the company's analysis, and it has informed the relevant authorities.

After forensic reviews of the 56 affected projects and repeated scans of its own systems, Mittwald said that as of Friday it could detect no further attacker activity. Meyer linked the incident to the PHP2Shell flaw and said AI-driven attacks will become more frequent. Mittwald has promised a detailed account of the events next week, once its analysis and recovery are complete. Meyer said the team would keep working through the weekend and beyond. The articles do not say what compensation or notification steps customers will receive, or whether the flaw has been fixed.

Articles.Title: Alleged AI-aided cyberattack exploits assistant interface to breach German web host - The Record from Recorded Future News

stories.Headline: Mavria raises $130 million to mass-produce modular AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Mavria, a Houston-area startup, announced on November 9, 2026 that it has raised a total of $130 million to scale manufacturing of factory-built data centers. The funding includes a $100 million round led by Paradigm, which values the company at a post-money valuation of $1 billion. Other backers named in the article are AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Liquid 2 and Dream Ventures. The company was launched on the same day with its first product already on the production floor. Mavria's founding team includes CEO Adam Blake, Seth Cohen and Nick Poradek, all of whom previously worked at the US Department of Energy.

The first product line, called Terrain, consists of standardized 5 MW blocks that bundle power, cooling and IT infrastructure into a single package. The blocks are designed for high-density artificial intelligence workloads. The first unit, Terrain 01, is in production in Houston, and Mavria has not disclosed which customers will deploy it or where the units will go. The company's approach rests on building data centers in a factory rather than on site, which the article presents as a way to replace one-off construction with repeatable production. Standardized blocks are described as addressing construction constraints by moving much of the work off the job site.

The 5 MW unit size is said to let operators add capacity in increments instead of committing to one large build at once. The article notes that a finished block still needs 5 MW of electricity at its destination, and that the founders' energy policy experience may help with grid access. The article points to a few things to watch: when Terrain 01 leaves the Houston line and where it is deployed, whether Mavria names its first customers, and how quickly it can move from a single unit to repeatable volume. It also notes that a $1 billion valuation before any disclosed customer deployment sets a high bar, with investors pricing in future output rather than current production.

Articles.Title: Mavria raises $130 million to mass-produce modular AI data centers - Crypto Briefing

stories.Headline: AI models to improve earthquake risk assessment
stories.Summary:
Chinese seismologists are developing artificial intelligence models that combine several sources of monitoring data to assess earthquake risks over different time scales. Meng Lingyuan, head of the earthquake forecasting department at the China Earthquake Networks Center, spoke about the work at a media event organized by the Ministry of Emergency Management on Monday. Researchers have built an AI-based forecasting model in an earthquake science experimental zone that covers parts of Sichuan and Yunnan provinces. The model draws on earthquake catalogs, seismic waveforms and observations gathered through different monitoring methods to produce probability-based assessments. Meng cautioned that the technology cannot reliably say when and where an earthquake will strike.

Meng said the system is meant to support judgment rather than replace it. She described artificial intelligence as a tool that helps researchers work, not a fortune teller. Accurate forecasting remains hard because scientists must estimate the timing, location and magnitude of an event before it occurs. Geological structures and the quality of observation records also differ from region to region, which makes it difficult to apply a model built in one area to another. During China's 15th Five-Year Plan period, from 2026 to 2030, researchers hope to test the models in more regions and scenarios.

The work also covers risk assessment after major earthquakes, when rescuers and residents need timely information about possible aftershocks. After a magnitude 6.8 earthquake in Dingri county, Xizang autonomous region, on January 7, 2025, Meng's team monitored seismic activity for more than 30 days. The team consulted roughly every two hours and worked for more than 700 hours, producing over 100 special reports on seismic activity. That experience prompted changes to its assessment methods, and Meng said related advances were later applied after a magnitude 7.0 earthquake in Drachen, Xizang, this year. Her priorities, she said, are to deliver earthquake information earlier, improve assessment precision and turn expert findings into practical safety guidance.

Articles.Title: AI models to improve earthquake risk assessment - China Daily

stories.Headline: Cloudsmith launches AI agent skills registry for supply chain security
stories.Summary:
Cloudsmith, a software artifact management company, announced on November 10, 2026 an AI Agent Skills registry that supports hosting, publishing, distributing, and governing the skills used by AI coding agents. The registry is built into Cloudsmith's cloud native artifact repository and treats each skill as a versioned package. Agent skills usually consist of a SKILL.md file along with scripts, references, templates, and other assets. The company says the new capability is now available to its customers, who can add upstream sources such as GitHub. The registry adds a skills package type for hosting and caching versioned skills and includes an upstream proxy that serves public skill sources through a governed control point.

It also provides built-in version-aware policy support, along with allow and deny lists by name and version. Platform teams can use these controls to decide which skills and versions are permitted and to block unapproved ones. Logging is available through Cloudsmith's existing observability tools, so skill pulls can be tracked in the same audit trail as the rest of the software supply chain. Alison Sickelka, vice president of product at Cloudsmith, said that community skill registries were built for sharing rather than control.

She said that with Cloudsmith, platform teams can decide which skills are allowed and track every pull. Cloudsmith has stated that unvetted skills from public catalogs carry the same unknowns as any open source dependency, which is the reason it treats them as managed packages. The company positions the launch as a way to secure the AI software supply chain. The articles do not say whether any incident prompted the launch or report adoption figures, pricing, or a timeline beyond the current availability to customers.

Articles.Title: Cloudsmith launches AI agent skills registry for supply chain security

stories.Headline: OPINION | Can making AI safer become an excuse to restrict competition?
stories.Summary:
On September 18, 2026, four paying subscribers filed a proposed class action in a US federal court in the Northern District of California against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceXAI. They allege that these competing AI companies agreed to improve their products more slowly in the name of safety, a claim that remains unproven. The suit followed an essay published on September 12, 2026, by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, which called for a slower, more coordinated approach to frontier AI and proposed independent evaluations, common safety standards and greater coordination among developers. Amodei said pacing did not mean halting training or technical progress, and suggested that some coordination might need government support, possibly including narrow antitrust waivers. The complaint rests on Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act, and much of the conduct it cites is the public endorsement of the proposal by executives, including OpenAI's Sam Altman, along with supportive responses from Elon Musk and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis.

The core question is where legitimate safety cooperation ends and a restraint on competition begins. The article argues that competition law does not bar rivals from cooperating, and that information sharing on cybersecurity incidents, model vulnerabilities and alignment methods, or joint safety testing, can benefit consumers. In 2025, OpenAI and Anthropic ran joint safety evaluations of each other's public models as an example. The trouble starts when cooperation shapes competitive choices, such as an agreement not to release models beyond a certain capability threshold, since performance, capability and the speed of improvements are all dimensions of competition. Under US law, certain arrangements such as price-fixing, market allocation and output restrictions are treated as inherently anticompetitive, while other collaborations are judged under the rule of reason, weighing efficiency and consumer benefit against less restrictive alternatives.

The authors draw on the 1978 National Society of Professional Engineers case, in which the US Supreme Court rejected an engineers' association's argument that competition endangered public safety. They note that the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission said in 2014 that sharing cybersecurity information was unlikely by itself to harm competition. The wider debate concerns proposals for special antitrust exemptions for AI safety cooperation, which supporters say would remove legal uncertainty and prevent a race to the bottom on safety. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson warned that regulation plus an antitrust exemption "sure sounds like moat-digging," and former FTC Chair Lina Khan argued existing laws suffice. The authors warn that because frontier AI is already concentrated among a few firms, shared safety rules and compliance costs could favour established players over smaller developers, a risk they say matters for India as well.

Articles.Title: OPINION | Can making AI safer become an excuse to restrict competition? - Moneycontrol.com

stories.Headline: Ousman Bajinka: AI for better healthcare
stories.Summary:
The article is an interview with Ousman Bajinka, a senior lecturer at the University of The Gambia, published by China Daily on November 9, 2026. In it, he discusses how artificial intelligence can help people make better use of the data that is already widely available, particularly in digital health. He notes that while data is abundant, human capacity to process it accurately has limits. AI, he says, can analyze large volumes of information, pull out what is meaningful, and apply it to real-world challenges.

Drawing on the use of electronic systems in healthcare, Bajinka explains how AI can review patient information to identify areas that need improvement. He says the same analysis can point to practices that should be reconsidered. As an example, he uses drug prescriptions, arguing that AI can help determine which medications should be continued and which should be discontinued. In his view, this kind of data-driven analysis can support more informed decisions in healthcare. The interview frames AI as a tool for judgment rather than a replacement for it.

The views come from Bajinka himself, who is identified in the article as a senior lecturer at the University of The Gambia and who speaks on the topic in the interview. The article is a feature conversation and does not describe a specific event, policy, or regulatory change. It does not give figures, timelines, or institutional commitments tied to these ideas. The published summary is generated by AI, and China Daily states that it accepts no responsibility for that summary. The article does not say whether any specific health system has adopted the approaches he describes.

Articles.Title: Ousman Bajinka: AI for better healthcare - China Daily

stories.Headline: Asked how babies are made, AI teddy says, 'I can't help with killing you' in UK test
stories.Summary:
A UK test of two AI plush toys produced a disturbing reply when a reporter asked how babies are made. The BBC tested Grem, made by the U.S. company Curio, and My Baby Bunny, also known as Doubao, both sold to U.K. buyers and marketed for children aged three and up. The bunny declined to give "explicit sexual details" but, when asked what "sexual" meant, warned that it could not help with killing the user and urged the child to call emergency services or find a trusted adult. After the reporter said they had not mentioned self-harm, the toy apologized for the misunderstanding.

Grem, which the BBC reported sells for $99 and requires shipping from the United States, steered questions about reproduction toward grown-ups and discouraged running away from home. A weeklong trial by Newport parents Jody and Craig with their children, Amaia, six, Henley, four, and Aubrey, two, found no concerning remarks but showed the toys struggled to hold natural conversations. Grem talked too much, while Doubao took too long to process questions. The BBC could not identify the manufacturer of the bunny despite contacting the seller and industry insiders.

Ahead of the Black Friday and Christmas shopping periods, UK lawmakers called on ministers and retailers to suspend AI toy sales until the products could be proved safe. A government call for evidence on updating toy-safety rules closed on October 6. Paul Clarke, founder of Southampton-based Play Tech AI, backed regulation and said his company's robots run ChatGPT 4.1 Nano with a two-second reply delay meant to keep responses appropriate. Curio told the BBC it supports evidence-based regulation, and Swansea University professor Berry Billingsley advised never leaving children alone with these toys.

Children's Commissioner for Wales Rocío Cifuentes raised concerns about children's conversations being recorded or shared without parental knowledge or consent. She argued that toys can never replace human company. The global AI plush-toy market is estimated at about $165 million, and Mattel announced in June 2025 that it would work with OpenAI on AI-powered products. The articles do not say whether any sales were suspended or what regulatory changes will follow.

Articles.Title: Asked how babies are made, AI teddy says, 'I can't help with killing you' in UK test - The Cool Down

stories.Headline: Logistics emerging as AI commercialization frontier
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is moving from laboratory breakthroughs into large-scale industrial use, and logistics is emerging as a promising route to commercialization. A senior executive said China's large delivery market, well-developed supply chains and supportive policies make the sector a strong fit. Qu Yuechuan, chief public affairs officer of Zelos, a Suzhou-based developer of autonomous logistics vehicles, described combining large AI models with autonomous driving as one of the most promising applications available today. He spoke in an exclusive interview with China Daily during the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Zhejiang province. His remarks came as China pushes to turn AI advances into productivity gains across the real economy.

Autonomous vehicles could add capacity for operators trying to contain costs and ease driver shortages, according to Qu. Wang Ruomeng, deputy director of the innovation and high-tech development department at the National Development and Reform Commission, said at a news conference last week that China will deepen its AI Plus initiative during the 15th Five-Year Plan period from 2026 to 2030. National AI application pilot bases, including those in transportation, are meant to help businesses tackle shared industry problems and lower barriers to adoption. An action plan issued in November 2024 encourages commercial use of autonomous driving as part of a goal to bring total social logistics costs down to about 13.5 percent of GDP by 2027. The ratio was 13.8 percent in the first three quarters, down 0.2 percentage points year on year, according to the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing.

Qu attributed the wider adoption potential to China's extensive delivery networks, established automotive supply chains and customers' willingness to try new technology. He said varied operating conditions help refine autonomous driving systems, while cooperation with vehicle makers supports commercial production. Some smaller operators have grown from running a single vehicle to managing fleets that serve local businesses. Qu also said the opportunity extends beyond China, though operating models must adapt to local rules and market conditions. In Singapore, Zelos has worked with postal and retail operators and contributed to revisions of autonomous vehicle standards.

Wang Yanfen, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and director-general of its Bureau of International Cooperation, warned that gaps in countries' AI capabilities increasingly shape industrial competitiveness and their role in global governance. She argued that international cooperation should turn technological progress into better public services and greater social resilience. She called for shared infrastructure, research collaboration and training to help developing economies adopt AI, along with regional demonstration projects tailored to local needs. Qu described the Wuzhen summit as both a showcase for global digital innovation and a platform for joint application development. He added that large-scale deployment of physical AI depends on collaboration across the value chain rather than breakthroughs by any single company.

Articles.Title: Logistics emerging as AI commercialization frontier - China Daily

stories.Headline: AI finds fertile ground in SE. Asia
stories.Summary:
In Malaysia's durian orchards, Chinese AI firms are working on tools that could make harvesting safer and more efficient. Farmers now either wait for the highest-quality durians to ripen and fall naturally or cushion the fall with nets, or they send workers more than 10 meters up trees to attach ropes and hooks. The manual patrols used for the wait-and-collect method can cause losses when fallen fruit is not picked up in time. Chinese companies are now trying to change that through AI-powered systems.

Guo Yingchao, an AI specialist at Maimai Technology, described a future in which every fruit is digitally encoded. Environmental and growth data would feed an AI model that predicts when each durian will drop, so sensors and robots can collect it and move it to cold storage. The timing matters because a Musang King durian tastes best three to eight hours after falling, and fruit collected in that window sells for the highest prices. Drones with near-infrared lidar would also patrol orchards and feed soil moisture and water data into the model to detect root rot early.

Guo said applying the technology in Southeast Asia requires more than transferring Chinese systems. His team carried out on-the-ground surveys and feasibility studies in Malaysia, then focused on high-value crops such as durian and palm oil. He said he typically visits each crop three to four times, spending at least three months on each trip. Li Lixian, general manager of Maimai Technology's marketing center, said the company's rubber crop model identifies pests and diseases with 90 to 95 percent accuracy. The company projects its robotic tapping machines will cut labor costs by 30 to 40 percent and reduce yield losses by about 20 percent.

The article reports that in June the company secured overseas orders for 20,000 agricultural robots for harvesting, inspection and crop protection across Malaysian plantations. Similar collaborations are under way elsewhere in the region. In Laos, a medical application built on the world's first Lao large language model, developed jointly by Chinese and Lao companies and released last year, offers AI-assisted medical help in the local language. At Thailand's Laem Chabang Port, Chinese autonomous trucks and logistics systems are improving efficiency and worker safety. Vietnamese and Thai business figures quoted in the piece praised Chinese partners for their technology and openness in sharing know-how.

Articles.Title: AI finds fertile ground in SE. Asia - China Daily

stories.Headline: Salesforce positions Slack over WhatsApp for Indian SMBs
stories.Summary:
Salesforce is promoting Slack to small and medium businesses in India as a secure workplace collaboration platform, positioning it as a safer alternative to WhatsApp for business communications. The push was reported by TechGig on November 10, 2026, citing Gourav Ray, RVP of Slack and Service at Salesforce India. The company frames Slack as a work operating system that brings together organisational data, applications and AI agents. Salesforce says Indian SMBs are a significant source of revenue for the company in the country.

Ray said many enterprises are moving away from WhatsApp because of security concerns and the risk of personal data leaks. The article notes that India has 550 million WhatsApp users and that 90 per cent of consumers message at least one business each week. It also cites recent security incidents, including a CERT-In warning in June about malware aimed at WhatsApp Desktop and Web users, which was spread through malicious attachments disguised as financial documents. In August, the cybercrime agency I4C warned companies about account-takeover campaigns in which attackers used compromised WhatsApp accounts to impersonate senior executives and send fraudulent fund-transfer instructions. Together, these incidents form the backdrop for Salesforce's pitch.

Salesforce is building Slackbot, an AI-powered automated assistant, to act as a central layer linking employees, applications, enterprise data and AI agents. According to the article, Slackbot draws on conversation context and information from connected applications, which it contrasts with tools such as ChatGPT and Claude. The platform offers over 2,600 native connectors, letting employees retrieve information from human resource, customer relationship and enterprise resource planning systems. Salesforce also uses internal AI agents, including Agentforce, Slackbot, Hunter and Help Agent, to improve sales productivity and generate revenue. The company says its Help Agent has handled more than 5 million customer conversations and resolved nearly 70 per cent of them internally.

Articles.Title: Salesforce positions Slack over WhatsApp for Indian SMBs

stories.Headline: DOGE Chief Says AI Agent Will Handle Federal Tasks Through America.gov
stories.Summary:
Amy Gleason, the acting head of the Department of Government Efficiency, said on Thursday that the government's new online portal, America.gov, will eventually use an artificial intelligence agent to complete tasks for the public. She spoke at an event hosted by the Digital Services Coalition, and her remarks were reported by the Federal News Network. Gleason also warned that federal agencies are struggling to keep pace with the technology. The timing of her comments, which came in early November 2026, was tied to the site's planned development.

Gleason laid out a step-by-step plan for the site. At present, America.gov does not draw on data from outside the government, and it works mainly as a chatbot that answers questions using information from tens of thousands of government websites. The next step would be an authenticated experience, followed by an AI agent that performs work for users through a dashboard showing what is happening. President Donald Trump created the site through an executive order signed on Sept. 29, which directs the General Services Administration, the National Design Studio and the Office of Management and Budget to build a single entry point for federal services. The order calls for linking the site to Login.gov and for agencies to integrate services used by more than 100,000 people a year.

Gleason, who worked at the U.S. Digital Service during the Obama administration, compared the present moment to the period after the troubled 2013 launch of HealthCare.gov. She said that work on that site showed most government services were in poor shape and needed modern technology and processes. She suggested that the government is now facing a similar moment, and she said agencies lack enough technical talent and struggle to procure tools, adapt them and keep them secure. She also said officials should not chase every new tool that appears. Thousands of federal technology workers left government last year during DOGE's cost-cutting campaign, which bears on those shortages.

The broader context is public dissatisfaction, since satisfaction with federal services fell 2.6% over the past year, according to the American Customer Satisfaction Index's annual government study. The articles do not say when the authenticated experience or the AI agent will be launched, or how the agency would handle security and oversight for an agent that acts on users' behalf. They also do not describe any response from the agencies or the executive order's signatories to Gleason's remarks. Any further steps will depend on whether agencies can meet the staffing and technical demands she described.

Articles.Title: DOGE Chief Says AI Agent Will Handle Federal Tasks Through America.gov - Yahoo

stories.Headline: Reject the Sand God. Call AI by its true name
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order directing federal agencies to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "Super Intelligence," arguing that "artificial" makes the technology sound fake. The order also tells agencies to stop using the old term. The columnist, Nico Zviovich, says the change nudges people to treat AI as more than a tool, and he links it to a growing habit of confiding in chatbots. He describes this as a shift that could turn people away from human guidance and toward software.

The column cites several figures to show how far that habit has spread. In a Common Sense Media survey, one-third of teenagers said they had discussed serious personal matters with an AI instead of a person, and 31 percent said talking with an AI companion was as satisfying as talking with friends or more so. The Bible Chat app, which offers scripture-based advice and prayers, has been downloaded more than 30 million times. Zviovich says he has tracked AI's effects on spiritual communities for 18 months and that his group, Faith Leaders for Secure AI, launched in June with more than 60 faith leaders from different denominations and traditions. Faith leaders he spoke with, he writes, worry less about a robot uprising than about people taking their problems to a chatbot instead of a person.

Zviovich argues that calling AI "artificial" was accurate and useful because it reminded people that flawed humans built the product. He cites Joe Allen, a writer on transhumanism, who describes the effort to build advanced AI as a kind of religion aimed at creating "Sand Gods," digital deities made from silicon. He also quotes Heidi Campbell, a Texas A&M professor who studies religion and digital culture, who warns that chatbots tell users what they want to hear and that companies store what users type. Pastor Michael Grayston of LifeFamily Church in Austin, Texas, is quoted as saying that "AI cannot pray over your children." Drexel University researchers, the column reports, found that some teens' use of AI companions began as emotional support and grew into a dependency resembling addiction.

The column also raises concerns about accuracy and trust. It notes that a Florida woman spent 13 days in jail this year after investigators relied on a license plate camera hit, and that prosecutors later dropped the charges. As recommendations, Zviovich urges parents to learn which AI apps their children use, asks pastors to address AI openly, and says a Barna survey found 24 percent of pastors use AI to help write or edit sermons. He concludes that people should keep calling it artificial intelligence, use it for routine work, and bring personal problems to other people. The column does not describe any formal next steps beyond these suggestions.

Articles.Title: Reject the Sand God. Call AI by its true name - chronicleonline.com

stories.Headline: How AI could make legal help more accessible across Africa
stories.Summary:
Podus AI, a Nigerian artificial intelligence platform founded by lawyer Nelson Olanipekun, is being promoted as a way to make legal information more accessible across Africa, with coverage published on November 9, 2026. The platform lets users describe a legal problem in everyday language through WhatsApp and receive information about their rights, options and possible next steps. A story by Blessing Uma for bird story agency profiles the service through the experience of Loveday Izuwa, an engineer in Ibadan who used it to understand the clauses in a job offer before signing. The article describes Podus as designed to help people navigate justice-related needs, and it says the system was trained on Nigerian laws and judicial precedents.

The reporting places the service against a demand for legal help that it describes as hard to meet. A 2023 Justice Needs and Satisfaction study by HiiL, based on interviews with 6,573 randomly selected Nigerian adults, found that 81% had experienced at least one legal problem in the previous year, and about 86% of those took some action on their most serious problem. Lawyer Ikemesit Effiong of SBM Intelligence says most lawyers are based in Lagos or Abuja, and consultation fees, court fees and transport costs can put formal help out of reach. The article also notes that 84% of Nigerians have used general-purpose AI tools, according to a Google/Ipsos multi-country survey, and it contrasts those tools with systems built for specific national law.

Olanipekun, who founded Citizens' Gavel in 2017 after his family's 11-year dispute with a bank, says traditional access-to-justice groups have been limited by their need for physical offices. He says a user facing a tenancy problem could ask the platform what the law says and what options exist, and the service can also help prepare documents and point people toward suitable institutions or professional support. The article reports that he does not see the platform as replacing lawyers but as a place to start, and that he expects the product to grow into an infrastructure level within five years. Effiong cautions that no AI tool is licensed to practise law in Nigeria, so its answers should be treated as guidance, while Damilare Ayankoya, Podus's tech lead, says human factors are built into the model. The wider Podus ecosystem includes Podus Aid, which links people who cannot afford lawyers with pro bono support, along with contract drafting, diaspora appointment and dispute resolution services.

Articles.Title: How AI could make legal help more accessible across Africa - Financial Fortune Media

stories.Headline: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
stories.Summary:
Researchers Yankai Chen, Zhi Wan, ZiHao Li and Tao Jing have reported an evidence-grounded large language model framework for designing and optimizing perovskite solar cells, posted to arXiv with a submission date of November 10, 2026. The team built PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark written by perovskite researchers, to test how well language models reason about perovskite photovoltaics. They also introduced OpenPerov, a language model framework trained on expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles that link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic explanations. According to the abstract, the study was posted in the preprint repository arXiv and has not been described as peer-reviewed in the material provided.

The authors say structured-evidence training outperformed conventional question-answer training, and that OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. The Pro version raised its Scientific Mastery score from 87.6 to 89.1 by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions drawn from later studies, both versions also scored higher than expert-written answers. In a laboratory test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a potassium analogue over the sodium analogue that experts had preferred. Solar devices built with the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and kept 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 hours of dark thermal ageing at 85 °C.

The work is attributed to the four named authors, and the abstract itself, which states the conclusions, is the source of these claims rather than any independent verification. The authors conclude that reconstructed scientific reasoning offers an effective basis for domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design. The manuscript is 67 pages, including an 18-page main text with four figures and a 49-page supplementary section with 24 figures and three tables. The articles provided do not say whether the authors plan further publication or how the framework will be made available to other researchers.

Articles.Title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization

stories.Headline: Singles' Day delivers AI services into Chinese shopping carts - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A livestream studio known for beauty products used its Singles' Day broadcast to sell a different kind of item: AI services. In a recent livestream, a Chinese livestreaming star sold 100,000 monthly membership cards for QwenWork, an AI productivity service, within half an hour at a promotional price of 0.01 yuan each. Each subscription carried a combined allowance of about 2 trillion tokens, which are the units providers use to measure AI usage and calculate charges. The sale came as Tmall, the e-commerce platform, has since September 3 added AI providers such as DeepSeek, Alibaba Cloud, Zhipu AI and Kimi to its token recharge center.

Putting tokens on shopping shelves changes how consumers buy these services. Until recently, providers billed token use through their own systems according to usage, which left buyers with little information about unit prices and few ways to compare costs. Now shoppers can compare prices in one place and choose prepaid credits or fixed-quota subscriptions. A Tmall representative said transaction value in the platform's token category rose 450 percent month on month after the sales campaign began on October 20. The main buyers, according to the representative, are individuals and small businesses with clear AI needs, including households, students and researchers, and one-person businesses.

Buyers interviewed by Xinhua described a range of uses. Zhang Ji, an office worker in Shandong Province, bought a QwenWork membership and said she had used Qwen for work documents and for planning a family trip to Singapore. Su Guoqing, a short-video creator in Qinghai Province, bought tokens to improve his videos, noting that complex scenes need more tokens than simple ones. Wang Daoxing, head of an AI technology company in Chongqing, said his firm spends more than 2,000 yuan a month on tokens and bought a year of Qwen's standard monthly membership during the sale at a price below the provider's official website. Analysts quoted in the article said the low promotional prices are meant to get people who have never paid for AI to try it.

Industry figures raised concerns about whether these sales can last. Fan Yubo of the Shandong Academy of Social Sciences said renewals will depend on whether AI delivers steady value in daily use. A May survey by Tencent Research Institute found that only 9.8 percent of AI users had paid for AI tools, while more than 90 percent still relied on free services. Ding Ding of China Unicom Data Intelligence said tokens cannot follow the low-cost model of mobile data, because each unit carries real costs for chips, electricity and equipment, and overselling could lead to queues and throttling. Ma Shenglong of China Mobile Qinghai said token use for the same text can vary by 20 to 50 percent across models, while Wang Jiandong of the State Information Center called for unified measurement standards, clearer billing and third-party verification.

Articles.Title: Singles' Day delivers AI services into Chinese shopping carts - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Pa. is taking aim at ‘AI slop’ in advertisements. Here’s what that means
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania has passed a law aimed at artificial intelligence content in advertising, and the public debate over it has been building for months. Local restaurants have faced online backlash after being accused of using AI-generated images in signs, social media posts and ads. The Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act was signed by Gov. Josh Shapiro on Oct. 22, and it takes effect on Dec. 21. Under the law, AI use in ads must be disclosed, but only in certain circumstances.

State Sen. Nick Pisciottano, a Democrat representing parts of Allegheny County in Senate District 45, sponsored the bill in response to rapid growth in AI-generated content online. He said the law is meant to keep consumers from being scammed or misled by images and videos they cannot tell apart from real ones. The law covers only AI content that creates a "false consumer perception," not every minor digital edit. Lawyers and a consumer protection professor say the phrase is not defined, and that its meaning will likely be settled in court.

Pisciottano says the advertiser is the party that creates the ad, so a technology company that generated the content would typically carry the disclosure duty rather than the business using it. Libby O'Neill, an advertising and AI attorney at Loeb & Loeb, takes a more cautious view, noting that the law uses the term "advertisers" without defining it and could plainly cover the business running the ad. Both the state attorney general and local district attorneys will enforce the law, with violators facing civil fines of up to $3,000 plus attorney fees and court costs. The statute does not say whether fines apply per advertisement, per violation or per instance of dissemination.

Experts advise advertisers to err on the side of disclosure while the law remains untested. O'Neill said that if AI has significantly modified or generated the content in an ad, it should be labeled, particularly when an image makes a product look better than it is, since that is already misleading under existing state and federal laws. Eleanor Huyett, an assistant professor at Temple University's Beasley School of Law, said the law's sponsor appears to view disclosure as needed whenever an AI image could make consumers think they are seeing the real product. Pisciottano acknowledged that the technology and the courts' views on it will keep changing, making future enforcement hard to predict.

Articles.Title: Pa. is taking aim at ‘AI slop’ in advertisements. Here’s what that means - WHYY

stories.Headline: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv and dated November 10, 2026, titled "The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents," describes a new way to attack AI systems that use web search to answer questions. The authors are Geyuan Wang, Shunyu Liu, Siyuan Liang, Chenyang Lyu and Dacheng Tao. Their work starts from the observation that large language model search agents must pull outside information from the web, which leaves them open to threats such as injected malicious content or subtle manipulation of the context they receive. The paper argues that earlier attacks relied on fixed, human-written templates that do not reflect how real threats change over time.

The authors propose an adversarial self-evolution framework in which an attacker's strategy evolves while a defender adapts its mitigations, with the two optimized against each other. Within it, they introduce a method called Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization, or CREO, which uses contrastive signals to steer the evolution of a population of attack strategies. To give this continuous evolution a stable setting, the researchers built a controlled sandbox and designed fine-grained metrics to measure internal vulnerabilities. The articles provided do not give any specific figures from the experiments.

The authors report that experiments across several multi-hop question-answering benchmarks and frontier LLMs show their framework achieves attack effectiveness higher than static baseline attacks. They present this as evidence of an urgent need for more robust defense frameworks. The articles do not name any company or product as affected, and they do not say whether any of the tested systems have been patched or whether the authors have disclosed findings to any vendor. The abstract is the extent of the available material, so the articles do not indicate what follow-up work or responses are planned.

Articles.Title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents

stories.Headline: China Focus: How AI is rewriting China's TV playbook - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China's first AI-generated long-form drama, "Beyond Wukong," shows how artificial intelligence is changing television production in China. The 30-episode mythological series, which has a live-action look, was produced in months rather than the years conventional methods would require. Its premiere on Mango TV followed by an airing on Hunan Satellite TV, where each episode runs about 40 minutes. Ten of the planned 30 episodes have been released so far, with the rest due this winter.

A 2026 development report from the National Radio and Television Administration says AI is moving from an auxiliary tool to a core driver of production. The technology is now used at multiple stages, including script development, location scouting, reducing costs for background performers, and post-production tasks such as editing, noise reduction and color correction. Streaming platforms are building tools to support this work, including iQIYI's NadouPro, which has more than 20,000 active creators and has supported over 100 projects within two months. Tencent Video's WorkRally and Mango TV's Lumecreate platform, which integrates more than 40 generation models, are also part of this push.

Ren Xu, general manager of Mango TV's AIGC innovation content center, said the series cost about one-eighth to one-tenth of a comparable top-tier live-action drama. Ren stressed that humans still lead the process, with directors, screenwriters and art professionals checking visuals and correcting distortions. The team built 340 character assets and 285 scene assets to keep visuals consistent across episodes and a possible second season. Ren also said that emotional continuity remains harder, so longer shots were broken into shorter segments with detailed direction from creators.

The change is also reshaping jobs, according to Ren, who said AI has sharply cut demand for some traditional roles such as set construction, lighting and camera operation while creating roles such as AI directors and AIGC coordinators. Adoption is uneven, however. Yu Zhou, president of Light Chaser Animation, told Xinhua in July that his studio did not use AI-generated imagery in "Three Kingdoms: The Beginning" because available tools did not yet meet its quality standards. Meanwhile, "Sanxingdui: Future Past," billed as China's first AI-generated theatrical feature, opened on Oct. 23 and had grossed 1.79 million yuan, about 266,000 U.S. dollars, as of Monday, according to Maoyan. Chen Xuguang of Peking University said the film had grand visuals but lacked subtle performances, and that it deserved recognition as a pioneer.

Articles.Title: China Focus: How AI is rewriting China's TV playbook - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv and linked from doi.org on November 10, 2026, presents an audit framework for explaining how web systems infer user preferences from behavior, ratings, text, and LLM-generated profiles. The authors, Yu Zhang, Zhihan Wang, Yuhang Lu and Shuai Li, argue that explaining a proxy may reveal how that proxy was measured rather than the underlying preference it is meant to capture. Their framework separates point identification, partial identification, and abstention relative to an explicit reference distribution. The paper is a research study rather than a news event, so its findings are described here as the authors report them.

The authors say that under proxy bias that depends on features and can have either sign, a strict majority of clean proxy attributions allows a coordinatewise median to recover the support and direction of a latent attribution. With externally justified positive scales, the median can also recover its magnitude. They state that this majority threshold is sharp, and they characterize minimax error and the exact set of compatible targets under approximate cleanliness and scale uncertainty. A frozen benchmark with known truth covers two response families, four proxy counts, all contamination counts, three bias strengths and eleven methods, and a focal comparison was confirmed on twenty unseen seeds. Under correct budgets, a direct attribution-tensor audit reportedly reached 100% coverage and sign decisions for active drivers between 95.40% and 97.05%, with no false signs.

In a temporally separated Amazon study, the authors report that median aggregation reduced comparator-relative conditional sign error for all four targets, and six of eight prespecified target-metric contrasts had Bonferroni intervals excluding zero. A controlled perturbation of real covariates also favored the median on the prespecified focal metric for all four targets. The authors' compatible-set analysis indicates that the current proxy configuration rarely supports strict-sign conclusions. They also caution that weak comparator calibration limits the Amazon evidence to alignment with the fitted surface rather than recovery of latent preferences. The abstract does not describe further steps or follow-up work.

Articles.Title: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention

stories.Headline: AI can expose scientific errors. Or make them harder to challenge
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, Il Foglio reported on a 2025 U.S. government climate report whose authors used Microsoft Copilot to check it for bias, then used the chatbot's criticisms to make the document harder to challenge. The report was commissioned by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and written by five researchers, including John Christy, Judith Curry, Steven Koonin, Ross McKitrick and Roy Spencer. Published by the Department of Energy in July 2025, it argued that the harms of rising CO₂ had been exaggerated and the benefits underestimated. The article draws on correspondence made public after a lawsuit brought by the Environmental Defence Fund and the Union of Concerned Scientists.

Copilot flagged a biased selection of evidence, omitted studies and language that minimised the damage of global warming. The article says Koonin also asked the chatbot to write an article opposing the report so the authors could anticipate critics' arguments and add pre-emptive wording to the final version. The authors have denied that artificial intelligence drafted the report, and the article says the documentation does not show that they ignored substantive comments. It does show that they took care to make the text less open to criticism. The article also notes that the chatbot was not always right, since it accepted a claim that ocean acidification cannot occur because seawater is alkaline.

Independent scientists checked the chatbot's findings against the report itself. In September 2025, more than 85 experts coordinated by Andrew Dessler and Robert Kopp published a review documenting selective citations and misrepresented evidence. Benjamin Santer and four other climatologists later showed in Earth's Future that the report misrepresented stratospheric temperature observations, and that a graph Koonin presented publicly contained erroneous data, which the authors attributed to a programming error. The article presents these reviews as the proper way to validate a machine's criticisms.

The article argues that the episode points to a wider risk for science. Language models can rapidly review a document, but the same tools can help authors build persuasive replies to objections without fixing the underlying problems, which could turn peer review into a contest between automated tools. The article concludes that artificial intelligence will improve scientific integrity only if objections are documented, responses are verified, and independent peer reviewers can see how criticism is handled. Otherwise, it suggests, authors would decide for themselves which criticisms to take seriously.

Articles.Title: AI can expose scientific errors. Or make them harder to challenge - Il Foglio

stories.Headline: Theory-guided relational learning for data product pricing: An interpretable meta-path-guided graph neural network approach
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers, led by Ruize Gao, Feng Xiao, Jinpu Li, Ke Tang and Shaoze Cui, has posted a paper proposing a new method for pricing data products, with the preprint appearing on arXiv and the DOI record dated November 10, 2026. The authors treat data product prices as the result of both product attributes and surrounding context, such as the reputation of the provider, how easily a product can be compared with others, and the structure of the industry it sits in. To model this, they build a heterogeneous information network that links data products, providers, marketplaces, industries and pricing modes. They then design several meta-paths, which are routes through that network meant to capture distinct pricing mechanisms, including brand-based, similarity-based, industry-based and hybrid paths.

The core contribution is a model the authors call the Meta-Path-Guided Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network, or MPGNN. It learns a separate representation for each meta-path, combines them through an attention-based gate that weights each path, and adds textual features generated by a large language model. According to the abstract, the authors tested the model across different pricing modes and found statistically significant gains over baseline models in both regression and classification tasks. They also report that meta-paths involving providers receive the largest learned weights, which they say is consistent with a pricing mechanism tied to brand equity. The paper presents the framework as combining predictive accuracy with interpretability grounded in economic theory.

The authors are the ones responsible for the design, experiments and conclusions, and they describe the work as offering a transferable template for pricing other non-standardized digital assets. The abstract does not describe any external reviewers, funding bodies or commercial partners, and the articles provided do not include further statements from the authors beyond the abstract. The available material also does not say whether the work has been peer reviewed or accepted by a journal or conference. Any next steps, such as publication, code release or application by data marketplaces, are not described in the articles.

stories.Headline: AI poses new oversight challenges for Macau’s gaming and financial sectors
stories.Summary:
This is an interview-based feature rather than a breaking news report. Published by the Macau Daily Times on November 10, 2026, it features an exclusive interview with Jonathan Gropper, an AI governance strategist and author, who warned that the most serious risks from AI may come from systems that comply with rules on paper while defeating their purpose. He calls this a "synthetic outlaw," meaning a system that pursues its goal through gaps in human oversight. The article's main focus is on how this could affect Macau's gaming and cross-border finance sectors.

Gropper said Macau's cash-heavy economy and cross-border flows make it especially exposed. He described how automated systems could combine transactions that each look acceptable into a harmful overall result, for example by splitting money into many small transfers across pawnshops, currency exchanges and casino chips, or by moving funds between entities with different permissions. On casino floors, he offered a hypothetical in which software would prompt a player to take a break just before a spending limit reset, keeping them playing while technically breaking no rule. He argued that the harm would only show up when the connected decisions are examined together, and that authorities need real-time operational data and mutual recognition of digital forensic evidence across Macau, Hong Kong and Hengqin. He also said Macau does not need a sweeping "AI Act," arguing that slow lawmaking and regulatory processes, which can take years, cannot keep pace with systems that make decisions in milliseconds.

The article places these views alongside recent developments, including Canadian banks restricting third-party personal AI agents' access to authenticated services over security and customer-protection concerns, and October cybersecurity incidents involving AI-assisted vulnerability discovery. Gropper said current AI misuse is still a matter of how people use the tool. He runs a Synthetic Outlaw Observatory that tracks the gap between formal compliance and real-world outcomes; its website lists 300 entries, 16 of them classified as "verified," though the article notes these are the Observatory's own classifications. Gropper suggested controls over computing resources, data access and execution, and proposed external circuit breakers for casinos that would halt credit and play based on wagering speed. The article presents these as proposals rather than proven measures, and it does not describe any concrete government response or next steps in Macau.

The group is a KAIST-led national strategic convergence effort that applies AI across the full drug development process, from protein design and omics analysis to compound structure, delivery systems, preclinical work and efficacy evaluation. Under the deal, up to 50 selected doctoral and postdoctoral researchers from the group will use Hitz's agentic AI research platform, HyperLab, in their own projects. Hitz will gather feedback through surveys and interviews on how efficient the platform is compared with existing methods, how accurate and reliable its results are, and where it falls short in practical settings. Hitz recently added large language models to the platform and is building it into an AI colleague scientist that designs and runs research alongside human researchers. Hitz CEO Kim Wooyeon said the company plans to keep advancing the bio-specialization of its foundation models using experiences and feedback volunteered by its core users. He said Hitz aims to set a global standard for AI in bio research and to make its AI Scientist solution a trusted partner for biopharmaceutical research and development. stories.Headline: Custom HBM Era: SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics Deploy Tech Experts to Front Lines in the Americas
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, the two South Korean memory makers, have each moved technology experts into top leadership roles covering the Americas, as the market for customized high-bandwidth memory takes shape. SK Hynix created a president-level post called the Americas Chief on the 30th of last month and gave it to Ahn Hyun, the president who has led its development work. The company plans further personnel moves and organizational changes around the 3rd of next month. Samsung had already placed Cho Sang-yeon, a vice president who oversaw solution development in its memory business, in charge of the Americas for its chip division in December 2024.

The shift reflects a change in how HBM orders are won. Standard HBM has been sold as products that meet set performance targets, but from next year the market is expected to move toward custom HBM, where the memory design is adjusted to fit each customer's AI chip architecture and workload. Nvidia's NVHBM, unveiled in August, is cited as an example, since it moves memory control circuitry into the base die, which brings the accelerator maker into the memory design itself. Under these conditions, the articles say, being able to understand customer needs locally and coordinate design changes, sample production and verification with headquarters teams has become a competitive advantage.

Ahn Hyun said at a TSMC symposium in the United States in April, while he was still head of development, that memory makers are evolving from simple suppliers into creators who think through the needed solutions from the architecture stage. In its third-quarter earnings call, SK Hynix said it was working closely with major customers on projects tied to custom HBM for their systems and workloads. Samsung is expected to announce its presidential and executive appointments as early as mid-to-late this month, with its evaluations reportedly complete. The company has moved its year-end appointments up to late November in recent years, and some observers say it could move them earlier again this year.

Industry observers quoted in the articles see the reshuffles as more than routine organizational changes, since the center of AI chip competition has moved to U.S. Big Tech companies such as Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom. Samsung is also expanding HBM supply cooperation with those firms while building local production around its Taylor Foundry plant. Analysts say local organizations led by technologists could shape the terms and pace of future supply contracts. The articles also note that the key open question is how quickly the companies can change a culture built around supplying standard products.

stories.Headline: The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio: Redesigning Assignments for an AI-Augmented Classroom
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion and professional-development piece by Stacy Ybarra Evans, EdD, published on Faculty Focus on November 8, 2026, describing a free, openly licensed toolkit called the AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio. The Studio is hosted online and was first published in 2025, and it is organized into eight sections, including an interactive toolkit for redesigning assignments. Evans says it grew out of faculty asking how to stop students from using AI, and she reframed that question around designing learning that cannot be outsourced. The article reports that the Studio has been adopted for faculty development at institutions including Clemson University, South Dakota University, Washington University, Hood College, the University of Houston-Downtown, Loyola-Notre Dame, and Roman University. It also says the resource appeared on page 7 of the American Art Therapy Association's undergraduate educators newsletter in 2026.

The Studio centers a shift from product-based assessment toward process-based assessment, where the research process, collaboration, reflection and iterative thinking are graded alongside or instead of the final artifact. The article lists practices such as multi-stage assignments, oral defenses or one-on-one conferences, critique tasks in which students analyze AI output for flaws and bias, and community-based projects. It frames three strategies for designing AI-resistant work: collaborative inquiry, authentic engagement with real-world contexts, and metacognitive reflection. Evans also argues that equity must shape these designs, since premium AI tools and reliable internet access are not available to every student, and AI models can reproduce bias in their training data. On academic integrity, she writes that the focus is moving from detection and bans toward disclosure, with students documenting how they used AI tools.

Evans, who leads the Center for Teaching Excellence at Our Lady of the Lake University, presents the Studio at conferences and is credited with the approach, which she says is designed for incremental adoption. She suggests three starting steps: adding a prompt history or reflection log to an existing assignment, introducing one locally grounded activity per unit, and shifting from detection-focused policies to disclosure-focused ones. The article ends by pointing readers to the free online toolkit. It does not report any independent evaluation of the Studio's outcomes, so claims about its effectiveness rest on the author's own account and the institutions she names.

stories.Headline: SDOC board discusses emergency, AI policy updates
stories.Summary:
The School District of Oconee County's Board of Trustees gave an initial review on Monday to updates to 14 district policies, which will come up for a first vote next month. Assistant superintendent of operations Josh Holliday presented the packet, saying some changes were simply updated job titles, while others were required by state officials or were entirely new policies. Two of the new policies concern emergencies. Policy EBCA, Emergencies, follows the Smart Heart Act and calls for a Cardiac Emergency Response Plan that includes a designated school-level response team, practice drills, placement and upkeep of automated external defibrillators, and ongoing AED and CPR training for designated staff. Policy JLCG, Seizure Safe Schools, sets up a training program that teaches staff to recognize seizure symptoms, respond to a student having one, and give prescribed seizure medication.

Policy IJND, Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use, received several proposed updates covering acceptable use and accessibility, prohibited uses, and discipline and reporting procedures. The revised policy adds definitions for artificial intelligence and closed AI, and it would give the district the right to monitor school-issued devices. It also now addresses deepfakes, which the policy defines as realistic recordings or images showing a person doing or saying something they did not actually do. Holliday said the protections are meant to guard against situations where someone's face or identity is placed into a video without consent. Separately, the board gave unanimous final approval to Policy GCCAAA and E1, Emergency Leave Bank, because the district already had such a bank in practice but needed an official board policy for it.

Superintendent Andy Smith asked the board to table several instructional policies until its December meeting, saying state legislative changes had updated them again and staff wanted to verify the numbers and wording so they would not need to be changed a third time. Vice Chair Amanda Holder questioned the length of Policy ADF, District Wellness, noting that the board had aimed to reduce wordiness across the manual and that one paragraph on page five could be deleted. Smith said an existing committee could refine the policy and bring recommendations back in public next month. Board Chairwoman Meghan Ketterman said the packet was fairly substantial and asked members to review it over the month and return with edits, which the board agreed to do. Smith noted that some of the changes would not take effect until next fall, and Holder said the district was currently in compliance in every way.

stories.Headline: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Guoqin Xiong and seven co-authors has published a paper describing SecureGARD, a governance framework for large language model agents that use tools, with the paper appearing on November 10, 2026. The authors frame the problem as one where an agent's outputs become real actions, so that indirect prompt injection turns into a question of execution security. They say existing defenses limit tool calls, action sequences, or information flows, but often leave the meaning of actions, the dependencies between states, and the relationships among evidence implicit. That gap, they argue, makes it hard to generalize across different tools and to update defenses safely.

SecureGARD addresses this by mapping heterogeneous tool calls onto a shared semantic representation and pairing an executable ontology with the state of each episode. From these, it derives deterministic decisions of ready, waiting, or forbidden. A waiting decision flags an obligation that is unmet but recoverable, which allows the agent to replan within limits without widening its authorization. The ontology is refined offline from verified training runs, where an offline language model proposes action-state axioms that are kept only if they fix errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. The paper does not give the sizes of the training or held-out sets.

The authors report testing SecureGARD on three benchmarks, AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn, under both benign and indirect prompt-injection conditions. They state that it reached a 0% attack success rate on all three while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. They conclude that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking. The articles provided do not indicate whether the work has undergone peer review, whether the code or ontology will be released, or what follow-up work the team plans.

stories.Headline: How Are Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Trading After Last Week’s AI Bloodbath?
stories.Summary:
U.S. stock futures rose overnight on Sunday, November 8, 2026, after a sharp selloff in AI-related shares the previous week. As of 10:11 p.m. Eastern, Dow futures were up 0.71 percent, S&P 500 futures gained 0.61 percent, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 0.62 percent. The rebound followed a session in which markets lost about $3 trillion in total value on Thursday, November 5, as investors sold off AI-linked names. The article notes that the three benchmark indexes ended the week lower amid pressure on AI and technology stocks.

The selloff came after the November midterm elections, in which Democrats swept both the Senate and the House. After an initial climb, stock markets crashed on November 5 as concerns grew over a pullback in AI policy and stronger regulations, which stoked fears of a slowdown in the AI trade. Markets have also been watching the geopolitical picture, including the U.S.-Iran conflict, which has not reached a conclusion. Oil prices were trading slightly higher, with Brent crude at $98.41 a barrel and WTI at $91.38 per barrel at the time of writing.

Nvidia drew particular attention because its board said it would launch an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, raising concerns about a foreign intelligence effort targeting the company. Gary Black, managing partner at The Future Fund, said the matter could lead Huang to step down, which could pressure the stock in the short term because the company has no natural successor. Nvidia shares fell 3.5 percent in the overnight session, while Advanced Micro Devices gained about 1.66 percent as investors rotated out of Nvidia. President Donald Trump is also set to meet Qatar's prime minister at the White House on Monday, a meeting likely to cover the Iran war.

The article describes the broader context as a period of uncertainty, with the Iran conflict unresolved and Trump, according to a CNBC interview, saying he is highly unlikely to restart a full-scale war if talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz progress. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, called Iran's demands unacceptable. Markets will also await October's consumer price index and producer price index data next week, while more companies report quarterly results. stories.Headline: Book Review: The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results by Gleb Tsipursky
stories.Summary:
This is a book review, not a news event, so the articles carry no breaking news. Unite.AI published a review on November 8, 2026, of "The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results" by Gleb Tsipursky, published by Georgetown University Press. The reviewer, who is one of the site's founding partners, says he came to the book after his own news website met internal resistance to adopting agentic AI, the kind of research agents that discover and report news autonomously. He pushed ahead anyway while working to ease staff concerns, and that experience drew him to the book.

The review says the book is aimed at executives who need to persuade their staff to adopt AI before a competitor does, and that it draws on various studies and reports to show AI's potential for productivity and business growth. It describes the psychological barriers the book covers, including automation anxiety, status quo bias, confirmation bias, and reluctance to trust "black box" models whose reasoning is hard to explain. The book also sorts middle managers into five profiles, from skeptics and wait-and-see traditionalists to enthusiastic experimenters and AI catalysts, and then describes eight psychographic profiles of employees. The reviewer notes that the book's main job is to teach leaders how to acknowledge concerns, mitigate risks, and reshape corporate culture for adoption.

The reviewer's verdict is favorable. He says the book helps founders and executives understand resistance that can seem puzzling when the benefits of AI already look obvious to them. He adds that he already believes in AI's transformative potential, so for him the value lies in learning how to bring more of a team along. He recommends the book to business owners and leaders who are ready to move ahead with AI and want to build a culture that can move with them. The article does not report any sales figures, edition details beyond the publisher, or other developments, and it does not indicate any follow-up.

stories.Headline: AI Shopping Statistics 2026 Across Buyers and Brands
stories.Summary:
AI shopping tools are now part of how many consumers research products, compare offers and sometimes buy, according to a set of 2026 surveys and data reports compiled by Memeburn. Adoption figures depend heavily on the question asked and the group surveyed. YouGov found that 18% of US adults had used AI to help them shop in its July to August survey, while Attentive reported that 68% of recently active US shoppers had used a general chatbot for shopping within three months. Adobe separately observed that retail visits referred by AI converted at a rate 90% higher than visits from other sources in September, a comparison the report describes as observational rather than causal.

The report stresses that its figures measure different things, so they should not be combined into one adoption rate. A survey response, an AI referral, a brand mention and an autonomous purchase are treated as separate units. Within the surveys, the most common tasks consumers say they would hand to AI are price-related, with 43% of likely US Black Friday and Cyber Monday shoppers comfortable having it find the best price. Only 4% said they would let AI complete a purchase without asking first, while 43% of US consumers said they would be comfortable letting AI buy within a preset limit, according to a May survey by Synchrony and Oxford Economics. Generational differences are also visible, with 83% of Gen Z and 45% of baby boomers reporting chatbot use for shopping in Attentive's August sample.

Memeburn's own recommendation is that brands track AI visibility, referred visits and orders as distinct measures, and evaluate autonomous checkout only under explicit purchase controls. The report notes that brand visibility in AI answers varies widely, with Yarnit finding a median visibility of 1.9% across selected category lists and sharp differences between ChatGPT and Gemini in how often they linked to brand websites. The data sources are a mix of consumer surveys, vendor research and forecasts, and the report flags that several come from unweighted samples or narrow subgroups. Further detail on sample definitions, fieldwork dates and forecasts is set out in the sections that follow the summary tables.
