stories.Headline: Neural Networks with Exciton-Polariton Waveguides
stories.Summary:
A group of eight researchers, led by Huawen Xu, Ruiqi Bao, Lingyu Tian, Yusong Gan, Junfeng Gao, Michal Matuszewski, Qihua Xiong and Timothy Liew, has published a proposal for a neural network built from exciton-polariton waveguide meshes. The paper was posted on doi.org on November 10, 2026, at 06:00 UTC, and the authors describe it as a numerical study rather than a built device. The articles provided present the work only through its abstract and the arXiv page, so the details of the simulations and their results are not available to report. According to the abstract, the scheme allows arbitrary programmable couplings between network layers, which suits a restricted Boltzmann machine architecture.

In this design, the phases of the polaritons act as stochastic variables in the network. The authors say the network can be trained with unsupervised Hebbian and anti-Hebbian updates, a learning approach that does not require labeled examples. The abstract states that this training makes it possible to build an associative memory, a system that recovers previously learned patterns when given imperfect or partial inputs. The articles do not give specific accuracy figures, sizes of the networks, or comparisons with other approaches.

They also do not describe any experimental fabrication or measurement of the proposed system. Context and next steps are not described in the articles, which contain no statements from the authors beyond the abstract, no information about peer review or publication in a journal, and no reactions from outside the research group. The articles do not indicate when, or whether, an experimental demonstration will follow. Readers should treat the work as a theoretical and simulation-based proposal at this stage.

Articles.Title: Neural Networks with Exciton-Polariton Waveguides

stories.Headline: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets rebounded sharply on Monday after a turbulent week, with the MSCI Asia Pacific index rising 2.3%, Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining 3.5% and South Korea's KOSPI climbing 1.6%. Taiwan's Taiex led the recovery, jumping as much as 6.4%, its biggest advance since July. The rally followed a week in which Japanese and Taiwanese equities entered bear-market territory and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each lost more than 16%. The rebound also came as Nvidia futures initially slipped as much as 1% after the company's board announced an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation.

Taiwan's market regulator and finance ministry moved to steady investors after the Taiex endured a seven-session losing streak, its longest since 2022. The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the permitted volume of intraday short-selling orders using borrowed securities to 3% of a stock's average daily trading volume over the previous 30 sessions, down from 30%. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short-selling to 130% from 90%. Authorities said the NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) national stock stabilization fund remained available. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and MediaTek each rose at least 6% in the rebound.

The Nvidia board said it had no reason to believe its secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised, and Huang had acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. Earlier in the week, U.S. chip stocks had rallied as investors bought beaten-down shares, easing worries that a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten restrictions on the AI industry after the party's midterm gains. Still, the S&P 500 posted its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 100 lost $2.3 trillion in market value on Thursday alone. Investors were also weighing inflation data due Tuesday, with markets pricing in nearly an 80% chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase by year-end.

Elsewhere in the region, mainland China's CSI 300 rose 0.3% and the Shanghai Composite gained 0.5%, while India's Nifty 50 fell 0.2%. Chinese October inflation showed higher factory-gate prices from energy and commodity costs, but weak domestic demand left many manufacturers unable to pass those costs on. Australia's ANZ Group shares fell 4.5% despite a full-year cash profit of A$7.59 billion that narrowly beat expectations, as the bank raised provisions. Analysts and investors remain cautious about AI valuations, regulatory risks and infrastructure spending, with attention now turning to the U.S. inflation report.

Articles.Title: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade

stories.Headline: Generative AI use in Japan nearly doubles as mobile habits shift - NTT Docomo
stories.Summary:
Generative AI use in Japan has nearly doubled in a year, according to research by NTT Docomo's Mobile Society Research Institute. The survey found that 51 percent of respondents now use the technology, up from 27 percent in February 2025. Use is spreading beyond younger people and beyond searching and writing, reaching business tasks and personal advice as well. The change comes as mobile habits shift among users in Japan. In the institute's 2025 survey, 54 percent of users said generative AI quickly resolves their questions or concerns.

Another 51 percent said consulting the tool was easier than talking to a person. The article notes that trust in the technology still lags behind its use. The figures point to a wider role for the tools in everyday decisions and problem solving. The research was carried out by NTT Docomo's Mobile Society Research Institute, which published the findings. The article attributes the survey results to the institute and does not describe any additional statements from company officials.

It also does not identify any regulatory or policy requirements arising from the data. The findings add to a picture of rapid adoption of generative AI in Japan over a short period. The article does not say what the institute expects next or whether usage will continue to climb. It also does not describe any planned changes to services or products. More detail on future trends was not included in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Generative AI use in Japan nearly doubles as mobile habits shift - NTT Docomo

stories.Headline: Masahiro Sakurai doesn’t use AI for his games, but believes that avoiding it entirely could cause devs to fall behind in the “far-too-demanding” industry climate
stories.Summary:
Masahiro Sakurai, the game designer behind the Kirby and Super Smash Bros. series, spoke at a stage event held on November 7 in Akihabara, Tokyo, as part of Famitsu's 40th Anniversary Festival. The talk was tied to the release of Thoughts on Games: Final, a compilation of columns Sakurai wrote for Famitsu that was published on November 6, and a portion of the festival was livestreamed on Famitsu's YouTube channel. During the event he addressed generative AI and current industry conditions, which the article reports as the main focus of his remarks.

Sakurai said he does not use generative AI in his own work, including for brainstorming ideas, and that he did not use it for recent projects such as Kirby Air Riders. He argued that game design involves many factors beyond raw ideas, such as whether a team can meet a fixed deadline and whether the work fits the budget, and that prompts alone cannot capture all of that. He also said AI may improve to the point where it becomes useful for such tasks, but he does not believe it has reached that stage yet. On graphics, he said the technology has not yet earned developers' trust, that it must not become a tool for exploitation, and that creating assets by hand is still quicker for now.

At the same time, Sakurai described the games industry as being in a very tight position, calling the current climate "far too demanding." He said Kirby Air Riders required ten times the workload of Kirby Air Ride, and the article notes that several recent titles have left developers operating at a loss even after selling millions of copies. He warned that refusing AI entirely could leave developers falling further behind, and that those who adopt it without hesitation may be able to produce many more games, so doing nothing could also be a poor choice. Because the question of where and how to use AI is complex, he said he is taking a cautious approach and did not commit to whether he will adopt the technology in the future.

Articles.Title: Masahiro Sakurai doesn’t use AI for his games, but believes that avoiding it entirely could cause devs to fall behind in the “far-too-demanding” industry climate

stories.Headline: InsurTech's AI Reckoning: Who's Winning the 2026 Race
stories.Summary:
Corgi, an AI-native commercial insurer, closed a $160 million Series B at a $1.3 billion valuation, led by TCV, according to coverage in Fintech Global and Dealroom. The raise came just four months after its Series A. Reporting from SiliconANGLE and Insurtech FFNews says the company is starting with trucking and plans to expand into adjacent verticals, using a single data model that links underwriting, claims, policy administration and reinsurance recovery. The articles frame this as a bet that collapsing many separate systems into one stack can cut the labor cost of moving information between them. A second startup, Klaimee, is pursuing a different niche: insurance for autonomous AI agents. Per Fintech Global and Coverager, Klaimee closed a $5.5 million seed round earlier this year and is backed by Y Combinator.

Its policies would cover the company deploying an agent when that agent causes harm, with pricing based on pre-deployment simulations of the agent's behavior. The articles present this as a new category of liability coverage for a world where the policyholder may not be human. The reinsurance and capital-markets side is also moving. EarthRe secured an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) reinsurance license earlier this year, according to CXO Digital Pulse, and InRisk Labs raised $27 million to build an AI-powered risk pricing engine for catastrophe and emerging perils. The same reporting describes a shift in which AI pricing lets risk be sliced, structured and sold to capital-markets buyers more quickly than the traditional primary-to-reinsurer cycle allowed.

Parametric insurance, which pays automatically when a defined trigger is met, is cited as the most visible example. On claims, COVR Global raised $2.5 million this year to speed AI-powered settlement for life and health coverage, according to InsurTech Insights. A May 2026 InsurTech NY roundup reports that some carriers have seen double-digit percentage reductions in claims operating expense after adopting generative AI triage. Funding overall looks healthier than recent headlines suggest: Fintech Global reports $420 million in InsurTech funding in January 2026 alone, and the articles say investors now favor AI-first underwriting, embedded distribution, climate-focused parametric products and reinsurance access for smaller firms over generic app-based pitches.

Articles.Title: InsurTech's AI Reckoning: Who's Winning the 2026 Race - FinanceX Magazine

stories.Headline: Raycast’s new Dictate to AI reads your Mac screen as you talk, for $10 a month
stories.Summary:
Raycast released version 2.11 of its Mac launcher on November 4, adding a command called Dictate to AI. The feature lets a user speak a request while the AI receives context from whichever app is in focus, so a spoken instruction such as turning an email into a polite reply can be handled without copying and pasting text first. Raycast suggests assigning a shortcut like Control and A so the command is always one press away. The company describes the change in its official changelog as a way to go from talking to responses in seconds. The command builds on Raycast's existing Screen Awareness feature, which already let its AI Chat pull in content from the active app or window.

Users can switch off the app context in the command's settings when they only want a plain dictated question. The article advises deciding that setting in advance, since an open banking site, private message or work document would otherwise be sent as context by default. The update also adds an AI usage meter in the menu bar, a Dictation AI extension, a Contacts AI extension, better dictation quality and speed, and smoother handling of chat renaming and unavailable models. Raycast itself is free, but its AI features and dictation require a paid plan. The Pro plan costs $10 a month or $96 a year and includes 500 AI credits a month along with dictation, while Plus costs $20 a month or $192 a year with 3,000 credits and Max costs $50 a month or $480 a year with 7,500 credits.

Plus and Max add access to top-tier AI models. Verified students receive 50 percent off the Pro plans, and new accounts can start a free Pro trial whose credits expire after seven days. The article compares Raycast with the free Dictation already built into macOS and with the Siri AI features Apple continues to add. Its distinction is that Raycast connects voice input to the AI model a user chooses, works across any focused app, and keeps everything within the launcher many people already use. The article concludes that existing Raycast Pro subscribers can update and assign a hotkey at no extra cost, while others may find Apple's free tools sufficient unless they use AI on their Mac every day.

Articles.Title: Raycast’s new Dictate to AI reads your Mac screen as you talk, for $10 a month

stories.Headline: China may have just solved AI's biggest bottleneck
stories.Summary:
China's Envision says it has put an integrated 800-volt direct-current power system into commercial operation at an AI facility in Inner Mongolia. The installation is at the Galaxy AI campus in Ulanqab, where trials of its Dubhe controller and supporting energy model began in August 2026. The company describes this as the first commercial use of this configuration, though independent performance figures have not been published. Conventional facilities usually convert incoming electricity through several stages before it reaches servers and accelerators, which adds equipment and possible conversion losses.

Envision's design uses a solid-state transformer to convert 10-kilovolt medium-voltage alternating current directly into an 800-volt direct-current distribution line. The company says this cuts the number of conversion steps, improves electrical efficiency and lets power equipment take up much less space in data centers. A higher-voltage network could also reduce the copper needed for cabling as computing installations expand. The architecture adds battery storage that responds quickly when processor demand changes and provides temporary backup during unexpected interruptions. Envision says the storage can give immediate support over seconds and sustain backup across periods of several minutes.

The controller coordinates the transformer and batteries within milliseconds to manage sudden shifts in electricity use from GPUs. This matters because AI workloads can cause large swings in demand that strain electrical systems supplying densely packed equipment. The company also says the arrangement can support higher-density server racks, letting operators fit more computing capacity into a given floor area. The Galaxy facility is expected to grow to 3 gigawatts, and Envision says its eventual capacity could serve one million AI accelerators. The company also plans to bring the technology to Mission Gobi, an initiative seeking 5 gigawatts of renewable-powered computing capacity by 2030 in desert locations.

The system is designed to work alongside renewable generation, with batteries intended to balance supply against changing computing needs. However, the company has not provided independently verified measurements of efficiency gains, installation costs or savings compared with conventional systems. The announcement also does not establish how the architecture performs under sustained full-load conditions or across facilities with different hardware setups. The deployment therefore marks a commercial milestone for Envision, while the scale of its claimed advantages awaits detailed independent evidence.

Articles.Title: China may have just solved AI's biggest bottleneck

stories.Headline: Innodisk says AI applications now generate more than 40% of revenue as 3Q26 profit jumps
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese memory and storage maker Innodisk said that AI-related applications now generate more than 40% of its revenue, a shift that helped lift its third-quarter 2026 profit. The company reported the results in a report published on November 8, 2026, according to Digitimes. Demand for high-end memory and storage used in AI servers drove the gains in its third-quarter numbers. The company's figures show that the AI business has grown into a major share of its overall sales.

The article gives no further figures for the size of the profit increase, the exact revenue totals, or the quarter-on-quarter and year-on-year comparisons. It does not describe any new product requirement, regulatory change or business restructuring tied to the results. The reported change is therefore limited to the share of revenue coming from AI applications and the stronger earnings that followed from demand for AI server memory and storage. Readers can see the trend in the company's revenue mix, but the article does not say how the company expects that mix to change next.

The article does not name a specific executive or statement beyond the company's own disclosure of these results. It also gives no comment from analysts, customers or rivals on what the figures mean for the wider market. Digitimes' page carries unrelated headlines and subscription notices, but none of them adds details about Innodisk's results. What happens next, including any guidance for the fourth quarter or later years, is not stated in the material provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Innodisk says AI applications now generate more than 40% of revenue as 3Q26 profit jumps

stories.Headline: An interview with Cognition CISO Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity, AI-powered red teaming, vulnerabilities in legacy codebases, and more (Nilay Patel/The Verge)
stories.Summary:
AI tools have made cyberattacks faster and more widespread, and the industry is struggling to keep pace. According to the interview with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition, a series of breaches in October 2026 hit AI-related companies in rapid succession. Stamos described a chain in which attackers breached Fireworks, a provider of AI services, and used stolen API keys to get into Cursor, then pushed a bad plugin that reached about 5,000 companies. He also cited the Binance hack, which he called the largest heist in human history.

The attackers include a range of actors, from private groups to state actors such as Russia and North Korea. Stamos said AI has changed the basic attack sequence, so that systems can now find vulnerabilities and write exploits in real time rather than doing that work in advance. He pointed to ARTEX, an open-source Chinese tool that anyone can download, which when run on an altered open-weight model can break into many organizations. The tool began with three South Korean banks, and Stamos said about 200 more companies had been hit in the week of the interview. He compared the moment to the late 1990s, when security weaknesses were widespread and attackers had few barriers.

Stamos framed the change in terms of the culture and economics that once governed security work. For roughly two decades, after Microsoft's 2002 "trustworthy computing" memo, companies hired former hackers to find flaws, and the industry built norms for responsible disclosure and bug bounties. Stamos argued that open-weight models and inexpensive hardware now let people act outside that culture, without the protections or logging that frontier models carry. He said he expects a difficult transition, which he described as a dark age, while defenders work out how to adapt. The article does not say what specific regulatory or industry steps will follow.

Articles.Title: An interview with Cognition CISO Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity, AI-powered red teaming, vulnerabilities in legacy codebases, and more (Nilay Patel/The Verge)

stories.Headline: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness
stories.Summary:
A new academic paper, published on arXiv and listed on doi.org on November 10, 2026, examines a problem in evaluating whether explanations of algorithmic systems are faithful. The paper is titled "Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness," and its authors are Grant Shanklin, Jiří Němeček and Asia Biega. The article states that faithfulness requires algorithmic explanations to accurately reflect a model's behavior. It also notes that existing ways of measuring faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation passes, which leaves developers and auditors choosing among conflicting evaluations. The authors introduce a faithfulness functional, a framework that locates where existing criteria diverge.

The divergence lies in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated. The authors use this framework to reconstruct existing evaluation criteria. They argue that these reconstructions support treating faithfulness as a shared but incompletely specified relation between a model and its explanation, so the differences among criteria reflect choices the general requirement leaves open. On their view, justifying a particular operationalization means justifying those choices, drawing on explanatory, institutional and normative considerations.

The paper says this gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate conflicting evaluations. The authors support their argument with a case study of adverse action notices, the explanations given to people when a decision goes against them. They reconstruct the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure for these notices. They then identify which of that procedure's choices the setting justifies and which remain open.

The article presents this as an illustration of how concrete settings can narrow the choice among competing operationalizations. The paper also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations to exist. The article describes the work as a contribution to the broader question of how a single shared requirement can support contextually justified evaluations even when existing metrics disagree. The source material does not describe any further steps, reactions or next actions by the authors or others.

Articles.Title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness

stories.Headline: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP
stories.Summary:
Zurich-based 0sec Labs has released 0, an open-source AI security harness that can run vulnerability investigations, code review, pentesting, reverse engineering and fix generation. Developers can drive it from a local browser console, a headless command line tool, or an MCP server. The project is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and is shipped as a research preview. It is a software harness rather than a model, so users connect their own large language model from one of 14 listed providers. It runs on Apple Silicon macOS, x64 or ARM64 Linux, or a container image, and it does not require a GPU.

The harness organizes security work into stages. A research agent plans and attacks, then filters remove weak findings before a separate session re-exercises each candidate to verify it. Reports can be produced in HTML, PDF, SARIF, Markdown and JSON formats. Compiled targets are handled by a separate engine called 0verse, which wraps Ghidra, angr and AFL++ and exposes nine tools through a local MCP server. Installation is a single script, and the browser console opens without an account.

The project's architecture documents state one rule: reproduce before trusting. The research team describes 0 as a self-evolving, multi-model harness, and the company is backed by Y Combinator. The articles report self-reported benchmark results. On XBOW web capture-the-flag challenges, the best cohort solved 93 of 95 (97.9%) using gpt-5.4, when any retained success counts.

A black-box-only union reached 81 of 104 (77.9%), and a 2026 cold run scored 45 of 104 (43.3%). On Cybench, the harness solved 36 of 40 (90.0%) with Azure gpt-5.4 and three retries. The recorded cost was about $5.20 per solved XBOW challenge. The articles also note that the headline scores are not pass@1 results.

Compared with other open-source AI pentesting tools named in the article, 0 uses an MIT OR Apache-2.0 license, while Shannon uses AGPL-3.0 and CAI uses a mix of MIT and a proprietary research-only license. Strix is listed as archived as of August 28, 2026. The article compares feature sets, interfaces and supported platforms, but it does not say how the tools perform against one another. More to follow.

Articles.Title: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP

stories.Headline: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Reason Machines has released Aspen, an open-source Git server designed for AI agent traffic, aimed at repositories that hundreds of agents push to at the same time. The project is pre-alpha and is distributed as a single Rust binary. Branch data lives in PostgreSQL or SQLite, while pack files are stored in object storage. The articles say Aspen independently implements a design that OpenAI described for its own system, called Pando.

Aspen can run on a laptop, on a single host through Docker Compose, or in cloud deployments managed with Helm and Terraform. Its main change is that writes scale per branch rather than per repository, so pushes to different branches do not wait on each other. Fetches reuse stored packs instead of building new ones each time. The articles say Aspen speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH and sends packs to S3-compatible storage. Each branch is kept as a chain of versions in a single database row that is updated with a compare-and-swap operation.

The articles attribute the design to Reason Machines and credit OpenAI's Pando as the model it follows. Reason Machines reports, as self-reported figures, that one 8-core server sustained 567 pushes per second for five minutes on a copy of the git.git repository, with a median push latency of 208 milliseconds. The articles note that landing on the main branch runs at about 4 pushes per second and that the project has no releases or web interface. They also say the 24-hour durability gate has not been met, and the README describes Aspen's figures as indicative rather than formal performance claims.

The articles place Aspen among other agent-scale Git backends, citing Cursor's Origin, OpenAI's Pando and GitHub's Spokes. Cursor reports up to 120 pushes per second on S3 Standard and more than 300 on S3 Express One Zone, though the articles note that its setup differs. OpenAI said its approach cut median push latency by nearly five times, and the articles describe Pando as serving nearly a petabyte daily. The articles do not say what comes next for Aspen's development or release plans.

Articles.Title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents

stories.Headline: Political parties across Asia adopt ‘Seoul Declaration’ on geopolitical stability, AI
stories.Summary:
Political parties from across Asia adopted the "Seoul Declaration" on Friday at the 13th General Assembly of the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP) in Seoul. The gathering ran from Wednesday to Saturday at The Shilla Seoul and drew around 200 party representatives from 83 political parties in 36 Asian countries, along with 30 Korean lawmakers. The ruling Democratic Party and the main opposition People Power Party jointly hosted the event, which carried the theme "Rebuilding Trust in a Transforming World." It was the first time in 20 years that Seoul had hosted the assembly, the previous one being the fourth gathering in 2006.

The declaration committed the participants to cooperation on geopolitical stability, democratic governance, climate change and AI. The declaration sets out specific steps for each area. It urges countries to keep diplomatic channels open during periods of heightened tension and to make government decision-making more transparent and accountable. It also calls for investment in climate monitoring and early warning systems, as well as cooperation on safeguards for high-risk AI technologies.

A separate media forum on Friday, the eighth ICAPP Media Forum, involved representatives of 35 parties and 19 journalists from 18 outlets in 14 countries. Those participants unanimously adopted the "Seoul Statement," which calls for transparency, verification and human oversight in AI-assisted journalism. It also urges governments to protect press freedom and technology companies to address the misuse of AI, including deepfakes and disinformation. At the opening ceremony on Thursday, National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik stressed that complex crises threaten humanity's shared future and that no single country can resolve them alone.

President Lee Jae Myung sent a video message encouraging parties to strengthen dialogue and cooperation amid ongoing geopolitical tensions. At the closing press conference, ICAPP Standing Committee chairperson Chung Eui-yong said the declaration showed that parties with different ideological views can find common ground. He added that trust must be rebuilt through sustained dialogue, mutual respect and concrete action rather than declarations alone. Vietnam will host the 14th ICAPP General Assembly in 2028, and the organization plans a second Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties in Istanbul in March 2027 to extend cooperation beyond Asia.

Articles.Title: Political parties across Asia adopt ‘Seoul Declaration’ on geopolitical stability, AI

stories.Headline: The Teacher in the World of Artificial Intelligence: Illuminating Literature, Awakening Emotions
stories.Summary:
Vietnam.vn and the education newspaper Giáo dục và Thời đại published a commentary on November 9, 2026, by a literature teacher, Ms. Duong Thi Huyen, under the headline about teachers in the age of artificial intelligence. The piece describes a ninth-grade lesson on the excerpt "Kim Kieu's Encounter" from the Vietnamese Literature textbook, in which the author noticed that student homework read unusually polished, as though produced by a tool. The article does not state a specific date for that lesson beyond saying it took place one October morning. It frames the story as a question for colleagues about where a teacher's intellectual guidance and literary passion now stand, given that AI tools can produce strong essays in seconds.

The author reports that she tested AI assistance in class by asking students to have an AI write a diary entry in the voice of Thuy Kieu after her meeting with Kim Trong. Students found the generated passages too rational and lacking the shyness and subtle psychological shifts in Nguyen Du's lines. In a separate lesson on Ho Chi Minh's 1951 essay "The Patriotic Spirit of Our People," from the Grade 8 textbook, she had students compare an AI-written essay on patriotism with the original. The students concluded that the machine could write fluently in general terms but could not reproduce the historical grounding and the forceful tone of the original. She also argues that students should learn to question AI output, for example by having them replace generic evidence about youth apathy with real examples from their own experience.

The article recommends that literature teaching shift toward dialogue, debate and multimedia projects, with students using AI as a tool but drawing their emotional content from their own experience. The author closes by arguing that AI can process language but cannot share the emotional response that literature is meant to awaken. The article offers no institutional policy, no official response and no data on how widely these methods are used. It is a first-person opinion piece, and its claims rest on the author's own classroom experiments rather than on any broader study.

Articles.Title: The Teacher in the World of Artificial Intelligence: Illuminating Literature, Awakening Emotions

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang’s journey: From Taiwan to washing dishes at Denny's to founding AI chip giant Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, has risen from a difficult childhood in Taiwan and a dishwashing job at a Denny's diner to become one of the most influential figures in technology. The profile, published by Hindustan Times on November 9, 2026, traces his path from a boy born in Tainan in 1963 to the leader of a company whose chips power modern artificial intelligence. His family first moved to Thailand, and later he was sent to live with an uncle in Tacoma, Washington, in 1972 while his parents prepared their own paperwork. Huang struggled with limited English and bullying at a boarding school in Kentucky, but he focused on his studies. He later attended Oregon State University, where he earned an electrical engineering degree.

After graduating, Huang worked at Advanced Micro Devices and then LSI Logic, where he held engineering, marketing and management roles between 1985 and 1993. He also earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1992 while working at LSI. In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, starting with $40,000 in capital after discussing the idea at a Denny's restaurant in San Jose. The company first concentrated on graphics technology for video games, and its RIVA 128 processor sold about one million units within four months, helping it survive a difficult early period. Over the following decades, its graphics processing units became essential for artificial intelligence development because they can handle large volumes of data at once.

Huang has credited his early restaurant work with teaching him discipline, resilience and how to perform under pressure, according to Quartr as cited in the article. He has also described his rise in the article's account as the product of long, hard work rather than luck, saying in a CBS 60 Minutes interview that there is no magic involved. Fortune named him Businessperson of the Year in 2017, and Harvard Business Review ranked him first on its list of the world's 100 best-performing CEOs over the lifetime of their tenure in 2019. The article also notes that Huang has been the subject of recent news items, including a remark by US President Donald Trump calling him honorable and a report about a US memo that mentioned his alleged ties to a Chinese spy, though it does not detail either matter further.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang’s journey: From Taiwan to washing dishes at Denny's to founding AI chip giant Nvidia

stories.Headline: Palantir vs. Snowflake: The AI Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference for 2027
stories.Summary:
Palantir Technologies and Snowflake are both enterprise AI companies, and an article by RJ Fulton on Fool.com, updated November 8, 2026, compares the two as a sell-off in technology stocks prompts investors to reassess them for 2027. The author argues that the pullback gives investors a chance to look again at how each company is valued. The piece is an opinion and analysis piece rather than a report on a discrete event, so it does not describe a single announcement or decision. The core of the comparison is that Palantir has shown stronger profitability while Snowflake still posts losses. Palantir's software, including its Gotham, Foundry, and Artificial Intelligence Platform products, serves government and commercial customers.

The article reports that its fiscal 2025 revenue was $4.5 billion, up 56 percent, with net income of about $1.6 billion, and that its third-quarter 2026 revenue rose 96 percent to $2.3 billion. Snowflake's cloud data platform generated about $4.7 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue, up 29 percent, but recorded a net loss of $1.3 billion. The author notes that Snowflake's second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue grew 35 percent to $1.55 billion, and that its stock-based compensation exceeded its operating cash flow. The article identifies risks for each company, including Palantir's reliance on large government and enterprise contracts and its exposure to sensitive defense work, and Snowflake's intense competition and consumption-based revenue model. The author says neither stock is cheap, with Palantir trading at 103 times forward earnings and Snowflake at 131 times.

On price-to-sales, Snowflake is cheaper at 18.9 times sales compared with Palantir's 54.5 times. The author states a personal preference for Palantir for 2027, while cautioning that its valuation leaves little room for disappointment. The article does not describe any upcoming decisions, deadlines, or regulatory changes, and it does not say what will happen to either stock next. It offers a view on the two companies' prospects but presents no forecast beyond the author's stated preference. Readers should weigh that preference as the opinion of one writer.

Articles.Title: Palantir vs. Snowflake: The AI Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference for 2027

stories.Headline: Musk Announces Two More Data Centers for Mid-South AI Expansion
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk has announced that two more data centers tied to SpaceXAI's expanding artificial intelligence operation in the Memphis area are expected to begin running before the end of the year. The announcement comes as the rapid growth of the facilities draws increasing scrutiny from residents and city officials worried about the effects of large-scale data center development. The two sites, known as Gun Range and Spam, are part of the company's Colossus 2 computing complex. Both are located in Southaven, Mississippi, just across the state line from Memphis.

Musk said Gun Range is expected to become operational by the end of November, with Spam following in December. These dates are his projections and have not been independently confirmed. Together the facilities are expected to house roughly 420,000 Nvidia GB300 graphics processing units. About 220,000 of those chips at Gun Range would be set up to train AI models, while about 200,000 at Spam would handle inference, which means responding to user requests with already-trained systems. The buildings will add to existing sites within Colossus 2, and Musk has said the full complex is expected to contain about 1.2 million Nvidia Blackwell chips by the end of 2026.

The company runs this computing infrastructure to support its Grok AI platform, and Musk has said he has been spending several days a week in Memphis overseeing construction. Gun Range was once a police and fire training facility, and Spam was a warehouse that stored Hormel Foods products, which is where the names come from. The projects have drawn opposition from nearby residents concerned about pollution, noise, electricity demand and water use. In April the NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that methane gas turbines were run at the Southaven site without required permits. A federal judge recently refused to dismiss that lawsuit, so the case will proceed.

Separately, the Memphis City Council approved a 135-day pause on new data center permits after rejecting a proposed yearlong moratorium. The pause gives city officials time to write land-use and siting rules covering neighborhood protections, infrastructure and environmental concerns. It does not shut down existing facilities or automatically halt projects that already hold protected approvals. The latest expansion highlights the challenge facing Mid-South communities as technology companies move quickly to build AI infrastructure while residents and local governments push for greater oversight.

Articles.Title: Musk Announces Two More Data Centers for Mid-South AI Expansion - The Tennessee Tribune

stories.Headline: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records
stories.Summary:
Baidu has released ERNIE Evolve, an automated research system that improves AI training and inference code. Given a code repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it selects research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept. Baidu announced the system on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI.

The system runs two nested loops. An outer loop, made up of a Director and a Selector, decides which direction to investigate and which candidate to test next. An inner loop, made up of an Executor, an Evaluator and a Reviewer, implements, measures and checks each change. The Evaluator is a fixed program kept outside the repository that no agent can see, and gains must exceed a noise threshold to count. Several research lanes run in parallel, and failed experiments are logged so later rounds avoid repeating them.

On three public benchmarks, Baidu reports that ERNIE Evolve beat the best public result on three of four metrics. It reached a validation BPB of 0.8763 on NanoChat AutoResearch within a five-minute single-GPU budget, and 38.9 seconds on NanoGPT Speedrun Track 1 against a 39.9-second record. It also reached 2,590 steps on Speedrun Track 3, against 2,690, but trailed the leaderboard on SOL-ExecBench with a mean of 0.819 against 0.827. Baidu also ran the system on live engineering tasks for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, a model still in development, reporting +33.7% deterministic throughput and +14.9% decode speed.

Baidu's own figures are self-reported, the system itself has not been released, and the margins on public benchmarks are small. The company has not disclosed which language models power its agents or which GPU model ran the production tests. Some comparisons in its table are not like-for-like, because the Speedrun times from other groups were measured against an older record. The articles do not say when the system will be made available or whether outside researchers will be able to verify the results.

Articles.Title: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records

stories.Headline: China’s AI datacenter buildout reveals scale, speed
stories.Summary:
China is building gigawatt-scale AI datacenter campuses, and an analysis published by TechGig, citing SemiAnalysis, points to one in Inner Mongolia as an example. The Galaxy campus in Ulanqab is planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity, and its first 120MW phase was reportedly delivered within a year. The buildout is described as notably fast, large, cheap and tightly integrated, with construction costs about a fifth of those in the United States. Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator, owns the facility.

Envision builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply the campus, and it plans to meet over 60 per cent of power use in the first two phases from its own wind farms. The article says this is made possible by siting, a total of 420MW of installed capacity for a 240MW load, and a 4-hour battery storage system. A pilot 5MW hall uses an 800V DC system, with solid-state transformers converting 10kV AC directly to 800V DC for the racks, a technology the article says is still on the US roadmap. Cooling uses a shared water loop for both liquid- and air-cooled servers, with no central chiller plant, a design the article calls common in northern China.

Envision is highly vertically integrated, manufacturing its own wind turbines, battery energy storage systems and power electronics, and it co-designed the prefabricated substation. The article does not attribute any specific statements to company executives. It notes that China's datacenter market is highly competitive, with rents roughly halved and capital expenditure down about 25 per cent over the past five years. SemiAnalysis's China Datacenter Model tracks over 1,000 facilities across more than 70 operators, including projects like Galaxy. The article does not say what comes next for the campus beyond the planned capacity.

Articles.Title: China’s AI datacenter buildout reveals scale, speed

stories.Headline: Zeta CEO Bhavin Turakhia says coding is overrated in AI era
stories.Summary:
Zeta CEO Bhavin Turakhia has said that coding is becoming overrated as artificial intelligence takes over more software development work. He made the remarks in a YouTube conversation with Vidit Jain, SVP and Head of Scaler Schools at Scaler Campus, published on November 8, 2026. The article was published by TechGig on November 9, 2026, at 4:40 AM IST. It reports that the comments were part of a discussion about how technology careers are changing. Turakhia argues that professionals often focus too much on execution without first considering the outcomes they want.

As AI handles more execution-heavy tasks, he believes skills such as high-level abstraction, clear problem definition, and quick communication of outcomes will matter more. He still stressed that mathematics, data structures, and algorithms remain core fundamentals for aspiring tech professionals. On entrepreneurship, he said execution adds more value than ideas, which he sees as increasingly commoditised. Turakhia, who began coding at age 10, founded Directi, Radix, and Zeta, and his current venture, NEO, focuses on AI. He also advocated building businesses with a co-founder to foster debate and diverse perspectives, which he said improves decision-making.

On hiring, he questioned how reliable resumes are now that AI tools make applications easy to produce. He expects employers to rely more on assessments, case studies, interviews, and proof of work to judge candidates' real abilities. The views come as AI-assisted coding tools reshape software development workflows, and the article frames Turakhia's comments within that shift. The article does not report any formal policy, company decision, or measurable change tied to his remarks. It does not say how other industry figures have responded.

Articles.Title: Zeta CEO Bhavin Turakhia says coding is overrated in AI era

stories.Headline: Entire Git forge rethinks AI agent collaboration with trails
stories.Summary:
Entire, a company led by CEO Thomas Dohmke, has launched a Git forge built for human developers and AI coding agents to work together. The platform was reported on November 9, 2026, and it is meant to address the limits of the traditional pull request model when AI agents generate and revise code at high speed. Its core features are called "trails" and "continuous memory," both aimed at keeping agent-driven development organized. The articles describe these as new tools for a workflow that existing forges were not built to handle.

Dohmke, a former GitHub CEO, argues that GitHub and GitLab were designed around asynchronous code review and version control between people. He says a multi-agent forge instead centers on asynchronous orchestration, versioning, and auditing of AI agents working alongside humans. The trails feature attaches evaluation scores to every code push so developers can judge whether a pull request is stable or needs another round of agent work. A merge should happen only when confidence is high, risk is low, and findings have been cleared. Trails can start from a bug report, a feature request, or manually, and they can span several repositories.

When new code is pushed, a review agent running in a cloud sandbox scores the changes and explains the score based on code quality, security, and "slop." Developers can then tell their coding agent to improve the code, which starts a new iteration, and review agents can suggest fixes that stay visible until resolved or closed. Evaluation agents can be configured through Entire's interface or through repository-level JSON, and developers can set repository-level Gates that define approval conditions. The platform also connects with continuous integration services such as Buildkite and Depot. The articles do not report pricing, availability dates beyond launch, or independent assessments of how the platform performs in practice.

The second concept, continuous memory, is meant to keep knowledge that agents build up available for reuse across sessions. Entire implements it with two open-source tools, entire-graph, which maps the Git repository, and entire-brain, which combines that map with earlier agent sessions and Git history to form a persistent memory layer. The stated purpose is to give agents the context behind code changes, including the reasons for them. The articles do not say what comes next for the platform, such as adoption figures or planned expansions.

Articles.Title: Entire Git forge rethinks AI agent collaboration with trails

stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
stories.Summary:
Chinese AI companies are recruiting engineers and staff in Silicon Valley and Seattle, aiming to tap into talent at American labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Hong Kong-listed MiniMax has about 16 San Francisco job openings, including a research lead for its core model, and it is also seeking specialists in finance, law, life sciences and cybersecurity. Moonshot AI, behind the Kimi model, is looking for U.S.-based solutions architects to help enterprise customers integrate its models. The reporting describes this as a strategic shift as Chinese firms try to compete and stay close to one of their most lucrative markets.

The push runs into a pay gap. MiniMax spent $84.3 million on employee remuneration in 2025, roughly $203,000 per person across its 415 staff, while Z.AI's annualized figure for the first half of 2026 came to about $140,000 per employee, though both figures cover all departments. OpenAI advertises base salaries of $250,000 to $445,000 for San Francisco research engineers before equity, and three Chinese researchers in Silicon Valley say peers often earn more than $1 million a year. ByteDance's Seed division reportedly offers a competing package 1.5 times higher than a rival's offer to lure researchers, and it lists 71 positions in San Jose, San Diego and Seattle. Even with matching pay, the researchers said they preferred American firms for better work-life balance and the chance to work on frontier models.

Yale researcher Cheryl Wu, who studies the economics of AI, said Chinese firms lack the funds to match U.S. salaries and still lag far behind their American rivals. A September Carnegie China study found that more than half of top AI researchers studied as undergraduates in China, yet the U.S. recorded a net gain of 2,145 researchers in 2025 while China lost 1,729. Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, suggested that Washington could eventually invoke national security arguments to make it harder for Chinese labs to operate or recruit, a concern tied to ongoing restrictions on chips, data centers and some engineers. Wu, meanwhile, doubted that Chinese startups could find enough top researchers to compete with leading American labs.

The article places this hiring in a wider contest. The U.S. has restricted Chinese access to advanced Nvidia chips, but no comparable limits stop Chinese AI firms from opening U.S. operations, and neither country has banned cross-border AI hiring outright. Beijing has proposed export controls on some advanced models, while U.S. officials and companies have accused Chinese labs of unauthorized distillation of their models. Not all Chinese firms are looking abroad, since DeepSeek continues to advertise about 150 engineering roles in China. The reporting does not predict how the recruitment race will end.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy

stories.Headline: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
stories.Summary:
Researchers Alex M Tseng and Luca Zancato, both affiliated with Amazon, published a Hugging Face blog post on November 9, 2026, describing a new method called HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts) for shrinking Mixture-of-Experts language models. The problem they address is that MoE models must keep every expert in memory during inference even though only a small fraction are active for any given token. Their example, Qwen3.5-122B, has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and about 95% of its roughly 250 GB memory footprint is taken up by those expert networks alone. Expert pruning, which permanently deletes the least useful experts, is a common fix, but the authors argue existing methods score each expert in isolation.

According to the post, HOPE is a second-order method that accounts for pairwise interactions between experts. The authors say experts form stable cooperative groups that are frequently activated together, so removing one expert can break a group even if that expert looks unimportant on its own. HOPE builds an interaction matrix from a calibration dataset, using one forward pass like other pruning methods, and then solves a quadratic program to choose which experts to remove. The extra computation is described as roughly one to two seconds per layer, which the authors say is small compared with the calibration pass itself. They note that the diagonal of this matrix closely matches the rankings of REAP, a leading first-order pruning method, with a Spearman correlation of 0.988, so any gains come from the off-diagonal interaction terms.

The authors tested HOPE on three models, Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B and GLM-4.5-Air, using two calibration datasets, and compared it against four first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN and Frequency) at pruning rates from 10% to 50%. Across all conditions HOPE achieved the best average rank of 2.07 out of five methods, and at 50% pruning its average rank improved to 1.58 against 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP. On the SWE-Bench Pro agentic coding benchmark, the post reports that Qwen3.5-35B pruned by 50% with HOPE scored 42.3, close to the unpruned model's 41.8, while REAP scored 36.2. The authors say HOPE's advantage is largest at high pruning rates and on agentic coding tasks, and that the post's own experiments showed code-focused calibration did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks. The article presents HOPE as a research result and does not describe a product release, though it includes guidance for applying the method to other models.

Articles.Title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

stories.Headline: DAPA to Build ‘Defense AI Hub’ with KAIST, ETRI and LG, Modernizing Defense Industry with Civilian Innovation
stories.Summary:
On the 9th, the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) announced that it had designated three institutions as leading research institutions in artificial intelligence: the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI), and LG AI Research. The designation sets up a hub for collaboration among industry, academia, and research institutes to drive AI innovation in the defense sector. The aim is to bring private-sector technologies and research infrastructure into defense work and to strengthen small and midsize defense companies. The announcement was reported by Financial News.

The lead institutions were chosen from organizations with strong AI research capabilities, technology, and infrastructure. They are expected to support small and midsize defense companies and venture firms from technology development through commercialization. DAPA plans to roll out two initiatives in phases. Starting this December, a "Defense Innovation Lab" program will have lead institutions and companies jointly develop and demonstrate prototypes of complete weapon systems.

From 2027, DAPA intends to link this with a "Lead Research Institution Support Program" that uses the institutions' infrastructure and technology to build companies' R&D capacity. Lee Hyung-seok, director general of DAPA's Defense Industry Promotion Bureau, said that AI is a key technology for national defense and that close cooperation between research institutions and companies is important for quickly applying private-sector technologies to defense. He said the lead institutions would support technology development and commercialization for small and midsize companies, promote defense AI innovation, and build a competitive defense industry ecosystem. The article presents these efforts as an application of a "spin-in" strategy, moving civilian technology into defense, alongside "spin-off," moving defense technology into civilian use.

It notes that major military powers have pursued similar approaches, since civilian technology is advancing faster than the military's weapons development cycle. South Korea has also pursued policies to break down barriers between defense and science and technology ministries, such as the Civil-Military Technology Cooperation Program run by the Ministry of National Defense and the Ministry of Science and ICT. The article describes the designation as a step forward because it brings together a university, a public research institute, and a leading private AI research institute. Whether the two programs succeed remains an open question, the article suggests, depending on whether they can ease the shortage of costly AI computing infrastructure that small defense firms face and help them field technologies as weapon systems while meeting military security requirements.

Articles.Title: DAPA to Build ‘Defense AI Hub’ with KAIST, ETRI and LG, Modernizing Defense Industry with Civilian Innovation - 파이낸셜뉴스

stories.Headline: Police flag the use of AI by criminals
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong police have warned that criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to carry out technology-related crimes, which has led to a rise in ransomware cases. According to the force, ransomware cases rose by 18 percent year-on-year to 40 in the first three quarters of this year. Overall, however, tech crimes fell by 12 percent to 21,573 cases, and total losses dropped by 15 percent to almost HK$3.9 billion. The figures were presented in the police's most recent update on cybercrime trends.

Chief Superintendent Raymond Lam of the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau said that criminals have widely adopted agentic AI, meaning autonomous systems that carry out tasks with little human supervision, to support hacking operations. He explained that such tools can be used for system scanning, vulnerability scanning and penetration testing. In his view, AI has increased the speed, volume and intrusiveness of attacks, making them more effective. Police believe criminals have also expanded their reconnaissance and phishing activity before launching AI-assisted ransomware attacks.

Police said the trend underscores the need for closer cooperation with mainland authorities and Interpol, since rapidly evolving AI presents a challenge for law enforcement. Hong Kong has joined Interpol's first year-long AI-powered cyber operation, which targets phishing and fraudulent links. Using an AI analysis engine developed by Hong Kong police, officers can examine a website's features, including its domain and technical infrastructure, and then take down or block sites judged risky. Enrique Hernandez-Gonzalez, Assistant Director of Cybercrime Operations at Interpol's Cybercrime Directorate, said intelligence from the campaign was shared with 47 jurisdictions, and about 90 percent of the roughly 57,000 links investigated have become inaccessible. A second phase, involving more than 20 jurisdictions across five continents, was launched last month.

Articles.Title: Police flag the use of AI by criminals - RTHK News

stories.Headline: Samsung sees AI chip shortage worsening, keeps investors in suspense on returns
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics reported on Thursday, October 29, 2026, that its quarterly chip profit jumped about fifteen times, driven by demand for artificial intelligence, yet its shares fell as much as 6.2 per cent in morning trade. The company posted an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won for the July-to-September period, in line with its own estimate and up from 12.2 trillion won a year earlier. Its semiconductor operating profit reached 106.5 trillion won, which was slightly below the 107.3 trillion won analysts had expected, according to LSEG. Investors had hoped for new shareholder-return plans after rival SK Hynix reported stronger earnings and outlined about US$75 billion in returns for 2026. Samsung instead said it would finalise its next shareholder-return policy in January.

Samsung said its high-bandwidth memory supply is sold out for 2027, and key customers are asking for more of the chips used in AI data centres. It expects the chip market to stay tight through 2028, since building new fabrication plants takes time. Its chip capital spending rose 62 per cent to 76.8 trillion won in 2026, and it expects a further sharp increase in 2027. The company said it has signed long-term supply contracts with 10 major customers and is in talks with 10 more, aiming for such deals to cover 60 to 70 per cent of its production capacity by 2030.

Its shareholder returns for 2026 were previously set at between 90 trillion and 110 trillion won, including 30 trillion won in third-quarter dividends. Samsung's management said the memory business expects AI infrastructure spending to reach a historic level in 2027 as the AI ecosystem grows. Analysts said Samsung's view on how long the shortage would last sounded less bullish than SK Hynix's, which weighed on the stock. Lee Min-hee of BNK Investment & Securities said Samsung had not changed its earlier guidance much, while SK Hynix had gone well beyond expectations.

Jing Jie Yu of Morningstar linked the share decline to the outlook on the length of the memory shortage. CLSA's Sanjeev Rana said the market had expected an extra buyback or dividend announcement, and the deferral to late January could disappoint near-term hopes. The report also placed the results against wider concerns about the sector. Demand for AI chips is expected to stay resilient, but worries about financing AI infrastructure and rising competition from China have weighed on chip stocks in recent months.

The pace of memory price gains is slowing as chipmakers sign more long-term contracts, and higher chip prices are weighing on smartphone and personal computer makers. Samsung's foundry business remained at a loss, though it reported better revenue from logic dies for HBM chips and new orders for advanced two-nanometre chips. Its mobile business fell to a loss of 800 billion won because higher memory costs squeezed margins. The company said it will start mass production in 2027 at its Taylor plant in Texas, making chips for Tesla, and is considering a new fab for advanced two-nanometre chips.

Articles.Title: Samsung sees AI chip shortage worsening, keeps investors in suspense on returns - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA and Elith released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan on November 9, 2026, a synthetic persona dataset built to help teams develop financial AI for Japanese users without using real customer data. The dataset extends the earlier Nemotron-Personas-Japan release and pairs Japan's official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. It contains about 9 million personas, 50% more than the earlier dataset, across 50 fields instead of 22. Each record includes 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics.

The dataset was generated with NVIDIA's NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework, and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. The developers said they added finer education categories, extra occupations such as business owners, and life stages like students, retirees, and periods of unemployment that rarely appear prominently in statistics. They also included household-level financial and real assets along with internet, smartphone, and financial literacy measures. The dataset was designed with feedback from financial institutions and industry groups, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association. It is released under the CC BY 4.0 license, which permits commercial use.

The article says the developers built the dataset to avoid privacy risk, stating that every persona is fully synthetic and that no real individuals are represented. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. The authors describe the release as the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan's official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. They also say it is designed to integrate with the NeMo User Sim framework and can be used to build customer-service agents, test sales conversations, run bias evaluations across regions, ages, and incomes, and support sovereign AI efforts. The article notes that Nemotron-PII-Japan, a set of 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, launched the same day for testing redaction models.

Articles.Title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

stories.Headline: A place for older generations in the age of AI
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column, not breaking news, so the breaking-story fallback does not apply. Its argument is that AI could help older adults adapt to digital life, while also noting risks and the need for training. The article gives no specific events or deadlines to report on, so I've written it as a summary of that argument. Macau Daily Times published an opinion piece on November 9, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence, often linked with younger and tech-savvy people, could be especially useful for older adults. The writer notes that people who did not grow up with smartphones or online banking have found it hard to keep up as everyday tasks move to websites, apps and automated systems.

The piece points out that the writer, though a millennial, also finds the pace of change difficult. The column describes how AI assistants can help with daily life, such as setting medication reminders, organizing appointments and drafting messages, and how real-time translation tools can make conversation easier across languages. It cites a 2025 University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging, which found that 55% of American adults aged 50 and older had used AI tools they could speak or type to, including voice assistants and generative AI chatbots. The writer also acknowledges concerns about privacy, inaccurate information and the loss of human contact, and argues that AI should supplement rather than replace the personal help and social ties older people need.

The author says there is little public data on how many older Macau residents use generative AI or voice assistants, which makes local adoption hard to judge. Because the government is expanding digital public services and e-governance, the writer argues that older residents should not be left behind. The column suggests training sessions that teach older people to give voice commands, set reminders, spot unreliable information and protect their personal data. The writer concludes that as societies age and digital services spread, technological inclusion should be a priority, so that older generations have the knowledge, confidence and support to benefit from the same advances as everyone else.

Articles.Title: A place for older generations in the age of AI - macau daily times 澳門每日時報

stories.Headline: Global media discuss mass communication in AI era
stories.Summary:
A sub-forum of the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, brought together representatives of media, think tanks, government departments and other institutions from China and abroad. They called on media organizations to use intelligent technologies to deliver reporting that is accurate, fair, authoritative and trustworthy. The breakout session was titled Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Chinese Modernization and centered on the theme of AI Plus and a new consensus on global communication governance. Participants discussed how media can adapt to change, seize opportunities and meet challenges together in the AI era.

The event also included several firsts and launches. The world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchor made its official debut there. The sub-forum held a signing ceremony for the Xinhua News Agency AI Industry Alliance (Beijing Base), along with a launch ceremony for a research project on mobile news image technology and authenticity standards. Participants urged their media colleagues to build consensus and to promote dialogue among civilizations through openness and inclusiveness. The summit itself runs from Nov. 5 to 9 and draws nearly 500 delegates from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government departments and international organizations across 112 countries and regions.

Two speakers were singled out in the reports. Huo Xiaoguang, vice president of Xinhua News Agency, said traditional mainstream media around the world are generally going through major transformations as AI develops. He said China's mainstream media are carrying out systematic reforms to secure new competitive advantages in the emerging communication ecosystem. Xinhua, he added, is willing to work with all parties to safeguard media credibility, promote the inclusive sharing of technological achievements, and strengthen mutual understanding and friendship among different civilizations.

Bayo Onanuga, the Nigerian president's special adviser on information and strategy and his spokesman, said the profound impact of AI can no longer be ignored, and that much of it is positive. He argued that, unless people were willing to return to the Stone Age, they must face the trend and treat it seriously. The summit is co-hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality. Ahead of the gathering, Khalid Mahmood, chairman of the Board of Governors of the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad and a former Pakistani ambassador to China, told Xinhua that the summit would give news organizations worldwide an important platform to explore how technological progress can serve the public interest. He noted that AI has made it possible to access, process, analyze and distribute information at unprecedented speed, and he planned to attend.

Articles.Title: "AI's future should be open to all": World Media Summit delegates discuss AI's promise for all - Xinhua
