Articles.Title: Best AI Chatbot for Customer Support: $1 vs $4 [2026]

stories.Headline: AI Model Predicts Fertilizer Spread Width from Video
stories.Summary:
A team at the University of Regina and its collaborators has built a computer vision system that estimates how wide a fertilizer spreader distributes material, using only video of the spreading. The work, published in Smart Agricultural Technology, pairs a ResNet-18 convolutional neural network with a Transformer encoder to read sequences of frames. The approach removes the need for collection trays placed on the ground or analysis of the field after the spreader has passed. The authors frame it as a way to assess spreading performance while the machine is running.

The problem being addressed is that swath width, the spacing between passes, controls how much adjacent passes overlap and therefore how evenly fertilizer lands. Uneven spreading can waste nutrients, raise costs and contribute to runoff and leaching. The standard tray-based methods in ISO 5690 and ASAE S341.2 are accurate but must be run offline and consume material, while Discrete Element Method simulations are too computationally heavy for field use. Because labeled footage of real fertilizer spreading was scarce, the team trained the model on synthetic video produced by a simplified Python model of particles moving under gravity and aerodynamic drag. The training set covered variations in disk diameter, disk speed, disk height, wind speed and wind direction.

The model extracts a 512-dimensional feature vector from each frame, and a Transformer encoder with two layers and eight attention heads reads the sequence to output one value in meters. The training set contained 297 simulation scenarios, 162 under baseline conditions and 135 with varying wind, and was fitted with the Adam optimizer over 30 epochs. On held-out synthetic data, the wide-field-of-view version reached a mean absolute error of 0.529 meters and an R² of 0.996. Against independent EDEM simulations, the error was 0.535 meters with an R² of 0.954. In laboratory tests with a Scotts Elite Spreader and a ZED 2 stereo camera, using real image sequences, the model recorded an error of 0.11 meters and a mean absolute percentage error of 7.26 percent against collector-bin measurements.

The researchers attribute the model's performance to its wide field of view, which captured the full spreading pattern, and to a pre-processing pipeline that applied lens undistortion, gamma correction and contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization to the real images. A full 25-frame sequence was processed in 1.318 seconds, or about 18.96 frames per second on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 GPU, and the authors say further optimization is needed before the system could drive closed-loop control. The study also notes limits: the lab test used a small spreader and few conditions, the training data was built for commercial-sized spreaders, and field factors such as soil, vegetation, shadows, dust and changing light remain untested. The authors call for commercial-scale field validation, estimates of distribution uniformity, and faster inference on embedded hardware.

Articles.Title: AI Model Predicts Fertilizer Spread Width from Video

stories.Headline: I Let AI Redesign a Key Living Room Feature (the Results Surprised Me!)
stories.Summary:
The only article supplied is a lifestyle piece from Apartment Therapy, republished on AOL on November 8, 2026, by writer Cori Sears. In it, Sears describes struggling to style the built-in shelves in her living room, a space that also holds an internet modem, TV remotes, and her husband's PlayStation. Ahead of the holidays, she tested ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude with the same prompt, asking for a minimalist, timeless winter or holiday look and uploading a photo of the shelf. Sears found the three tools gave very different results.

ChatGPT produced several inspiration images that she found the most useful, though she noted that its renderings distort proportion and look heavily filtered. Gemini generated mockups she disliked, and she said they focused too heavily on the word "minimalist." Claude's free version could not generate images, so it offered written guidance and web inspiration photos instead, which she found less helpful as a visual learner. Sears chose ChatGPT's suggestions and rebuilt her shelves using decor she already owned, with no shopping trips.

She kept the lamp, a framed picture, a potted plant, and a wicker basket, then added brass candlesticks, wintry artwork, tonal books, vases, white ceramic Christmas houses, and greenery she foraged from her backyard. She kept the PlayStation and modem on the middle shelf because they are part of daily life. She concluded that the AI blueprint helped her past a creative block, though she noted that she already owned many of the suggested items. The article does not say what, if anything, happens next beyond her plan to use the approach for future seasonal vignettes.

Articles.Title: I Let AI Redesign a Key Living Room Feature (the Results Surprised Me!)

stories.Headline: AI Vehicle Maintenance System Merges Environmental Context With Internal Sensor Diagnostics
stories.Summary:
The study was published in the journal Discover Vehicles by researchers Kushal Khemani and Anjum Nazir Qureshi, who introduced an artificial intelligence system that predicts when connected vehicles will need maintenance. The system combines the car's own internal sensor readings with outside conditions such as weather and road quality. The authors tested the approach in four stages, from controlled simulations to a real-world pilot across several countries. Their work aims to close the gap between laboratory results and performance on actual roads. Most current vehicle health tools depend mainly on internal data gathered through on-board diagnostics ports, such as engine temperature, fault codes and vibration.

Those tools generally ignore the surrounding stresses a car faces every day. The authors found that adding contextual information improves the prediction of component failures. The system uses nine internal mechanical measurements along with driver behavior, environmental factors and interaction terms, for a total of twenty-three variables. Pavement roughness is monitored at fifty hertz with an inertial measurement unit, and weather and road data are updated within a sixty-second window. In a simulation built on two thousand vehicle-month observations, the full contextual model reached a macro F1-score of 0.855.

Removing the environmental features lowered that score by 0.026, and relying only on internal mechanical data produced an F1-score of 0.807. Removing the internal signals caused a much larger drop to 0.655, which the authors say confirms that internal measurements remain the core of failure prediction. To test the method on real industrial data, the team used the AI4I 2020 benchmark of ten thousand milling-machine records, where the model reached a macro F1-score of 0.814 and an area under the curve of 0.973. Performance was strongest for heat dissipation failures at 0.972 and weakest for random failures at 0.497. The field pilot covered five privately owned vehicles driven in Germany, India and Brazil, which together logged 992 trips and roughly one hundred thirty million sensor observations.

Wear was checked against service records and physical measurements of brake pads and tire tread. Across six wear-driven events, the framework detected every one, though fine-tuning each vehicle's model roughly halved the timing error, from 25.9 days to 12.2 days. The authors also reported clear limits: the Brazilian Toyota Etios produced an average error of about 206 days per event, and predictions for scheduled preventive maintenance had a mean error of 93.5 days, since the algorithm tracks physical wear rather than calendar intervals. Shapley analysis confirmed that environmental factors such as rain and road roughness contribute to the predictions. The article ends by noting structural limitations and outlining priorities for future research.

Articles.Title: AI Vehicle Maintenance System Merges Environmental Context With Internal Sensor Diagnostics

stories.Headline: Feeling AI in Fashion Retail: Mixed Effects on Employee Creativity
stories.Summary:
A study published in Fashion and Textiles on November 8, 2026, found that emotionally responsive artificial intelligence, often called "feeling AI," does not uniformly boost creativity among fashion retail employees. The researchers, led by Ishtehar Sharif Swazan, reported that the psychological effects depend on the context and on which AI features are involved. Some features raised employees' confidence in their creative work, while others produced anxiety that changed how they approached creative tasks. The authors stressed that this distinction matters for an industry that depends on human innovation and aesthetic judgment.

The study examined two capabilities of feeling AI, anthropomorphism and personalization, and how they shape creative self-efficacy and job replacement anxiety. Those psychological states in turn affect two forms of creativity: proactive creativity, which is self-initiated, and responsive creativity, which is prompted by outside demands. The researchers treated AI as a psychological stimulus rather than only a technical tool. The survey covered 302 professionals working in U.S. fashion retail across buying, merchandising, planning, forecasting, marketing, product development, and customer service. The sample was 55.6 percent female and 43.7 percent male, and most participants held a bachelor's degree and had four to six years of experience.

The researchers analyzed the data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling, and the model explained 22 percent of the variance in creative self-efficacy and 14.1 percent in proactive creativity. The results showed that anthropomorphism significantly reduced creative self-efficacy while also significantly increasing job replacement anxiety. Personalization strongly boosted creative self-efficacy, though its hypothesized effect on reducing job replacement anxiety was not statistically significant. Creative self-efficacy predicted proactive creativity, and job replacement anxiety significantly increased responsive creativity without significantly reducing proactive creativity. Subgroup analyses found that personalization varied by job function, with planning and forecasting roles reporting more of it than customer service, while the other mechanisms were consistent across departments.

The study notes several limitations, including its cross-sectional design, which limits causal conclusions, and its U.S.-only sample, which may not generalize globally. Sales, marketing, and customer service staff were more heavily represented than design and merchandising professionals. For managers, the authors suggest favoring personalized, adaptive tools over highly human-like agents, investing in training that builds creative self-efficacy, and communicating openly about how work is changing. The research adds to the literature on human-AI collaboration by focusing on psychological effects rather than operational utility. The authors call for future work to test the model across cultural contexts and to study the effects of AI integration over time.

Articles.Title: Feeling AI in Fashion Retail: Mixed Effects on Employee Creativity

stories.Headline: Fire hawks inspire encryption and AI pairing to guard healthcare cloud data
stories.Summary:
Researchers have published a two-layer security system for healthcare cloud data that combines an encryption scheme with a machine-learning screen for access requests. The framework, called OFHXOR-PSL, appeared as an open-access paper in Discover Computing and was tested on two Internet of Health Things datasets. It reported a detection accuracy of 95.68 percent and a security level of 98.56 percent, with an attack level of 4 percent. The work is described in an article dated November 8, 2026, which was reported by Scienmag.

The system addresses a concern that hospitals face as they store electronic medical records on third-party cloud infrastructure. The authors say that common tools such as AES, RSA, and ECC, along with standard classifiers, can be computationally inefficient and weak at spotting threats. Their approach treats encryption and intrusion detection as one jointly designed pipeline instead of two separate tasks. The encryption layer uses XOR with a key chosen by the Fire Hawks Optimizer, a method modeled on birds of prey, and each session gets its own key. The paper reports an average key entropy of 7.94 bits per byte, close to the theoretical maximum of 8.

The second layer screens every request to reach stored records. A gateway extracts features such as IP address, query pattern, access frequency, session duration, and a geolocation anomaly score, then passes them to an ensemble of three classifiers. If uncertainty exceeds a threshold of 0.45, the request is blocked as suspicious. The authors also say the detection module keeps learning after a malicious classification, which they describe as a way to handle new attacks. The experiments used the WUSTL-EHMS-2020 and ECU-IoHT datasets, and the proposed ensemble outperformed artificial neural network, K-nearest neighbors, and support vector machine baselines.

The authors state that the research was carried out by A. CG, A. C, and R. Neerukonda, and they acknowledge several open questions. They note that key distribution assumes a pre-established secure channel such as TLS 1.3, and that user authentication and trust management were not tested experimentally. They also say that ciphertext integrity would need separate protection, for example with an HMAC, because XOR offers no diffusion. Future plans include post-quantum key encapsulation based on CRYSTALS-Kyber, federated learning, and validation on more datasets. The source code is openly available on GitHub under an MIT licence.

Articles.Title: Fire hawks inspire encryption and AI pairing to guard healthcare cloud data

stories.Headline: Hybrid AI Model Predicts Postoperative Lung Function from Preoperative CT Scans
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers has developed a hybrid artificial intelligence model that can estimate how well a patient's lungs will work after surgery, using only a routine preoperative CT scan. The study, published in European Radiology Experimental in 2026 and reported by bioengineer.org on November 8, 2026, was led by Wang, Sun, Ma and Li. The model combines transfer-learned deep neural representations with elastic net regression to predict forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in one second, without requiring preoperative lung function tests or detailed surgical planning. The researchers say it is aimed at patients with pulmonary nodules who may undergo lobectomy, segmentectomy or wedge resection.

The motivation is that lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide, and rising detection of nodules has increased the number of thoracic operations. Surgeons must weigh removing enough tissue to treat the disease against preserving functioning lung. The traditional segment-counting method works only for anatomical segmentectomies and lobectomies, not wedge resections, and it depends on baseline spirometry while often overestimating functional loss. The study used data from 105 surgical patients at Huadong Hospital affiliated to Fudan University, drawn from 7,494 screened between October 2014 and October 2023, with 61 women and 44 men averaging 65.4 years old, and a separate external cohort of 31 patients from Heilongjiang Provincial Hospital treated between January 2017 and January 2023. In external testing, the hybrid model outperformed four alternative approaches and the segment-counting method, with a concordance correlation coefficient of 0.707 for forced vital capacity and 0.729 for forced expiratory volume in one second.

The authors, Wang, Sun, Ma and Li, presented the approach as an automated tool to support individualized decisions in common thoracic resections, though they were careful to describe its limits. Their own summary, paraphrased here, is that the study was retrospective, that the sample was modest because postoperative spirometry is not routinely performed, and that the clinical inputs were limited to six basic parameters. They concluded that larger prospective multicenter studies with standardized postoperative testing will be needed before the tool can be used in surgical practice. The article does not report any regulatory review or clinical rollout, so the model currently remains a research finding.

Articles.Title: Hybrid AI Model Predicts Postoperative Lung Function from Preoperative CT Scans

stories.Headline: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
stories.Summary:
The author, writing on sergeykuhne.com on November 8, 2026, describes a problem many people face when working with AI coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex from the terminal. Running several tasks at once means each agent reply pulls them into another tab, and the constant switching eventually exhausts the brain, breaks focus, and leaves them unsure where they started or what remains. Other advice, such as taking breaks or limiting scope, is mentioned, but the author has tried a different approach. They identified two core problems, sequencing and context, and organized their work along the lines of a priority queue.

The queue lives in git, with each ticket stored as a markdown file in the repository beside the code it concerns, and the board's state kept as a committed snapshot. An agent cycles through the board to research new tickets, build those a human has marked as safe, run tests and a browser check, and verify deployed work. Sensitive changes are built on a branch with approval requested first, and the agent never deploys to production, which the author keeps for themselves. Items needing human judgment are gathered into an owner inbox, where a script ranks them.

The author reads them through a Claude artifact, a page rebuilt from git each cycle, and records verdicts back onto the ticket card in git. The author says closing each item returns its context to the queue, so the next item can be approached with focus. The article notes that the work remains tiring, and that the main difficulties have been the tooling that delivers context quickly and the risk of tickets looping while they wait for a ruling only the author can give. The author calls the system a living project that is still being improved and says it has produced a large gain in productivity.

Articles.Title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
